free.upa-2026-an1-1a:
Illness vs diseaseExplanatory modelsMedical pluralismCultural concepts of distress

Biomedicine treats health as a measurable bodily state; the WHO Constitution (1948) widened it to complete physical, mental and social well-being. Anthropologists show that what counts as sickness, what causes it and who should heal it are shaped by culture. Arthur Kleinman (Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture, 1980) called these shared ideas explanatory models, making health a cultural construct as much as a biological fact.

1. Sickness is defined by culture

  • Disease, illness, sickness: Leon Eisenberg (1977) and Kleinman separated disease, a malfunction diagnosed by the doctor, from illness, the sufferer's own experience; Allan Young (1982) added sickness, the social role a community grants to the sufferer.
  • Shifting boundaries: conditions such as obesity, alcoholism and ageing have been medicalised over time, so the line between normal and abnormal is drawn socially, not only by laboratories.
  • Three bodies: Nancy Scheper-Hughes and Margaret Lock (1987) showed that health is lived through the individual body, the social body and the body politic.

2. Causes and cures follow cultural logic

  • Etiologies: George Foster (1976) contrasted personalistic systems, where sickness is sent by a sorcerer, spirit or deity, with naturalistic ones based on balance of humours, hot and cold, or the doshas of Ayurveda. Among the Azande, E.E. Evans-Pritchard (1937) found that witchcraft explained why misfortune struck a particular person.
  • Culture-specific syndromes: dhat syndrome in South Asia, anxiety over loss of semen, and susto in Latin America make sense only within local ideas of the body; DSM-5 (2013) lists them as cultural concepts of distress.
  • Medical pluralism: Charles Leslie (Asian Medical Systems, 1976) showed patients moving between biomedicine, Ayurveda, Unani and folk healers; a Santal family may consult the ojha and the primary health centre for the same fever.

3. Why the construct matters

  • Health programmes: immunisation, institutional delivery or TB treatment succeed when they fit local explanatory models, which is why India's ASHA workers (2005) are recruited from the community and the AYUSH ministry (2014) recognises plural systems; the Abhay Bang expert committee on tribal health (2018) proposed trained local tribal youth (Aarogya Mitras) as a bridge.
  • Caution: critical medical anthropologists such as Paul Farmer warn that cultural explanations must not hide poverty and structural violence, which also make people ill.

Health is thus a biocultural reality: germs and genes are universal, but the meaning of suffering, the choice of healer and the idea of recovery are cultural. Culturally sensitive care is a practical necessity, not a courtesy.
free.upa-2026-an1-1b:
CanalizationCatch-up growthTarget-seeking growthGrowth centiles

Human growth follows a genetically set path that resists disturbance. C.H. Waddington (1942; The Strategy of the Genes, 1957) called this buffering canalization, picturing development as a ball rolling along valleys of an "epigenetic landscape". Catch-up growth, a term introduced by Prader, Tanner and von Harnack (1963), is its visible proof: once an illness or shortage ends, a child grows faster than normal and returns towards its original curve.

1. Canalization

  • Meaning: a developmental system that reaches the same end-point despite genetic or environmental disturbance; a growing child tends to stay in its own channel, a centile line on the growth chart.
  • Target-seeking growth: J.M. Tanner (1963) argued that a child behaves as if it had a target size set by its genotype and corrects deviations from it.
  • Evidence: healthy children keep close to the same height centile from early childhood to adolescence; in infancy many shift up or down to settle into the channel set by their genes rather than by the conditions in the womb.

2. Catch-up growth

  • Process: illness, hunger or hormone deficiency slows growth; when the cause is removed, height velocity rises well above the normal for that age until the deficit is made up, then slows again.
  • Examples: children treated for coeliac disease or hypothyroidism; most low-birth-weight babies, who catch up within the first two years; Romanian orphans adopted into English families in the early 1990s, who showed rapid gains in Michael Rutter's English and Romanian Adoptees study.
  • Limits: catch-up is incomplete when the insult is long or falls in a critical period, especially the first 1,000 days from conception to age two. David Barker's foetal-origins work linked rapid weight gain after poor foetal growth with later diabetes and heart disease.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Plasticity within limits: Franz Boas (1912) showed that children of immigrants in New York differed in body form from their parents, yet canalization explains why individuals rebound after short insults.
  • Public health: growth monitoring under ICDS and POSHAN Abhiyaan uses WHO growth standards to spot children who leave their channel; NFHS-6 (2023–24) found 29.3% of children under five stunted, down from 35.5% in NFHS-5, a sign of failed catch-up.

Canalization is the self-righting tendency of growth, and catch-up growth is how it shows itself. Both reveal growth as a bio-cultural process in which nutrition, health care and timing decide whether genetic potential is reached.

Oral literatureMyth, legend and folktaleMythical charterMytheme

Oral literature is the verbal art of a community: songs, proverbs, tales and myths composed, performed and passed on by word of mouth. Within it, a myth is a sacred narrative about the origins of the world and of customs, set in a primordial time and held to be true by those who tell it. Ruth Finnegan's Oral Literature in Africa (1970) established such texts as literature in their own right.

1. Myth as a form of oral literature

  • A distinct genre: William Bascom (1965) separated three kinds of prose narrative: myths, legends and folktales, which differ in belief, time and attitude.
  • Performance: a myth lives in its telling, at a ritual, festival or funeral, and its wording changes with narrator and audience (Richard Bauman, Verbal Art as Performance, 1977).
  • Many versions: with no fixed text, myths survive in variants; Milman Parry and Albert Lord (The Singer of Tales, 1960) showed how oral poets compose through set formulas and themes while performing.
  • Collective ownership: myths belong to the group, but the right to recite them may lie with priests, elders or bards, such as the Pardhans who sing for the Gonds.

2. How anthropologists read myth

  • Early views: E.B. Tylor saw myth as early people's explanation of nature, Max Müller as a "disease of language", while Robertson Smith and J.G. Frazer derived myths from rituals.
  • Functional: Bronislaw Malinowski (Myth in Primitive Psychology, 1926) called Trobriand myth a charter that justifies clan rank, land rights and magic.
  • Structural: Claude Lévi-Strauss ("The Structural Study of Myth", 1955) broke myths into mythemes and showed that they mediate contradictions such as nature and culture or life and death.
  • Morphological: Vladimir Propp (Morphology of the Folktale, 1928) found 31 recurring functions in Russian wonder tales.

3. Indian examples

  • Santal: the creation story of Pilchu Haram and Pilchu Budhi accounts for the first humans, the clans and the rules of marriage.
  • Gond: the epic of Lingo, sung by Pardhan bards, explains the origin of Gond clans and their gods.
  • Recording: Verrier Elwin's Myths of Middle India (1949) collected hundreds of such narratives from central Indian tribes.

As oral literature, myth is at once the art, history and law of a people, transmitted without writing. Recording these texts in tribal languages and using them in mother-tongue schooling helps protect an intangible heritage threatened by language loss.

Genetic polymorphismBalanced polymorphismHeterozygote advantageTransient polymorphism

Genetic polymorphism is the presence in a population of two or more alleles at one locus, too common to be maintained by recurrent mutation alone (E.B. Ford, 1940); by convention the rarer allele reaches a frequency of at least 1%. ABO and Rh blood groups, haemoglobin variants, HLA types and enzyme variants are examples. Natural selection can keep such variation stable or replace one allele by another.

1. Balanced polymorphism

  • Heterozygote advantage: A.C. Allison (1954) showed that carriers of sickle-cell haemoglobin (HbAS) resist falciparum malaria, while HbSS people suffer sickle-cell disease and HbAA people are more vulnerable to malaria; the HbS allele therefore stays common in malarial Africa and in parts of tribal central and southern India.
  • Other malaria-linked variants: β-thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency and HbE, which is frequent in north-east India and South-East Asia, follow a similar logic.
  • Culture shapes selection: Frank Livingstone (1958) linked the spread of HbS in West Africa to forest clearing for yam farming, which created pools for mosquitoes.
  • Rare-allele advantage: HLA alleles are favoured when they are rare because pathogens have not adapted to them, which keeps the HLA system highly polymorphic.

2. Transient polymorphism

  • Meaning: a temporary state while directional selection pushes a favoured allele towards fixation.
  • Examples: industrial melanism in the peppered moth (H.B.D. Kettlewell's experiments in the 1950s); lactase persistence, which spread in dairying populations of Europe, East Africa and north-west India; the Duffy-null allele, which protects against vivax malaria and is almost fixed in West Africa.

3. Limits and significance

  • Neutral theory: Motoo Kimura (1968) argued that most molecular polymorphisms, including many SNPs, are selectively neutral and change through drift.
  • Relaxed selection: medicine, diet and marriage rules now alter fitness; India's National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) uses carrier screening and counselling.
  • Uses: polymorphic markers trace migrations and serve in forensic identification.

Polymorphism is both the raw material and the record of adaptation: balanced forms show selection preserving variation, transient forms show it replacing alleles. Together they explain population differences without any recourse to the idea of race.

EthnoarchaeologyClassical archaeologyEthnographic analogyMiddle-range theory

Classical archaeology studies the material remains of ancient Greece and Rome, and by extension other literate ancient civilisations, reading excavated objects alongside inscriptions and texts. Ethnoarchaeology studies living communities to learn how behaviour turns into material traces, so that the archaeological record can be read by ethnographic analogy. Jesse Walter Fewkes (1900) first called himself an "ethno-archaeologist" for his work among the Hopi.

1. Classical archaeology

  • Origins: it grew out of antiquarian and art-historical interest: J.J. Winckelmann's History of the Art of Antiquity (1764), Heinrich Schliemann at Troy (1870s) and Arthur Evans at Knossos (from 1900).
  • Method: it is text-aided; architecture, sculpture, coins, inscriptions and pottery styles are dated and interpreted with the help of written history.
  • Focus: cities, temples, elites and art, with a historical rather than anthropological aim. B.B. Lal's excavation at Hastinapura (1950–52), guided by the Mahabharata tradition, shows a similar text-led approach in India.

2. Ethnoarchaeology

  • Middle-range theory: Lewis Binford's Nunamiut Ethnoarchaeology (1978) watched Alaskan caribou hunters to link butchery and camp activities with the bone patterns they leave.
  • Foragers and farmers: John Yellen (1977) mapped !Kung San camps in the Kalahari; Richard Gould's Living Archaeology (1980) studied Aboriginal people of Australia's Western Desert; Ian Hodder's Symbols in Action (1982) showed how objects mark ethnic identity in the Baringo district of Kenya.
  • Indian studies: M.L.K. Murty (1985) used present-day exchange between forest foragers and villagers in the Kurnool cave area to interpret Mesolithic and Neolithic sites; Daniel Miller (Dangwara, Madhya Pradesh) and Carol Kramer (Pottery in Rajasthan, 1997) studied how potters make, use and discard vessels.

3. Complementarity and limits

  • Complementary: ethnoarchaeology supplies models of pottery life-span, discard and site layout that help interpret any excavation, including classical sites.
  • Limits: analogy can project the present onto the past, a danger Martin Wobst (1978) called the tyranny of the ethnographic record; living communities are not relics of prehistory, and research must respect their consent.

Classical archaeology mainly tells what past societies made and when; ethnoarchaeology explains how the record came to be formed. Used together, with critical analogy, they give a fuller picture of past human life.
free.upa-2026-an1-2a:
SomatotypeHeath-Carter anthropometric methodSheldon's somatotypingKinanthropometry

A somatotype is a quantified description of the present shape and composition of the human body, given as a three-number rating of endomorphy, mesomorphy and ectomorphy. The idea was introduced by W.H. Sheldon in The Varieties of Human Physique (1940), building on older typologies of Hippocrates and Kretschmer (1921). Barbara Heath and J.E. Lindsay Carter (1967) modified it into the method most widely used today.

1. Meaning of somatotype

  • Endomorphy: relative fatness, the first component.
  • Mesomorphy: relative musculo-skeletal robustness in relation to height, the second component.
  • Ectomorphy: relative linearity or slenderness, the third component.
  • Rating: always written in the order endo–meso–ecto; for example, 2-5-2 is a balanced mesomorph, with muscularity dominant and fatness and linearity equal and lower.

2. The Heath-Carter anthropometric method

  • Ten measurements: stature, body mass, four skinfolds (triceps, subscapular, supraspinale and medial calf), two bone breadths (biepicondylar humerus and femur) and two girths (flexed and tensed arm, and calf).
  • Endomorphy: from the sum of triceps, subscapular and supraspinale skinfolds, corrected for height (multiplied by 170.18 ÷ height in cm).
  • Mesomorphy: from the two bone breadths and the arm and calf girths, each girth corrected for its skinfold, adjusted for height.
  • Ectomorphy: from the height–weight ratio (height ÷ cube root of weight); when this ratio is 40.75 or more, ectomorphy = 0.732 × ratio − 28.58.
  • Somatochart: the rating is plotted on a two-dimensional chart using X = ectomorphy − endomorphy and Y = 2 × mesomorphy − (endomorphy + ectomorphy).
  • Three routes: anthropometric, photoscopic, or both combined as the criterion method; the anthropometric route is the most used because it needs no photographs.

3. Advantages over Sheldon's method

  • Objectivity: measurements by trained observers give reproducible ratings, while Sheldon's depended on the judgement of an expert rater.
  • Change is recognised: Heath and Carter accept that physique changes with age, nutrition and training, rejecting Sheldon's idea of a permanent body type.
  • No determinism: Sheldon's link between physique and temperament (The Varieties of Temperament, 1942) is dropped, and the method needs no nude photographs, which raised ethical concerns.
  • Wider use: the open scale can rate extreme physiques, such as heavyweight lifters, and the components can be analysed statistically.

4. Applications in sports sciences

  • Sport profiles: J.M. Tanner's The Physique of the Olympic Athlete (1964) and Carter's later Olympic studies showed that each event has a typical somatotype: throwers tend to be endomorphic mesomorphs, gymnasts balanced mesomorphs, and distance runners and high jumpers more linear.
  • Talent identification: comparing young athletes with elite profiles helps guide them towards sports that suit their build.
  • Monitoring training and diet: because the rating changes, repeated somatotyping tracks loss of fat and gain of muscle, useful in weight-category sports such as wrestling and boxing.
  • Positional roles: in team games like football, hockey or kabaddi, players in different positions show different somatotypes.

Somatotyping has moved from Sheldon's photographic typology, tied to temperament, to an objective, phenotypic tool. With its open scale and somatochart, the Heath-Carter method is now the standard of kinanthropometry and a practical aid in sports anthropology.

Cultural ecologyRitual regulationSacred grovesAdaptive function of religion

From Julian Steward (Theory of Culture Change, 1955) onward, anthropologists have treated culture as humanity's chief means of adapting to its environment. Religious beliefs, such as taboos, rituals, sacred places and divination, form part of this toolkit: they store ecological knowledge, regulate the use of resources and calm anxiety in uncertain conditions. Roy Rappaport and Marvin Harris gave the classic ecological readings of religion.

1. Rituals that regulate resources

  • Tsembaga Maring, New Guinea: in Pigs for the Ancestors (1968), Rappaport showed that the kaiko festival is held when pigs become too many for the gardens and for women's labour; the mass sacrifice to the ancestors reduces the herd, shares out protein and ends a truce, so that warfare spaces groups across the land.
  • Bali: J. Stephen Lansing (Priests and Programmers, 1991) showed that a hierarchy of water temples schedules irrigation and fallow for subak rice cooperatives, sharing water and controlling pests.
  • Chotanagpur: Sarhul, celebrated by Oraon, Munda and Ho villagers when the sal trees flower, is held at the sarna (sacred grove) and opens the agricultural year.

2. Taboos and sacred places that conserve nature

  • Sacred cattle: Harris (1966) argued that India's ban on killing cattle keeps oxen for ploughing, dung for fuel and manure, and milk, an efficient use of energy in a monsoon economy.
  • Sacred groves: Khasi forests such as Mawphlang in Meghalaya, kavu in Kerala, devarakadu in Karnataka and orans in Rajasthan protect forests, springs and biodiversity under the guardianship of deities.
  • Bishnoi: their rules forbid felling green trees and killing animals; at Khejarli in 1730, 363 Bishnois led by Amrita Devi died protecting khejri trees.
  • Food taboos: Fijian women avoid certain reef fish in pregnancy and breastfeeding, lowering their exposure to ciguatera poisoning (Joseph and Natalie Henrich, 2010).
  • Dongria Kondh: reverence for Niyam Raja, the deity of the Niyamgiri hills, underlay their gram sabhas' rejection of bauxite mining in 2013.

3. Beliefs that reduce risk and anxiety

  • Divination: Omar Khayyam Moore (1957) argued that Naskapi scapulimancy, reading cracks in a burnt caribou shoulder blade to choose a route, randomised hunting and prevented over-hunting of any one area.
  • Magic: Malinowski observed that Trobrianders used magic for dangerous open-sea fishing but not for safe lagoon fishing, giving confidence where technology could not guarantee success.

4. Critical assessment

  • Functionalist bias: critics call such explanations post hoc; Rappaport's balance was not measured over long periods, and Frederick Simoons disputed Harris's sacred-cow thesis.
  • Maladaptive beliefs: mortuary feasting among the Fore of Papua New Guinea spread the brain disease kuru until the practice ended (Shirley Lindenbaum, Kuru Sorcery, 1979).
  • Meaning beyond utility: Clifford Geertz and Mary Douglas stress that religion is first a system of meanings, not merely an ecological device.

Religion helps people adapt by turning ecological experience into sacred rules that are followed without calculation. Today the traditional ecological knowledge carried by sacred groves and taboos is gaining recognition in conservation, as in community forest rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
free.upa-2026-an1-2c:
StructuralismBinary oppositionsPurity and pollutionNature and culture

Structuralism, developed by Claude Lévi-Strauss from Saussure's linguistics, holds that social institutions are surface expressions of unconscious mental structures built on binary oppositions such as nature and culture, raw and cooked, or pure and impure. Since caste and gender are both systems of classification and exchange, structuralism helps uncover their underlying logic rather than their history.

1. Basic premises

  • Relations, not items: meaning arises from contrasts within a system; kinship, myth and classification work like languages.
  • Exchange: The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949) treats marriage as an exchange between groups, made necessary by the incest taboo.
  • Anomaly and danger: things that fall between categories are treated as sacred or polluting (Mary Douglas, Purity and Danger, 1966).

2. Structuralism and caste

  • Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus (1966): caste is a whole founded on one opposition, the pure and the impure, with the Brahmin and the Untouchable at its two poles; separation, division of labour and hierarchy, the features Célestin Bouglé (1908) had identified, all follow from it.
  • Status encompasses power: ritual status is disjoined from political and economic power, which is why the king, however powerful, ranks below the priest.
  • Holism: caste expresses homo hierarchicus, a value of hierarchy opposed to the Western homo aequalis.
  • "The Bear and the Barber" (1963): Lévi-Strauss treated castes and totemic groups as transformations of one logic: totemic clans borrow their differences from nature and exchange women by exogamy, while castes borrow theirs from culture, exchanging services but keeping women within by endogamy.

3. Structuralism and gender

  • Ortner's argument: in "Is Female to Male as Nature Is to Culture?" (1972, reprinted 1974) she argued that women are seen as closer to nature because of childbirth and domestic roles, and men as makers of culture; since culture claims to rise above nature, women are ranked lower.
  • Exchange of women: Gayle Rubin ("The Traffic in Women", 1975) used Lévi-Strauss to show how kinship turns women into objects of exchange between men.
  • Indian studies: Nur Yalman (1963) showed that caste purity in Sri Lanka and Malabar is guarded through control of women's sexuality; Leela Dube analysed the seed-and-field metaphor that gives men rights over children; menstrual pollution places women temporarily on the impure side.

4. Usefulness and limits

  • Strength: it reveals one grammar linking caste endogamy and the control of women, since the purity of a caste rests on the purity of its women.
  • Critiques of Dumont: Gerald Berreman and Dipankar Gupta saw caste as power and multiple competing hierarchies, not one Brahmanical value; McKim Marriott stressed transactions, and Nicholas Dirks (Castes of Mind, 2001) colonial history.
  • Critiques of Ortner: Carol MacCormack and Marilyn Strathern (Nature, Culture and Gender, 1980) showed that the nature–culture divide is a Western category; Ortner later revised her view (Making Gender, 1996).

Structuralism uncovers the hidden grammar of purity and impurity, nature and culture, that ties caste and gender together. To explain how these hierarchies are lived, contested and changing, it must be joined with history, power and agency, including Dalit and feminist voices.
free.upa-2026-an1-3a:
Power and authorityLegitimacyBand, tribe, chiefdom, stateSocial control

Power is the ability to make others act as one wishes, even against resistance; authority is power accepted as rightful, and legitimacy is the belief that makes it rightful (Max Weber, Economy and Society, 1922). Social control covers the sanctions, informal and formal, that keep conduct within norms. Along Elman Service's (1962) sequence of band, tribe, chiefdom and state, each of these changes in source, scale and form.

1. The concepts

  • Political process: Swartz, Turner and Tuden (Political Anthropology, 1966) stressed that legitimacy, more than force, sustains power.
  • Sanctions: A.R. Radcliffe-Brown separated diffuse sanctions (gossip, ridicule, ostracism) from organised ones (fines, courts, punishment); E.A. Hoebel (The Law of Primitive Man, 1954) found law wherever a recognised authority may legitimately use force.

2. Band societies

  • Power and authority: small, mobile, egalitarian foragers such as the !Kung San, the Inuit and the Chenchus have leaders who advise but cannot command; influence rests on age, skill and generosity.
  • Legitimacy and control: rests on kinship and consensus; disputes end through gossip, ridicule, sharing or the group splitting, and Inuit song duels let rivals shame each other before the camp (Hoebel).

3. Tribal and segmentary societies

  • Dispersed authority: there is no permanent central office; authority lies with lineage elders, age-sets or achieved leaders. Melanesian big men gain followers by giving feasts but cannot pass on their position (Marshall Sahlins, 1963).
  • Ritual legitimacy: the Nuer leopard-skin chief mediates feuds through ritual standing, not coercion (E.E. Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer, 1940); order rests on balanced opposition between lineage segments.
  • Control: bloodwealth in cattle, feud, oaths, ordeals, witchcraft accusations and supernatural sanctions; in India, Santal village councils under the manjhi and wider pargana councils impose fines or outcasting.

4. Chiefdoms

  • Centralised power: a hereditary, ranked office controls the redistribution of surplus, as among Polynesian and Trobriand chiefs; potlatch feasts on the Northwest Coast validated rank.
  • Sacred legitimacy: Polynesian chiefs held mana and were protected by tapu; Khasi syiems ruled their himas with the advice of clan-based councils (dorbars).
  • Control: the chief's court, fines and fear of tapu. Edmund Leach (Political Systems of Highland Burma, 1954) showed the Kachin moving back and forth between hierarchical gumsa and egalitarian gumlao forms, so change is not always one-way.

5. The state

  • Monopoly of force: Weber defined the state by its monopoly of legitimate physical force over a territory; Morton Fried (The Evolution of Political Society, 1967) linked its rise to stratification.
  • New legitimacy: divine kingship and dharma give way to constitutions, elections and courts.
  • Formal control: codified law, police and prisons; Michel Foucault (Discipline and Punish, 1975) argued that modern power also works through surveillance and self-discipline.
  • Indian blend: Article 371A protects Naga customary law, Sixth Schedule district councils and PESA (1996) recognise traditional bodies, while the Lushai Hills chiefs lost their rights under a 1954 Act.

As scale grows, power moves from persons to offices, legitimacy from kinship and the sacred to law, and social control from diffuse to organised sanctions. Kachin oscillation and India's legal pluralism show that this change is neither linear nor complete.
free.upa-2026-an1-3b:
Biocultural evolutionGene–culture coevolutionFeedback loopNiche construction

Human beings evolved through a biocultural process: natural selection shaped bodies able to create culture, and culture in turn changed the conditions under which selection acted. Charles Darwin (The Descent of Man, 1871) already linked upright walking, free hands, tools and a larger brain. Modern gene–culture coevolution (Robert Boyd and Peter Richerson, 1985) and niche construction theory formalise this two-way traffic.

1. Biological factors

  • Evolutionary forces: mutation, natural selection, genetic drift and gene flow produced bipedalism, seen in the Laetoli footprints (about 3.66 mya), smaller canines and a brain that grew from roughly 400–500 cc in australopiths to about 1,350 cc in modern humans.
  • Life history: a long childhood and dependence on adults gave time for learning, the precondition of culture.
  • Climate: Rick Potts's variability-selection hypothesis holds that fluctuating East African environments favoured flexible, generalist hominins.

2. Cultural factors

  • Tools: stone tools from Lomekwi 3, Kenya (about 3.3 mya), and the Oldowan (from about 2.6 mya) opened access to meat and marrow; S.L. Washburn (1960) argued that tool use itself selected for the human hand and a larger brain.
  • Fire and cooking: Richard Wrangham (Catching Fire, 2009) argued that cooking softened food, reduced teeth and gut, and freed energy for the brain, in line with Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler's expensive-tissue hypothesis (1995).
  • Language and social learning: cumulative culture made humans dependent on teaching and cooperation; Sarah Hrdy (Mothers and Others, 2009) stressed shared child care.
  • Clothing and shelter: let modern humans live in cold regions; studies of clothing lice suggest that clothes came into use roughly 170,000–83,000 years ago.

3. Gene–culture coevolution in recent humans

  • Farming and herding as selective forces: after the Neolithic, culture changed diets and disease loads fast enough to leave marks in the genome, while medicine now relaxes some selection.

4. Interaction, not either-or

  • Biology sets capacities, culture sets pressures: a large brain made culture possible, and culture then decided which bodies survived.
  • Culture as a buffer: clothing, fire and housing replaced fur and cold adaptations; today spectacles, vaccines and caesarean births weaken older selective pressures.
  • Corrections to old models: the "Man the Hunter" view (1968) overstated male hunting; gathering, women's work and cooperative breeding are now recognised as equally formative.

Human evolution is a dialectic of genes and culture: from Lomekwi tools to dairying, culture built new environments that selected bodies, and those bodies built more culture. With genetic medicine and climate change, this biocultural interplay continues today.
free.upa-2026-an1-3c:
SoanianSiwalik AcheulianPebble-tool traditionSub-Himalayan duns

The sub-Himalayan belt of Siwalik hills, dun valleys and river terraces, from the Potwar plateau to Nepal, was where South Asian Palaeolithic studies first gained a geological frame, through de Terra and Paterson (1939) in the Soan valley. It holds two Lower Palaeolithic traditions, the pebble-tool Soanian and the biface-making Acheulian, followed by flake-based Middle Palaeolithic industries.

1. Distribution of sites

  • Soan valley and Potwar plateau (Pakistan): de Terra and Paterson's 1935 expedition collected pebble tools from terraces of the Soan near Rawalpindi, and handaxes at Chauntra. The British Archaeological Mission later found Acheulian handaxes at Dina and Jalalpur (palaeomagnetically about 700,000–400,000 years old), and Robin Dennell's team (1988) claimed artefacts about 1.9 million years old at Riwat, a date still disputed.
  • Kashmir: an ASI team under H.D. Sankalia (1969) found a massive flake and a crude handaxe in glacial deposits at Pahalgam in the Liddar valley; Levallois-type flakes were noted near Pampur.
  • Himachal Pradesh and adjoining duns: B.B. Lal (1956) reported Soan-type choppers and a few handaxes at Guler in the Beas–Banganga valley of Kangra; G.C. Mohapatra traced handaxe clusters in the Shimla–Kalka area, and many Soanian sites were mapped in the Pinjore–Nalagarh duns.
  • Punjab and Chandigarh Siwaliks: Mohapatra collected about 120 Acheulian bifaces from 21 sites in the Hoshiarpur Siwaliks, and Atbarapur is a well-studied Acheulian locality. At Masol near Chandigarh an Indo-French team (2016) reported possible cut marks on bovid bones about 2.6 million years old, a claim not widely accepted.
  • Nepal: Gudrun Corvinus found Acheulian handaxes at Gadari in the Dang valley and at Satpati, and a Middle Palaeolithic workshop at Arjun 3 in Deukhuri.

2. Typo-technology of the tools

  • Soanian: made on rounded quartzite pebbles and cobbles from river gravels; choppers (flaked on one face), chopping tools (an edge flaked on both faces), discoids, core-scrapers and many flakes. De Terra and Paterson divided it into Pre-Soan (large, crude flakes), Early Soan (pebble choppers and chopping tools) and Late Soan (smaller flakes, some from prepared cores).
  • Siwalik Acheulian: handaxes, cleavers and picks of quartzite, shaped by bifacial flaking; unlike the late Acheulian of the peninsula, these assemblages usually lack Levallois cores.
  • Middle Palaeolithic: scrapers, points and Levallois-type flakes struck from prepared cores, as at Pampur and Arjun 3.

3. Debates on chronology and meaning

  • Shaky sequence: de Terra and Paterson tied five Soan terraces to Himalayan glacial cycles, but the terraces later proved largely erosional, so the stage-wise sequence is no longer a dated succession; most Siwalik finds are undated surface collections.
  • Soanian versus Acheulian: Hallam Movius (1948) placed the Soan within an Asian chopper–chopping-tool province; Claire Gaillard sees technical links with the Acheulian, while Parth Chauhan argues that the Siwalik Acheulian is older and the Soanian a late Lower or early Middle Palaeolithic industry.

The Himalayan foothills thus show a dual tradition: pebble-based Soanian and biface-based Acheulian, linking South Asia with both East Asian chopper industries and the African Acheulian. Absolute dating of stratified sites is the main need for settling their sequence.

ParanthropusRobust australopithecinesMegadontiaSagittal crest

Paranthropus ("beside man") was named by Robert Broom in 1938 for the Kromdraai skull TM 1517 from South Africa. It groups the robust australopithecines of eastern and southern Africa, which lived from nearly 3 million to about 1 million years ago, side by side with early Homo. Their massive jaws and teeth were an adaptation to tough, low-quality plant foods.

1. Phylogenetic status

  • Species: P. aethiopicus, the earliest; P. boisei of East Africa; and P. robustus of South Africa. In 2025 Clément Zanolli and colleagues proposed P. capensis for the Swartkrans jaw SK 15, earlier assigned to Homo; this remains debated.
  • Valid genus or not: many cladistic studies find the robust species form one clade, supporting a separate genus; others think the eastern and southern forms acquired heavy chewing independently (homoplasy) and keep them in Australopithecus.
  • Side branch: whatever its rank, Paranthropus is an extinct side branch of the hominin tree, not an ancestor of Homo.

2. Characteristic features

  • Skull: a sagittal crest (mainly in males), wide flaring cheekbones, a broad dished face, low forehead and marked postorbital constriction; cranial capacity about 410–550 cc.
  • Teeth: megadont, molar-like premolars and huge molars with very thick enamel, but small incisors and canines; P. boisei had the largest cheek teeth of any hominin, hence the nickname "Nutcracker Man".
  • Body: bipedal and small, roughly 1.0–1.4 m tall, with marked sexual dimorphism. Hand bones from Koobi Fora, about 1.5 million years old (Carrie Mongle and colleagues, Nature, 2025), combine human-like thumb proportions with broad, gorilla-like fingers.

3. Geographical distribution

  • East Africa: Omo and Konso (Ethiopia); West Turkana, Koobi Fora and Chesowanja (Kenya); Olduvai and Peninj (Tanzania); Malema in Malawi. Two molars at Nyayanga, Kenya, dated about 3.0–2.6 million years, are the oldest fossils attributed to Paranthropus.
  • South Africa: limestone caves of the Cradle of Humankind, including Kromdraai, Swartkrans, Drimolen and Cooper's Cave. No Paranthropus fossil is known from outside Africa.

4. Lifeways

  • Diet: carbon isotopes show that P. boisei ate mainly C4 plants such as grasses and sedges (Thure Cerling and colleagues, 2011), while P. robustus had a more mixed diet that included hard foods in lean seasons.
  • Tools: worn bone tools at Swartkrans, used to dig into termite mounds, may belong to P. robustus; at Nyayanga, Oldowan tools and butchered hippo bones lie with Paranthropus teeth (Thomas Plummer and colleagues, Science, 2023), though early Homo could also have made them.
  • Social life: delayed male growth in P. robustus suggests gorilla-like competition among males (Charles Lockwood and colleagues, 2007); enamel proteins from Swartkrans teeth have identified both sexes and unexpected genetic variation (Palesa Madupe and colleagues, Science, 2025).
  • Extinction: the genus vanished about a million years ago, perhaps because a specialised diet left it vulnerable to drier climates and competition from the more flexible Homo erectus.

Paranthropus was a successful specialist lineage for over a million and a half years. New fossils, isotopes and ancient proteins show it was more variable and capable than once thought, while its extinction highlights the value of dietary flexibility in Homo.

Incest tabooExogamyAlliance theoryReciprocity

The incest taboo forbids sexual relations and marriage between close kin. It is found in every known society, at least for members of the nuclear family (G.P. Murdock, Social Structure, 1949), though how far it extends varies widely. For Claude Lévi-Strauss (The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1949) it is the rule through which humanity passed from nature to culture, and the foundation of exogamy, alliance and kinship systems.

1. Explanations of the taboo

  • Support for Westermarck: children reared together in Israeli kibbutzim almost never married one another (Joseph Shepher, 1971), and Taiwanese "minor marriages", where a girl grew up in her future husband's home, showed more divorce and fewer children (Arthur Wolf, 1995).
  • Limits of biology: genetic or psychological theories explain avoidance between close relatives but not why taboos cover distant classificatory kin, or why parallel cousins are forbidden while cross-cousins are preferred. The scope of the rule is cultural.

2. How the taboo builds kinship systems

  • Exogamy: extending the ban from the family to the lineage, clan, gotra or moiety forces groups to seek spouses outside; Tylor (1889) put the early choice as marrying out or being killed out.
  • Reciprocity and alliance: for Lévi-Strauss the prohibition is the negative face of a positive rule of exchange: a group that gives up its sisters and daughters gains wives from others. Restricted exchange links two groups through bilateral cross-cousin marriage; generalised exchange, as among the Kachin described by Edmund Leach, links several groups in a circle through matrilateral cross-cousin marriage.
  • Kinship terminology: marriage rules shape kin terms; in Dravidian kinship cross-cousins are classed as potential spouses and parallel cousins as siblings (Louis Dumont, 1953).
  • Wider society: exogamous clans and phratries tie villages into networks of in-laws, so marriage becomes politics.

3. Indian illustrations

  • Hindu law and custom: gotra and sapinda rules bar marriage within one's patriline and within set degrees; the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 forbids sapinda marriages and those within prohibited degrees unless custom allows them, a clause that protects South Indian cross-cousin marriage.
  • Tribal clan exogamy: Oraon and Munda totemic clans, Gond clans and Khasi clans (kur) are exogamous, and breaches can lead to fines or expulsion.

4. Critical assessment

  • Male bias: Gayle Rubin (1975) and other feminists criticised the exchange-of-women model for treating women as objects.
  • Descent versus alliance: Radcliffe-Brown and Meyer Fortes held that descent groups, not marriage alliance, are the core of kinship, especially in Africa.
  • Exceptions: royal brother–sister marriages in Ptolemaic Egypt, the Inca empire and Hawaii show the rule could be suspended to keep sacred blood and power within a line.

The incest taboo is less a biological instinct than a cultural rule of reciprocity: by forcing marriage outward it turns families into alliances and lays the base of kinship. Same-gotra disputes and the Supreme Court's Shakti Vahini ruling (2018) against khap interference show it still shapes social control in India.
free.upa-2026-an1-4c:
AneuploidyNon-disjunctionTrisomy and monosomySex chromosome aneuploidy

Human cells normally carry 46 chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and XX or XY, a number established by J.H. Tjio and A. Levan in 1956. Numerical aberrations alter this number, as aneuploidy, the gain or loss of single chromosomes, or as polyploidy, extra whole sets. Most arise from non-disjunction in meiosis, and their effects depend on whether autosomes or sex chromosomes are involved.

1. Causes and types

  • Non-disjunction: homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II) fail to separate, producing gametes with one chromosome too many or too few; the risk rises with maternal age.
  • Mosaicism: errors after fertilisation, such as anaphase lag, create mixed cell lines (for example 46,XX/47,XX,+21), usually with milder features.
  • Types: monosomy, trisomy and tetrasomy; triploidy (69 chromosomes) usually ends in miscarriage.
  • Survival: most aneuploid conceptions are lost early, and chromosomal errors are a leading cause of miscarriage; among autosomes only trisomies 21, 18 and 13 commonly survive to birth.

2. Autosomal aneuploidies: severe, body-wide effects

  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21): described by John Langdon Down (1866) and traced to an extra chromosome 21 by Jérôme Lejeune and colleagues (1959); intellectual disability, low muscle tone, flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes, epicanthic folds, a single palmar crease, heart defects, and higher risk of leukaemia and early Alzheimer's disease.
  • Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18): low birth weight, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, small jaw, heart and kidney defects; most infants die within the first year.
  • Patau syndrome (trisomy 13): defects of forebrain development, cleft lip and palate, extra fingers, small or absent eyes and scalp defects; few survive infancy.

3. Sex chromosome aneuploidies: milder effects

  • Turner syndrome (45,X): the only viable full monosomy; short stature, webbed neck, broad chest, swelling of hands and feet at birth, ovarian failure with infertility and heart defects such as coarctation of the aorta; intelligence is usually normal.
  • Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): tall stature, small testes, low testosterone, infertility, breast development and learning or language difficulties; cells show a Barr body.
  • Triple X (47,XXX) and 47,XYY: usually tall, with mild learning difficulties or none; many are never diagnosed. Claims in the 1960s linking XYY to crime were not upheld.
  • Why milder: X-inactivation (Mary Lyon, 1961) silences every X but one, so the number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one, and the Y carries few genes; an extra autosome changes the dosage of hundreds of genes.

4. Detection and management

  • Diagnosis: karyotyping, FISH, prenatal screening including cell-free DNA tests, and amniocentesis, followed by genetic counselling.
  • Care: heart surgery and early stimulation in Down syndrome, growth hormone and oestrogen in Turner syndrome, testosterone in Klinefelter syndrome; India's Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (2013) screens children for birth defects including Down syndrome.

Numerical aberrations show that gene dosage matters: extra autosomes disturb development throughout the body, while sex-chromosome imbalances are partly buffered by X-inactivation. Early screening, therapy and genetic counselling reduce their burden on families.
free.upa-2026-an1-5a:
Informed consentDo no harmConfidentialityReciprocity

Fieldwork ethics are the moral duties an anthropologist owes to the people studied, and also to sponsors, colleagues and the public. Long participant observation makes the researcher a guest in homes, rituals and disputes, so the responsibility exceeds that of a one-time survey. Project Camelot (1965) and the use of fieldwork for counter-insurgency in Thailand during the Vietnam War led the American Anthropological Association (AAA) to adopt its first code, the Principles of Professional Responsibility (1971), revised in 2012.

1. Core principles

  • Informed consent: people should know the purpose, sponsor, methods and likely use of the study and may withdraw at any time; in non-literate communities consent is usually oral, renewed during fieldwork and sought from community leaders as well as individuals.
  • Do no harm: the AAA (2012) puts the safety and dignity of those studied above the researcher's goals, including harm that may follow publication.
  • Confidentiality: pseudonyms protect people and places, as in M.N. Srinivas's "Rampura" (The Remembered Village, 1976) and Gerald Berreman's "Sirkanda" (Behind Many Masks, 1962).
  • Openness and reciprocity: covert research and hidden sponsors are unacceptable; results should be shared in an accessible form; collaborative research treats community members as partners, not mere "subjects".

2. Dilemmas in practice

  • Rapport versus exploitation: close rapport can lead people to reveal more than they intend; Berreman showed that villagers and the ethnographer both manage impressions.
  • Taking sides: in caste or factional conflict, closeness to one group can endanger informants from another.
  • Payment and gifts: paying people for their time is fair, but money can shape answers and create dependence.
  • Dual loyalties: governments, companies or armies funding research may want information that harms the community.

3. Indian context

  • Protected access: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation, 1956 restricts entry to tribal reserves, so work among groups such as the Jarawa needs permission and must respect isolation policies.
  • Guidelines: ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017) require community engagement and benefit sharing in research with vulnerable groups, including tribes.
  • Benefit sharing: the Kani of Kerala receive a share of licence fees for Jeevani, a drug based on their knowledge of arogyapacha, a model for fair use of traditional knowledge.

Fieldwork ethics is reflexive and continuous, not a form signed once. With digital ethnography and genomic sampling, the anthropologist's first loyalty must remain to the dignity and rights of the people studied.
free.upa-2026-an1-5b:
Nuclear genomeMitochondrial DNAMaternal inheritanceHaplogroups

Every human cell carries two genomes. Nuclear DNA (nDNA) holds almost all our genes and is inherited from both parents. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), a remnant of an ancient bacterial endosymbiont (Lynn Margulis, 1967), lies in the mitochondria and passes from mother to child. Their contrasting properties make them complementary tools in human genetics and anthropology.

1. Structural differences

  • Size and form: the nuclear genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs spread over 23 pairs of linear chromosomes; mtDNA is a small closed circle of 16,569 base pairs (the Cambridge Reference Sequence, Anderson and colleagues, 1981).
  • Gene density: nDNA carries roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes broken by introns and separated by long non-coding stretches; mtDNA packs 37 genes (13 respiratory-chain proteins, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs) with no introns, plus one control region, the D-loop.
  • Packaging and copy number: nuclear DNA is wound on histones and present in two copies per cell; mtDNA is not, and occurs in hundreds to thousands of copies, which is why it survives in old bones and hair.
  • Genetic code: mtDNA reads a few codons differently; UGA, a stop signal in the nucleus, codes for tryptophan.

2. Genetic behaviour

  • Inheritance: nDNA is biparental and reshuffled by crossing over in every generation; mtDNA comes almost entirely from the mother and does not recombine, so it passes down as a single unit (haplotype).
  • Mutation rate: mtDNA changes several times faster, especially in the hypervariable segments HVS-I and HVS-II, giving fine detail for recent population history.
  • Heteroplasmy: a cell may hold both normal and mutant mtDNA, so mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS and MERRF vary in severity and do not follow Mendelian ratios.

3. Uses in anthropology

  • mtDNA: traced "Mitochondrial Eve" to Africa about 200,000 years ago (Cann, Stoneking and Wilson, 1987), identified Neanderthal (1997) and Denisovan (2010) lineages, and showed that Andaman islanders carry ancient haplogroups M31 and M32 (Thangaraj and colleagues, 2005).
  • nDNA: genome-wide data revealed the Ancestral North Indian and Ancestral South Indian components (Reich and colleagues, 2009) and Neanderthal admixture; the Genome India Project (about 10,000 genomes, data released in January 2025) supports disease research; autosomal STRs serve forensic and paternity work.

The two genomes are complementary: mtDNA, like the Y chromosome for fathers, tells the story of one line of descent and survives in ancient remains, while nuclear DNA gives the full picture of ancestry, admixture and disease.
free.upa-2026-an1-5c:
PatriarchyGender and kinshipUnpaid domestic workEgalitarian family

The feminist movement moved from the first wave (suffrage, late 19th to early 20th century) to the second wave of the 1960s–80s, whose slogan "the personal is political" carried the struggle into the home, and then to intersectional campaigns. Its main target was patriarchy within the family. In anthropology it gave rise to feminist anthropology, which asked whether the family is natural and universal at all.

1. Feminist critique of the family

  • A site of inequality: Engels (The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, 1884) tied women's subordination to private property; Betty Friedan (The Feminine Mystique, 1963) attacked the confinement of educated women to housework.
  • Invisible labour: Ann Oakley (The Sociology of Housework, 1974) showed housework to be real, unpaid work, and Arlie Hochschild (The Second Shift, 1989) found that employed women still do most of the home and care work.
  • Questioning universality: in Woman, Culture, and Society (1974, edited by Michelle Rosaldo and Louise Lamphere), Rosaldo traced women's lower status to the domestic–public divide and Sherry Ortner to their symbolic link with nature; Jane Collier and Sylvia Yanagisako (Gender and Kinship, 1987) treated family and kinship as cultural constructs, and Gayle Rubin (1975) criticised Lévi-Strauss's idea of the "exchange of women".

2. Impact on family structure and roles

  • New forms: dual-earner, single-parent, female-headed and live-in households have grown; marriage comes later and families are smaller.
  • Shared authority: the ideal shifted to a symmetrical family (Michael Young and Peter Willmott, 1973) with joint decisions and more involved fathers.
  • Autonomy: access to education, contraception and divorce gave women control over marriage and childbearing.
  • Strains: critics point to women's double burden, gaps in care and weaker kin support.

3. Indian context

  • Legal reform: campaigns that followed the Towards Equality report (1974) helped bring the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 and the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which made daughters coparceners (Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, 2020).
  • Indian scholarship: Leela Dube showed how kinship shapes girls' lives, and Bina Agarwal (A Field of One's Own, 1994) argued for women's land rights.
  • Matriliny is not matriarchy: among the Khasi, the youngest daughter (khadduh) inherits the ancestral house, yet the maternal uncle and men hold much public authority.

The feminist movement has not destroyed the family but democratised it, turning a hierarchy into a negotiated partnership. The remaining task is a fair sharing of care work, so that equality inside the home matches equality outside it.
free.upa-2026-an1-5d:
AnthropometryPercentilesHuman-centred designPopulation variation

Anthropometry is the systematic measurement of the size, shape and proportions of the human body, standardised by Rudolf Martin's Lehrbuch der Anthropologie (1914). Ergonomics, a term revived by K.F.H. Murrell in 1949, fits tasks, tools and spaces to the people who use them. Anthropometric data are its foundation, because nothing can fit users whose body dimensions are unknown.

1. Measurements used

  • Static (structural) dimensions: stature, sitting height, eye height, shoulder and hip breadth, popliteal height and buttock–knee length, taken with anthropometer, calipers or 3D body scanners.
  • Dynamic (functional) dimensions: reach envelopes, joint ranges, grip strength and clearances needed while working.
  • Mass and proportions: body weight and segment lengths matter for load handling, seating and safety equipment.

2. Design principles

  • No "average person": wartime sizing of cockpits, oxygen masks and flight clothing made anthropometry central to design; Gilbert Daniels (1952) then found that none of over 4,000 US Air Force pilots was average on all ten key dimensions, so designers use percentiles, usually the 5th to 95th.
  • Design for extremes: clearances such as doorways suit the tallest users; controls must be within reach of the smallest.
  • Adjustability and inclusion: seats, desks and steering columns adjust across the range; data on children, the elderly and persons with disabilities support accessible design, as required by the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.

3. Applications in India

  • Farm tools: ICAR's Central Institute of Agricultural Engineering, Bhopal, has compiled body-size and strength data of Indian farm workers to design sickles, weeders and tractor controls, including tools for women workers.
  • Clothing: NIFT's INDIAsize survey 3D-scanned over 25,000 Indians to build Indian size charts in place of borrowed Western sizes.
  • Other uses: school furniture matched to children's leg length, helmets, and protective masks that seal on Indian faces.

4. Anthropological insights

  • Population variation: dimensions differ by sex, age, region, ethnic group and nutrition, so machines designed for Europeans often misfit shorter Indian users.
  • Secular trend: average height changes over generations, so databases need regular updating.
  • Cultural posture: squatting and floor-sitting, common in Indian homes and workshops, call for designs different from chair-based work.

Anthropometry turns human variation into numbers designers can use. Population-specific, up-to-date data make work safer and more productive and give physical anthropology a direct role in human-centred design.
free.upa-2026-an1-5e:
ThermoluminescenceTrapped electronsPalaeodoseBurnt flint and pottery

Thermoluminescence (TL) dating is an absolute (chronometric) method based on the light that crystalline minerals give off when heated, releasing energy stored from natural radiation. Suggested by Farrington Daniels and colleagues (1953) and developed for pottery by Martin Aitken at Oxford in the 1960s, it dates the last time an object was strongly heated.

1. Principle

  • Storage of energy: grains of quartz and feldspar receive a small, steady dose of radiation from uranium, thorium and potassium-40 in the surroundings and from cosmic rays; freed electrons are caught in defects ("traps") in the crystal.
  • Resetting: firing a pot, burning a flint or using a hearth at about 500 °C or more empties the traps and sets the clock to zero.
  • Release as light: when the sample is reheated in the laboratory, trapped electrons escape and emit light (a glow curve) in proportion to the radiation absorbed since the last heating.

2. Method

  • The equation: age equals the palaeodose (equivalent dose, in grays) divided by the annual dose rate; the palaeodose comes from comparing natural light with light produced by known laboratory doses, and the dose rate is measured on site.
  • Range and precision: from a few hundred to a few hundred thousand years, usually with an error of 5–10%.
  • Materials: pottery, terracotta, burnt flint and chert, burnt stones, bricks, kilns and hearths; for unheated sediments the related optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) is now preferred.

3. Significance

  • Human origins: TL on burnt flints dated early modern humans at Qafzeh, Israel, to about 92,000 years (Valladas and colleagues, 1988) and the Jebel Irhoud fossils, Morocco, to about 315,000 years (Richter and colleagues, 2017), the oldest known Homo sapiens.
  • Beyond radiocarbon: it dates inorganic objects and reaches far beyond the roughly 50,000-year limit of radiocarbon.
  • Authentication: it exposes forged ceramics and terracottas.
  • Indian use of luminescence: OSL dated Middle Palaeolithic tools below and above the Toba ash (about 74,000 years) at Jwalapuram, Andhra Pradesh (Petraglia and colleagues, 2007).

4. Limitations

  • Dose-rate errors: changes in soil moisture, radon loss and burial conditions affect results.
  • Incomplete resetting and fading: low-temperature firing, anomalous fading in feldspars and saturation of traps give unreliable ages.
  • Sampling demands: samples are destroyed and must be shielded from light.

TL dating gave archaeology a clock for fired and burnt materials, bridging the gap between radiocarbon and potassium–argon dating. With OSL, luminescence remains central to dating Palaeolithic sites and ancient ceramics.
free.upa-2026-an1-6a:
Pedigree analysisTwin and adoption studiesModes of inheritanceMolecular confirmation

A disorder that "runs in families" is not necessarily genetic, because relatives share food, habits and surroundings as well as genes. Human geneticists therefore combine family (pedigree) studies, twin and adoption studies, population data and laboratory tests. Archibald Garrod's work on alkaptonuria (1902), noting that many affected children had first-cousin parents, was the first such demonstration of a recessive human trait.

1. Establishing that a disorder is inherited

  • Familial aggregation: the risk among relatives of an affected person (the proband) is higher than in the general population and falls with distance of relationship, from first- to second- to third-degree relatives.
  • Twin studies: much higher concordance in identical (monozygotic) than in fraternal (dizygotic) twins points to genes, an approach pioneered by Francis Galton (1875); the co-twin control method then tests environmental effects.
  • Adoption (foster-child) studies: if adopted children resemble their biological rather than their adoptive parents, heredity outweighs upbringing.
  • Ruling out the environment: the disorder does not spread to unrelated spouses or neighbours and often appears at a typical age without an outside trigger.
  • Laboratory proof: karyotyping (trisomy 21 in Down syndrome, Lejeune, 1959), enzyme assays (phenylketonuria) and DNA tests locate the defect; linkage analysis (LOD score above 3) and genome-wide association studies map the genes.

2. Finding the mode of inheritance

  • Pedigree analysis: standard symbols are used to chart affected, unaffected and carrier members; the pattern is then matched with expected models and checked by segregation analysis, which compares observed with Mendelian ratios after correcting for how families were selected.

3. Examples

  • Huntington disease: an expanded CAG repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4 is dominant and shows anticipation, with earlier onset in successive generations.
  • Haemophilia in Europe's royal families: Queen Victoria was a carrier; DNA from the Russian imperial family identified the disease as haemophilia B (Rogaev and colleagues, 2009).
  • Sickle cell disease in India: a recessive disorder common among tribal communities of central, western and southern India; the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) had screened over 7 crore people by June 2026 and issues genetic status cards for marriage counselling.
  • Consanguinity and endogamy: cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriages in South India raise recessive disorders, and caste endogamy has produced strong founder effects (Nakatsuka and colleagues, 2017).

4. Pitfalls

  • Shared environment: kuru among the Fore of Papua New Guinea clustered in families and was first thought hereditary, but proved to be a prion disease spread through mortuary feasts (Carleton Gajdusek; Shirley Lindenbaum, Kuru Sorcery, 1979).
  • Masked patterns: reduced penetrance, variable expressivity, new mutations, imprinting (Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes) and small family size can hide the true pattern.

Proof of inheritance rests on converging evidence: pedigrees suggest a pattern, twin and adoption data separate genes from environment, and molecular tests confirm it. In India, with widespread endogamy and consanguinity, such studies are the basis of screening and genetic counselling.
free.upa-2026-an1-6b:
CulturologySymbolEnergy and technologyTechnological determinism

Leslie A. White (1900–1975), the leading neo-evolutionist of American anthropology, held that human behaviour is shaped not by instinct or individual psychology but by culture, a symbol-based, extrasomatic system that follows its own laws. He called the study of this system culturology (The Science of Culture, 1949) and tied cultural evolution to the capture of energy.

1. How culture determines behaviour

  • The symbol: "All human behavior originates in the use of symbols" (White, 1940). Only humans freely give meanings to things, such as holy water or a mourning colour; things and acts that depend on this capacity he later called symbolates (1959).
  • Culture outside the individual: culture exists before and beyond any person; a child born into a Gond or a Toda household will speak, eat, marry and worship as that tradition prescribes. For White, behaviour is a function of culture, not the reverse.
  • The individual as carrier: simultaneous inventions, such as calculus by Newton and Leibniz and natural selection by Darwin and Wallace, show that ideas appear when culture is ready; in his essay on Ikhnaton he argued that even a pharaoh's religious reform expressed cultural forces.
  • Incest taboo: White (1948) explained exogamy as a cultural device that forced groups to marry out and so build alliances and cooperation, not as an instinctive aversion; clan and gotra exogamy in India illustrate such rules.

2. Energy, technology and the three subsystems

  • Law of cultural development (1943): culture advances as the energy harnessed per person per year increases, or as tools use it more efficiently (C = E × T).
  • Three subsystems: technological (tools, energy), sociological (kinship, economy, polity) and ideological (beliefs, knowledge); technology is primary and conditions the other two.
  • Stages: human muscle power among foragers, the agricultural revolution, and the fuel revolution of coal and oil, each producing new social forms and beliefs (The Evolution of Culture, 1959).
  • Indian illustration: tube wells, tractors and fertilisers of the Green Revolution weakened jajmani ties and spread cash wages in Punjab.

3. Critical evaluation

  • Strengths: White gave anthropology an objective, materialist and comparative framework, revived evolutionism after the Boasian reaction and inspired Marvin Harris's cultural materialism (1979) and ecological anthropology.
  • Determinism: the same technology coexists with very different behaviour; Milton Singer (When a Great Tradition Modernizes, 1972) found Madras industrialists keeping joint-family and ritual obligations.
  • Ethnocentric ranking: measuring progress by energy use ranks high-consuming societies as "higher" and ignores ecological costs, a serious flaw in the age of climate change.

White rightly showed that culture, not instinct, patterns human behaviour, and that technology and energy set its limits. Yet behaviour arises from culture, ecology, history and human agency together, so his culturology is a powerful but partial explanation.

StrepsirhiniToothcomb and rhinariumLemurs and lorisesHaplorhini

Living primates fall into two suborders. Strepsirhini ("turned nose", from the moist, comma-shaped nostrils) comprise the lemurs and the lorises and galagos; Haplorhini ("simple nose") comprise tarsiers, monkeys, apes and humans. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire coined Strepsirhini (1812); R.I. Pocock (1918) revived it and named Haplorhini on the basis of nose structure, a split now preferred to the prosimian–anthropoid scheme because tarsiers share key traits with monkeys and apes.

1. What strepsirhines are

  • The most conservative living primates: they keep ancestral mammalian features such as a strong sense of smell, a moist nose and, in many species, nocturnal habits.
  • Two main groups: Lemuriformes (true lemurs, indri and sifakas, mouse and dwarf lemurs, aye-aye) and Lorisiformes (lorises, pottos, angwantibos and galagos or bushbabies).
  • Fossil roots: Eocene adapiforms such as Notharctus are usually placed near this line; the earliest toothcombed fossil, Karanisia, and the early galago Saharagalago come from the Fayum, Egypt, about 40 million years ago.

2. Geographical distribution

  • Madagascar: isolated from Africa, lemur ancestors (probably arriving by rafting) radiated into more than 100 species; IUCN assessments place over 90% of them under threat, making lemurs among the most endangered mammals.
  • India: the Bengal slow loris lives in the forests of the north-east, and the grey slender loris in the Eastern and Western Ghats; Tamil Nadu notified India's first slender loris sanctuary at Kadavur (Karur and Dindigul) in 2022.

3. Characteristics that distinguish them from haplorhines

  • Smell versus sight: strepsirhines depend on smell, with a working vomeronasal organ and scent glands; ring-tailed lemur males hold "stink fights" by wafting tails rubbed on wrist glands. Haplorhines rely on sight, with a fovea and, in Old World monkeys and apes, routine trichromatic colour perception.
  • Grooming and feeding: the toothcomb, cleaned by a "sublingua" under the tongue, combs fur and scrapes gum and resin; haplorhines groom with their fingers.
  • Reproduction: a two-horned (bicornuate) uterus and frequent twins, against a single-chambered uterus and usually one infant in monkeys and apes.
  • Behaviour and physiology: many are nocturnal, solitary foragers, female dominance is common among lemurs, and fat-tailed dwarf lemurs hibernate for up to seven months, the longest of any primate.
  • Tarsiers bridge the gap: they look prosimian (nocturnal, grooming claws) but share the dry nose, haemochorial placenta and loss of vitamin C synthesis with haplorhines.

Strepsirhines are a living window on early primate adaptation: smell-guided, often nocturnal and arboreal. Their survival in Madagascar and in India's loris habitats depends on forest conservation.
free.upa-2026-an1-7a:
Mixed methodsTriangulationEmic and eticBiocultural holism

Mixed methods research collects both qualitative and quantitative data in one study and integrates them to answer a question more completely (John Creswell and Vicki Plano Clark, Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research, 2007). Anthropology practised it long before the name: Malinowski (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922) joined statistical documentation with the "imponderabilia of actual life". Its logic is triangulation (Norman Denzin, The Research Act, 1970).

1. Why anthropology needs mixed methods

  • Holism: human life has measurable sides (income, diet, stature, fertility) and interpretive sides (meanings, values, beliefs); no single method captures both.
  • Emic and etic together: a survey shows the outsider's pattern, while ethnography gives the insider's reasons.
  • Validity: agreement between methods raises confidence, and disagreement opens new questions.
  • Policy relevance: planners need numbers, communities need their voices heard, and applied anthropology must supply both.

2. Designs

  • Forms of triangulation: Denzin distinguished triangulation of data sources, investigators, theories and methods; mixed methods is mainly the last.
  • Priority: Janice Morse (1991) wrote designs as QUAN → qual or QUAL + quan to show which strand leads.

3. Tools commonly combined

  • Qualitative: participant observation, key-informant and in-depth interviews, case studies, life histories, genealogies, focus groups and participatory rural appraisal (Robert Chambers).
  • Quantitative: household schedules, structured questionnaires, time-allocation records, anthropometry, blood and genetic tests and GIS mapping, analysed with statistical software alongside qualitative coding (NVivo, ATLAS.ti).

4. Examples

  • Village studies: S.C. Dube's Indian Village (1955) on Shamirpet near Hyderabad combined household data with ethnography; T. Scarlett Epstein (1962) compared irrigated Wangala and dry Dalena in Mysore through economic surveys and fieldwork.
  • People of India project: the Anthropological Survey of India (1985–92, under K.S. Singh) profiled 4,635 communities through standard schedules and ethnographic notes.
  • Biocultural research: studies of sickle cell disease or child malnutrition among tribes link blood tests and anthropometry with ethnography of diet, marriage rules and healing practices.

5. Challenges

  • Paradigm conflict: positivist and interpretive assumptions differ, and critics doubt whether the two can be truly integrated rather than placed side by side.
  • Cost, time and skills: one researcher must master both, or work in a team.
  • Integration: results may conflict, and deciding which strand to trust needs judgement.
  • Ethics: surveys can reduce people to numbers, while long fieldwork raises issues of consent and confidentiality.

Mixed methods suit anthropology's holistic, biocultural outlook: numbers show how widespread a pattern is, ethnography explains what it means. Used reflexively, they make research both rigorous and grounded in people's own voices.
