Fertility and fecundityMortalityProximate determinantsBiosocial factors

Fertility is the actual reproductive performance of a woman or population, measured by live births, whereas fecundity is the biological capacity to reproduce. Mortality is the occurrence of deaths in a population. With migration they determine population size and structure, and both are biosocial: biology sets the limits, while ecology, economy and culture decide where a population falls within them.

1. Meaning and measures

  • Fertility measures: crude birth rate, general and age-specific fertility rates and total fertility rate (TFR); India's TFR was 1.9 in SRS 2024 (rural 2.1, urban 1.5), from 2.9 in Bihar to 1.2 in Delhi.
  • Mortality measures: crude death rate, infant mortality rate (IMR), maternal mortality ratio (MMR) and life expectancy; India's IMR was 24 per 1,000 live births (SRS 2024) and MMR 87 per 100,000 live births (SRS 2022–24).
  • Frameworks: Kingsley Davis and Judith Blake (1956) showed that social factors act on fertility only through intermediate variables; John Bongaarts (1978) reduced these to a few proximate determinants, and W. Henry Mosley and Lincoln Chen (1984) built a similar model for child deaths.

2. Biological factors

  • Reproductive span: ages at menarche and menopause set the limits; better nutrition has lowered the age at menarche over generations.
  • Fecundability and sterility: the chance of conceiving in a single cycle is low even for young couples; genital infections and sexually transmitted diseases cause sterility.
  • Lactation and nutrition: among the !Kung San, frequent nursing and a mobile life kept births about four years apart (Nancy Howell, 1979); Rose Frisch linked regular ovulation to a minimum level of body fat.
  • Age and sex: deaths cluster in infancy and old age, giving a U-shaped age curve; males are biologically more vulnerable, though in India neglect of girls has raised female child mortality.
  • Genetic factors: consanguinity raises foetal loss and infant deaths through recessive disorders; sickle cell disease and G6PD deficiency affect survival in some tribal groups.

3. Socio-ecological factors

  • Marriage customs: early and universal marriage raises fertility; the Hutterites of North America, marrying early and rejecting contraception, averaged about ten children per woman, whereas celibacy, polyandry and bans on widow remarriage lower it.
  • Value of children: where children work and support parents, families are large (John Caldwell's wealth-flow theory, 1976); urban, educated parents invest in fewer children.
  • Women's education and status: Kerala and Tamil Nadu reached low fertility and child mortality through female literacy and health services; son preference keeps fertility up and skews child deaths against girls.
  • Environment and health care: endemic malaria in forest belts, unsafe water, poor sanitation, high-altitude hypoxia and distance from clinics raise infant and maternal deaths; famines and epidemics raise mortality sharply.
  • Contact and displacement: small groups such as the Onge and Great Andamanese declined after colonial contact through epidemics and low fertility.

Fertility and mortality are biosocial outcomes: biology defines the potential, while marriage rules, economy, ecology and health systems decide actual levels. Below-replacement fertility alongside high infant mortality in some states and tribal groups calls for community-specific health policy.
free.upa-2026-an1-7c:
MagdalenianUpper PalaeolithicBone and antler industryCave art

The Magdalenian is the last major culture of the Upper Palaeolithic in Western Europe, named by Gabriel de Mortillet after the rock shelter of La Madeleine in the Dordogne, France, which Édouard Lartet and Henry Christy excavated in the 1860s. Made by anatomically modern humans of the Cro-Magnon type, it is known for reindeer hunting, barbed harpoons and the climax of Ice Age cave art.

1. Chronology

  • Dates: roughly 21,000 to 14,000 calendar years ago (about 17,000–12,000 radiocarbon years BP), from the end of the Last Glacial Maximum to the Late Glacial warming.
  • Sequence: it followed the Solutrean (with the Badegoulian as a transitional phase in France) and gave way to the Azilian and related cultures as forests spread and reindeer moved north.
  • Phases: Henri Breuil divided it into Magdalenian I–VI on the basis of bone and antler tools, now often grouped as Lower, Middle and Upper.

2. Geographical distribution

  • Core area: south-west France (Vézère valley sites such as La Madeleine and Laugerie-Basse; Pyrenean sites such as Mas d'Azil, Isturitz, Niaux and Les Trois-Frères) and Cantabrian Spain (Altamira, El Castillo).
  • Expansion: after the glacial maximum, groups recolonised the north and east: Belgium, Switzerland (Kesslerloch), Germany (Gönnersdorf, Andernach), the Czech Republic, southern Poland and Britain (Gough's Cave, Cheddar), with open-air camps in the Paris Basin (Pincevent, Étiolles).

3. Tool types

  • Lithic: a blade-based industry rich in burins, end-scrapers and borers, with tiny backed bladelets that foreshadow Mesolithic microliths.
  • Organic: the real hallmark is bone and antler, worked by the groove-and-splinter technique into points, harpoons and needles.

4. Lifeways

  • Economy: specialised, seasonal hunting of reindeer, with horse, red deer, bison and ibex; salmon fishing and fowling added variety. Édouard Lartet called this period the "age of the reindeer".
  • Settlement: caves, rock shelters and open-air tent camps with hearths (Pincevent, studied by André Leroi-Gourhan); large sites such as Altamira (Margaret Conkey, 1980) and Isturitz may have been seasonal gathering places.
  • Art and belief: the polychrome bison of Altamira, Niaux's Salon Noir, the "Sorcerer" of Les Trois-Frères, the clay bison of Tuc d'Audoubert and Lascaux, usually placed in the early Magdalenian; engraved plaques at Gönnersdorf. Interpretations range from hunting magic to shamanism and Leroi-Gourhan's male–female symbolism.
  • Society: shells and flint moved over long distances, personal ornaments were common, and skull cups from Gough's Cave suggest ritual treatment of the dead.
  • Population history: ancient DNA links Magdalenian groups to an older western European ancestry, later largely replaced by incoming hunter-gatherers from the south-east around 14,000 years ago.

The Magdalenian marks the climax of Ice Age hunter-gatherer life: specialised hunting, refined bone and antler technology and unmatched art. Its change into the Azilian as the climate warmed shows culture adapting to environment, the prelude to the Mesolithic.
free.upa-2026-an1-8a:
British structuralismInterpretive anthropologyThick descriptionSymbol and meaning

Edmund Leach (1910–1989) brought Lévi-Strauss's structuralism into British social anthropology while keeping Malinowski's empiricism, and treated politics, myth and ritual as systems of communication. Clifford Geertz (1926–2006) founded interpretive anthropology (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), reading culture as public meaning, almost like a text. Both moved the discipline from function to symbol, but by different routes.

1. Leach's structuralism

  • Structure in motion: Political Systems of Highland Burma (1954) showed Kachin communities swinging between hierarchical gumsa and egalitarian gumlao ideals, with the Shan state as a third model; structure was an ideal, not the fixed equilibrium Radcliffe-Brown assumed.
  • Against typology: in Rethinking Anthropology (1961) he mocked the classification of societies as "butterfly collecting" and urged comparison of underlying principles such as marriage alliance (the Kachin mayu–dama, wife-giver and wife-taker, relation).
  • Oppositions and mediation: in Genesis as Myth (1969) and his essay on animal categories and verbal abuse (1964), sacredness and taboo cluster at the ambiguous boundary between paired categories.
  • Culture as communication: Culture and Communication (1976) decoded ritual and dress as signs and symbols.
  • Testing against data: Pul Eliya (1961), on a Sri Lankan village, treated kinship as an idiom of land and property, a warning that models must fit the facts.

2. Geertz's interpretive anthropology

  • Webs of meaning: man is "an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun", and their analysis is "not an experimental science in search of law but an interpretive one in search of meaning" (1973).
  • Thick description: borrowing Gilbert Ryle's contrast between a twitch and a wink, the ethnographer records the layers of meaning behind an act, not just the act.
  • Exemplary studies: "Deep Play" read the Balinese cockfight as "a story they tell themselves about themselves"; The Religion of Java (1960) described abangan, santri and priyayi traditions; Negara (1980) portrayed the Balinese kingdom as a theatre state.
  • The particular over the universal: in "The Cerebral Savage" (1967) he faulted Lévi-Strauss for losing living people in abstract codes.

3. Comparison

  • Common ground: both rejected mechanical functionalism, saw culture as symbolic and used myth and ritual as central data.
  • Core difference: Leach sought general principles hidden beneath diverse customs, while Geertz distrusted universals; Leach explains, Geertz interprets.
  • Indian echoes: Louis Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus (1966) read caste through the structural opposition of pure and impure, while McKim Marriott's "The Feast of Love" (1966) interpreted Holi in Kishan Garhi as a festive reversal of village hierarchy.

4. Criticisms

  • Of Leach: structural readings can be subjective and hard to verify, and individual intentions get lost, though his Kachin study brought politics and change into structure.
  • Of Geertz: Talal Asad (Genealogies of Religion, 1993) argued that he ignored how power authorises meanings; Roger Keesing (1987) asked whose meanings are being read; the Writing Culture debate (James Clifford and George Marcus, 1986) questioned the ethnographer's authority.

Leach looks for the grammar beneath cultural expressions, Geertz for their meaning in context. A mature anthropology uses both, while attending to the power that both underplayed.
free.upa-2026-an1-8b:
SerogeneticsCytogeneticsPrenatal diagnosisReproductive ethics

Serogenetics studies inherited variation in blood groups and serum proteins (ABO, Rh, MN, HLA, haptoglobin, transferrin); cytogenetics studies the number and structure of chromosomes, a field set on its modern footing when Tjio and Levan (1956) established the human count of 46. Both are central to reproductive biology: they explain infertility and pregnancy loss, predict risk to offspring and guide assisted reproduction.

1. Serogenetics in reproductive biology

  • Rh incompatibility: an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive foetus may form anti-D antibodies that destroy the red cells of later foetuses (haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn); antenatal typing and anti-D immunoglobulin have made it largely preventable, while ABO incompatibility causes milder newborn jaundice.
  • HLA and immune factors: studies of Hutterite couples (Carole Ober and colleagues) linked HLA sharing between spouses with longer time to pregnancy and more miscarriages; antiphospholipid and antisperm antibodies are tested in repeated loss.
  • Carrier screening: haemoglobin tests detect sickle cell and beta-thalassaemia carriers before marriage or early in pregnancy; India's Sickle Cell Mission issues genetic status cards for counselling.

2. Cytogenetics in reproductive biology

  • Infertility: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is a leading chromosomal cause of absent sperm, Turner syndrome (45,X) causes ovarian failure, and Y-chromosome (AZF) microdeletions reduce sperm counts; karyotyping is therefore advised before ICSI.
  • Recurrent miscarriage: about half of first-trimester miscarriages carry chromosome errors, mostly trisomies; a parent with a balanced reciprocal or Robertsonian translocation may produce unbalanced embryos.
  • Prenatal diagnosis: chorionic villus sampling (10–13 weeks) or amniocentesis (15–20 weeks), with karyotype, FISH or microarray, detects trisomies 21, 18 and 13; cell-free foetal DNA in the mother's blood (Dennis Lo, 1997) now allows non-invasive screening.
  • Assisted reproduction: preimplantation genetic testing (PGT-A for aneuploidy, PGT-M for single-gene disorders, PGT-SR for rearrangements) selects embryos in IVF.

3. Ethical issues in reproductive technology

  • Sex selection and eugenics: prenatal tests can be misused to select sons, which the PCPNDT Act, 1994 prohibits; screening out disability raises eugenic fears, as Rayna Rapp's study of amniocentesis (Testing Women, Testing the Fetus, 1999) showed.
  • Commodification: commercial surrogacy hubs such as Anand in Gujarat (Amrita Pande, Wombs in Labor, 2014) exposed poor women to market pressures; India's Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 now permits only altruistic surrogacy, and the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021 regulates clinics and gamete banks.
  • Access and equity: IVF is costly, and the surrogacy law excludes single men and same-sex couples; in October 2025 the Supreme Court held that the Act's age limits do not bind couples who had frozen embryos before it came into force (25 January 2022).
  • Germline change: He Jiankui's gene-edited twins (2018) and mitochondrial donation (eight babies born in the UK, reported 2025) raise questions of consent for future generations.
  • Kinship and identity: donors and surrogates split genetic, gestational and social parenthood (Marilyn Strathern, Reproducing the Future, 1992), raising questions of donor anonymity and a child's right to know.

Serogenetics and cytogenetics have made reproduction safer and more predictable, from preventing Rh disease to choosing healthy embryos. Their use needs firm bioethics and sensitivity to gender, kinship and inequality.

Basic personality structureModal personalityNational characterChild-rearing

The culture and personality school held that every society moulds a typical personality through child-rearing. Abram Kardiner and Ralph Linton (The Individual and His Society, 1939) called it the basic personality structure; Cora Du Bois (The People of Alor, 1944) recast it as the statistically most frequent, or modal, personality. During the Second World War these ideas were scaled up from tribes to nations as national character studies.

1. Basic personality types

  • Kardiner's model: primary institutions (family form, feeding, weaning, toilet training, discipline) give children common experiences that form a basic personality, which is then projected into secondary institutions such as religion, folklore and taboos; he tested it on Linton's data from the Marquesas and the Tanala, and later on the Comanche, Alor and Plainville, USA (The Psychological Frontiers of Society, 1945).
  • Ethnographic tests: among the Alorese, irregular maternal care was linked to suspicious, insecure adults, an inference supported by Rorschach tests read blind by a psychiatrist.
  • Linton's addition: besides the basic personality, individuals carry status personalities tied to age, sex and class.
  • Benedict's configurations: Patterns of Culture (1934) contrasted the restrained Apollonian Zuni with the ecstatic Dionysian Kwakiutl, showing whole cultures selecting a temperament.

2. From basic personality to national character

  • Child-rearing as the root: Geoffrey Gorer and John Rickman (The People of Great Russia, 1949) linked tight swaddling of Russian infants to alternating restraint and emotional outbursts in adults; Gorer had earlier tied strict Japanese toilet training to compulsive orderliness.
  • Moral codes: Ruth Benedict (The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, 1946) explained Japanese conduct through obligations such as on, giri and gimu, contrasting a shame culture with the American guilt culture.
  • A nation's self-image: Margaret Mead (And Keep Your Powder Dry, 1942) portrayed Americans as achievement-driven and moralistic; with Rhoda Métraux she set out methods for studying "culture at a distance" through films, novels and migrants (1953).
  • Statistical version: Alex Inkeles and Daniel Levinson (1954) defined national character as the modal personality of a nation's adults, to be tested by sampling; Francis Hsu (Americans and Chinese, 1953) contrasted individual-centred and situation-centred ways of life.
  • India: G. Morris Carstairs (The Twice-Born, 1957) related upper-caste upbringing in Rajasthan to adult anxieties, and Sudhir Kakar (The Inner World, 1978) linked intense mother–son bonds and joint-family life to a relational self, though India's diversity of region, caste and tribe resists one national type.

3. Critical appraisal

  • Stereotyping: nations hold many classes, regions and ethnic groups, and conclusions drawn from a few informants or wartime enemies easily become stereotypes.
  • Childhood determinism: critics mocked swaddling theories as "diaperology"; adult experience, economy and politics shape behaviour too.
  • Political use: much of this work served wartime governments.
  • Empirical test: Antonio Terracciano and colleagues (Science, 2005) found that beliefs about national character in 49 cultures did not match measured average personality traits.

Basic personality can produce shared dispositions within a nation, but national character is better seen as a tendency shaped by history, institutions and ideology than as a fixed type. Used cautiously, the idea helps explain cultural diversity without stereotyping peoples.
free.upa-2026-an2-1a:
Dravidian familyGondi and KurukhLanguage shiftLinguistic identity

The term Dravidian for India's second-largest language family was established by Robert Caldwell in his Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages (1856). Census 2011 lists 17 Dravidian languages spoken by about 19.6% of Indians. Besides the four great literary languages, the family includes many unwritten tribal languages spread across the central Indian highlands, the Nilgiris and the Rajmahal hills.

1. Branches and their tribal speakers

  • Four branches: Bhadriraju Krishnamurti (The Dravidian Languages, 2003) groups about two dozen languages into South, South-Central, Central and North Dravidian; apart from Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada, Telugu and Tulu, most of them are spoken by Scheduled Tribes.
  • Largest tribal languages: Gondi of the Gonds and Kurukh of the Oraons each have well over a million speakers (Census 2011); Kui and Kuvi of the Kondhs of Odisha come next.
  • Small communities: Toda, Kota, Kurumba, Irula and Koraga belong to small communities, the Toda and Kota only a few thousand strong and several of them PVTGs, so every lost speaker matters.
  • Historical clues: Oraon tradition, recorded by S.C. Roy (The Oraons of Chota Nagpur, 1915), recalls an earlier home at Rohtas, from where one branch went to the Rajmahal hills and another to Chotanagpur; the close kinship of Kurukh and Malto supports this shared origin of the Oraons and the Sauria Paharia.

2. Socio-linguistic features

  • Bilingualism and shift: most speakers also use a regional language; in many Oraon villages the lingua franca Sadri has displaced Kurukh, and many Gonds of Madhya Pradesh now speak Hindi dialects.
  • Language as identity: a shared tongue links a tribe across state borders, for example Kurukh speakers from Jharkhand to the tea gardens of Bengal and Assam, and has become a rallying point of ethnic assertion.

3. Revitalisation

  • Scripts and status: the Masaram and Gunjala Gondi scripts are now in Unicode, Tolong Siki is promoted for Kurukh, and Kurukh is an additional official language in Jharkhand and, since 2017, West Bengal; demands for Eighth Schedule status continue.
  • Mother-tongue schooling: Odisha's multilingual education programme in Kui, Kuvi and other tribal languages, and the NEP 2020 emphasis on the home language, aim to cut dropout among tribal children.

Dravidian tribal languages carry oral traditions and ecological knowledge; surveys such as the People's Linguistic Survey of India (from 2010) show that many are endangered, so schooling, media and official recognition decide their future.

Clifford Jolly (1970)Gelada analogySmall-object feedingRamapithecus

The Seed Eaters Model was proposed by Clifford J. Jolly in The Seed-Eaters: A New Model of Hominid Differentiation Based on a Baboon Analogy (Man, 1970). Using the grassland-dwelling gelada baboon (Theropithecus gelada) as an analogy, Jolly argued that the first hominids split from the apes by adapting to small-object feeding (seeds, grass and roots) in open country, not by hunting. It was applied directly to Ramapithecus of the Indian Siwaliks.

1. The model

  • Analogy, not ancestry: geladas are not human ancestors, but they live in open, seasonal grassland; features they share with hominids, and not with forest apes, were read as convergent adaptations to the same diet.
  • Phase I, seed-eating: a ground-feeding primate picking up tiny, hard items while sitting or squatting would evolve small incisors, reduced canines, thick-enamelled grinding molars, a robust jaw, a precision grip and an upright trunk.
  • Phase II, meat-eating: hunting and tool use were added later in the line leading to Homo, while the robust australopithecines kept the seed-eating specialisation.
  • Against the hunting hypothesis: canine reduction was explained by the need for side-to-side grinding, not by tools replacing teeth as weapons, as Darwin (1871) and later Washburn had suggested.

2. Indian relevance: Ramapithecus

  • Siwalik fossil: Ramapithecus, named by G. Edward Lewis in 1934 from a Siwalik upper jaw, was treated by Elwyn Simons and David Pilbeam in the 1960s as the earliest hominid because of its thick enamel and small canines; Jolly's model gave it a dietary rationale.
  • Collapse of the claim: fuller Sivapithecus remains from the Potwar Plateau, especially a face described by Pilbeam in 1982, showed orangutan affinities; Ramapithecus was merged into Sivapithecus, and molecular dating (Sarich and Wilson, 1967) had already placed the human–ape split much later.

3. Evaluation

  • Weaknesses: geladas mainly eat grass blades rather than seeds; early hominins such as Ardipithecus ramidus (4.4 mya) lived in woodland, and dental microwear shows mixed diets, not a single grassland niche.
  • Partial support: carbon isotopes show that Paranthropus boisei ate mostly C4 grasses and sedges (Cerling and colleagues, 2011), echoing Jolly's view of the robust line.
  • Rival models: the gathering hypothesis of Tanner and Zihlman (1976) and Owen Lovejoy's food-sharing model (1981) offered other routes to bipedalism.

The Seed Eaters Model is now seen as heuristic: wrong about Ramapithecus, but lasting in its insight that diet and ecology shape teeth, hands and posture, an idea that isotope and microwear studies still test.
free.upa-2026-an2-1c:
Jatra Oraon (1914)Kurukh DharamGandhian non-cooperationRevitalisation movement

The Tana Bhagat movement began among the Oraons of Chotanagpur in 1914, when Jatra Oraon (Jatra Bhagat), a young man of the present Gumla district, announced a message from Dharmes, the supreme Oraon deity. It joined religious purification with protest against landlords, moneylenders and colonial demands, and fits Anthony Wallace's idea of a revitalisation movement.

1. Causes

  • Agrarian distress: loss of land to non-tribal landlords (dikus), rising rents, forced unpaid labour (begari) and debt.
  • Cultural crisis: costly sacrifices to spirits and dependence on exorcists, along with pressure from missionaries and Hindu reformers, unsettled the Oraon world.
  • Example of Birsa: the memory of Birsa Munda's ulgulan (1899–1900) offered a model of prophet-led resistance.

2. Features and phases

  • Purification: followers gave up liquor, meat, animal sacrifice and belief in ghosts and witchcraft, worshipping Dharmes through devotion; the word tana ("to pull") recurs in their hymns.
  • Economic defiance: Jatra told Oraons to stop ploughing landlords' fields and working for outsiders and to withhold rent; he was jailed in 1914 and released in 1915, after which others led the movement.
  • Gandhian phase: from 1919–21 the Tana Bhagats joined non-cooperation, wore khadi and Gandhi caps, took vows in Gandhi's name and carried the Congress flag; many lost land by refusing rent.

3. Interpretation and legacy

  • Anthropological readings: S.C. Roy (Oraon Religion and Customs, 1928) treated it as a religious answer to economic hardship; Sangeeta Dasgupta (1999) shows how it reordered Oraon society by challenging the authority of the pahan (priest) and mahto (headman).
  • Sanskritisation or self-rule? Vegetarianism, the sacred thread and purity rules resemble Sanskritisation, but the aim was a reformed Kurukh dharam and freedom from oppression, not a place in the caste order.
  • Legacy: the Ranchi District Tana Bhagat Raiyats' Agricultural Lands Restoration Act, 1947 returned land lost by followers; Tana Bhagats, in white khadi, still live in Gumla, Lohardaga and Ranchi districts and marked the movement's centenary in 2014.

The movement shows tribal protest moving from millenarian revival to nationalist politics; its non-violent, reformist character makes it a distinctive chapter of Jharkhand's Adivasi history.
free.upa-2026-an2-1d:
PVTGAndamanese and ShompenANPATR 1956Protection with consent

Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), identified as Primitive Tribal Groups from 1975 and renamed in 2006, are the most vulnerable Scheduled Tribes, marked by pre-agricultural technology, very low literacy and a stagnant or declining population. Of India's 75 PVTGs, five live in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands: the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese of the Andamans and the Shompen of Great Nicobar.

1. Ethnographic profile

  • Ancient lineages: genetic work on the Onge and Great Andamanese (Thangaraj and colleagues, 2005) shows very old, distinct maternal lineages from an early dispersal out of Africa.
  • Classic studies: A.R. Radcliffe-Brown's The Andaman Islanders (1922) described Great Andamanese and Onge society; T.N. Pandit of the Anthropological Survey of India led the first friendly contact with the Sentinelese in 1991.
  • Traditional knowledge: the Onge and Jarawa are reported to have read sea and animal signs and moved to high ground before the 2004 tsunami, suffering few losses.

2. Vulnerabilities

  • Demographic collapse: the Great Andamanese fell from several thousand in the 19th century to a few dozen after colonial contact and epidemics; the last speaker of Bo died in 2010.
  • Contact and disease: measles outbreaks among the Jarawa, poaching, and "human safari" tourism along the Andaman Trunk Road expose them to harm.
  • Development pressure: the Great Nicobar project (port, airport, township and power plant, costing over ₹80,000 crore) diverts about 130 sq km of forest used by the Shompen and Nicobarese; the NGT declined to interfere with its environmental clearance on 16 February 2026, but petitions alleging Forest Rights Act violations are before the Calcutta High Court, which the Supreme Court let proceed in October 2026.

3. Protection

  • Legal shield: the A&N Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation, 1956 creates tribal reserves; a 2012 amendment set a 5-km buffer zone round the Jarawa reserve and penalised "human safari" contact and photography. The Supreme Court ordered the trunk road through the reserve closed in 2002, yet it still carries regulated traffic.
  • Policies: the Jarawa Policy (2004) and Shompen Policy (2015) favour minimal, need-based intervention; for the Sentinelese the rule is "eyes on, hands off".
  • Inclusion: seven Shompen voted for the first time in the 2024 Lok Sabha election.

Island PVTGs show that survival depends on consent-based, culturally sensitive development: Nehru's principle that tribes should develop "along the lines of their own genius" is most urgent here.
free.upa-2026-an2-1e:
K.S. SinghBirsa Munda movementTypology of tribal movementsAnthropo-historical method

Kumar Suresh Singh (1935–2006), a historian by training, an IAS officer in Bihar and later Director-General of the Anthropological Survey of India, joined archival history with fieldwork and folklore. His The Dust-Storm and the Hanging Mist (1966), on Birsa Munda's movement in Chotanagpur (1874–1901), made him India's leading interpreter of tribal movements.

1. Study of the Birsa Munda movement

  • Method: he combined colonial records with Munda songs, oral memory and long fieldwork, an anthropo-historical approach later set out in Tribal Society in India (1985).
  • Interpretation: the ulgulan (1899–1900) was both millenarian and agrarian: the breakdown of khuntkatti (clan-founders' joint land rights) under landlords and colonial law drove Birsa, hailed as Dharti Aaba, to preach a new faith and a Munda Raj.
  • Fuller account: a later book, Birsa Munda and His Movement (1983), also traced how the earlier Sardari larai, a long land agitation, fed into Birsa's revolt.

2. Typology and phases

  • Edited volumes: Tribal Movements in India (2 vols, 1982–83) brought together case studies from all regions and set the categories above.

3. Key insights

  • Dual character: because tribes are both ethnic communities and peasants, their movements mix identity goals with land and forest grievances; in middle India they were mainly agrarian and forest-based, in the north-east mainly political.
  • Beyond rebellion: he saw reform and Sanskritising movements, and later language and script campaigns, as part of the same search for dignity and power.
  • Broader work: the People of India project, which he led from 1985, profiled about 4,600 communities and their changing identities.
  • Limitations: critics note that his categories overlap, since a single movement may be agrarian, religious and political at once, and that the People of India drew on colonial categories.

Singh turned tribal movements from a list of uprisings into a field of structured analysis, and his blend of history and anthropology remains the model for studying Adivasi assertion today.
free.upa-2026-an2-2a:
JajmaniReciprocity vs exploitationRitual vs material basisPatron–client ties

Jajmani denotes hereditary, non-market exchange in which patron households (jajman, usually landholders) receive economic and ritual services from service castes (kamin or praja), who are paid mainly in grain at harvest and in gifts at festivals and life-cycle rites. William Wiser gave the term its sociological meaning in The Hindu Jajmani System (1936), based on Karimpur in Uttar Pradesh. Since then its nature, basis and very existence have been debated.

1. Integrative or exploitative?

  • Reciprocity view: Wiser stressed mutual service, with each caste both serving and being served; Pauline Kolenda (1963) modelled it as a functional system that gave security and shared risk.
  • Exploitation view: Oscar Lewis and Victor Barnouw (1956), in Rani Khera near Delhi, and Thomas Beidelman (1959) argued that it rested on landholders' power; Beidelman called it feudal.
  • View from below: Joan Mencher (1974) showed that untouchable labourers in Tamil Nadu experienced it as coercion, not harmony.
  • Patronage turning into exploitation: Jan Breman (Patronage and Exploitation, 1974) traced how the hali tie in south Gujarat lost its protective side as markets expanded.

2. Ritual order or material power?

  • Ritual basis: Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966) read jajmani as an expression of the hierarchy of pure and impure: priests, barbers and washermen remove pollution, and grain shares follow religious values rather than market logic; Harold Gould ("The Hindu Jajmani System", 1958) likewise traced the ties to the divide between pure and impure castes rather than rich and poor.
  • Material basis: Beidelman and later critics placed land, grain and power at the core, with ritual service only a part.
  • Centrality, not only hierarchy: Gloria Goodwin Raheja (The Poison in the Gift, 1988) found in Pahansu (western UP) that the dominant Gujar landholders stood at the centre of gift-giving, passing inauspiciousness to Brahmins and service castes through dan.

3. Was it ever a "system"?

  • Fuller's critique: C.J. Fuller ("Misconceiving the Grain Heap", 1989) argued that harvest shares, ritual fees and customary dues were wrongly fused into a single pan-Indian system by anthropologists.
  • Historical contingency: Simon Commander (1983) showed that its form in north India varied with labour supply and agrarian conditions over two centuries; regional forms such as Maharashtra's balutedari differ in detail.

4. Decline or persistence?

  • Erosion: cash crops, factory goods, mechanisation, education, migration and Dalit assertion turned most ties into wage contracts; T. Scarlett Epstein (1962) found older ties surviving longer in irrigated Wangala than in diversified Dalena.
  • Residues: barbers, priests and drummers still serve at weddings and funerals for customary payments.

The debates show that jajmani is best seen not as a timeless harmony but as a changing bundle of patron–client relations, shaped by ritual values and material power alike; its study remains a key test of theories of caste.
free.upa-2026-an2-2b:
DAJGUASaturation approachSustainable Development GoalsConvergence

Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DAJGUA), approved by the Union Cabinet on 18 September 2024 (as the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Unnat Gram Abhiyan) and launched at Hazaribagh on 2 October 2024, is named after Birsa Munda, "Dharti Aaba". With an outlay of ₹79,156 crore over five years, it seeks saturation of basic services in about 63,000 tribal villages through 25 interventions of 17 ministries, which maps it closely onto the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

1. Design of the Abhiyan

  • Coverage: villages of 500 or more people, at least half of them tribal, and villages in aspirational districts with 50 or more tribal people; 549 districts in 30 States/UTs and over 5 crore tribal people.
  • Funding and convergence: the Centre bears ₹56,333 crore and the States ₹22,823 crore, routed through the Development Action Plan for Scheduled Tribes; villages are mapped on the PM Gati Shakti portal and the best districts are rewarded.
  • People and governance: the Adi Karmayogi programme (2025) aims to train about 20 lakh grassroots functionaries and village change leaders for responsive, participatory delivery.

2. Links with the SDGs

3. Strengths: why it can advance the SDGs

  • Leaving no one behind: STs lag on most indicators (literacy 58.96% against 72.98% nationally, Census 2011); an area-based, multi-sector approach attacks several deprivations together.
  • Rights with services: support for Forest Rights Act claims and community forest management links livelihoods to ecology (SDGs 13 and 15).
  • Builds on experience: it extends the saturation model of PM-JANMAN (2023) for PVTGs to all tribal villages.

4. Gaps and concerns

  • Assets versus outcomes: buildings and connections do not by themselves raise learning, nutrition or health; staff shortages in tribal areas persist.
  • Slow delivery: the sister mission PM-JANMAN shows the risk: by December 2025 only 8 of 500 sanctioned hostels and about 1,200 of some 8,000 km of roads were complete (PIB).
  • Participation: plans must be made by gram sabhas under PESA 1996 and in tribal languages, or the scheme becomes top-down.
  • Land and displacement: as the Xaxa Committee (2014) warned, loss of land to projects and mining can erase welfare gains.
  • Data: SDG monitoring rarely disaggregates by tribe, making progress hard to judge.

DAJGUA can deliver on SDGs 1–4, 6–9 and 15 for tribal India if it is driven by gram sabhas and backed by secure land and forest rights; Nehru's warning not to overwhelm tribal areas "with multiplicity of schemes" is a useful guide.
free.upa-2026-an2-2c:
Rabi and kharif cropsZebu cattleLogo-syllabic scriptUndeciphered

The Indus (Harappan) Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) stood on a mixed farming and herding economy whose roots go back to Mehrgarh (from c. 7000 BCE) in Balochistan. Evidence comes from charred seeds, phytoliths, starch and fat residues, animal bones, seals and terracottas. Its script, found on seals and tablets, remains undeciphered.

1. Evidence of crops

  • Winter (rabi) staples: wheat and hulled barley, with lentil, pea and chickpea; both cereals were grown at Mehrgarh in the Neolithic.
  • Summer (kharif) crops: millets at Rojdi and other Gujarat sites, and rice husks at Lothal and Rangpur; Cameron Petrie and Jennifer Bates (2017) argue that Harappans practised multi-cropping suited to varied rainfall.
  • Fibre, oil and fruit: cotton (cloth traces at Mohenjo-daro, earlier fibres at Mehrgarh), sesame, linseed, mustard, dates and ber.
  • Field and cooking evidence: a furrowed field at Kalibangan, a terracotta plough model from Banawali, large storehouses at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro (the "granary" label is debated), and starch grains of ginger and turmeric at Farmana (Kashyap and Weber, 2010).

2. Evidence of domesticated animals

  • Zebu cattle: humped cattle, domesticated locally by the Mehrgarh period, dominate bone collections; the humped bull is a favourite seal motif, and terracotta carts show draught use.
  • Other animals: water buffalo, sheep, goat, pig, dog and donkey; camel bones at Kalibangan; elephants on seals.
  • Dairying: fat residues in pots at Kotada Bhadli in Gujarat point to milk processing around 2500 BCE (Chakraborty and colleagues, 2020).
  • Horse debate: Sándor Bökönyi identified true horse bones at Surkotada, but Richard Meadow and Ajita Patel disagreed; horses are absent from seals.

3. Nature of the Indus script

  • Corpus: a few thousand inscribed objects with about 400 signs; texts are short, around five signs on average; the ten large signs of the Dholavira signboard are the biggest known.
  • Direction and type: B.B. Lal (1966) showed from overlapping strokes that it ran right to left; the sign count suggests a logo-syllabic script, with word signs and sound signs.
  • Why undeciphered: no bilingual inscription, short texts and an unknown language.

4. Views of scholars

  • Current status: no reading is accepted; in January 2025 the Tamil Nadu government announced a prize of US$1 million for a verified decipherment.

The crop and animal record shows a diversified, risk-spreading agro-pastoral economy whose zebu-and-grain base still underlies South Asian farming; the script awaits a bilingual find or a much larger corpus.
free.upa-2026-an2-3a:
F.G. BaileyEconomic frontierCaste mobilityTribe–caste continuum

F.G. Bailey, trained in Max Gluckman's Manchester school, worked in the early 1950s in Bisipara, an Oriya village set among Kond villages in the Kondmals (now Kandhamal district) of Odisha. His Caste and the Economic Frontier (1957), followed by Tribe, Caste and Nation (1960) and Politics and Social Change: Orissa in 1959 (1963), showed how a mercantile economy and the modern state remade caste ranks.

1. The study and its findings

  • A frontier village: Bisipara's castes (dominant landowning Warriors, Brahmins, Distillers, service castes and Pan untouchables) lived in Kond country, opened by British annexation in the mid-19th century to officials and traders.
  • The economic frontier: land became saleable, and new wealth from trade, liquor and government jobs lay outside the old land-based order; Warriors sold land to meet new needs.
  • Mobility accepted: the Boad and Ganjam Distillers grew rich under the government's liquor-sale policy and, by the time prohibition came in 1910, held much of the land the Warriors once owned; they then Sanskritised their customs and were accepted as clean, having used wealth in the old idiom of land and ritual.
  • Mobility resisted: the Pans (Bailey's "Boad Outcastes"), enriched by trade in hides and backed by laws against untouchability, claimed higher rank; clean castes and even other untouchables opposed them, so they turned to officials, courts and politics beyond the village.

2. Salience: contributions

  • Economy drives caste mobility: wealth must be turned into land and ritual style before rank changes, which adds an economic base to M.N. Srinivas's ideas of Sanskritisation and the dominant caste.
  • Village not an isolate: against Charles Metcalfe's "little republics" (1830), Bailey set the village within linked arenas of market, administration and state politics.
  • Two kinds of change: the system absorbed the Distillers (change within the structure) but not the Pans, whose demand challenged its principle (structural change).
  • Tribe–caste continuum: comparing Oriyas and Konds, he treated tribe and caste as poles of one continuum, measured by the share of people with direct access to land ("'Tribe' and 'Caste' in India", 1961).
  • Political anthropology: his work on brokers and factions grew into transactionalism (Stratagems and Spoils, 1969).

3. Criticisms

  • Ideology neglected: Louis Dumont and David Pocock argued in Contributions to Indian Sociology that village studies under-rated the all-India values of purity and hierarchy; Bailey's reply, "For a Sociology of India?" (1959), defended field-based study of interests and power.
  • Economic bias: reading status through land and money slights belief and meaning.
  • Continuum questioned: one criterion cannot define a tribe; André Béteille (1986) showed how tribe and caste overlap in Indian history.
  • Narrow base: one frontier village is thin ground for generalisation; his actors appear as calculating individuals.

4. Contemporary relevance

  • Kandhamal: Pan–Kond tensions over land, ST status and conversion, rooted in the relations Bailey described, erupted in the Kandhamal violence of 2007–08.

Bailey's Bisipara remains salient because it showed caste as dynamic and negotiated, tied to land, market and state; his questions still guide studies of caste, tribe and local politics.
free.upa-2026-an2-3b:
Gossner Mission (1845)Lievens and HoffmannSarna–Christian divideEducation and assertion

Organised missions reached Chotanagpur when four German Lutheran missionaries of the Gossner Mission arrived at Ranchi in 1845; Anglican work followed from 1869 and the Catholic mission with the Belgian Jesuit Constant Lievens in 1885. Conversion spread mainly among the Oraon, Munda and Kharia. In Census 2011 Christians formed 4.3% of Jharkhand's population and about 15.5% of its Scheduled Tribes.

1. Why conversion spread

  • Land and law: Lievens helped tribal tenants fight landlords in the courts in the 1880s, and the Jesuit John Baptist Hoffmann helped draft the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908, which recognised khuntkatti land rights.
  • Relief from debt: Hoffmann's Catholic cooperative credit society (1909) freed members from moneylenders; famine relief and schooling drew others.
  • Escape from costly rites: Christianity, like the Tana Bhagat movement, offered release from expensive sacrifices to spirits.

2. Positive impacts

  • Education and health: mission schools, colleges such as St Xavier's College, Ranchi (1944), and hospitals reached remote villages; Christian Adivasis gained early access to jobs and professions.
  • Language and literature: Hoffmann's Mundari grammar (1903) and Encyclopaedia Mundarica, Ferdinand Hahn's Kurukh grammar and Bible translations brought tribal languages into print.
  • Political leadership: educated Christians led the Chotanagpur Unnati Samaj, which asked the Simon Commission (1928) for a separate province; Jaipal Singh Munda, schooled at St Paul's mission school in Ranchi and at Oxford, became president of the Adivasi Mahasabha (formed 1938) in 1939 and later founded the Jharkhand Party, laying the base of the Jharkhand movement.
  • Sport: the hockey tradition of Simdega and Khunti grew from mission schools.

3. Cultural change and tensions

  • Culture change: converts left sacrifice, rice beer and the village priest's rites, and dormitories such as the dhumkuria declined; yet clan exogamy, language and dance largely survived, and Catholic inculturation uses drums and tribal music in worship; K.N. Sahay (Under the Shadow of the Cross, 1976) and Sachchidananda (Culture Change in Tribal Bihar, 1964) recorded this selective change.
  • Resistance in history: Birsa Munda, once a pupil of the Lutheran school at Chaibasa, broke away, and his movement opposed missionaries as well as landlords.
  • Sarna–Christian divide: splits within tribes and villages fuel the "delisting" demand, first raised by Kartik Oraon in the late 1960s and revived by the Janjati Suraksha Manch, to remove converts from the ST list; Christians reply that ST status rests on community, not religion.
  • State response: the Jharkhand Freedom of Religion Act, 2017 regulates conversion, and in 2020 the Assembly sought a separate Sarna religion code in the census.

Christianity gave many Adivasis of Jharkhand education, legal protection and political voice, strengthening tribal identity, but it also created a religious cleavage that shapes today's debates on identity, census codes and ST status.
free.upa-2026-an2-3c:
EthnoarchaeologyGeneral comparative analogyDirect historical approachTesting analogies

Ethnoarchaeology studies living communities to learn how material remains are made, used and discarded, so that the archaeological record can be read. Its inferences rest on analogy. A general comparative analogy draws parallels from societies with similar environment, technology and economy, without assuming historical links; it differs from the direct historical approach (Julian Steward, 1942), which projects back from descendants living in the same region.

1. The method

  • Cross-cultural regularities: forager group size, seasonal mobility, camp layout and the roles of men and women recur across continents and can be used as models.
  • Choosing analogues: Robert Ascher (1961) advised selecting societies with similar environment and subsistence; Lewis Binford's Nunamiut Ethnoarchaeology (1978) showed how observed behaviour leaves patterned traces, the basis of middle-range theory.

2. Indian examples

  • Acheulian settlement (Hunsgi valley, Karnataka): K. Paddayya (The Acheulian Culture of the Hunsgi Valley, 1982) used ethnographic accounts of hunter-gatherers to model Acheulian sites as seasonal camps tied to water and food.
  • Foraging ecosystems (Andhra Pradesh): M.L.K. Murty (1981, 1985) studied how Yanadi and Chenchu groups forage, make tools and choose shelters, building a model for Palaeolithic and Mesolithic sites of the south-east coast and the Kurnool caves.
  • Mesolithic camps: Malti Nagar and V.N. Misra (1990) observed the Kanjars, a mobile hunting-gathering community of the Ganga valley, as a guide to camp size, hearths and food remains at the region's Mesolithic sites.
  • Neolithic ash mounds: F.R. Allchin (Neolithic Cattle-Keepers of South India, 1963) explained the Deccan ash mounds (Utnur, Kupgal) as burnt dung of seasonal cattle pens, drawing on present-day herders' camps and suggesting a ritual, perhaps purificatory, side to the burning; later excavations confirmed burnt dung.
  • Megaliths and rock art: living menhir and memorial-stone traditions of the Khasi, Munda, Ho and the Maria Gonds of Bastar are used to suggest how Iron Age megaliths of the peninsula were raised and used, and present tribal life helps read hunting and honey-gathering scenes in the Bhimbetka paintings (Yashodhar Mathpal, 1984).

3. Limitations

  • Not living fossils: Indian foragers have long traded forest produce with farmers; Richard Fox (1969) called them "professional primitives", so their behaviour reflects contact with states and markets.
  • Tyranny of the record: Martin Wobst (1978) warned that past societies may have had forms with no modern parallel.
  • Equifinality: different activities can leave similar remains, so analogies must be tested; Alison Wylie (1985) argued for relational analogies based on causal links.
  • Ethics: using living tribes as proxies for the past can stigmatise them as "primitive".

In India, general comparative analogy has enriched the study of Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic life; joined with the direct historical approach and scientific tests, it turns India's living diversity of foragers, herders and artisans into a laboratory for the past.
free.upa-2026-an2-4a:
Verrier ElwinTribal PanchsheelNEFA philosophyIntegration without assimilation

Verrier Elwin (1902–1964), an Oxford-educated churchman who came to India in 1927 and became the ethnographer of the Gonds, Baigas, Murias, Bondos and Saoras, was the most influential voice in shaping post-independence tribal policy. As Adviser for Tribal Affairs in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA) from 1954 and a confidant of Jawaharlal Nehru, he gave shape to the Tribal Panchsheel.

1. From protection to integration

  • Ethnographic base: The Baiga (1939), The Muria and Their Ghotul (1947), Bondo Highlander (1950) and The Religion of an Indian Tribe (1955) recorded land loss, forest restrictions and cultural decline.
  • The "national park" idea: in The Baiga and The Aboriginals (1943) he proposed temporary protection of the most vulnerable groups in reserved areas under a tribes commissioner; he later admitted the label was badly chosen.
  • Ghurye's critique: G.S. Ghurye (The Aborigines—"So-called"—and Their Future, 1943) attacked him as an isolationist and called tribes "backward Hindus".
  • Middle path: after Independence Elwin argued for integration without assimilation, rejecting both isolation and forced absorption.

2. Contribution to policy

  • Tribal Panchsheel: Nehru's five principles, set out in his foreword (1958) to the second edition of Elwin's A Philosophy for NEFA (1957), became the charter of tribal policy.
  • NEFA approach: protection of land and forests, use of local languages, gradual change through institutions such as the Adi village council (kebang), training of local officials, and limits on outsiders under the Inner Line.
  • Elwin Committee (1959–60): his Home Ministry committee on the Special Multipurpose Tribal Blocks urged slower, people-centred programmes and trained staff; the Tribal Development Block approach of the Third Plan followed.
  • Recognition: he took Indian citizenship in 1954 and received the Padma Bhushan in 1961.

3. Evaluation

  • Strengths: his respect for tribal culture, land and self-governance is echoed in Article 371A, PESA 1996 and the Forest Rights Act 2006, and protective rules helped the north-east keep its land base.
  • Criticisms: nationalists saw him as a romantic who wanted tribes as museum pieces; after the 1962 war, NEFA's slow development was blamed on his caution; Rammanohar Lohia attacked his non-interventionist approach.
  • Balanced view: Ramachandra Guha's biography Savaging the Civilized (1999) presents him as a humanist whose ideas changed with experience.

Elwin moved Indian tribal policy from isolation versus assimilation to integration with dignity; his Panchsheel still offers a test for schemes, mining and displacement in tribal India.
free.upa-2026-an2-4b:
Racial typologySomatometry and somatoscopyClinal variationPopulation genetics

From the 1901 Census, scholars tried to sort India's people into "races" using somatometric traits (measured: stature, cephalic and nasal indices) and somatoscopic traits (observed: skin colour, hair form, eye fold, nose shape). H.H. Risley, B.S. Guha, S.S. Sarkar and others produced very different schemes, and none gave a shared picture of India's population diversity.

1. The main classifications

2. Why they failed to agree

  • Continuous variation: traits change gradually across space, so any boundary is arbitrary; as Frank Livingstone (1962) put it, "there are no races, there are only clines".
  • Non-concordance of traits: stature, head form, nasal index and skin colour vary independently, so each trait yields a different map and the result depends on the trait chosen.
  • Subjective observation: grading skin colour, hair or nose shape by eye differed between observers, and small convenience samples were treated as typical of whole castes and tribes.
  • Plasticity: Franz Boas (1912) showed that head form changed in the children of immigrants to the United States; nutrition and climate also shape stature and nasal index, so these are not fixed racial markers.
  • Race confused with language and caste: "Aryan" and "Dravidian" are language labels; Risley even claimed that "the social position of a caste varies inversely as its nasal index", turning colonial census ranking into biology, a link criticised by Nicholas Dirks (Castes of Mind, 2001).
  • Admixture with endogamy: long migration and mixing, followed by strict endogamy, produced a mosaic that fits no set of discrete types; disputed elements such as Guha's mainland "Negrito" showed how fragile the categories were.

3. What replaced the typologies

  • New concepts: the UNESCO statements on race (1950, 1951) and Richard Lewontin's finding (1972) that about 85% of human genetic variation lies within populations ended typological thinking.
  • Genetic evidence: David Reich and colleagues (2009, Nature) showed that most Indian groups descend from a mixture of Ancestral North Indians and Ancestral South Indians in varying proportions, with strong founder effects from endogamy; ancient DNA, including the Rakhigarhi genome (2019), refined this.
  • GenomeIndia: whole genomes of 10,000 people from 99 communities, released in January 2025, now map diversity for medicine and history.

The older schemes failed because human variation is continuous, multi-causal and shaped by history and environment; modern anthropology studies populations and clines, while anthropometry remains useful for growth, nutrition and forensic work.
free.upa-2026-an2-4c:
NiyamgiriDongria KondhGram sabha consentForest Rights Act

The Niyamgiri hills of Rayagada and Kalahandi districts in Odisha are home to the Dongria Kondh, a PVTG of hill horticulturists who revere the mountain as Niyam Raja, their law-giver and provider. A plan to mine bauxite there for Vedanta's alumina refinery at Lanjigarh provoked a decade-long movement that ended in what is often called India's first environmental referendum (2013).

1. Achievements

  • Rights-based victory: in Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment and Forests (2013) the Supreme Court held that the Forest Rights Act protects religious and cultural rights, including worship of the hill, and that gram sabhas must decide on them, a landmark for consent.
  • Sacred ecology: the Dongria tied the hill's streams, forests and orchards to their deity, a case of what L.P. Vidyarthi called the nature–man–spirit complex, so identity and environment became one argument; this resonates with ILO and UN norms on indigenous peoples.
  • Organisation and alliances: the Niyamgiri Suraksha Samiti, led by Dongria such as Lado Sikaka, and strong women's participation drew support from lawyers, activists and international campaigns; Norway's pension fund (2007) and the Church of England (2010) sold their Vedanta holdings. Felix Padel and Samarendra Das (Out of This Earth, 2010) set the struggle within the aluminium industry's record of displacement in Odisha.
  • Wider influence: the verdict strengthened the FRA and PESA consent norms that communities now invoke in other mining and forest disputes, showing that a small PVTG can shape national law.

2. Limitations: a critical appraisal

  • Narrow consultation: the state selected only 12 villages for the gram sabhas, leaving out many others that use the hills, and the judgment covered the mining lease, not the refinery and its red-mud waste.
  • Pressure continues: the refinery runs on bauxite from elsewhere, and the nearby Sijimali bauxite project faces fresh protests; in September 2026 Vedanta announced a ₹1 lakh crore Odisha investment plan that includes reviving Niyamgiri mining, which local tribal communities vowed to resist.
  • Criminalisation: activists have faced arrests and have been branded as Maoist sympathisers, which weakens peaceful protest.
  • Development deficit: saying no to mining did not bring better schools, health care or fair markets; the Dongria still need PVTG-sensitive development under schemes such as PM-JANMAN.
  • Romantic framing: media portrayals of a pristine tribe defending its "Avatar" mountain hid internal debates and the community's own aspirations.

Niyamgiri shows that sacred geography and legal consent can stop extraction, but lasting justice needs full FRA and PESA implementation and Dongria-led development, all the more as India's push for critical minerals intensifies.
free.upa-2026-an2-5a:
Vajrayana and TheravadaGompaHimalayan and North-East tribesSyncretism

Buddhism faded from the plains after about the 12th century, but it survives among tribal communities along the Himalayan and north-eastern frontier. Two streams reached them: Tibetan (Vajrayana) Buddhism, from Tibet and Bhutan into Ladakh, Lahaul-Spiti, Sikkim and western Arunachal Pradesh, and Theravada Buddhism, from Myanmar and the Chittagong hills into eastern Arunachal, Mizoram and Tripura. In both, Buddhism has blended with older nature and ancestor cults.

1. Distribution and major tribes

  • Western Himalaya: the Bot (Boto), the Changpa herders of the Changthang plateau and the Brokpa of Ladakh; the Bhot of Lahaul-Spiti and Buddhist sections of the Kinnaura in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Eastern Himalaya: the Bhutia, Lepcha, Sherpa and Tamang of Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills; the Monpa, Sherdukpen, Memba and Khamba of Arunachal Pradesh.
  • North-East (Theravada): the Khamti and Singpho of eastern Arunachal, the Chakma of Mizoram, Tripura and Arunachal, and the Marma (Mog) of Tripura.
  • Numbers: in Census 2011 Buddhists formed about 27% of Sikkim's and 12% of Arunachal Pradesh's population, largely from these communities.

2. Socio-religious features

  • Monastery at the centre: the gompa is the ritual, educational and social centre of village life. Tawang monastery (1680–81) anchors Monpa society, and families traditionally gave a son to the monastic order.
  • Festivals: Losar (Tibetan New Year) and Torgya among the Monpa, Losoong among the Bhutia, Hemis Tsechu in Ladakh, Sangken (a water festival) among the Khamti and Bizu among the Chakma.
  • Learning and script: monasteries kept alive the Tibetan (Bhoti) script and texts; the Khamti write in a Tai script of their own.
  • Family: fraternal polyandry, once linked to scarce land in Ladakh, Spiti and Kinnaur, has largely given way to monogamy.

3. Syncretism and change

  • Layered religion: Geoffrey Gorer's Himalayan Village (1938) showed the Lepcha turning both to lamas and to their own shamans (mun and bongthing). The Brokpa and Sherdukpen likewise keep pre-Buddhist deities beside Buddhist rites.
  • Identity and politics: Buddhism underpins ethnic identity, as in the Chakma Autonomous District Council in Mizoram under the Sixth Schedule.
  • New pressures: schooling, tourism, migration and border development are changing monastic roles, while the citizenship question of Chakma settlers in Arunachal remains contentious.

In Buddhist tribes a world religion has been "tribalised" and tribal culture "Buddhicised" at the same time: the lama and the shaman coexist. Their monasteries make them custodians of Himalayan heritage, while development and border politics now test this syncretic identity.
free.upa-2026-an2-5b:
Hathnora calvariumHomo erectus narmadensisArchaic Homo sapiensMiddle Pleistocene Homo

Narmada Man (now often called the Narmada hominin) is still India's only Pleistocene hominin cranium: a partial skull-cap (calvarium) found by Arun Sonakia of the Geological Survey of India on 5 December 1982 at Hathnora, Sehore district, Madhya Pradesh. It lay in the boulder conglomerate of the Narmada with Acheulian tools and fossils of Stegodon, horse, pig and bovids. Its place in human evolution has been debated ever since.

1. The rival classifications

  • Homo erectus narmadensis (Sonakia, 1984): the thick vault, strong brow ridge (supraorbital torus), broad low skull and small mastoid processes resembled Asian Homo erectus; the Acheulian context suggested an age of 0.5–0.6 million years. De Lumley and Sonakia (1985) called it an "evolved" Homo erectus.
  • Archaic Homo sapiens (Kenneth A.R. Kennedy and colleagues, 1991): the cranial capacity, about 1,200 cc by Sonakia's estimate and 1,155–1,421 cc in Kennedy's later estimate, is well above the Asian Homo erectus average of about 1,000 cc; with a fuller vault, it placed the skull with early sapiens-like forms.
  • Homo heidelbergensis-like (Cameron, Patnaik and Sahni, 2004; Sheela Athreya, 2007): a cladistic study linked it most closely to the Steinheim skull of Germany; Athreya excluded Homo erectus and grouped it with "Middle Pleistocene Homo". Anek Sankhyan, who later found two clavicles and a rib at the site, also came to favour heidelbergensis affinities and inferred a short, sturdy body.

2. Why the debate persists

  • Uncertain age: estimates fall from 0.5–0.6 million years (Sonakia, from fauna) to a tentative minimum of about 236,000 years (uranium-series dating of associated bovid bones, 2004) and to electron spin resonance dates by Patnaik and others (2009) giving a minimum of about 49,000 years, with other model ages near 160,000 years. The skull lay in reworked gravels, so no date is direct.
  • One incomplete specimen: there is no face, jaw or teeth, and the cranium shows a mosaic of archaic and derived traits; even its sex was revised from male to probably female.
  • Shifting taxonomy: the status of Homo heidelbergensis itself is disputed, so the label changes with the framework used.

Most specialists now reject a simple Homo erectus label and treat Narmada as an archaic Middle Pleistocene Homo with heidelbergensis-like features. Direct dating and new finds from the Narmada valley are needed to settle its phylogenetic position and its link with India's Acheulian and Middle Palaeolithic cultures.

Article 371AThirteenth Amendment, 1962Naga customary law16-Point Agreement

Article 371A, inserted by the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1962, gives Nagaland a special constitutional status. It grew out of the 16-Point Agreement (1960) between the Naga People's Convention and the Government of India, which led to statehood on 1 December 1963. For anthropology it is a constitutional guarantee of Naga customary institutions and of community control over land.

1. Main clauses

  • Legislative shield, clause 1(a): no Act of Parliament on (i) the religious or social practices of the Nagas, (ii) Naga customary law and procedure, (iii) civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, or (iv) ownership and transfer of land and its resources applies to Nagaland unless the Legislative Assembly so decides by a resolution.
  • Governor's special responsibility, clause 1(b): for law and order while internal disturbances continued, exercised in his individual judgement after consulting the Council of Ministers.
  • Tuensang district: a regional council of 35 members and, for the first ten years, special arrangements for its administration, funds and representation in the State ministry.

2. Anthropological significance

  • Living customary law: village councils and customary courts work with constitutional backing; the Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978 builds on them, and the Communitisation Act, 2002 hands schools and health centres to village communities.
  • Land and resources: most land is owned by clans, villages and individuals rather than the State, so central laws on land, forests or minerals depend on the Assembly's consent. In September 2023 the Assembly resolved to seek exemption from a Uniform Civil Code, invoking Article 371A.
  • Plural legal order: it embodies the policy of integration without assimilation associated with Nehru and Verrier Elwin.

3. Tensions

  • Custom versus gender equality: the 33% reservation for women in urban local bodies was opposed as a violation of customary law; Part IX on panchayats does not apply to Nagaland (Article 243M), but Part IXA on municipalities does. After Supreme Court pressure the quota was kept and elections were held in 2024.
  • Political settlement: Naga peace talks since the Framework Agreement (2015) test how far special status can be widened within the Constitution.

Article 371A is a working model of asymmetric federalism that protects a living tribal legal order. Its future lies in customary institutions evolving from within, especially on women's participation, as the 2024 municipal elections showed.

L.P. VidyarthiMaler (Sauria Paharia)Eco-cosmologyHolistic approach

The Nature-Man-Spirit complex is an analytical framework proposed by L.P. Vidyarthi in The Maler (1963), based on fieldwork among the Maler (Sauria Paharia) of the Rajmahal hills in the Santal Parganas, then in Bihar and now in Jharkhand. It holds that a tribe's physical environment, its social life and its supernatural world form a single interdependent whole, so that none can be understood alone.

1. The three components

  • Nature: the hills, forests, streams and thin soils of the Rajmahal range set the economy: shifting cultivation on the slopes, collection of forest produce and hunting.
  • Man: family, lineage and village with its headman, together with life-cycle rites, socialisation and personality; social units are organised around the use of hill land and forest.
  • Spirit: the Maler recognise benevolent deities called gossaiyan (among them the sun and moon gods), ancestral spirits (jiwe urrkya), malevolent spirits (alchi) and the power of witchcraft (chergani). They dwell in hills, forests and the sky, control rain, crops, health and misfortune, and are approached through sacrifices, priests and diviners.

2. The interconnection

  • Nature shapes the spirit world: spirits are located in particular hills, groves and springs, so sacred geography mirrors the landscape.
  • Spirit regulates nature: rites before clearing a plot, sowing or harvesting, and taboos on certain places, act as a check on the use of resources.
  • Man mediates: household and village rituals restore balance; illness or crop failure is read as a breach between man and spirits to be repaired.
  • One whole: a change in one element, such as loss of forest, unsettles the other two.

3. Significance and critique

  • Method: a holistic, ecological way of studying tribal world view, close to Julian Steward's cultural ecology (Steward wrote the book's foreword) and Robert Redfield's idea of world view; it complements Vidyarthi's Sacred Complex (The Sacred Complex in Hindu Gaya, 1961).
  • Application: it explains why displacement causes cultural as well as economic loss. The Dongria Kondh's defence of Niyamgiri, seat of their deity Niyam Raja, through the gram sabhas of 2013 is a clear instance.
  • Criticism: the model is largely descriptive and functionalist; it presents an equilibrium and underplays history, markets, the State and inequality within the tribe, which later political-ecology studies emphasised.

The Nature-Man-Spirit complex remains a key Indian contribution to ecological anthropology. It reminds planners that, for tribes, land and forest are sacred as well as economic, a view now reflected in community rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

Cochin Tribes and CastesCalcutta department, 1920Ethnographic surveyLectures on Ethnography

L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer (1861–1937) of Palakkad was one of the first Indian scholars to make anthropology a profession. As Superintendent of Ethnography of Cochin State he documented Kerala's communities, and in 1920 he became head of the new Department of Anthropology at the University of Calcutta, the first university department of the subject in India.

1. Ethnographic surveys

  • Cochin: working within the Ethnographic Survey of India launched with the 1901 Census under H.H. Risley, he prepared monographs that became The Cochin Tribes and Castes (two volumes, 1909 and 1912; the second introduced by A.C. Haddon).
  • Range: volume I covered hill tribes such as the Kadar and lower groups such as the Pulaya and Izhava; volume II the Nambudiri Brahmins, Nayars, Christians, Muslims and Jews, so communities were grouped roughly by social rank rather than alphabetically.
  • Mysore: after H.V. Nanjundayya's death he completed the Mysore ethnographic survey, published as The Mysore Tribes and Castes (from 1928).
  • Christians: The Anthropology of the Syrian Christians (1926) was among the first studies of a Christian community in India.

2. Academic and methodological contribution

  • Institution builder: he led postgraduate teaching at Calcutta until his retirement in the early 1930s; his Lectures on Ethnography (1925) was one of the earliest Indian textbooks of the subject.
  • Fieldwork: he met people in their own settings rather than relying only on official returns, and gave special weight to life-cycle rites, kinship and customary law.
  • Photography: his 150-odd photographs in the Cochin volumes show people in everyday, natural settings, unlike the stiff anthropometric "type" pictures of the period.
  • Beyond tribes: by studying literate castes and Christians as well as tribes, he widened anthropology to the whole of Indian society, and he noted how contact with the plains was changing tribal life.
  • Recognition: the title Dewan Bahadur, the French Officier d'Académie and, after retirement, lectures in Florence, Rome, Paris, Berlin and Cambridge; his son L.A. Krishna Iyer carried the work forward in Travancore.

3. Assessment

  • Strengths: his volumes remain reliable baseline data for Kerala and Karnataka communities and brought Indian scholars into world anthropology.
  • Limitations: he worked inside the colonial survey framework; his accounts are descriptive and encyclopaedic, treat each group in isolation and carry some racial ideas of the time.

Ananthakrishna Iyer turned colonial ethnography into an Indian academic discipline. With his Cochin and Mysore volumes and the Calcutta department he, alongside S.C. Roy, laid the foundation of Indian anthropology.

Ox-bow lakesGeometric microlithsSarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha, DamdamaEarly Holocene burials

The Mesolithic marks the early Holocene shift to hunting-gathering with microliths after the last glacial phase. In the middle Ganga plain, which has no natural stone, G.R. Sharma and the University of Allahabad excavated open-air sites beside the ox-bow (horseshoe) lakes of Pratapgarh district, Uttar Pradesh: Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama. They give one of the fullest pictures of Mesolithic life in South Asia.

1. Settlements

  • Lake-side camps: perennial water, fish, turtles, waterfowl and game drew people to the lakes. Thick habitation deposits and many hearths, some plastered at Damdama, show long and repeated stays.
  • Wider basin: Chopani Mando in the Belan valley has huts and, in its last phase, hand-made pottery and wild rice; rock shelters such as Lekhahia add burials and paintings.

2. Artifacts

  • Microliths: geometric lunates, triangles and trapezes with backed bladelets, points and scrapers, of chert, chalcedony, agate and carnelian carried from the Vindhyas about 100 km away, implying mobility or exchange.
  • Bone and antler: arrowheads dominate, with points and knives; ornaments include bone-ring necklaces on two Mahadaha men and an ivory pendant at Damdama.
  • Grinding stones: sandstone querns, mullers, anvils and hammerstones; charred wild grains at Damdama point to plant processing. The plains sites have no pottery.

3. Faunal remains

  • Broad-spectrum diet: wild cattle including gaur, several deer species, wild boar and rhinoceros, with tortoise, fish, birds and rodents.
  • Contested claims: reported sheep, goat and hippopotamus were re-identified; the "hippo" was a rhinoceros, and no domestic animal is proven.

4. Human skeletal remains

  • A large skeletal series: over 90 individuals from the three sites (see table).
  • Burial rites: shallow pits within the settlement, bodies extended and supine, mostly west–east with the head to the west; grave goods of microliths, bone ornaments and animal bones. Double male–female burials occur at Mahadaha and Damdama, a four-person grave at Sarai Nahar Rai and a triple burial at Damdama.
  • Biology: tall, robust people with long, large skulls, strong brow ridges and big teeth; osteoarthritis was common. Dental studies (J.R. Lukacs, J.N. Pal) show heavy wear from a gritty diet.
  • Violence: a microlith lodged in a rib at Sarai Nahar Rai suggests death by an arrow.

5. Critical appraisal

  • Strengths: the earliest Ganga-plain evidence of semi-sedentary life, planned burial and ritual, and a rare biological record of early Holocene foragers, leading into the rice-growing Neolithic of Lahuradewa and Koldihwa.
  • Chronology: dates conflict: Sarai Nahar Rai gave about 10,350 BP, while Mahadaha's early dates (about 4,000–2,900 BP) are too young; Damdama's newer dates are about 8,800 BP.
  • Reports and samples: detailed reports were slow to appear, early faunal identifications were unreliable and plant remains were not systematically sampled.
  • Interpretation: whether these were seasonal camps or year-round settlements is debated; very high stature estimates, even for women, may reflect the formulae used.

These sites show complex foragers living semi-permanently around lakes. Secure dating and full publication would clarify their place in the transition to farming in the Ganga valley.

Political participationPESA, 1996Sixth Schedule councilsElite capture

Since 1950 tribal communities, once governed by their own councils, have been drawn into democratic institutions: universal adult franchise, reserved seats, Panchayati Raj (73rd Amendment, 1992), its extension to Fifth Schedule areas through PESA, 1996 and the Sixth Schedule councils of the North-East. F.G. Bailey's Tribe, Caste and Nation (1960) on the Konds of Odisha was an early study of how tribes learnt to work these new arenas. The impact has been real but uneven.

1. Positive impacts

  • Political voice: reserved constituencies produce tribal MPs, MLAs and Chief Ministers, and in 2022 Droupadi Murmu became the first tribal President. Movements such as the Jharkhand movement used democratic means to win statehood in 2000, the year Chhattisgarh was also created.
  • Grassroots participation: reserved panchayat seats and chair posts, and women's quotas, have brought new leaders, including tribal women, into public life.
  • Gram sabha as a shield: in 2013, after a Supreme Court order, twelve Dongria Kondh palli sabhas rejected bauxite mining in Niyamgiri; Mendha-Lekha in Gadchiroli manages its bamboo forest under community forest rights.
  • Autonomy in the North-East: Sixth Schedule councils such as the Khasi Hills council and the Bodoland Territorial Council (2003) protect land and custom.

2. Negative impacts

  • Erosion of traditional institutions: statutory panchayats overlap with customary councils such as the Santhal manjhi-pargana and Munda manki systems, creating dual authority. The Pathalgadi movement (2017–18) in Khunti asserted gram sabha sovereignty against the State.
  • Elite capture: benefits concentrate among educated and better-off families, and party patronage splits villages into factions.
  • Diluted PESA: states framed rules late (Maharashtra 2014; Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh 2022; Jharkhand only in January 2026), state laws narrow gram sabha powers and consent is bypassed in land acquisition, as the Xaxa Committee (2014) noted.
  • Representation without leverage: in many reserved constituencies non-tribal voters are the majority, so tribal legislators depend on them; Sixth Schedule and customary bodies often exclude women.

3. Anthropological reading

  • Integration and identity: democracy integrates tribes into the nation-state while giving them a platform to assert ethnic identity, as in demands for autonomy in Bodoland and for Sixth Schedule safeguards in Ladakh.
  • Changing leadership: authority moves from hereditary headmen and elders to elected, educated leaders, often younger.

Democracy has turned tribes from objects of administration into citizens with a voice, but the gains are uneven. Strong PESA gram sabhas, recognition of customary councils and checks on elite capture would make tribal participatory democracy real in substance as well as form.
