Sickle cell diseaseHbS (beta-globin mutation)Balanced polymorphismElimination by 2047

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an autosomal recessive blood disorder caused by a single change in the beta-globin gene (HBB): at codon 6, glutamic acid is replaced by valine, producing haemoglobin S (HbS). Under low oxygen HbS polymerises and red cells become rigid and sickle-shaped, causing anaemia, painful crises, infections and organ damage. In India it was first reported by Lehmann and Cutbush (1952) among tribal people of the Nilgiri hills.

1. Prevalence among tribal populations

  • Carrier rates: the sickle trait (HbAS) ranges from about 1% to 40% across tribal groups.
  • The sickle cell belt: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra (especially Vidarbha), southern Gujarat, Odisha and Jharkhand, with pockets in Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, the Nilgiris and Wayanad.
  • High-prevalence groups: Bhil, Madia, Pawara, Pardhan and Otkar in Maharashtra (20–35%); Dhodia, Dubla, Gamit and Naika in Gujarat (13–31%); 18–34% among Wayanad tribes; 10–33% in 27 districts of Madhya Pradesh (2015 review).
  • National picture: by June 2026 the national mission had screened over 7.19 crore people and identified more than 20 lakh carriers and about 2.46 lakh people with the disease.

2. Why it is concentrated among tribes

  • Malaria and balanced polymorphism: carriers resist falciparum malaria (A.C. Allison, 1954), so the gene spread in malarious forest and hill tracts.
  • Endogamy and small populations: tribal endogamy and founder effects raise the chance of two carriers marrying.
  • The Arab-Indian haplotype: high foetal haemoglobin and frequent alpha-thalassaemia make many Indian cases milder than African ones, yet severe disease and child deaths occur where care is distant.
  • Compounding factors: malnutrition, poor access to hospitals and low awareness.

3. Initiatives by the affected states

  • Screening and counselling: school, pre-marital and antenatal screening with genetic counselling, so that carrier couples know their risk.
  • Newborn screening: pilots in Valsad, Nagpur, Raipur and Kalahandi detect affected babies early.
  • Care: free hydroxyurea, folic acid, vaccines and transfusions at district hospitals and medical colleges.

4. National support

  • National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission: launched on 1 July 2023 at Shahdol; it targets about 7 crore people aged 0–40 in 278 districts of 17 states, gives sickle cell status cards and aims to end SCD as a public health problem by 2047.
  • Other measures: blood disorders count as disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and India's indigenous CRISPR gene therapy, BIRSA 101, was launched in November 2025.

5. Gaps

  • Follow-up and drug supply in remote hamlets, fear of stigma in marriage, too few counsellors and the cost of new therapies.

Sickle cell disease is a public health and anthropological problem at once: it follows malaria ecology, endogamy and marriage rules. Counselling that respects kinship norms, delivered through local health workers and gram sabhas, is the key to elimination.

Colonial ethnographyAssam monograph seriesHutton and MillsExcluded Areas

The hill peoples of North-East India were first described systematically by colonial administrators, army officers and missionaries, and their writings remain the foundation of the region's anthropology. The high point was the official monograph series sponsored by the Assam administration, beginning with P.R.T. Gurdon's The Khasis (1907), and the Naga studies of J.H. Hutton and J.P. Mills, both district officers in the Naga Hills. Their contribution must be weighed for its documentary value and its colonial purpose.

1. Phases of colonial study

  • Early accounts (1830s–1880s): after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826), officers recorded the hill peoples: John Butler's A Sketch of Assam (1847), T.H. Lewin's Wild Races of South-Eastern India (1870), E.T. Dalton's Descriptive Ethnology of Bengal (1872) and Alexander Mackenzie's 1884 history of government relations with the frontier hill tribes.
  • Monographs (1907–1937): the Assam series in a standard format, followed by the Naga volumes of Hutton and Mills (see table).
  • Late phase: C. von Fürer-Haimendorf's The Naked Nagas (1939) on the Konyak and Himalayan Barbary (1955) on the Apa Tani and their neighbours; Ursula Graham Bower's Naga Path (1950) on the Zeme. G.A. Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India classified the Tibeto-Burman languages, and missionaries produced scripts and grammars, such as Thomas Jones's Roman script for Khasi (1842).

2. Contributions

  • A documentary baseline: detailed accounts of clans, village government, land tenure, the morung (youth dormitory), feasts of merit, head-hunting, megaliths and customary law, still primary sources for Naga, Mizo and Khasi scholars.
  • Field method: long residence, knowledge of local languages, photographs and large object collections, such as Hutton's and Mills's at the Pitt Rivers Museum, Oxford.
  • Analysis: Gurdon explained Khasi matriliny and the youngest daughter's (ka khadduh's) inheritance; Hutton compared Naga megaliths and head-hunting with South-East Asian cultures in a diffusionist frame.
  • Building the discipline: Hodson became the first William Wyse Professor of Social Anthropology at Cambridge (1932–37) and Hutton, who directed the 1931 Census, succeeded him (1937–50); Mills became Assam's honorary director of ethnography.
  • Policy: administrator-ethnographers backed the protective regime of the Inner Line, the "backward tracts" (1919) and the Excluded Areas (1935), a legacy carried into the Sixth Schedule.

3. Limitations

  • Knowledge for control: these studies served pacification, revenue and indirect rule, a link examined in Anthropology and the Colonial Encounter (1973), edited by Talal Asad.
  • Exoticism: the stress on head-hunting, nakedness and "wild" tribes produced stereotypes and a timeless picture that ignored history, trade and hill-plain ties.
  • Fixed categories: neat tribal labels hardened fluid identities, with lasting political effects among Naga, Kuki and Mizo groups.
  • Isolation: the protective policy kept the hills apart from the national movement; G.S. Ghurye attacked it in The Aborigines "So-called" and their Future (1943).
  • Missing voices: women's lives and people's own histories were little recorded.

Colonial scholars gave North-East India a rich ethnographic archive and shaped protective constitutional safeguards, yet their work carried the colonial gaze. Today's Naga, Mizo and Khasi scholars use it critically, reading it against oral history and their own experience.

Caste-like stratificationAshraf, Ajlaf and ArzalDalit Christians and SikhsEndogamy

Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966) tied caste to the Hindu ideology of purity and pollution. Ethnography shows, however, that caste as a social category — hereditary, endogamous, ranked groups linked to occupations — persists among Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Jains, largely because converts carried their jati identities into the new faith. The answer is "yes, but in a modified form".

1. Muslims

  • Three broad strata: the Ashraf, claiming foreign descent (Sayyid, Shaikh, Mughal, Pathan); the Ajlaf, converted occupational groups such as Ansari weavers and Qureshi butchers; and the Arzal, who did tasks seen as unclean, such as Halalkhor and Lalbegi. The 1901 Census recorded this three-fold ranking.
  • Ethnography: Ghaus Ansari's Muslim Caste in Uttar Pradesh (1960) and the volume edited by Imtiaz Ahmad (1973) describe biradari endogamy, caste councils and ranked occupations. Fredrik Barth's study of Swat (1960) found a full caste-like hierarchy in a Muslim society.
  • Today: the Pasmanda movement mobilises backward and Dalit Muslims; many Muslim groups are on OBC lists, and the Sachar Committee (2006) documented their deprivation.

2. Christians

  • Carried-over jati: Syrian Christians of Kerala trace descent from Brahmins converted by St Thomas and remain endogamous, ranking above Latin Catholics and Dalit converts.
  • Ethnography: David Mosse's The Saint in the Banyan Tree (2012) shows caste shaping seating, festival roles and burial in a Tamil Catholic village; separate cemeteries have been reported in Tamil Nadu.
  • Law: under the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, SC status is limited to Hindus, Sikhs (1956) and Buddhists (1990). The Ranganath Misra Commission (2007) recommended delinking it from religion, and the K.G. Balakrishnan Commission, set up in 2022 on this question, was reported to have completed its report in June 2026 after several extensions.

3. Sikhs

  • Ideal and practice: the Gurus rejected caste and the langar symbolises equality, yet Jat Sikhs dominate land, while Dalit Sikhs (Mazhabi, Ramdasia, Ravidasia) often have separate gurdwaras and cremation grounds. Surinder S. Jodhka's studies show Dalits asserting through deras, notably the Ravidassia movement.

4. Buddhists, Jains and others

  • Neo-Buddhists: converts following B.R. Ambedkar's 1956 diksha are still identified by their former caste in village life.
  • Ladakh: hereditary blacksmith (Garra) and musician (Mon, Beda) groups have been ranked low.
  • Jains: endogamous jatis such as Oswal, Porwal and Agarwal share caste names and marriage rules with Hindu Banias.

5. Assessment

  • Supports a wider view: caste is a feature of South Asian society, not of Hindu doctrine alone, as Gerald Berreman's comparative work (1960) and the essays in Aspects of Caste (1960), edited by Edmund Leach and including Barth on Swat, suggest.
  • Differences: it lacks scriptural sanction, pollution rules are weaker, and status is more negotiable; a north Indian proverb mocks how a prosperous weaver could become a Shaikh and then a Sayyid.

Caste exists among non-Hindus as a social category without religious legitimacy. This is why debates over SC status for Dalit Christians and Muslims and Pasmanda assertion remain live issues.

The Development Action Plan for Scheduled Tribes (DAPST) is the present name of the Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP) strategy at the Union level. Adopted in the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974–75) on the advice of the expert committee chaired by S.C. Dube, it requires government departments to set aside funds for Scheduled Tribes, who form 8.6% of the population (Census 2011), so that benefits do not depend on the trickle-down of general schemes.

1. Features and mechanism

  • Earmarking: besides the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, over 40 Union ministries and departments must earmark between 4.3% and 17.5% of their scheme allocations for STs every year.
  • Coverage: over 200 schemes in education, health, agriculture, irrigation, roads, housing, drinking water, electrification, skills and livelihoods.
  • Budget visibility: allocations appear in a separate statement on the welfare of Scheduled Tribes in the Union Budget.
  • Scale: actual spending rose from about ₹21,500 crore in 2013-14 to over ₹1 lakh crore a year from 2023-24 (PIB, 2025); the Union Budget allocation for STs is about ₹1.41 lakh crore in 2026-27, up from about ₹1.29 lakh crore in 2025-26.
  • States: state TSPs work through ITDPs and ITDAs; Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka (2013) and Telangana (2017) gave their sub-plans legal backing.

2. Monitoring

  • STC-MIS portal: the Ministry of Tribal Affairs tracks ministry-wise and scheme-wise allocation and use online.
  • Reviews: periodic meetings check adherence to the earmarking norm, choice of ST-beneficial schemes and physical targets, following NITI Aayog guidelines.

3. Convergence with flagship missions

  • PM-JANMAN (2023): ₹24,104 crore for housing, roads, water, health and education in habitations of the 75 PVTGs.
  • DAJGUA (2024): ₹79,156 crore across 17 ministries for about 63,800 tribal-majority villages until 2029, built on DAPST funds.

4. Critical assessment

  • Notional allocation: general schemes, such as highways or telecom, are booked as tribal spending without clear direct benefit.
  • Under-use and diversion: funds are released late, left unspent or diverted to general works.
  • No statutory backing: the Union-level plan rests on guidelines; the Ministry of Tribal Affairs can monitor but not enforce.
  • Outlays over outcomes: gram sabha planning under PESA is weak, and results in literacy, health and income lag behind spending; the Xaxa Committee (2014) also pointed to poor utilisation.

DAPST has made tribal development a shared duty of the whole government, and its scale has grown sharply. Legal backing, outcome budgeting and gram sabha-based planning would turn its earmarked funds into real gains for tribal communities.

Tribe-caste continuumRajput myth and state formationLittle and great traditionBhumij

Surajit Sinha, drawing on Robert Redfield's civilizational approach and on N.K. Bose's "Hindu method of tribal absorption" (1941), argued that tribes and castes are not isolated categories but points on a continuum within Indian civilization. His argument rests on his study of the Bhumij of Manbhum and on papers such as "Tribal cultures of peninsular India as a dimension of little tradition" (1958), "State formation and Rajput myth" (1962) and "Tribe-caste and tribe-peasant continua" (1965).

1. Sinha's line of argument

  • Tribe as little tradition: tribal cultures of peninsular India are a dimension of the little tradition of Indian civilization, not separate worlds.
  • Ideal types: a tribe is marked by isolation from the great tradition, ethnic homogeneity, clan-based segmentary structure, close tie to territory and little hierarchy; a caste by hierarchy, interdependence and Brahmanical values. Real groups lie between these poles.
  • The Bhumij case: the Bhumij of Barabhum took Brahmin priests, Hindu deities and caste norms, and in the early 20th century a Bhumij-Kshatriya movement claimed Kshatriya status, which Sinha analysed in a 1959 paper on south Manbhum.
  • Rajput myth and state formation: tribal chiefs who built kingdoms legitimised their rule by claiming Rajput descent and patronising Brahmins and temples. Such secondary state formation drew Bhumij, Gond, Chero and Nagvanshi rulers and their subjects into the caste order.

2. Strengths

  • Historical and dynamic: it replaced both Verrier Elwin's picture of isolated tribes and G.S. Ghurye's label of "backward Hindus" (1943) with a process traced over centuries.
  • Empirical support: Gond kingdoms of Garha-Mandla and Chanda, the Nagvanshi rajas of Chotanagpur and the Rajput claims of many central Indian chiefs fit the model; it parallels M.N. Srinivas's Sanskritisation and F.G. Bailey's continuum based on access to land (1961).
  • Lasting relevance: it explains why many communities sit on the tribe-caste border and why scheduling is contested.

3. Criticisms

  • One-way and Hindu-centred: Hinduisation is treated as the only path; Christianisation among the Oraon and Munda, Islamisation and secular change are neglected, and "Indian civilization" is equated with the Brahmanical great tradition.
  • Neglect of agency and resistance: Virginius Xaxa (1999) argued that tribes have not dissolved into castes; they keep distinct identities, often move towards a peasant economy, and assert themselves through movements such as the Jharkhand movement and the demand for a Sarna religion code.
  • Limited reach: the model fits central India, not the Naga, Mizo, Khasi or Andaman islanders.
  • Conceptual blurring: André Béteille (1986) held that tribe and caste rest on different principles, isolation versus hierarchy, even if the boundary is historically fluid.
  • Reverse flows: de-Sanskritisation, tribal revival and some castes' demands for ST status, such as the Kurmi-Mahato in Jharkhand and West Bengal, show movement in both directions, shaped by State policy.

Sinha rightly showed that tribes have long been part of Indian civilization and its state systems. Today, however, tribes are better seen as distinct communities negotiating with that civilization and with the State, which calls for integration without assimilation.
free.upa-2026-an2-8b:
Land alienationDevelopment-induced displacementHealth and education gapsIdentity and governance

Scheduled Tribes, 10.43 crore people or 8.6% of India's population (Census 2011) in over 700 notified communities, remain at the bottom of most development indicators. Their problems arise from the encounter between forest- and land-based tribal economies and a market-driven State. The Xaxa Committee (2014) identified livelihoods, education, health, legal safeguards and displacement as the main areas of concern.

1. Land, forests and displacement

  • Land alienation: debt, fraud, benami transfers and acquisition continue despite tenancy laws such as the Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act (1908) and the Samatha judgment (1997) barring transfer of Scheduled Area land to private miners.
  • Displacement: tribes are 8.6% of the population but, by Walter Fernandes's estimates, around 40% of those displaced by dams, mines and industries since 1950, with poor rehabilitation, as in Sardar Sarovar and Polavaram.
  • Forest rights: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 is unevenly applied; many claims are rejected and community forest rights move slowly. The Supreme Court's 2019 eviction order, later stayed, showed the insecurity.
  • Conservation conflicts: relocation from tiger reserves and mega-projects such as Great Nicobar, home of the Shompen, raise new fears.

2. Economic deprivation

  • Poverty and debt: low incomes, indebtedness to moneylenders and bonded labour persist in pockets.
  • Distress migration: seasonal work in brick kilns, construction and plantations exposes migrants, especially women, to exploitation.
  • Shrinking livelihoods: restrictions on shifting cultivation and low prices for minor forest produce weaken traditional economies.

3. Health and nutrition

  • Disease burden: malnutrition, anaemia, malaria, tuberculosis and sickle cell disease are higher than average; PVTGs such as the Jarawa and Shompen are especially vulnerable to outside infections.
  • Access: health centres are distant and understaffed, and traditional healers are rarely linked to formal care.

4. Education and employment

  • Learning gap: ST literacy was 58.96% against 72.99% nationally (Census 2011); teaching in an unfamiliar language, poor schools and dropout widen it.
  • Jobs: few tribals reach the organised sector, and reserved posts often stay unfilled.

5. Identity, security and governance

  • Cultural erosion: many tribal languages are endangered, and institutions such as youth dormitories are fading.
  • Conflict: Adivasis were caught between Maoists and the State in central India (Salwa Judum was held unconstitutional in 2011), and the ethnic violence that broke out in Manipur in 2023 displaced tens of thousands.
  • Weak self-rule: PESA is diluted, elites capture benefits and non-tribal influx alters demography.

Tribal challenges are interlinked: losing land and forest sets off a chain of deprivation. Secure rights, strong gram sabhas, culturally sensitive schooling and health care, and development with consent are needed to break it.
free.upa-2026-an2-8c:
Article 17Protective discriminationArticle 46National Commission for Scheduled Castes

Scheduled Castes are communities notified by the President under Article 341 (defined in Article 366(24)), historically subjected to untouchability; they numbered 20.14 crore, or 16.6% of the population, in Census 2011. Building on the Poona Pact (1932) and the Government of India Act, 1935, the Constitution drafted under B.R. Ambedkar combined protection against discrimination with compensatory measures.

1. Social safeguards

  • Article 17: abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence, enforced through the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, strengthened in 2015 and 2018.
  • Article 15(2): no restriction on access to shops, wells, tanks, roads and public places on grounds of caste.
  • Article 23: bans begar and forced labour, the basis of the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.
  • Article 25(2)(b): allows laws throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes.

2. Educational and economic safeguards

  • Article 15(4): special measures for the advancement of SCs, added by the First Amendment (1951).
  • Article 15(5): reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided ones except minority institutions (93rd Amendment, 2005).
  • Article 46: directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of SCs and protect them from social injustice and exploitation; it underpins scholarships and the Development Action Plan for SCs.

3. Safeguards in public employment

  • Article 16(4): reservation in posts; 15% for SCs in direct central recruitment.
  • Article 16(4A): reservation in promotion (77th Amendment, 1995), with consequential seniority (85th Amendment, 2001).
  • Article 16(4B): unfilled reserved vacancies carried forward beyond the 50% ceiling (81st Amendment, 2000).
  • Article 335: claims to be considered consistently with efficiency; a proviso (82nd Amendment, 2000) allows relaxed qualifying marks.

4. Political safeguards

  • Articles 330 and 332: seats reserved in the Lok Sabha (84) and State Assemblies in proportion to population; Article 334, amended by the 104th Amendment (2019), extends this to 2030; under the 106th Amendment (2023), a third of these SC seats will go to SC women once it comes into force after the next delimitation.
  • Articles 243D and 243T: reservation in panchayats and municipalities, including chairpersons, with a third of SC seats for SC women.

5. Institutional safeguards

  • Article 338: the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, a separate body since the 89th Amendment (2003), investigates violations and advises on development.
  • Article 341: only Parliament can add to or remove from the notified list.

These safeguards have produced an SC middle class and political leadership, yet atrocities, manual scavenging and unfilled quotas persist. As Ambedkar warned, "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." Social change must match legal equality for true social justice.
free.upa-2025-an1-1a:
Mendelian inheritancePolygenic traitsExtranuclear inheritanceGenomic imprinting

A Mendelian trait is controlled by a single gene and is transmitted according to the laws of segregation and independent assortment that Gregor Mendel derived from pea crosses (Experiments on Plant Hybridization, 1866), rediscovered in 1900. Non-Mendelian traits depart from these simple ratios because many genes, the environment, or inheritance outside the nuclear genes shape them.

1. Mendelian (monogenic) traits

  • Discrete phenotypes: individuals fall into clear classes (affected or unaffected), and matings give predictable ratios such as 3:1 or 1:1.
  • Modes of transmission: autosomal dominant (brachydactyly, which William Farabee in 1905 showed to be the first human trait inherited as a Mendelian dominant; Huntington disease), autosomal recessive (alkaptonuria, which Archibald Garrod tied to cousin marriage in 1902; albinism; sickle-cell anaemia) and X-linked recessive (haemophilia, red–green colour blindness).
  • Catalogue: Victor McKusick's Mendelian Inheritance in Man (1966), now the online OMIM database, lists thousands of such conditions.

2. Non-Mendelian traits

  • Polygenic and multifactorial: stature, skin colour, finger-ridge counts and blood pressure vary continuously along a bell curve; R.A. Fisher (1918) showed that many small Mendelian effects add up to such variation.
  • Departures from simple dominance: codominance (the AB and MN blood groups), multiple alleles (ABO), epistasis (the Bombay phenotype, in which an hh genotype hides ABO antigens, reported by Y.M. Bhende and colleagues in 1952) and incomplete penetrance.
  • Sex-influenced and sex-limited traits: pattern baldness is expressed far more often in men because of hormones, and some traits appear in one sex only, so ratios differ between sons and daughters.
  • Extranuclear (mitochondrial) inheritance: passed only through the mother, as in Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy; this maternal transmission underlies the "mitochondrial Eve" studies of human origins.
  • Imprinting and anticipation: the same chromosome 15 deletion causes Prader–Willi syndrome when inherited from the father and Angelman syndrome when inherited from the mother; repeat expansions (fragile X, myotonic dystrophy) worsen over generations.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Population history: Mendelian markers such as blood groups and haemoglobin variants trace gene flow and selection; the high frequency of the sickle-cell gene in tribal belts of central and southern India reflects balanced polymorphism against malaria.
  • Critique of race: skin colour and stature are polygenic and vary in clines, so they cannot sort humanity into discrete races.

The two classes are ends of a continuum: "simple" traits have modifier genes, and complex traits contain genes of large effect. Genomics and epigenetics now study both together to explain human variation and disease.
free.upa-2025-an1-1b:
PurumAsymmetric alliancePrescriptive marriageStructure and statistics

The Purum are a small Old Kuki, Tibeto-Burman-speaking community of the Manipur hills, numbering about 300 in four villages when T.C. Das described them in The Purums: An Old Kuki Tribe of Manipur (1945). Their rule of marrying into the mother's brother's group made them the classic test case of alliance theory, and one of the most re-analysed kinship systems in anthropology.

1. The kinship system

  • Descent: five exogamous patrilineal sibs (Marrim, Makan, Kheyang, Thao and Parpa), subdivided into lineages.
  • Marriage rule: matrilateral cross-cousin marriage: a man should take a wife from his mother's brother's lineage and must not take one from his father's sister's lineage.
  • Wife-givers and wife-takers: each lineage receives women from one set of lineages and gives them to another, so women move in one direction and the relation is never reversed.

2. Theoretical significance

  • Test of generalised exchange: Claude Lévi-Strauss (The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1949) argued that matrilateral marriage links groups in a circle and builds wider solidarity than direct sister exchange. Rodney Needham's "A Structural Analysis of Purum Society" (American Anthropologist, 1958) used Das's data to show such a circulating connubium among Purum lineages.
  • Structure versus sentiment: George Homans and David Schneider (Marriage, Authority, and Final Causes, 1955) explained the matrilateral preference psychologically, by a boy's affection for his mother's brother in patrilineal societies. Needham's Structure and Sentiment (1962) replied that the rule follows from the logic of alliance between groups, not from individual feelings.
  • Prescription versus preference: Needham held that the Purum terminology itself defines a category of marriageable women, so marriage is prescribed, not merely preferred; Lévi-Strauss later played this distinction down (preface to the 1967 edition).
  • Model versus behaviour: Charles Ackerman ("Structure and Statistics: The Purum Case", 1964) tested Das's marriage records and found no clear avoidance of direct exchange. The debate sharpened the contrast between normative (mechanical) and statistical models.

3. Wider relevance

  • Similar one-way alliance among the Kachin (mayu–dama), analysed by Edmund Leach, points to a regional pattern in north-east India and Myanmar.
  • The Purum case shows the lasting value of detailed genealogies, which allow later scholars to test new theories.

A community of a few hundred people thus shaped a worldwide debate: it established alliance theory as a rival to descent theory and taught anthropologists to test elegant models against actual marriages.
free.upa-2025-an1-1c:
Raymond DartMakapansgatOsteodontokeraticTaphonomy

Osteodontokeratic ("bone–tooth–horn") was the name Raymond Dart gave to a supposed tool culture of the australopithecines, inferred from thousands of animal bones at the Makapansgat Limeworks cave in northern South Africa, whose hominin layers are about 3 million years old. He set out the full case in The Osteodontokeratic Culture of Australopithecus prometheus (1957).

1. Dart's claims

  • Selected bones: some skeletal parts, such as the lower ends of antelope humeri, jaws and horn cores, were far more common than others, so Dart argued that hominins chose and carried them as implements.
  • A tool kit: heavy limb bones served as clubs, horn cores as daggers, jaws with teeth as saws and scrapers, and split bones as scoops.
  • The "killer ape": dented baboon and hominin skulls were read as blows from bone clubs. In "The Predatory Transition from Ape to Man" (1953) Dart pictured our ancestors as violent hunters, an image popularised by Robert Ardrey's African Genesis (1961).

2. The makers

  • Dart named the Makapansgat hominin Australopithecus prometheus (1948), believing that blackened bones showed the use of fire. Later work found no reliable evidence that the blackening came from fire, and the fossils are now usually placed in Australopithecus africanus, a small-brained (about 450 cc), bipedal gracile australopithecine.

3. Criticism and reinterpretation

  • Carnivore collectors: Sherwood Washburn (1957) argued that hyenas and other predators could build up such bone heaps.
  • Taphonomy: C.K. Brain, in The Hunters or the Hunted? (1981), showed that the "selected" parts are simply the densest bones, which survive chewing and weathering; leopards, hyenas and porcupines were the main accumulators.
  • Hominins as prey: the juvenile skull SK 54 from Swartkrans has two holes that match a leopard's lower canines, reversing Dart's picture.
  • A partial vindication: worn bone fragments from Swartkrans and Sterkfontein (about 1.8–1.0 mya) were later shown to have been used to dig into termite mounds, so early hominins did use bone, though not as weapons.

The osteodontokeratic culture has been rejected, but the debate it provoked made taphonomy, the study of how bone assemblages form, central to palaeoanthropology and shifted the image of early hominins from "man the hunter" to the hunted.
free.upa-2025-an1-1d:
Olfactory communicationScent markingVomeronasal organChemical signals

Primates communicate by sight, sound, touch and smell. Olfactory communication, through scent glands, urine and faeces, is richest in the "wet-nosed" strepsirrhines (lemurs, lorises, galagos), remains important in New World monkeys and plays a smaller but real role in Old World monkeys and apes. Scent signals last after the sender has left, which makes them ideal for scent marking of space.

1. Anatomical basis

  • Strepsirrhines: a moist rhinarium, large olfactory bulbs and a working vomeronasal organ (VNO) that detects pheromone-like compounds.
  • Haplorhines: a dry nose and reduced smell apparatus; New World monkeys keep a VNO, but Old World monkeys and apes have largely lost a functional one. Yoav Gilad and colleagues (2004) linked the loss of olfactory receptor genes to the rise of full trichromatic colour sight, though later work questioned how close the link is.
  • Scent glands: on the wrists and upper arms of ring-tailed lemurs, the chest (sternal gland) of male sifakas and mandrills, the genital region of marmosets and tamarins and the base of the tail (subcaudal gland) in owl monkeys.

2. Messages carried by smell

  • Space and territory: galagos and lorises "urine-wash" their hands and feet, leaving trails along branches; lemurs mark trunks at range boundaries.
  • Identity and quality: lemur scent encodes sex, individual identity and even genetic diversity, which helps mate choice and kin recognition.
  • Reproductive state: female odours advertise fertility; among common marmosets, the dominant breeding female suppresses ovulation in subordinate females partly through scent.
  • Rank and conflict: male ring-tailed lemurs hold "stink fights", drawing their tails across their wrist glands and waving them at rivals (Alison Jolly, Lemur Behavior, 1966).
  • Food: spider monkeys and other fruit-eaters sniff fruit to judge ripeness.

3. Evolutionary significance

  • From smell to sight: the arboreal theory and Matt Cartmill's visual predation theory (1974) explain why primates came to rely more on sight, yet calling apes "microsmatic" overstates the loss: humans still carry roughly 400 working olfactory receptor genes.
  • Caution: the "copulins" reported in rhesus macaques by Richard Michael's team (1971) were not confirmed by later studies, showing how hard chemical signals are to prove.

Smell is thus an ancient channel that persists beside sight and sound. Its study links primate socio-ecology, genetics and the evolution of the human senses.
free.upa-2025-an1-1e:
EmbodimentTechniques of the bodyHabitusMindful body

Embodiment treats the body not as a natural object on which culture is written, but as the living ground through which culture is experienced and reproduced. Thomas Csordas proposed it as "a paradigm for anthropology" (1990), building on Marcel Mauss's "Techniques of the Body" (1934 lecture, published 1935), Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology and Pierre Bourdieu's habitus.

1. From body as symbol to body as subject

  • Body as symbol: Robert Hertz (1909) showed that the pre-eminence of the right hand is a religious and social value, not a biological given; Mary Douglas (Natural Symbols, 1970) argued that the physical body mirrors the social body and its boundaries.
  • Techniques of the body: Mauss noted that walking, swimming, sleeping and giving birth are done differently in each society and are learnt by imitating respected others.
  • Habitus: Bourdieu (Outline of a Theory of Practice, 1977) described lasting dispositions, inscribed in posture, gesture and taste, that reproduce class and gender order without explicit rules.
  • Disciplined bodies: Michel Foucault (Discipline and Punish, 1975) showed how schools, armies and prisons train "docile bodies" through timetables, drill and surveillance.
  • Three bodies: Nancy Scheper-Hughes and Margaret Lock ("The Mindful Body", 1987) separated the individual body, the social body and the body politic, bringing in power and control.

2. Ethnographic and Indian illustrations

  • Body marking: facial tattoos and nose plugs once marked Apatani women of Arunachal Pradesh, and godna tattoos remain a sign of identity for Baiga women of central India.
  • Caste and purity: rules on touch, food and seating, which Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966) traced to the opposition of purity and impurity, make hierarchy a felt bodily experience.
  • Everyday habitus: squatting, sitting cross-legged, eating with the right hand and touching elders' feet are learnt dispositions.
  • Gender: Iris Marion Young's "Throwing Like a Girl" (1980) showed how girls learn restrained ways of moving.

3. Significance

  • Beyond dualism: embodiment dissolves the mind–body and nature–culture splits and connects cultural with biological anthropology.
  • Embodied inequality: stunting, chronic stress and disease show how poverty and discrimination become biology; Scheper-Hughes's Death Without Weeping (1992) on hunger in north-east Brazil is a classic study.

Culture, then, lives not only in minds and texts but in muscles, senses and health. Embodiment is now central to medical anthropology and to the study of structural inequality.
free.upa-2025-an1-2a:
Miocene hominoid radiationProconsulSivapithecusLast common ancestor

The Miocene epoch (about 23–5.3 mya) was the "age of apes": dozens of hominoid genera lived across Africa and Eurasia, against a handful today, as warm forests gave way to drier, seasonal habitats. Fossils from Proconsul to Sivapithecus show how the ape body plan was assembled in stages, and the first hominins appear at its very end.

1. Early Miocene (23–16 mya): African stem apes

  • Proconsul and Ekembo (Kenya): named by A.T. Hopwood in 1933; Mary Leakey's 1948 skull from Rusinga Island is the best-known Miocene ape. They had no tail but a monkey-like body that walked along the tops of branches.
  • Morotopithecus (Uganda): its vertebrae hint at an early upright trunk, though its date is debated.

2. Middle Miocene (16–11.6 mya): thick enamel and spread into Eurasia

  • Kenyapithecus (Fort Ternan, Kenya, about 14 mya): thick enamel for hard foods; partly ground-living.
  • Out of Africa: once Afro-Arabia joined Eurasia, apes spread: Griphopithecus in Turkey, Dryopithecus in France (described by Édouard Lartet in 1856) and Pierolapithecus in Spain (over 12 mya), with an upright climber's broad trunk.
  • Kapi ramnagarensis (Ramnagar, Jammu and Kashmir, about 13 mya; described 2020): the earliest known gibbon relative, suggesting that great and lesser apes reached Asia together.
  • Danuvius (Germany, about 11.6 mya; 2019): claimed to combine extended legs with climbing arms; its locomotion is contested.

3. Late Miocene (11.6–5.3 mya): Asian apes and the first hominins

  • Sivapithecus and Ramapithecus (Siwalik Hills): G.E. Lewis found Ramapithecus in the Siwaliks in 1932 and named it in 1934; Elwyn Simons and David Pilbeam later hailed it as the earliest hominid for its short face and thick enamel. Pilbeam's 1982 Sivapithecus face from Pakistan's Potwar Plateau showed orangutan features, and Ramapithecus was merged into Sivapithecus.
  • Other Eurasian apes: the giant Gigantopithecus bilaspurensis of the Indian Siwaliks (Simons and Chopra, 1969), Oreopithecus of Italy and Ouranopithecus of Greece.
  • African ape ancestors: Nakalipithecus (Kenya, about 10 mya) and Chororapithecus (Ethiopia, about 8 mya) lie near the African ape and gorilla lines.
  • Earliest hominins: Sahelanthropus tchadensis (Chad, about 7 mya), Orrorin tugenensis (Kenya, about 6 mya) and Ardipithecus kadabba (Ethiopia, 5.8–5.2 mya). A January 2026 Science Advances study of Sahelanthropus limb bones argued for habitual, not obligate, bipedalism; debate continues.

4. Significance in evolution

  • Mosaic evolution: ape teeth, an upright trunk and suspension arose at different times; there is no single "missing link".
  • Molecular clock: Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson (1967) dated the human–African ape split to about 5 mya; the fall of Ramapithecus showed that fossils and molecules must be read together.
  • Biogeography: David Begun argues that the African ape–human lineage evolved in Europe and returned to Africa; most scholars favour an African origin.
  • Climate and bipedalism: late Miocene cooling and spreading grasslands fragmented forests, setting the stage for bipedalism.

Miocene hominoids show that human ancestry lies in a bushy radiation of apes, not a ladder; the Indian Siwaliks, with Sivapithecus and Kapi, hold one of Asia's richest records of it.
free.upa-2025-an1-2b:
Symbolic anthropologyThick descriptionDominant symbolsLiminality

Symbolic and interpretive anthropology arose in the 1960s as a reaction to materialist and structural-functional explanations. Its two leading figures were Clifford Geertz, who treated culture as a system of public meanings to be interpreted (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), and Victor Turner, who treated symbols as forces at work in social processes (The Forest of Symbols, 1967; The Ritual Process, 1969).

1. Common ground

  • Meaning before function: both placed symbols, ritual and religion at the centre of culture, not as mere reflections of economy or structure.
  • Public symbols: meaning lies in shared, observable symbols, not hidden inside individual minds.
  • The actor's view: both relied on long fieldwork and local commentary: Geertz in Java, Bali and Morocco; Turner among the Ndembu of Zambia.

2. Geertz: culture as a text

  • Webs of significance: following Max Weber, he saw man as "an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun", so anthropology is an interpretive search for meaning, not a search for laws.
  • Thick description: borrowing Gilbert Ryle's contrast between a twitch and a wink, the ethnographer must unpack the layers of meaning behind an act.
  • Model of and model for: in "Religion as a Cultural System" (1966), symbols both describe reality and shape moods and motivations.
  • Deep Play (1972): the Balinese cockfight is a status drama, "a story they tell themselves about themselves".

3. Turner: symbols in action

  • Dominant symbols: the mudyi (milk tree) in the Ndembu girls' puberty rite is multivocal and condenses many meanings, with an ideological pole (matriliny, social order) and a sensory pole (breast milk, nurture).
  • Three levels of meaning: exegetical (what people say), operational (how the symbol is used) and positional (its relation to other symbols).
  • Social drama: in Schism and Continuity in an African Society (1957), conflict passes through breach, crisis, redressive action and reintegration or schism.
  • Liminality and communitas: extending van Gennep, Turner showed that the "betwixt and between" phase suspends rank and creates communitas, as when Sabarimala pilgrims dress alike and address one another as "Swami".

4. Contrast and critique

  • Static versus processual: Geertz reads culture as a finished text; Turner shows symbols operating within conflict and change, and so keeps a link with social structure.
  • Critics of Geertz: Talal Asad (1983) argued that he ignored the power and discipline that produce religious meaning; Roger Keesing (1987) asked whose meanings are being read, since women and juniors may disagree with elite readings.
  • Critics of Turner: he relied heavily on male ritual experts, and communitas was romanticised: John Eade and Michael Sallnow (Contesting the Sacred, 1991) showed pilgrimage as an arena of competing claims.

Geertz offered a way of reading culture and Turner a way of seeing culture at work; together they moved anthropology from structure to meaning and prepared the ground for practice and performance theory.
free.upa-2025-an1-2c:
Biocultural synthesisHuman adaptabilityPolitical ecologyStructural violence

Biocultural anthropology studies how human biology and culture shape each other. Its earlier ecological and adaptability approaches explained variation as adaptation to physical stresses such as cold, heat and altitude. From the 1990s, Alan Goodman and Thomas Leatherman (Building a New Biocultural Synthesis, 1998) and others brought political economy (power, history and unequal access to resources) into the definition of the human environment.

1. Ecological and adaptability perspectives

  • Cultural ecology and systems: Julian Steward (1955) linked a "culture core" to the environment; Roy Rappaport's Pigs for the Ancestors (1968) read Tsembaga Maring ritual as an ecological regulator.
  • Human adaptability: the International Biological Programme (1964–74) studied populations under stress; Paul Baker's team at Nuñoa in the Peruvian Andes measured responses to low oxygen, cold and scarce energy.
  • Levels of adaptation: genetic (EPAS1 variants in Tibetans), developmental (larger chests in Andean children), physiological acclimatisation and cultural buffering.
  • Limits: populations were treated as closed and in balance with nature; colonial history, markets and poverty were left out, and adaptation was assumed to be beneficial.

2. The political-economy challenge

  • Global connections: Eric Wolf (Europe and the People Without History, 1982) and Sidney Mintz (Sweetness and Power, 1985) showed that local populations are shaped by capitalism and colonialism.
  • Political ecology: a term given currency by Wolf (1972), it studies how ownership and power govern access to land and resources.
  • Structural violence and syndemics: Paul Farmer and Merrill Singer showed that diseases cluster and interact where poverty and exclusion converge.

3. How the perspectives are integrated

  • Environment redefined: stressors now include landlessness, wage dependence and market prices as well as altitude or climate. Leatherman's work in southern Peru linked illness and its effects on work to households' access to land, wages and markets, not only to hypoxia.
  • Adaptation with costs: small body size or reduced activity may aid survival under scarcity but lowers health and productivity, so "adaptation" must be judged by who pays its price.
  • Linked levels and methods: global and national forces, households and individual bodies are studied together, combining anthropometry and biomarkers with ethnography and history.

4. Indian illustrations

  • Sickle-cell trait: its frequency in central Indian tribal belts is an ecological adaptation to malaria, but its burden today depends on access to screening and care.
  • Tribal undernutrition: child deaths among the Korku of Melghat (Maharashtra) and the Sahariya of Madhya Pradesh reflect forest loss, land alienation, distress migration and weak services, not natural food shortage alone.

The new synthesis keeps the biological rigour of adaptability studies but asks who is exposed to stress and why. Critics warn against reducing biology to politics, yet the approach has made biocultural anthropology more critical, historical and policy-relevant.
free.upa-2025-an1-3a:
Nutritional anthropologyAnthropometryIntersectionalityHidden hunger

Nutritional anthropology studies food and nutrition as both biological and cultural facts, a field opened by Audrey Richards' Land, Labour and Diet in Northern Rhodesia (1939) on the Bemba. Anthropologists measure a community's nutritional status with the clinical ABCD methods and ethnography, and increasingly interpret the results through intersectionality, Kimberlé Crenshaw's (1989) idea that disadvantages overlap and compound.

1. Assessing nutritional status

  • Anthropometry: height, weight, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) and skinfolds are compared with the WHO Child Growth Standards (2006) as z-scores: stunting shows chronic and wasting acute undernutrition, while adult BMI below 18.5 marks chronic energy deficiency.
  • Biochemical tests: haemoglobin for anaemia, ferritin, retinol and urinary iodine reveal "hidden hunger".
  • Clinical signs: Bitot's spots, goitre, angular stomatitis and the oedema of kwashiorkor.
  • Dietary surveys: 24-hour recall, food-frequency questionnaires, weighed intake and dietary diversity scores.
  • Ethnography: observing who eats what, when and in what order, and recording food categories (hot/cold, pure/impure), taboos and seasonal calendars, explains causes that numbers alone cannot.
  • India: NFHS-6 (2023–24) found 29.3% of children under five stunted (35.5% in NFHS-5), 19.0% wasted and 31.8% underweight; NFHS-5 (2019–21) recorded anaemia in 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months.

2. Ecology, culture and inequality as intersecting causes

  • Ecology: lean-season hunger before harvest, drought, iodine-poor Himalayan soils, malaria-driven anaemia and the loss of forest foods (tubers, greens, mahua) through deforestation and displacement.
  • Culture: "eating down" in pregnancy to have a smaller baby, post-partum food restrictions, hot–cold beliefs and women eating last; Mary Douglas and Marvin Harris (Good to Eat, 1985) showed that food choices follow both symbolic and material logics.
  • Social inequality: caste, class, gender and tribal status govern land, income and access to services; Amartya Sen's entitlement approach (Poverty and Famines, 1981) showed that people starve when their entitlements fail, even when food is available.

3. Significance of the intersectional approach

  • Explains differences within a community: a Dalit or tribal girl in a drought-prone district faces risks that caste, gender or ecology alone cannot explain.
  • Reveals intergenerational cycles: undernourished mothers bear low-birth-weight babies, so inequality becomes embodied.
  • Improves policy: POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018, now part of Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0), Anaemia Mukt Bharat and millet promotion work best when tailored to local food cultures, ecologies and social barriers.

Assessment tells us how much undernutrition exists; an intersectional, biocultural reading tells us why and for whom, which is what effective action needs.
free.upa-2025-an1-3b:
HolismBounded cultureGlobal flowsAgency and power

Classical anthropology often pictured each society as an integrated whole and a closed, bounded unit. Malinowski's functionalism treated institutions as interlocking parts meeting needs, and Ruth Benedict's Patterns of Culture (1934) gave each people a single configuration. This holism produced rich ethnography, but as a model of contemporary society it has serious drawbacks.

1. Merits of the model

  • Interconnection: it showed how institutions fit together, as the Trobriand kula linked trade, magic, politics and prestige (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922).
  • Relativism and fieldwork: it supported cultural relativism and long fieldwork in small, fairly isolated groups.

2. Drawbacks

  • Static and ahistorical: the "ethnographic present" froze societies in time. Eric Wolf (Europe and the People Without History, 1982) criticised the image of cultures as separate "billiard balls" and traced centuries of trade, colonialism and migration.
  • Hides conflict and inconsistency: Edmund Leach's Kachin (Political Systems of Highland Burma, 1954) oscillated between egalitarian gumlao and hierarchical gumsa forms; Max Gluckman showed conflict built into custom.
  • Homogenises: treating culture as equally shared hides differences of gender, age, caste and class; Lila Abu-Lughod's "Writing against Culture" (1991) argued that the concept freezes difference and creates "others".
  • Ties culture to territory: Akhil Gupta and James Ferguson (1992) showed that people, places and cultures no longer coincide; Arjun Appadurai's Modernity at Large (1996) described global flows of people, media, technology, money and ideas.
  • Denies agency and hybridity: practice theory (Bourdieu, Sherry Ortner) and Marshall Sahlins (Islands of History, 1985) showed people remaking culture through action; Ulf Hannerz described cultural creolisation.
  • Harmful policy uses: Oscar Lewis's "culture of poverty" was read as blaming the poor, and colonial images of "isolated tribes" justified segregation.

3. Indian evidence

  • Tribes were never sealed: N.K. Bose's "Hindu method of tribal absorption" (1941) and Surajit Sinha's tribe–caste continuum show long interaction; the Elwin–Ghurye debate on isolation or assimilation rested on these assumptions.
  • Open, hybrid cultures today: Gond painting in global art markets, Naga Christianity alongside the Hornbill Festival, Gulf migration reshaping Kerala households and tribal youth on social media.

4. A balanced view

  • Pattern is real: the Toda buffalo-dairy complex studied by W.H.R. Rivers (1906) tied economy, ritual and rank together, so integration should not be denied altogether.
  • Partial integration: Clifford Geertz compared culture to an octopus, loosely integrated rather than a seamless web; the task is to study pattern together with process, power and connection.

A closed, integrated notion of culture cannot explain a world of globalisation, mobility and contested identities; anthropology now treats culture as open, historical and negotiated.
free.upa-2025-an1-3c:
Pedigree analysisGenealogical methodW.H.R. RiversMode of inheritance

Both methods chart relatives across generations but ask different questions. Pedigree analysis is a tool of human genetics that follows a biological trait through blood relatives to infer how it is inherited. The genealogical method, systematised by W.H.R. Rivers (1900, 1910), is a fieldwork technique that uses an informant's knowledge of kin to reveal social organisation.

1. Differences

  • Biology versus social recognition: a pedigree treats an adopted child as genetically unrelated, while a genealogy records the child as a full member of the lineage, because kinship is socially defined.
  • Accuracy versus meaning: pedigrees need correct biological parentage; genealogies record what people believe and claim, including mythical founders.

2. History of pedigree analysis

  • Francis Galton (Hereditary Genius, 1869) traced talent through eminent families, an approach later misused by eugenics.
  • After the rediscovery of Mendel, Archibald Garrod (1902) used family data on alkaptonuria to identify a recessive human disorder, and William Farabee (1905) showed brachydactyly to be dominant.
  • Haemophilia among Queen Victoria's descendants became the textbook X-linked pedigree; a large kindred around Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela, helped locate the Huntington disease gene (marker 1983, gene 1993).
  • Pedigree symbols were standardised by the US National Society of Genetic Counselors (1995, revised 2008 and 2022).

3. History of the genealogical method

  • Lewis Henry Morgan collected kin terms worldwide for Systems of Consanguinity and Affinity (1871).
  • Rivers developed the method on the Torres Strait Expedition (1898), used it in The Todas (1906) and set it out in "A Genealogical Method of Collecting Social and Vital Statistics" (1900) and "The Genealogical Method of Anthropological Inquiry" (1910).
  • It became standard in British lineage studies (Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer, 1940; Meyer Fortes) and in India in Iravati Karve's Kinship Organisation in India (1953) and T.C. Das's The Purums (1945).
  • David Schneider's A Critique of the Study of Kinship (1984) exposed its biological bias, leading to the "new kinship" studies of relatedness (Janet Carsten).

4. Applications in anthropology

  • Pedigree: inheritance of sickle-cell disease, thalassaemia and G6PD deficiency in Indian tribal and caste groups; genetic counselling in communities practising consanguineous marriage; inbreeding coefficients and linkage studies.
  • Genealogy: kin terminology, descent and alliance (the Purum debate), succession to office, land and inheritance disputes, and data on fertility, mortality and migration.
  • Combined: biocultural studies link marriage rules such as cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriage to recessive disease, and genetic genealogy now joins DNA with family histories.

Pedigree analysis reads biological inheritance; the genealogical method reads social relatedness. Used together, they make anthropology truly biocultural.
free.upa-2025-an1-4a:
HolismFour-field approachBiocultural perspectiveScientific humanism

Anthropology studies human beings both as biological organisms and as makers of meaning. Its holistic, comparative and four-field design (biological, archaeological, linguistic and socio-cultural), shaped by Franz Boas, joins the methods of natural science with the interpretive concerns of the humanities; Eric Wolf (1964) called it "the most scientific of the humanities, the most humanist of the sciences".

1. Anthropology as a science

  • Empirical and comparative: hypotheses are tested across cultures; George Murdock's Social Structure (1949) and the Human Relations Area Files made statistical comparison possible.
  • Search for laws: Radcliffe-Brown wanted a natural science of society, Malinowski wrote A Scientific Theory of Culture (1944), and Leslie White, Julian Steward and Marvin Harris (Cultural Materialism, 1979) sought causal regularities.
  • Laboratory tools: evolutionary biology, genetics and ancient DNA, radiometric dating, anthropometry and forensic identification.

2. Anthropology as a humanity

  • Interpretation: Clifford Geertz (1973) called it an interpretive search for meaning, and Evans-Pritchard's Marett Lecture (1950) likened it to history rather than natural science.
  • Insider's view: participant observation and the emic perspective capture how people experience their world.
  • Expressive culture: myth, art, language, music and ritual; reflexive writing after Writing Culture (James Clifford and George Marcus, 1986).
  • Ethics and voice: collaboration and informed consent, as in the American Anthropological Association's Principles of Professional Responsibility (2012).

3. The bridge in practice

  • Kuru among the Fore (Papua New Guinea): Carleton Gajdusek (Nobel Prize, 1976) studied the fatal brain disease, while Shirley Lindenbaum (Kuru Sorcery, 1979) and Robert Glasse linked its spread to mortuary feasting; neither biology nor culture alone could explain it.
  • Sickle-cell and malaria: Frank Livingstone (1958) linked the gene's spread in West Africa to forest clearing for farming, joining genetics, ecology and history.
  • Lactase persistence: dairying cultures selected for adult milk digestion, a case of gene–culture co-evolution.
  • Epidemics: during the 2014–16 Ebola outbreak, anthropologists helped design safe burials that respected local rites (Paul Richards, Ebola, 2016).

4. Indian illustrations

  • People of India project: the Anthropological Survey of India under K.S. Singh documented the biological and cultural traits of thousands of communities.
  • Sickle-cell mission: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) in tribal belts needs both genetic screening and culturally sensitive counselling on marriage.
  • GenomeIndia: data on about 10,000 genomes from tribal and non-tribal groups, released in January 2025, raise humanistic questions of consent and benefit-sharing.

5. Tensions

  • Institutional rifts: the two sides do pull apart: Stanford's anthropology department split into scientific and cultural wings in 1998 and reunited only in 2007.
  • Lesson: such episodes show that each side needs the other, since questions of health, heredity or migration have both biological and cultural answers.

Anthropology is multidimensional because it refuses to separate the body from meaning; this synthesis of science and humanities is its distinctive contribution to understanding and serving humanity.
free.upa-2025-an1-4b:
Mousterian industryLevallois techniqueNeanderthalsMiddle Palaeolithic

The Mousterian is the main Middle Palaeolithic flake industry of Europe and West and Central Asia (about 300,000–40,000 years ago), named by Gabriel de Mortillet after the rock shelter of Le Moustier in the Dordogne, France. It is linked above all with the Neanderthals, though early modern humans in the Levant made similar tools.

1. The tool tradition

  • Prepared cores: the Levallois technique shaped a core like an upturned tortoise shell so that a single blow removed a flake of planned size and shape; disc cores yielded several flakes.
  • Tool types: side-scrapers, triangular Mousterian points, denticulates and notches, backed knives and, in some assemblages, small handaxes; most tools are retouched flakes.
  • Hafting: some tools were fixed to wooden handles with birch-bark tar, made by controlled heating.
  • Variants and debate: François Bordes listed 63 tool types and grouped assemblages into facies (Typical, Charentian or Quina–Ferrassie, Denticulate, and Mousterian of Acheulian Tradition). He saw these as separate cultural groups; Lewis and Sally Binford (1966) read them as tool kits for different tasks, and later scholars added time and resharpening as explanations.

2. Mousterian culture

  • Subsistence: skilled hunting of large mammals such as reindeer, bison, horse and mammoth, often by ambush, along with plant foods.
  • Fire and shelter: regular hearths in caves and rock shelters; circles of broken stalagmites at Bruniquel, France (about 176,000 years ago).
  • Burial and care: deliberate burials at La Chapelle-aux-Saints, La Ferrassie and Shanidar (Iraq, excavated by Ralph Solecki); the badly injured Shanidar 1 survived for years, implying care. The "flower burial" of Shanidar 4 is now doubted, as burrowing animals may have brought the pollen.
  • Symbolic behaviour: ochre and manganese pigments, eagle-talon ornaments from Krapina (Croatia, about 130,000 years ago) and perforated shells.
  • Speech capacity: a modern-looking hyoid bone from Kebara (Israel) suggests the anatomy for speech.

3. The makers

  • Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis): robust, cold-adapted bodies with short limbs, a large nose, heavy brow ridges, no chin, an occipital bun and brains as large as or larger than ours (roughly 1,400–1,500 cc on average); found from Spain to the Altai (Feldhofer, La Chapelle, Spy, Shanidar, Teshik-Tash).
  • Early modern humans: Homo sapiens at Skhul and Qafzeh (Israel, about 120,000–90,000 years ago) made Levantine Mousterian tools, so the industry is not the mark of one species.
  • Genetic legacy: the Neanderthal genome (2010) proved interbreeding; non-Africans today carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA. Neanderthals disappeared about 40,000 years ago.

4. Indian Middle Palaeolithic

  • Flake industries: India has no Neanderthal fossils. H.D. Sankalia named the flake industry of Nevasa (Maharashtra) "Nevasian", and scrapers, points and borers on fine-grained stones occur widely.
  • Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu): Levallois tools dated to about 385,000–172,000 years ago (2018) have reopened the question of who made them.

The Mousterian reveals planned toolmaking, care, burial and symbolism, overturning the image of Neanderthals as brutish; it marks a key stage in the evolution of human cognition.
free.upa-2025-an1-4c:
Classical evolutionismSympathetic magicSecularisationDesecularisation

Sir James Frazer, a Cambridge "armchair" scholar, set out in The Golden Bough (1890; twelve volumes by 1915) an evolutionary scheme in which human thought passed from magic to religion to science. Like E.B. Tylor and L.H. Morgan, he assumed the psychic unity of humankind and relied on the comparative method.

1. Frazer's theory

  • Magic: a mistaken association of ideas, "a false science as well as an abortive art". Sympathetic magic has two forms: homoeopathic (like produces like, as in harming an effigy) and contagious (things once in contact stay linked, as in sorcery with hair or nail clippings).
  • Religion: "a propitiation or conciliation of powers superior to man", adopted when people realised that magic failed.
  • Science: a return to the idea of an ordered nature, now governed by correct, tested laws.
  • Other themes: the priest-king of Nemi, divine kingship and dying-and-reviving gods; Totemism and Exogamy (1910).

2. Critical examination

  • Armchair method: he used missionaries' and travellers' reports torn from context; Malinowski's fieldwork replaced this.
  • Coexistence, not sequence: Malinowski (Magic, Science and Religion, 1925) showed Trobrianders relying on skill in the safe lagoon but adding magic for dangerous open-sea fishing; magic relieves anxiety rather than marking an earlier stage.
  • Other rationalities: Evans-Pritchard (Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande, 1937) showed witchcraft beliefs to be logical within their premises, and later (Theories of Primitive Religion, 1965) mocked the "if I were a horse" guesswork of intellectualists; Wittgenstein's remarks on Frazer found him narrower than the peoples he described.
  • Religion as social: Durkheim (The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, 1912) traced religion to collective life; R.R. Marett proposed animatism before animism.
  • Ethnocentrism: placing European science at the summit justified colonial hierarchy.
  • Lasting value: his classification of magic is still used, and neo-evolutionists revived evolutionism in universal (Leslie White) and multilinear (Julian Steward) forms.

3. Place of religion in modernity

  • Secularisation thesis: Max Weber's "disenchantment of the world" predicted religion's retreat; Peter Berger (The Sacred Canopy, 1967) agreed but later (The Desecularization of the World, 1999) admitted religion had revived.
  • Religion in public life: José Casanova (1994) traced its return to politics; Charles Taylor (A Secular Age, 2007) saw belief as one option among many; Talal Asad (2003) showed the secular itself to be a historical construct.
  • New forms: guru movements, televangelism, online darshan and e-puja, and mass pilgrimages such as the Kumbh Mela managed with modern technology.
  • Magic persists: Jean and John Comaroff (Modernity and Its Malcontents, 1993) found occult beliefs thriving in market economies; in India, witch-hunting continues, prompting laws such as Maharashtra's anti-black-magic Act (2013), passed after Narendra Dabholkar's murder.
  • Coexistence: scientists praying before launches and sacred groves protecting biodiversity show science and religion working side by side.

Frazer was right that thought changes but wrong to arrange magic, religion and science as a ladder. Modernity has transformed rather than replaced religion, which persists as identity, ethics and community.
free.upa-2025-an1-5a:
Multi-sited ethnographyMultispecies ethnographyCritical ethnographyReflexivity

Classic ethnography, as Bronislaw Malinowski practised it in the Trobriand Islands (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922), meant long fieldwork in one bounded village, focused on human beings alone. After the Writing Culture debate (James Clifford and George Marcus, 1986), three newer forms stretched this model: multi-sited ethnography follows connections across places, multispecies ethnography widens the cast beyond humans, and critical ethnography turns description into an inquiry into power.

1. Multi-sited ethnography

  • Origin: George Marcus set out the method in a 1995 essay in the Annual Review of Anthropology, arguing that a world system cannot be understood from one locality.
  • Method: the researcher follows the people, the thing, the metaphor, the story, the life or the conflict as it moves. Sidney Mintz's Sweetness and Power (1985), which traced sugar from Caribbean plantations to English tea tables, was an early model.
  • Indian example: Xiang Biao (Global Body Shopping, 2007) followed IT workers from Andhra Pradesh through recruiting agencies to jobs in Australia.
  • Criticism: breadth can cost depth, since each site receives less time.

2. Multispecies ethnography

  • Meaning: it studies how human lives are entangled with animals, plants, fungi and microbes. Eben Kirksey and Stefan Helmreich named the field in Cultural Anthropology (2010), building on Donna Haraway's When Species Meet (2008).
  • Examples: Anna Tsing's The Mushroom at the End of the World (2015) follows the matsutake mushroom through ruined forests and global trade; Eduardo Kohn's How Forests Think (2013) studies the Runa of Ecuador's Amazon.
  • Indian example: Radhika Govindrajan's Animal Intimacies (2018) shows how villagers of Kumaon (Uttarakhand) form bonds of relatedness with goats offered to deities, cows, monkeys and bears.

3. Critical ethnography

  • Meaning: ethnography guided by critical theory (Marxist, feminist, postcolonial) that exposes domination and aims at change; D. Soyini Madison's Critical Ethnography (2005) treats it as an ethical responsibility of the researcher.
  • Examples: Paul Willis's Learning to Labour (1977) showed how working-class boys' rebellion at school led them into working-class jobs; Alpa Shah's In the Shadows of the State (2010) argued that elite-led indigenous and environmental activism could work against poor Munda villagers in Jharkhand.
  • Features: reflexivity about the researcher's position, collaboration with participants and advocacy.

Together these approaches fit ethnography to a globalised, ecologically fragile and unequal world: the field is no longer one village, humans are not the only actors, and description carries an ethical commitment. They extend, rather than replace, holistic participant observation.
free.upa-2025-an1-5b:
MenopauseGrandmother hypothesisPost-reproductive lifespanLife history

Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation, caused by exhaustion of ovarian follicles and confirmed after twelve months without a period. It occurs at about 51 years in Western populations and at a mean of about 46 years in India (Indian Menopause Society survey, 2016). The evolutionary puzzle is the long post-reproductive lifespan: selection should favour reproduction until death, yet women live for decades after fertility ends, a life-history trait shared with only a few mammals such as killer whales.

1. Adaptive explanations

  • Mother hypothesis: George C. Williams (1957) argued that, as late births are risky and infants stay dependent for long, an older mother gains more by stopping early and raising the children she has.
  • Grandmother hypothesis: Kristen Hawkes and colleagues observed that older Hadza women of Tanzania dig tubers that feed weaned grandchildren, letting daughters bear the next child sooner; their 1998 model links such help to the evolution of long human life. Lahdenperä and colleagues (Nature, 2004), using old church records from Finland and Canada, found that women gained about two extra grandchildren for every ten years they lived beyond 50.
  • Reproductive conflict: Michael Cant and Rufus Johnstone (2008) proposed that where young wives move into the husband's family, older women lose out in competition with younger breeders, so stopping early avoids conflict; killer whale studies (Croft and colleagues, 2017) support this.

2. Non-adaptive explanations

  • By-product of longevity: lifespan may simply outlast a fixed stock of eggs; but many hunter-gatherer women reach their sixties without modern medicine (Michael Gurven and Hillard Kaplan, 2007).
  • Patriarch hypothesis: Frank Marlowe (2000) suggested that long life was selected in older, high-status fathers, leaving menopause in women as a side-effect.

3. Comparative and bio-cultural evidence

  • Primates: Brian Wood and colleagues (Science, 2023) found hormonal and demographic signs of menopause in wild Ngogo chimpanzees of Uganda, though these females do not help grandchildren, so the trait may arise in more than one way.
  • Grandmother effect: Rebecca Sear and colleagues (2000) found that maternal grandmothers improved children's nutrition and survival in rural Gambia. In Indian joint families too, grandmothers share childcare and pass on knowledge.
  • Cooperative breeding: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy (Mothers and Others, 2009) places post-menopausal helpers within humans' shared childcare, long childhood and cultural learning.

Menopause is best seen as part of the human life-history package of long life, slow childhood and cooperative care, in which older women's labour and knowledge raise the survival of kin, a clear case of bio-cultural evolution.
free.upa-2025-an1-5c:
Fission track datingUranium-238Absolute datingOlduvai Gorge

Fission track dating is a radiometric (absolute) dating method that counts microscopic damage trails left in minerals and natural glass by the spontaneous fission of uranium-238. Developed in the early 1960s by the physicists R.L. Fleischer, P.B. Price and R.M. Walker, it dates the last time a sample was heated above a critical temperature, such as a volcanic eruption, the firing of pottery or the burning of obsidian.

1. Principle

  • Nuclear clock: U-238 nuclei split at a constant, known rate; the two heavy fragments fly apart and leave a narrow trail of damage in the crystal lattice.
  • Accumulation: the number of tracks per unit area grows with time and with the uranium content of the grain.
  • Resetting: heating erases (anneals) old tracks, for example in apatite at roughly 70–110°C and in zircon at about 230–250°C, so the clock restarts when a volcanic ash cools or a stone is burnt in a hearth.
  • Materials: zircon, apatite, sphene, mica, volcanic glass and obsidian, and some man-made glass.

2. Procedure

  • Uranium measurement: the second count gives the uranium content; many laboratories now measure uranium by laser-ablation mass spectrometry instead of reactor irradiation.

3. Applications in anthropology

  • Cross-checking hominin sites: at Olduvai Gorge, tracks in Bed I pumice gave 2.03 ± 0.28 million years (Fleischer and colleagues, 1965), supporting the potassium-argon age of about 1.75 million years for Zinjanthropus and Homo habilis.
  • Settling disputes: zircon dates by Andrew Gleadow (1980) helped resolve the KBS Tuff controversy at Koobi Fora, Kenya, supporting an age of about 1.9 million years rather than the earlier 2.6 million.
  • Wide range: usable from about 100,000 years to well over a billion years, it suits the volcanic sequences of the East African Rift where hominin fossils lie.
  • Archaeology: it dates burnt obsidian, heated stones and glass, and helps source obsidian to trace prehistoric exchange; geologists use apatite tracks to study the uplift of the Himalaya.

4. Limitations

  • Young or uranium-poor samples contain few tracks, so errors are large.
  • Partial annealing, especially in glass, shortens tracks and gives ages that are too young.
  • Counting is partly subjective, so results are best checked against potassium-argon or argon-argon dates.

Fission track dating is valuable as an independent check on other chronometric methods; together with argon dating it built the absolute chronology of early hominin evolution in East Africa.
free.upa-2025-an1-5d:
Mitochondrial DNAMitochondrial EveRecent African originHaplogroups

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a small circular genome of about 16,569 base pairs carrying 37 genes, present in hundreds to thousands of copies in each cell. Because it is inherited only from the mother, does not recombine and mutates faster than most nuclear DNA, it works as a molecular clock and a record of female lineages, which makes it a powerful tool for tracing human origins and migrations.

1. Why mtDNA is useful

  • Maternal inheritance: each person carries the mtDNA of the mother, her mother and so on, so all lineages join into one family tree.
  • No recombination: lineages differ only through mutation, so the number of differences indicates time since they separated.
  • Fast-mutating control region: the hypervariable segments of the D-loop separate closely related populations.
  • High copy number: it survives better in old bones, making ancient DNA studies possible.

2. Contributions to human evolution

  • Mitochondrial Eve: Rebecca Cann, Mark Stoneking and Allan Wilson (Nature, 1987) compared mtDNA of 147 people from five regions and traced all lineages to a woman in Africa about 200,000 years ago. This strongly supported the recent African origin model against Milford Wolpoff's multiregional model.
  • Whole mitochondrial genomes: Max Ingman and colleagues (2000) confirmed the African root; Africans carry the deepest and most diverse L lineages.
  • Routes of dispersal: only one African lineage, L3, gave rise to haplogroups M and N found outside Africa. In India, the Andamanese carry ancient M31 and M32 lineages (Kumarasamy Thangaraj and colleagues, Science, 2005), supporting an early southern coastal route.
  • Archaic humans: Neanderthal mtDNA (Krings and colleagues, 1997) falls outside modern variation; mtDNA from a finger bone in Denisova Cave revealed the Denisovans (2010); in 2025 mtDNA from dental calculus, together with ancient proteins, linked the Harbin cranium from north-east China (at least 146,000 years old) to the Denisovans.

3. Limitations

  • Single maternal line: Mitochondrial Eve was not the only woman alive, only the one whose female line survived; male history needs Y-chromosome data.
  • Clock and selection: mutation rates need calibration, and selection may act on mitochondrial genes; Alan Templeton (1992) questioned the early tree-building.
  • Blind to admixture: mtDNA missed the roughly 2% Neanderthal ancestry later found in the nuclear genomes of non-Africans (Richard Green and colleagues, 2010).

mtDNA turned human evolution into a testable molecular history. Read together with Y-chromosome and whole-genome evidence, it supports a recent African origin of modern humans with limited interbreeding with archaic groups.
free.upa-2025-an1-5e:
Foetal origins hypothesisDavid BarkerThrifty phenotypeDOHaD

The foetal origins hypothesis, also called the Barker hypothesis, holds that undernutrition and stress in the womb and in infancy programme the body's metabolism, raising the risk of coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and stroke in adulthood. It was developed by the British epidemiologist David J.P. Barker (1938–2013) of the University of Southampton and grew into the field of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD).

1. Barker's contribution

  • Geographical clue: Barker and Clive Osmond (Lancet, 1986) found that areas of England and Wales with high infant mortality in the 1920s later had high heart-disease death rates, pointing to poor early nutrition and not only adult affluence.
  • Hertfordshire records: using weights recorded by midwives and health visitors from 1911, Barker and colleagues (1989) showed that men lightest at birth and at one year had the highest death rates from ischaemic heart disease.
  • Thrifty phenotype: with C. Nicholas Hales (1992) he proposed that a poorly fed foetus spares the brain at the cost of organs such as the pancreas; the saving turns harmful when food later becomes plentiful, causing type 2 diabetes.
  • Synthesis: Mothers, Babies and Disease in Later Life (1994).

2. Supporting evidence

  • Dutch Hunger Winter (1944–45): those exposed to famine in the womb later showed more obesity, glucose intolerance and heart disease, varying with the stage of pregnancy.
  • Mysore: Barker's team with Caroline Fall (Claudia Stein and colleagues, 1996) linked low birth weight to adult coronary heart disease in south India.
  • Pune: C.S. Yajnik's Pune Maternal Nutrition Study described the ‘thin-fat Indian baby’, small but with relatively high body fat, and linked low maternal vitamin B12 with high folate to insulin resistance in the children.

3. Mechanisms and anthropological significance

  • Epigenetics: DNA methylation and hormone settings fixed in the womb shape gene expression throughout life.
  • Predictive adaptive response: Peter Gluckman and Mark Hanson (2004) see programming as a forecast of the outside world; disease follows when the forecast fails, as in a rapid nutrition transition.
  • Bio-cultural lens: poverty, gender bias in food and early marriage transmit ill-health across generations; hence policies for the first 1,000 days, such as POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018, now Poshan 2.0).
  • Criticism: social class may confound the link, and effect sizes are modest.

Barker shifted attention from adult lifestyle alone to the intrauterine environment, showing that chronic disease can begin before birth. For India's double burden of undernutrition and diabetes, better maternal and child nutrition is a key preventive strategy.
free.upa-2025-an1-6a:
Genetic markerPolymorphismDisease associationDNA profiling

A genetic marker is a gene or DNA sequence with a known chromosomal location that varies between individuals and is inherited in a simple Mendelian manner, so it can identify people, compare populations or flag a nearby gene. Useful markers are polymorphic (the commonest allele below 99% frequency), easy to detect and ideally co-dominant. From Karl Landsteiner's ABO blood groups (1900) to genome-wide SNP panels, markers have been central to biological anthropology.

1. Types of genetic markers

2. Understanding population variation
