  • Beginnings: Ludwik and Hanna Hirszfeld (1919) tested the ABO groups of soldiers of many nationalities on the Salonika front and found regular geographical gradients, the first population-genetic survey; A.E. Mourant later mapped blood-group frequencies worldwide (1954).
  • Against racial typology: Richard Lewontin (1972) used classical markers to show that about 85% of human genetic variation lies within populations; frequencies change gradually as clines.
  • Selection: the sickle-cell allele is common where malaria was intense (balanced polymorphism), and lactase persistence where herding spread, examples of gene–culture co-evolution. In India HbS clusters among tribal communities of central and western India, and HbE in the Northeast.
  • Indian population history: SNP studies (David Reich and colleagues, 2009) identified Ancestral North Indian and Ancestral South Indian components; the GenomeIndia project (Nature Genetics, 2025) sequenced 9,772 people from 83 populations, 30 of them tribal, recording about 180 million variants.

3. Disease association

  • Blood groups: group A was associated with stomach cancer and group O with duodenal ulcer (Ian Aird and colleagues, 1953–54).
  • HLA: about 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis carry HLA-B27; HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 predispose to coeliac disease; HLA-B*15:02 predicts severe skin reactions to the anti-epileptic drug carbamazepine in many Asian populations, a case of pharmacogenomics.
  • Mapping genes: markers co-inherited with a disease in families (linkage) and genome-wide association studies locate genes for diabetes, heart disease and cancers.
  • Public health: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) set out to screen 7 crore people aged 0–40 in affected, mainly tribal, areas; over 7 crore had been screened by June 2026, enabling carrier counselling towards elimination by 2047.

4. Forensics

  • DNA fingerprinting: Alec Jeffreys (1984–85) showed that hypervariable minisatellites give each person a unique pattern; it convicted Colin Pitchfork in 1988 after clearing an innocent suspect. In India, Lalji Singh at CCMB, Hyderabad, developed indigenous DNA fingerprinting in the late 1980s.
  • STR profiling: PCR-based STR panels now identify suspects, disaster victims and parents; Y-STRs isolate male DNA in sexual-assault mixtures, and mtDNA identifies degraded bones and hair.
  • Historical remains: mtDNA and isotopes traced the Ajnala (Punjab) skeletons to soldiers from the Gangetic plain killed in 1857 (2022).

Genetic markers have moved anthropology from typology to population thinking, opened the way to precision medicine and made forensic identification reliable. Their use needs safeguards for privacy and consent, and care that ancestry data do not revive ideas of race.
free.upa-2025-an1-6b:
New Physical AnthropologyModern SynthesisPopulation thinkingMolecular anthropology

Until the 1940s physical anthropology was largely descriptive and typological, measuring skulls and bodies to sort humanity into fixed races. From the middle of the twentieth century, the Modern Synthesis of Darwinism and genetics and Sherwood Washburn's programme of a New Physical Anthropology (1951) turned the field to testing hypotheses about evolutionary process, as biological anthropology.

1. The older agenda: classification

  • Typology: J.F. Blumenbach's five varieties (1795), Anders Retzius's cephalic index (1842), Paul Broca's craniometry and E.A. Hooton's racial types assumed fixed and often ranked types.
  • Colonial India: H.H. Risley's The People of India (1908) used the nasal index to rank castes and tribes, mixing measurement with social prejudice.
  • Early dissent: Franz Boas's study of immigrants' children (1912) showed head form changing in a new environment, but plasticity was not yet the mainstream view.

2. Why the agenda became scientific

  • Population thinking: Theodosius Dobzhansky (Genetics and the Origin of Species, 1937) and Julian Huxley (Evolution: The Modern Synthesis, 1942) made the breeding population, gene frequencies and the forces of mutation, selection, drift and gene flow the units of analysis.
  • Process, not types: Washburn asked how traits function and evolve; his own experiments removing chewing muscles in rats showed how skull form responds to function. He joined fossils to primate behaviour, and field primatology grew, from his baboon studies with Irven DeVore to Jane Goodall's work at Gombe (from 1960).
  • Race replaced by clines: Ashley Montagu (1942), the UNESCO statements on race (1950, 1951), Frank Livingstone (1962), who wrote "There are no races, there are only clines", and Richard Lewontin (1972) replaced racial boxes with continuous variation.
  • Bio-cultural hypothesis testing: Livingstone (1958) explained the spread of the sickle-cell gene in West Africa through yam farming, forest clearance, mosquitoes and malaria.

3. New tools

  • Dating: radiocarbon (Willard Libby, 1949) and potassium-argon (Olduvai Bed I, 1961) gave absolute ages; fluorine and other tests exposed the Piltdown forgery (1953).
  • Molecules: the DNA double helix (1953), Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson's immunological clock (1967) placing the human–African ape split at about 5 million years ago, the mtDNA studies of 1987 and the Neanderthal genome (2010), for which Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022.
  • Human adaptability: the International Biological Programme (1964–74) measured responses to altitude, cold and heat with physiology and statistics.

4. Indian developments

  • Statistics: D.N. Majumdar's 1941 anthropometric survey of the United Provinces was analysed with P.C. Mahalanobis and C.R. Rao using the D² statistic (Sankhyā, 1949).
  • Genetics: the Anthropological Survey of India (1945) moved from anthropometry to serology, genetics and growth studies; the GenomeIndia project (2025) sequenced 9,772 genomes from 83 populations.

5. A qualification

  • Science did not begin in 1950, and mid-century work was not free of bias: Carleton Coon's The Origin of Races (1962) still ranked races. Today science also means ethics: consent and community rights over samples.

The statement is justified: biological anthropology moved from description to explanation, from races to populations and processes, and from callipers to genomes, while remaining bio-cultural and ethically aware.
free.upa-2025-an1-6c:
Linguistic relativityEthnoscienceEthnography of speakingLanguage ideology

Linguistic anthropology studies language as a cultural resource and speaking as a cultural practice. Since Franz Boas's Handbook of American Indian Languages (1911), its central question has been how language, culture and thought shape one another. Perspectives range from linguistic relativity, through universalism, to practice approaches that locate meaning in social use.

1. Boas and the Sapir–Whorf hypothesis

  • Boas: every language classifies experience in its own way, largely below awareness, but language does not fix culture.
  • Edward Sapir: argued that "the 'real world' is to a large extent unconsciously built up on the language habits of the group" (1929).
  • Benjamin Lee Whorf: contrasted English with Hopi, claiming that Hopi grammar lacks English-style countable time; his essays appeared as Language, Thought, and Reality (1956).
  • Strong and weak forms: linguistic determinism is rejected; Ekkehart Malotki's Hopi Time (1983) showed that Hopi has many time expressions. The weaker claim, that language influences habitual thought, still has support.

2. Cognitive and universalist perspectives

  • Ethnoscience: Ward Goodenough (1957) saw culture as "whatever it is one has to know or believe in order to operate in a manner acceptable to its members"; Harold Conklin (Hanunóo colour terms, 1955) and Charles Frake (Subanun disease terms, 1961) mapped native categories through componential analysis.
  • Universals: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay (Basic Color Terms, 1969) found a regular order in which languages add colour terms; Eleanor Rosch showed that the Dani of New Guinea, with two colour words, still remembered focal colours well.
  • Structuralism: Claude Lévi-Strauss, borrowing from Saussure and Jakobson, analysed myth and kinship like language, through binary oppositions produced by a universal human mind.

3. Neo-Whorfian research

  • Space: Stephen Levinson's group found that speakers of Guugu Yimithirr (Australia) describe and remember arrangements by cardinal directions rather than left and right.
  • Number: John Lucy (1992) found that Yucatec Maya speakers attend less to number than English speakers, matching their grammar. Language thus guides habits of attention without imprisoning thought.

4. Language in social context

  • Ethnography of speaking: Dell Hymes (1962) asked who speaks what, to whom and when; his idea of communicative competence and SPEAKING model shifted attention to use.
  • Contact and convergence: John Gumperz studied dialects in Khalapur village (Uttar Pradesh) and, with Robert Wilson (1971), showed Marathi, Kannada and Urdu converging in grammar at Kupwar, Maharashtra, after generations of multilingual life.
  • Variation and power: William Bright and A.K. Ramanujan (1964) described caste dialects in Tamil and Kannada; Basil Bernstein's restricted and elaborated codes and Pierre Bourdieu's linguistic capital tie speech to class. Hindi pronouns tu, tum and aap encode hierarchy and intimacy.
  • Language ideology: Michael Silverstein (1979) showed that speakers' beliefs about their language shape its use and change; such beliefs also rank languages and speakers, as in the Hindi–Urdu divide.

The field has moved from asking whether language determines thought to how language, culture and cognition interact in practice. A weak relativity view, enriched by attention to context and power, is most widely accepted today.
free.upa-2025-an1-7a:
Definition of marriageSocial reproductionRelatednessUniversality of family

Classical anthropology defined marriage as a union of a man and a woman that makes children legitimate (Notes and Queries, 1951) and treated the nuclear family as universal (G.P. Murdock, Social Structure, 1949). Ethnographic variation in forms of marriage broke these assumptions and pushed anthropologists to rethink family, kinship and social reproduction, the process by which a society renews its people, statuses and structures across generations.

1. Variation in forms of marriage

2. Rethinking marriage

  • Bundle of rights: Edmund Leach (1955) argued that marriage allocates separable rights, to legal fatherhood, sexual access, labour and property, which societies combine differently, so no single definition fits all.
  • Gough's definition (1959): to include Nayar unions she defined marriage as a relationship between a woman and one or more persons that gives her children full birth-status rights, shifting the focus from the couple to the child's legitimacy.
  • Pater and genitor: in Nuer woman–woman marriage a woman pays bridewealth and becomes the social father, showing fatherhood to be a social role.

3. Rethinking family

  • Universality questioned: the Nayar taravad, where brothers, sisters and sisters' children formed the unit, did not fit Murdock's model; Melford Spiro (1954) raised the same question for the Israeli kibbutz. Such cases led some scholars to treat only the mother–child bond as universal.
  • Indian forms: the Khasi household centred on the youngest daughter (khadduh) and the patrilineal joint family show family form following descent and property.
  • Contemporary families: single-parent, live-in, transnational and same-sex families; in Supriyo Chakraborty v. Union of India (2023) the Supreme Court declined to recognise same-sex marriage, leaving it to Parliament.

4. Rethinking kinship

  • Critique of biology: David Schneider (American Kinship, 1968; A Critique of the Study of Kinship, 1984) showed that kinship studies rested on a Western idea of blood and procreation.
  • Relatedness: Janet Carsten (The Heat of the Hearth, 1997) showed that Malays of Langkawi create kinship by sharing rice and living in one house; kinship is made, not only given.
  • Reproductive technologies: Marilyn Strathern (Reproducing the Future, 1992) showed that IVF, donors and surrogacy split genetic, gestational and social parenthood; India's Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021, permits only altruistic surrogacy.

5. Rethinking social reproduction

  • Alliance: Claude Lévi-Strauss (The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1949) saw marriage as exchange linking groups; Gayle Rubin (1975) criticised the treatment of women as objects of exchange.
  • Property and power: Jack Goody (1973, 1976) linked dowry to plough agriculture and inheritance by daughters, and bridewealth to African hoe farming; Claude Meillassoux (1975) showed elders controlling bridewealth to reproduce their authority.
  • Caste: B.R. Ambedkar (Castes in India, 1916) identified endogamy as the mechanism that reproduces caste.
  • Gender: Jane Collier and Sylvia Yanagisako (1987) called for one analysis of gender and kinship.

The study of marriage variation moved anthropology from biological universals to cultural constructions of relatedness, and from functional stability to power and reproduction, insights that remain central as surrogacy, same-sex unions and migration reshape families.
free.upa-2025-an1-7b:
Neolithic RevolutionOasis theoryHilly flanks theoryBroad-spectrum revolution

From about 11,500 years ago, at the close of the Pleistocene, people in the Fertile Crescent began cultivating wheat and barley and later herding goats and sheep; food production also arose independently in China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea and Africa. V. Gordon Childe called this shift the Neolithic Revolution (Man Makes Himself, 1936). Explanations range from environmental and demographic to social and ideological theories.

1. Major theories

  • Climate trigger: the Younger Dryas cold phase (about 12,900–11,700 years ago) may have pushed the settled Natufian foragers of the Levant to cultivate wild cereals (Ofer Bar-Yosef).
  • Ritual first: monumental carved pillars at Göbekli Tepe, Turkey, built by foragers about 11,600 years ago (Klaus Schmidt), suggest that large gatherings encouraged cultivation.
  • Multiple centres: Nikolai Vavilov (1926) traced crops to several centres; most scholars now combine climate, sedentism, population and social factors that varied by region.
  • India: Mehrgarh in Baluchistan (from about 7000 BCE) shows barley, wheat and humped cattle; Burzahom in Kashmir has pit dwellings; the ash mounds of the Southern Neolithic (Utnur, Budihal) record cattle pastoralism.

2. How the new subsistence economy brought a revolution

  • Sedentism and population: reliable harvests and storage allowed permanent villages; births were spaced more closely and population grew.
  • Technology: polished stone celts, sickles, querns, pottery for storage and cooking, weaving and, later, the plough.
  • Surplus and inequality: stored grain created property, inheritance, chiefs and craft specialists, the base of Childe's Urban Revolution (1950).
  • Society and belief: territoriality, warfare, fertility cults and ancestor worship grew; women's work became tied to grain processing.
  • Environment and disease: forests were cleared, and close living with animals spread zoonotic infections.

3. A critical view

  • Health costs: skeletal studies (Mark Cohen and George Armelagos, 1984) show shorter stature, more caries, enamel defects and infections in early farmers; Jared Diamond called agriculture "the worst mistake in the history of the human race" (1987).
  • Revolution or evolution: the change took millennia, and Marshall Sahlins's idea of the original affluent society reminds us that foraging was not constant hunger.

No single cause explains food production; it emerged from interacting ecological, demographic and cultural factors. Its consequences, surplus, sedentism and inequality, laid the foundation of civilisation, at a cost to health and equality.
free.upa-2025-an1-7c:
Cradle of humankindRecent African originAdmixtureReticulate evolution

Charles Darwin reasoned in The Descent of Man (1871) that "it is somewhat more probable that our early progenitors lived on the African continent than elsewhere", because the gorilla and chimpanzee live there. Fossils, archaeology and genetics have since made Africa the cradle of both the hominin lineage and Homo sapiens. Yet Asian and European finds and admixture complicate the story.

1. Evidence for African centrality

  • Earliest hominins: Sahelanthropus (Chad, about 7 million years ago), Orrorin (Kenya, about 6 mya) and Ardipithecus ramidus (Ethiopia, 4.4 mya) are all African.
  • Australopithecines and early Homo: hominin fossils older than about 2 mya, such as the Taung child (1925), Lucy (A. afarensis, Hadar, 1974), the Laetoli footprints (3.66 mya) and Homo habilis at Olduvai, are known only from Africa.
  • First technology: Lomekwi 3 tools (3.3 mya), Oldowan tools at Nyayanga, Kenya (about 2.6–3.0 mya) and the earliest Acheulean handaxes (about 1.76 mya) are African.
  • Our species: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils are from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (about 315,000 years) and Omo Kibish, Ethiopia (at least 233,000 years); engraved ochre at Blombos Cave, South Africa (about 75,000 years) shows early symbolism.
  • Genetics: Africans are the most genetically diverse, mtDNA and Y-chromosome trees root in Africa, and diversity falls with distance from it (serial founder effect).

2. Critical issues

  • Early exits: small-brained Homo at Dmanisi and 2.1-million-year-old tools at Shangchen, China, show that hominins left Africa early; some evolution of Homo may have occurred in Asia.
  • Asian diversity: H. floresiensis, H. luzonensis (2019) and the Denisovans make Asia a second centre of hominin diversity. Ancient proteins and mtDNA (2025) indicate that the Harbin cranium (at least 146,000 years) was Denisovan. A 2025 study placed the Yunxian 2 skull (about 1 mya) on that lineage, pushing its split from sapiens beyond a million years; this rests on skull shape alone and clashes with younger genetic estimates.
  • Admixture: non-Africans carry about 2% Neanderthal DNA and Melanesians a few per cent Denisovan DNA, favouring Fred Smith's assimilation model over strict replacement.
  • No single cradle: Eleanor Scerri and colleagues (2018) argue that sapiens evolved across subdivided populations throughout Africa, not in one East African Eden.
  • Early sapiens outside Africa: Misliya, Israel (about 177,000–194,000 years) and the disputed Apidima 1, Greece (about 210,000 years).
  • Bias: finds cluster where Rift Valley sediments are exposed and datable; colonial-era scholars favoured non-African origins (Piltdown); African scientists remain under-represented.

3. The Indian dimension

  • Siwalik apes: Ramapithecus, once claimed as a human ancestor, is now placed in Sivapithecus on the orangutan line.
  • A corridor of dispersals: Acheulean tools at Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu (about 1.5 mya), Middle Palaeolithic tools there by about 385,000 years, Jwalapuram tools around the Toba eruption (about 74,000 years) and the Hathnora (Narmada) cranium show repeated dispersals into South Asia.

Africa remains central as the source of the hominin line, the first tools and our species. But human evolution was reticulate, a braided stream of dispersals and interbreeding across Afro-Eurasia with a larger Asian role than once thought.
free.upa-2025-an1-8a:
PostmodernismPower/knowledgeDeconstructionVoice and representation

Postmodernism questions grand theories and claims of objective truth; Jean-François Lyotard described it as "incredulity toward metanarratives" (The Postmodern Condition, 1979). In anthropology it arrived through Writing Culture (James Clifford and George Marcus, 1986), which showed ethnographies to be partial texts shaped by power. By asking who speaks for whom, it became a resource for social justice for women, Dalits, Adivasis, sexual minorities and colonised peoples.

1. Postmodern ideas relevant to justice

2. Relevance for social justice

  • Deconstructing stigma: the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871, branded whole communities criminal by birth; though they were denotified in 1952, the stigma persists. Foucauldian critique shows such categories as products of colonial power, and the Budhan Theatre of the Chhara community in Ahmedabad, supported by Mahasweta Devi and G.N. Devy, performs against it.
  • Critique of development discourse: Arturo Escobar (Encountering Development, 1995) and James Ferguson (The Anti-Politics Machine, 1990) showed how development talk depoliticises poverty and extends state control. This strengthens Adivasi claims, as at Niyamgiri, where the Supreme Court (2013) let Dongria Kondh gram sabhas decide on bauxite mining; all twelve rejected it.
  • Plural knowledges: rejecting a single standard of rationality legitimises oral history, indigenous knowledge and customary law, as recognised in the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) and India's Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Gender and sexuality: Judith Butler (Gender Trouble, 1990) treats gender as performative; the Supreme Court's NALSA (2014) and Navtej Singh Johar (2018) judgments affirmed gender and sexual diversity.
  • Intersectionality: Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) and Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint (1998) show caste, gender and class overlapping.

3. Empowerment through method

  • Reflexivity and polyphony: dialogic ethnographies such as Kevin Dwyer's Moroccan Dialogues (1982) share authorship with informants.
  • Decolonising research: Linda Tuhiwai Smith (Decolonizing Methodologies, 1999) demands research that is accountable to, and serves, indigenous communities.
  • Writing against culture: Lila Abu-Lughod (1991) warned that bounded culture concepts freeze difference and hierarchy, and urged ethnographies of particular lives.

4. Limits

  • Relativism: if all truths are equal, universal rights and claims of injustice lose a firm basis (Melford Spiro, Roy D'Andrade).
  • Textualism: a focus on discourse can neglect material inequality in land, wages and caste violence, as Marxist critics such as Terry Eagleton argued.
  • Fragmentation: identity politics may divide collective struggles; Nancy Scheper-Hughes (1995) urged anthropologists to put ethics first and stand with the oppressed.

Postmodernism offers no programme of justice by itself, but by unmasking power in knowledge and amplifying silenced voices it has strengthened rights-based movements. Joined to universal human dignity and material change, it supports an engaged, emancipatory anthropology.
free.upa-2025-an1-8b:
GWASSingle nucleotide polymorphismPolygenic riskPrecision medicine

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) scans hundreds of thousands to millions of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) across the genomes of many people with and without a disease or trait, to find variants that are more frequent in one group. Made possible by the Human Genome Project (completed 2003) and the HapMap catalogue of common variation, GWAS has since 2005 mapped thousands of loci for common, complex diseases.

1. How GWAS works

  • Hypothesis-free: unlike candidate-gene studies, it scans the whole genome without prior assumptions.
  • Indirect association: a marker SNP usually tags a nearby causal variant through linkage disequilibrium, so fine-mapping and functional work must follow.

2. How GWAS advanced understanding of health and disease

  • First successes: Robert Klein and colleagues (2005) linked the complement factor H gene to age-related macular degeneration, revealing a role for inflammation; the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) studied seven common diseases in 14,000 cases and 3,000 shared controls.
  • New biology: Crohn's disease loci (ATG16L1, IRGM, IL23R) pointed to autophagy and immune pathways; most type 2 diabetes loci act through insulin-secreting beta cells.
  • Polygenic architecture: common diseases involve hundreds or thousands of variants of small effect; polygenic risk scores can identify people at several-fold higher risk of coronary artery disease (Amit Khera and colleagues, 2018).
  • Pharmacogenomics: variants near IL28B predicted response to hepatitis C treatment (Ge and colleagues, 2009) and helped explain poorer response among people of African ancestry.
  • Causes and drugs: Mendelian randomisation uses GWAS variants to test causation, for example confirming LDL cholesterol but not HDL as a cause of heart disease; drug targets with genetic support succeed more often in trials.
  • Infection and evolution: a COVID-19 risk region on chromosome 3 was inherited from Neanderthals (Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020); a Greenlandic Inuit variant in TBC1D4 (2014) raises diabetes risk, showing population-specific architecture.

3. Indian and anthropological relevance

  • South Asians: a GWAS by Jaspal Kooner and colleagues (2011) found six new type 2 diabetes loci in people of South Asian ancestry; the GenomeIndia data (2025) of 9,772 genomes from 83 populations now provide a reference.
  • Endogamy: India's many endogamous groups carry founder variants, so population-specific studies can find recessive disorders.

4. Limitations

  • Eurocentric samples: in 2016 about 81% of GWAS participants were of European descent (Alice Popejoy and Stephanie Fullerton), so risk scores perform poorly in Africans and South Asians.
  • Missing heritability: identified SNPs explain only part of heritability; rare variants and gene–environment interactions are missed.
  • Association is not causation: effects are small, and results risk genetic determinism, stigma and misuse of race.

GWAS has moved medicine from single genes to polygenic and pathway thinking and laid the base for precision medicine. Anthropology adds needed cautions: diverse samples, attention to environment and culture, and vigilance against reviving race through genes.
free.upa-2025-an1-8c:
Forensic anthropologyBiological profileFacial reconstructionCraniofacial superimposition

Forensic anthropology applies physical anthropology and osteology to legal questions, above all identifying the dead and reconstructing how they died. T. Dale Stewart (Essentials of Forensic Anthropology, 1979) described it as the branch that identifies skeletonised remains for legal purposes, building on W.M. Krogman's The Human Skeleton in Forensic Medicine (1962). Because bones and teeth outlast soft tissue, human remains are often the only witness in murders, mass disasters and human-rights cases.

1. Utility of human remains

  • Human or not, and how many: bone shape and microscopic structure separate human from animal bones; duplicated elements give the minimum number of individuals.
  • Biological profile (the big four): sex from the pelvis (T.W. Phenice's three traits, 1969) and skull; age from tooth eruption, epiphyseal union, cranial sutures and the pubic symphysis (T. Wingate Todd, 1920); stature from long bones by regression formulae (Mildred Trotter and Goldine Gleser; N. Pan, 1924, for Indians); ancestry, estimated cautiously because variation is clinal.
  • Individual identity: healed fractures, dental work, implants with serial numbers, occupational markers and disease.
  • Cause and manner of death: trauma analysis separates ante-mortem, peri-mortem and post-mortem damage from blunt force, sharp weapons and bullets.
  • Time since death: decomposition, insects, weathering and scavenging help estimate the post-mortem interval.
  • DNA and isotopes: DNA from teeth and dense bone identifies individuals; oxygen and strontium isotopes show where a person grew up. In India, mtDNA and isotopes traced the Ajnala (Punjab) skeletons to Gangetic-plain soldiers killed in 1857 (2022), and ancient DNA showed South Asian and eastern Mediterranean groups among the Roopkund lake skeletons (2019).
  • Human rights: teams trained by Clyde Snow formed the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team (1984) to identify the disappeared.

2. The facial reconstruction technique

Forensic facial reconstruction (approximation) rebuilds the likely face of an unknown person on the skull, so that the public may recognise it when other leads fail.

  • History: Wilhelm His (1895) measured soft-tissue depths on cadavers to model J.S. Bach's face; Mikhail Gerasimov in Russia developed the anatomical method, modelling muscles (Tamerlane, 1941); Krogman (1946) popularised the tissue-depth method in the USA; Richard Neave's Manchester method combines both.
  • Forms: two-dimensional drawings over skull photographs, clay sculpture on a cast, and computer modelling from CT scans. Faces of two individuals from the Harappan cemetery at Rakhigarhi, Haryana, were reconstructed from CT data (2019).
  • Related method: craniofacial superimposition overlays the skull on a photograph of a missing person to test a match.

3. Limitations

  • Tissue-depth standards vary with age, sex, nutrition and population, and Indian data are limited.
  • Ears, lips, hair, skin colour and body weight cannot be read from bone, so a reconstruction only aids recognition; identity must be confirmed by DNA, dental records or superimposition.

Human remains speak for the dead, establishing identity, cause of death and justice, and facial reconstruction gives an unknown skull a recognisable face. With DNA and isotopes, forensic anthropology now serves criminal justice, disaster victim identification and historical inquiry.
free.upa-2025-an2-1a:
SoanianPebble toolsSiwalik terracesMovius Line

The Soanian (or Sohanian) is a Lower Palaeolithic pebble-tool tradition named after the Soan, a tributary of the Indus on the Potwar plateau, now in Pakistan. It was defined by Helmut de Terra and T.T. Paterson of the Yale–Cambridge expedition of 1935, who in Studies on the Ice Age in India and Associated Human Cultures (1939) linked the tools to river terraces of a supposed Himalayan glacial sequence.

1. Distinctive features

  • Pebble technology: rounded quartzite pebbles from the Upper Siwalik boulder conglomerate were flaked to give a cutting edge, while the smooth cortex served as the grip.
  • Tool kit: unifacial choppers, bifacial chopping tools, discoids, scrapers and simple flakes; hand-axes and cleavers are rare or absent.
  • Phases: de Terra and Paterson separated an Early Soan of rolled pebble tools on the higher terrace from a Late Soan with more flakes, some from prepared cores, on a lower terrace; Acheulian hand-axes also turned up at Chauntra in the same valley.
  • Setting: open-air sites on terraces and fans of the Siwalik frontal zone.

2. Distribution in India

  • Sub-Himalayan belt: the Beas and Banganga valleys of Kangra (Guler, Dehra), described by B.B. Lal (1956); the Sirsa valley near Nalagarh and the Chandigarh–Pinjore area, explored by G.C. Mohapatra; the Jammu foothills.
  • Wider spread: choppers also occur within peninsular Acheulian assemblages, so pebble tools are not unique to the north.

3. Significance and re-evaluation

  • Movius Line: Hallam Movius (1948) grouped the Soanian with a "chopper–chopping tool" complex of East and South-East Asia, set against the hand-axe world of Africa and western Eurasia.
  • Dating revised: Robin Dennell and Helen Rendell's re-survey of the Potwar in the 1980s rejected the glacial-terrace scheme; many Soanian pieces are surface finds, and several assemblages are Middle or Late Pleistocene.
  • Facies, not a people: Soanian and Acheulian tools are now found together in the Siwalik frontal zone, so many scholars treat the Soanian as a raw-material or activity facies rather than a separate, older culture.
  • Early claims: artefacts at Riwat (Pakistan, about 2 mya) and cut-marked bones at Masol near Chandigarh (about 2.6 mya, reported in 2016) keep the question of the first toolmakers open, but both claims are contested.

The Soanian is best understood as a pebble-tool facies of the Lower Palaeolithic in the Siwalik zone. It shaped the early history of Indian prehistory and the Movius debate, but its age and its separateness from the Acheulian still need firm dating.
free.upa-2025-an2-1b:
Dominant casteFactionalismVote bankPoliticisation of caste

M.N. Srinivas first used the idea of the dominant caste in "The Social System of a Mysore Village" (1955) and developed it in "The Dominant Caste in Rampura" (American Anthropologist, 1959). Caste domination, internal factionalism and political power form a chain: the dominant caste controls the village, its rival factions compete for that control, and electoral democracy has carried the contest to district and state politics.

1. Caste domination

  • Attributes: a caste dominates when it is numerically strong, owns much of the arable land, wields political power and holds a fairly high ritual rank; Srinivas later added Western education, government jobs and urban income.
  • Examples: Okkaligas in Rampura and Lingayats in Karnataka, Reddis and Kammas in Andhra, Jats in Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, Marathas in Maharashtra and Patidars in Gujarat.
  • Exercise of power: it settles disputes, sets local norms and controls patronage, as Jat khap panchayats do.

2. Factionalism

  • Nature: Ralph Nicholas (1965) described factions as political conflict groups that are not corporate; a leader recruits followers through kinship, patronage, debt or economic dependence.
  • Inside the dominant caste: Srinivas found factionalism endemic within the dominant caste. Rival leaders belong to it and draw followers vertically from lower castes, so factions cut across caste lines. Oscar Lewis (Village Life in Northern India, 1958) found Jat factions in a village near Delhi organised along lineage lines.
  • Triggers: land disputes, panchayat polls, schemes and party rivalry.

3. Political power

  • Vote bank: Srinivas coined the term in 1955 for the bloc of votes a patron could deliver; factions became the local units of party politics, as Paul Brass showed for the Congress in Uttar Pradesh (1965).
  • Politicisation of caste: Rajni Kothari (Caste in Indian Politics, 1970) argued that caste was organised for politics while politics drew on caste loyalties; the Rudolphs (1967) saw caste associations as vehicles of democratic participation.
  • Shifting power: André Béteille (Caste, Class and Power, 1965) showed power in Sripuram passing from Brahmin landlords to non-Brahmin politicians, separating power from ritual rank.
  • Challenges: reserved seats in panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992) and assertion by Dalits and backward classes now contest old dominance, sometimes provoking violent backlash.
  • Critique: later village studies found power resting with a few lineages or leaders rather than the whole caste, and A.C. Mayer (1958) showed that dominance often works across a region rather than within one village.

Domination, faction and power form a single cycle in rural India. Democratic decentralisation has widened access to office, but it has also turned caste into a resource for electoral mobilisation.
free.upa-2025-an2-1c:
RegionalismAutonomySixth ScheduleEthnic identity

Regionalism is attachment to a region defined by language, ethnicity, history or economic interest, expressed as a demand for a larger share of power and resources. Autonomy is the institutional response: self-government within the Union, ranging from statehood to autonomous councils under the Sixth Schedule. Anthropologists read both as the politics of ethnic boundaries (Fredrik Barth, Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, 1969), not merely as threats to unity.

1. Roots of regionalism

  • Language and culture: the Telugu agitation, climaxing in Potti Sriramulu's death after a fast in 1952, produced Andhra State (1953) and the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
  • Uneven development: a sense of internal colonialism, where resources leave but benefits do not return, drove the Jharkhand (2000) and Telangana (2014) movements and the Vidarbha demand.
  • Ethnic and tribal identity: Naga, Mizo and Bodo movements rested on distinct histories, customary law and fear of being outnumbered by migrants; Myron Weiner called this "sons of the soil" politics (1978).
  • Elite competition: regional parties and educated tribal elites turn cultural grievances into political demands, often by mobilising language, history and symbols of a homeland.

2. Forms of autonomy in India

3. Assessment

  • Accommodation works: the Mizo Accord (1986) turned an insurgency into statehood; linguistic states defused early separatism; councils protect land, customary law and language.
  • Problems: autonomy is often captured by the dominant tribe or elite; minorities inside autonomous areas feel excluded, as in clashes in the Bodoland area (2012, 2014); councils depend on state funds.
  • Current debate: Ladakh, a Union Territory without a legislature since 2019, has sought statehood and Sixth Schedule safeguards. In May 2026 the Centre agreed in principle to an elected UT legislature with Article 371-type safeguards, but in October 2026 the Leh Apex Body and Kargil Democratic Alliance rejected the Home Ministry's draft as too weak, and talks were continuing.

Regionalism becomes divisive when ignored but strengthens the Union when channelled into federal accommodation. Real devolution of funds and powers, with protection for minorities within regions, is the key to keeping autonomy a means of integration.
free.upa-2025-an2-1d:
Verrier ElwinA Philosophy for NEFATribal PanchsheelIntegration

Verrier Elwin (1902–1964), ethnographer of the Baiga, Muria and Saora of central India, was appointed Adviser for Tribal Affairs to the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), today's Arunachal Pradesh, in 1954. His book A Philosophy for NEFA (1957; second edition 1959, with a foreword by Jawaharlal Nehru) laid down a middle path between isolation and assimilation that guided administration of the frontier.

1. From protection to integration

  • Central Indian phase: in the late 1930s Elwin argued for protected areas, a kind of "national park", for the most vulnerable groups; G.S. Ghurye (1943) attacked this as isolationist and called tribes "backward Hindus".
  • NEFA phase: among the Adi, Apatani, Mishmi, Nyishi and Monpa he moved to integration: the tribes should join national life, but on their own terms and at their own pace.

2. Core principles of his philosophy

  • Neither museum nor melting pot: he rejected both freezing tribal life and forcing it into the plains model.
  • Protection of land and forests: the Inner Line (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873) was retained to keep out moneylenders, traders and land-grabbers.
  • Work through tribal institutions: village councils such as the Adi kebang and the Apatani buliang were to be strengthened, not replaced.
  • Local cadre, few outsiders: officers of the Indian Frontier Administrative Service were expected to learn local languages and respect custom, and tribal youth were to be trained to run their own affairs.
  • Pride in culture: dress, weaving, architecture, dance and oral tradition were to be encouraged; his Myths of the North-East Frontier of India (1958) and The Art of the North-East Frontier of India (1959) documented them.

3. Assessment

  • Achievements: Arunachal's communities retained most of their land and a confident identity, with far less land alienation than in central India.
  • Criticism: the approach was called paternalistic and slow; roads and economic growth lagged, a weakness exposed in the 1962 war, and later generations sought faster change.
  • Legacy: NEFA became a Union Territory as Arunachal Pradesh (1972) and a state (1987); Elwin's emphasis on consent, land rights and self-governing institutions anticipates PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).

Elwin's NEFA philosophy turned his anthropology into policy: integration with dignity. Its central lesson, that development must respect cultural autonomy, still guides tribal policy in the North-East.
free.upa-2025-an2-1e:
Robert RedfieldUniversalisationParochialisationCultural media

Robert Redfield (Peasant Society and Culture, 1956) held that "In a civilization there is a great tradition of the reflective few, and there is a little tradition of the largely unreflective many." The Chicago school, notably McKim Marriott and Milton Singer, applied this idea to India, treating Indian civilisation as a continuous exchange between a textual, all-India tradition and countless local, folk traditions.

1. Characteristics

2. Channels of communication

  • Universalisation and parochialisation: in Kishan Garhi (Uttar Pradesh), Marriott ("Little Communities in an Indigenous Civilization", 1955) showed local elements rising upward: the wall-drawn goddess Saurti was identified with Lakshmi at Diwali, and the local Saluno rite with Raksha Bandhan. Elements of the great tradition also moved downward: Navaratri became the worship of a single mud goddess, Naurtha, and Krishna's Govardhan became a cow-dung mound, Gobardhan.
  • Cultural performances and specialists: studying Madras, Singer (When a Great Tradition Modernizes, 1972) traced how recitations, devotional singing, dance and temple festivals, carried by priests, storytellers and musicians, translate texts into popular forms.
  • Sacred centres: L.P. Vidyarthi's The Sacred Complex in Hindu Gaya (1961) showed sacred geography, rituals and priests linking pilgrims from every region to the textual tradition.
  • Social processes: Sanskritisation (Srinivas), the absorption of tribes into Hindu society (N.K. Bose, 1941) and Surajit Sinha's studies of tribal little traditions show traffic in both directions.
  • Modern media: vernacular epics such as the Ramcharitmanas, print, TV serials and now social media carry great-tradition themes into homes and bring local cults to wider audiences.

3. Critique

  • One civilisation: Louis Dumont and David Pocock (1957) argued that the two levels cannot be cleanly separated in India.
  • Cultural bias: Yogendra Singh (Modernization of Indian Tradition, 1973) noted that the model explains orthogenetic, internal change but neglects structural and external sources of change.
  • Hierarchy assumed: Dalit and tribal traditions are treated as "little", though they form great traditions of their own.

The model remains a useful lens on India's cultural continuity: a civilisation held together by constant two-way communication between text and village, not by a single uniform culture.
free.upa-2025-an2-2a:
Siwalik GroupSivapithecusRamapithecus debateHaritalyangar and Ramnagar

The Siwaliks are the outermost foothills of the Himalaya, built of river sediments shed into the foreland basin as the mountains rose from the Middle Miocene to the Middle Pleistocene (roughly 18 to 0.2 mya). Their long, well-dated fossil record, first described by Hugh Falconer and Proby Cautley in Fauna Antiqua Sivalensis (1840s), makes them the richest source of Miocene apes in Asia and India's key evidence for hominoid evolution.

1. The three-fold Siwalik sequence

  • Three-fold scheme: Guy Pilgrim (1913) divided the Siwalik Group into Lower, Middle and Upper Siwaliks; their formations are named after type sections on the Potwar plateau.
  • Changing environments: the sediments record a shift from moist forest to open, seasonal woodland and grassland.

2. Fossil primate fauna

  • Sivapithecus: Richard Lydekker described a Siwalik ape palate in 1879, and Pilgrim named Sivapithecus indicus (1910). Thick molar enamel and robust jaws suggest hard foods; David Pilbeam's GSP 15000 face from Potwar (1982), with its concave profile and narrow space between the eyes, links it to the orangutan lineage.
  • "Ramapithecus": G.E. Lewis named R. brevirostris (1934) from a maxilla found near Haritalyangar in 1932. In the 1960s Elwyn Simons and Pilbeam presented it as the earliest hominid; complete jaws with a V-shaped tooth row and molecular dates for the human–ape split led to its merger with Sivapithecus.
  • Giant ape: Simons and S.R.K. Chopra (1969) described Gigantopithecus bilaspurensis from a near-complete mandible near Haritalyangar; it is now often called Indopithecus giganteus, a relative of the Chinese G. blacki.
  • Kapi ramnagarensis: a lower molar from Ramnagar about 13 mya, described by Christopher Gilbert and colleagues (2020), is the earliest known gibbon, extending the lesser-ape record by about five million years.
  • Strepsirrhines and monkeys: Sivaladapis, Indraloris and Ramadapis are among the last adapiform primates; cercopithecid monkeys dominate the Upper Siwaliks.

3. Major primate fossil localities

  • Haritalyangar (Bilaspur–Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh): late Miocene, about 9 mya; Ramapithecus type area, Indopithecus, Sivapithecus, Indraloris; worked by Yale and Panjab University teams.
  • Ramnagar (Udhampur, Jammu and Kashmir): Chinji-age beds of about 13–12 mya; Sivapithecus, Kapi, Sivaladapis, Ramadapis.
  • Pinjor–Chandigarh belt (Haryana, Punjab): Upper Siwalik mammals and monkeys; Masol, where cut-marked bones of about 2.6 mya were claimed (2016), a disputed report.
  • Beyond India: the Potwar plateau (Pakistan) and Tinau Khola (Nepal).

4. Palaeoanthropological significance

  • Ape radiation in Asia: great and lesser apes reached South Asia by about 13 mya; Sivapithecus belongs to the orangutan branch, not to human ancestry.
  • Method lesson: the Ramapithecus episode showed the danger of reconstructing ancestry from fragments and the value of molecular evidence.
  • Climate and extinction: carbon isotopes in Siwalik soils show C4 grasslands replacing forests around 8–7 mya, when apes vanish from the record.
  • Human prehistory: Upper Siwalik terraces carry Soanian and Acheulian tools, linking the primate record with early toolmakers.

The Siwaliks are a natural laboratory of hominoid evolution: they record the arrival, diversification and extinction of Asian apes and frame the search for the earliest hominins of South Asia.
free.upa-2025-an2-2b:
S.S. SarkarCephalic indexRisley's nasal indexRacial typology

S.S. Sarkar (Sasanka Sekhar Sarkar), an Indian physical anthropologist, classified the peoples of India in The Aboriginal Races of India (1954) into six ethnic elements, using mainly head form (cephalic index) with stature, skin colour, hair and nose. His scheme came half a century after H.H. Risley's seven-fold classification in the Census of India, 1901 and The People of India (1908).

1. Major features of Sarkar's classification

  • Six elements: Australoid, Indo-Aryan, Irano-Scythian, Munda-speaking, Far Eastern and Mongolian.
  • Long-headed majority: he found India mainly dolichocephalic; broad-headedness was regional, which contradicted B.S. Guha's widespread brachycephalic element.
  • Australoid base: he saw the Australoid (Veddid) as the oldest layer, best preserved among tribes of south and central India such as the Paniyan, Kadar and Urali, and present in many castes.
  • No mainland Negrito: a study of the Kadar by his team (1959), using measurements, blood groups, finger-prints and hair, found no Negrito element; he confined Negritos to the Andaman Islands.
  • Munda and eastern elements: he recognised the Munda-speaking peoples of Chota Nagpur and a Far Eastern (Malayan) element on the eastern margins as distinct strands.

2. Risley's scheme in brief

  • Seven types: Turko-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Scytho-Dravidian, Aryo-Dravidian, Mongolo-Dravidian, Mongoloid and Dravidian.
  • Method and theory: he measured castes and tribes, relied chiefly on the nasal index, and held that a caste's social rank varied inversely with its nasal index, reading caste as a product of Aryan conquest and race mixture.

3. Was Sarkar's classification better?

  • Yes, in method: Sarkar did not treat castes as races, dropped speculative hybrid types such as "Scytho-Dravidian", tested the Negrito claim with several kinds of data, and identified an Australoid base and a separate Munda element that later work broadly supports.
  • Less colonial bias: Risley's census ranking of castes served administrative purposes; Sarkar's scheme carried no social hierarchy.
  • But equally typological: both assumed fixed racial types; head form is plastic, as Franz Boas (1912) showed among immigrants' children, and Sarkar still mixed language labels (Indo-Aryan, Munda-speaking) with biology.
  • Superseded by genetics: Lewontin (1972) found most human variation within populations, and genome studies (Reich and colleagues, Nature, 2009; Narasimhan and colleagues, Science, 2019) show Indians as mixtures of Ancestral North and South Indian components, the latter with deep local hunter-gatherer roots.

Sarkar's scheme was more scientific and less hierarchical than Risley's, but both belong to the age of racial typology. Today the peopling of India is studied through population genetics, which treats variation as continuous rather than as fixed races.
free.upa-2025-an2-2c:
Missionary encounterLiteracy and scriptEthnic identityRevival of indigenous faith

Christianity reached the hills of North-East India through American Baptist and Welsh Presbyterian missions in the nineteenth century, under colonial protection. It is now the majority faith in Nagaland (87.9%), Mizoram (87.2%) and Meghalaya (74.6%), and large in Manipur (41.3%) and Arunachal Pradesh (30.3%) (Census 2011). Its impact on Scheduled Tribe societies is deep and mixed.

1. Education, literacy and language

  • Script and standard languages: missionaries gave Khasi, Mizo, Ao, Garo and other languages a Roman script, grammars and Bible translations, creating written literatures.
  • Literacy: mission schools made the region's Christian-majority states highly literate; Mizoram recorded 91.3% literacy in 2011.
  • New elite: educated converts became teachers, officials and political leaders, giving tribes a voice in modern institutions.

2. Changes in social life

  • Old institutions weakened: the end of headhunting (with colonial law), the decline of feasts of merit, rice-beer rituals and youth dormitories such as the Naga morung followed conversion.
  • Health and welfare: mission dispensaries and hospitals reduced deaths from epidemics; churches and bodies such as the Young Mizo Association (1935) run welfare and community work.
  • Gender: girls gained schooling, yet customary councils remain male; Nagaland held urban local body elections with women's reservation only in 2024 after long resistance.
  • Peace-building: church leaders mediated in the Mizo and Naga conflicts and supported the Mizo Accord (1986).

3. Identity and politics

  • Pan-tribal identity: a shared faith and English helped scattered Naga clans and villages see themselves as one people, feeding Naga nationalism.
  • Conversion as choice: Richard Eaton (Indian Economic and Social History Review, 1984) showed that Naga Christianity grew fastest after 1947, when foreign missionaries had largely left; as colonial rule widened their world, Nagas identified their own high god with the Christian God, as Robin Horton's theory of conversion predicts.
  • New rifts: denominational rivalries and converts versus non-converts create tension within villages and tribes.

4. Loss and revival of indigenous faiths

  • Erosion: oral rituals, priests and ancestor rites faded in converted areas; Verrier Elwin criticised missions for discouraging dance, rice beer and dormitories.
  • Revitalisation: Seng Khasi (1899) among the Khasi, Heraka among the Zeliangrong (Jadonang and Rani Gaidinliu), Donyi-Polo among the Adi and Rangfraism among the Tangsa in Arunachal reassert indigenous religion.
  • Current debate: after a 2024 Gauhati High Court direction, Arunachal began framing rules under its 1978 anti-conversion law; a high-powered committee submitted its recommendations in June 2026 amid church protests, while indigenous-faith groups press for the rules to be notified.

Christianity brought literacy, health and a modern identity to North-East tribes but also eroded older institutions and created new fault lines. A balanced view sees conversion as a tribal adaptation to change, and supports cultural pluralism that respects both church and indigenous faiths.
free.upa-2025-an2-3a:
Blade-and-burin industryBone toolsOstrich eggshellLate Pleistocene

The Upper Palaeolithic of India belongs to the later Upper Pleistocene, broadly c. 40,000 to 10,000 years ago, and is associated with Homo sapiens. Its hallmarks are a blade-and-burin technology on finer stone, the first bone tools, and the earliest ornaments and art. Its study took shape through M.L.K. Murty (Renigunta, 1968), S.A. Sali (Patne) and G.R. Sharma (Belan valley).

1. Distinctive features

  • Blades and burins: long, parallel-sided blades were struck from prismatic cores and turned into backed blades, burins, end-scrapers, borers and points, some tanged. Indian assemblages often mix flakes and blades ("flake-blade" industries), and blades are less standardised than in Europe.
  • Finer raw material: toolmakers moved from coarse quartzite towards chert, jasper and chalcedony; tools became smaller and more symmetrical.
  • Bone tools: the Kurnool caves, Billa Surgam (first dug by Robert Bruce Foote in 1884) and Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi, yielded bone scrapers, perforators, chisels and shouldered points, with a hearth dated to about 17,000 BP.
  • Ornament and art: ostrich eggshell beads and engraved fragments come from Patne (Jalgaon, Maharashtra), central India and Rajasthan; a carved bone object from Lohanda Nala (Belan) was read by G.R. Sharma as a mother-goddess figure, though this is debated; the earliest green and dark-red paintings at Bhimbetka are often assigned to this period.
  • Ritual: at Baghor I in the Son valley a natural triangular stone with concentric bands stood on a rubble platform (Kenoyer, Clark, Pal and Sharma, 1983); Kol and Baiga people still worship such stones as the mother goddess.
  • Environment and economy: a cold, arid phase peaking around 20,000 years ago spread dunes in the Thar; people hunted wild cattle, deer and other game, gathered plants and camped near rivers, lakes and rock shelters.
  • Overlap with microliths: microblade industries at Jwalapuram 9 (Andhra Pradesh) begin about 35,000 years ago, so many scholars prefer the term Late Palaeolithic.

2. Distribution

  • Pattern: sites cluster on river terraces, lake margins, dunes and rock shelters of the peninsula and the Vindhyas; the Ganga alluvium and the North-East are largely blank, owing to deep sediments and limited survey.
  • Open-air factory sites lie close to sources of fine stone, while rock shelters show repeated seasonal use.

3. Significance

  • Modern human behaviour: blades, bone tools, beads and art in India parallel the Upper Palaeolithic elsewhere and reflect the spread of Homo sapiens.
  • Continuity: the same rock shelters and valleys carry on into the Mesolithic, and the Baghor parallel shows the value of ethnoarchaeology.

The Indian Upper Palaeolithic is thus a regionally varied blade and microblade tradition that adapted to a harsh late-glacial climate and laid the foundation for the Mesolithic way of life.
free.upa-2025-an2-3b:
Biocultural approachSickle cell and malariaForest ecologyHealth culture

Tribal health in India, among 10.4 crore Scheduled Tribe people (Census 2011), reflects the interplay of habitat, genes and culture that medical anthropology calls the biocultural approach. The Expert Committee on Tribal Health (chaired by Dr Abhay Bang, 2018) found tribal people bearing about 30% of India's malaria cases and a tuberculosis prevalence of 703 per lakh against 256 elsewhere.

1. Environmental factors

  • Forest and hill ecology: shaded forest streams breed malaria vectors, so falciparum malaria concentrates in tribal Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
  • Zoonoses: forest dwellers face Kyasanur Forest Disease (identified in Karnataka in 1957), snakebite and animal attacks.
  • Water and soil: unsafe water causes diarrhoea; iodine-poor hill soils once made goitre common.
  • Remoteness: scattered hamlets, poor roads and vacant posts in rural health centres delay care.
  • Ecological change: deforestation, dams and mines take away forest foods, as seen in child deaths among the Korku of Melghat and the Irula of Attappadi; Bhil migrants from Jhabua and Alirajpur have developed silicosis in Gujarat's quartz-crushing units.

2. Biocultural factors

  • Sickle cell gene: first reported in India among Nilgiri tribes (Lehmann and Cutbush, 1952), it is frequent among central Indian groups such as Bhil, Gond and Pawara. A.C. Allison (1954) showed the trait protects against falciparum malaria, so gene and environment have evolved together.
  • Small endogamous groups: G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia and genetic drift in very small PVTGs raise inherited disorders; cross-cousin marriage in some southern groups adds to it.
  • Food culture: millets, tubers, greens, mahua and red-ant chutney once gave a varied diet; the shift to polished rice and packaged food brings anaemia, hypertension and diabetes. NFHS-5 (2019–21) found 40.9% of ST children stunted (35.5% nationally) and 64.6% of ST women anaemic (57%).
  • Alcohol and tobacco: rice beer (handia) and mahua liquor have ritual value, but commercial liquor and tobacco harm health.
  • Beliefs about illness: sickness is often traced to spirits, deities or sorcery, so the healer (gunia, ojha) is consulted first; L.P. Vidyarthi's nature–man–spirit complex (The Maler, 1963) captures this worldview.
  • Reproductive customs: early marriage, home births, food restrictions in pregnancy and menstrual huts among the Madia Gond raise risks to mothers and infants.
  • Positive heritage: the Kani of Kerala shared knowledge of the herb arogyapacha, which led to the drug Jeevani under a benefit-sharing arrangement.

3. Responses

  • Sickle cell mission: launched at Shahdol on 1 July 2023 with elimination by 2047 as the goal, it had screened over 7.19 crore people, diagnosed over 2.46 lakh patients and identified more than 20 lakh carriers by June 2026; genetic counselling cards guide marriage choices.
  • Culturally sensitive care: the Bang Committee proposed local health workers (Aarogya Mitras), a Tribal Malaria Action Plan and a Tribal Health Index; training healers and traditional birth attendants and home-based newborn care (pioneered by SEARCH, Gadchiroli) build trust.

Tribal health cannot be improved by hospitals alone: it needs secure forest rights and food systems, genetic screening and services that work with, not against, local health culture.
free.upa-2025-an2-3c:
B.S. GuhaIrawati KarveS.R.K. ChopraIndian anthropology

In the mid-twentieth century Indian anthropology grew from colonial ethnography into a discipline with its own institutions. B.S. Guha built its physical anthropology and its national survey, Irawati Karve opened up kinship and caste from an Indian standpoint, and S.R.K. Chopra made India a centre of research on fossil primates of the Siwaliks.

1. B.S. Guha (1894–1961)

  • Training: after a Harvard PhD (1924) on the racial basis of the caste system, he joined the anthropological section of the Zoological Survey of India (1927).
  • Racial survey: using anthropometric data from the 1931 Census, he published The Racial Affinities of the Peoples of India (1935) and Racial Elements in the Population (1944), recognising six main races with sub-types, from the Negrito (seen in the Kadar) and Proto-Australoid to the Nordic; he used Karl Pearson's coefficient of racial likeness.
  • Institution builder: he headed the Anthropological Survey of India, set up in 1945, as its first Director (1946–1954), founded the Indian Anthropological Institute (1936) and later directed the Bihar Tribal Research Institute, Ranchi.
  • Applied work: he led a multidisciplinary study of social tensions among refugees from East Pakistan and advised on tribal welfare; later he called racial purity a myth.

2. Irawati Karve (1905–1970)

  • Physical anthropology: her doctorate at Berlin (1930), under Eugen Fischer, studied asymmetry in the human skull; her anthropometric surveys of Maharashtra showed that castes of one region differ from one another.
  • Kinship: Kinship Organisation in India (1953) mapped four zones: a northern zone of distant, exogamous marriage and hypergamy; a southern zone of cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriage; a central mixed zone; and an eastern zone of Munda and other groups.
  • Caste: in Hindu Society: An Interpretation (1961) she treated caste as an extended kin group, endogamous within a linguistic region, formed by the incorporation of separate groups rather than by the splitting of the four varnas.
  • Village and text: Group Relations in Village Community (1963) studied inter-caste ties; Yuganta (1967), which won the Sahitya Akademi Award, read the Mahabharata as a human, social document.
  • Institution: as head of Sociology and Anthropology at Deccan College, Pune (from 1939), she trained a generation of scholars and stands as India's pioneer woman anthropologist.

3. S.R.K. Chopra

  • Department builder: he founded the Department of Anthropology at Panjab University, Chandigarh, in 1960 as its first head; its Museum of Man now bears his name.
  • Siwalik primates: with Elwyn Simons of Yale he described Gigantopithecus bilaspurensis (1969) from a near-complete mandible found near Haritalyangar, Himachal Pradesh.
  • Further finds: with R.N. Vasishat he reported a fossil tree shrew from Haritalyangar (Nature, 1979), and joint Yale–Panjab University teams kept adding Siwalik primate fossils to the Ramapithecus debate.
  • School of research: Panjab University became a hub for Siwalik palaeontology and prehistory with international links.

Together they gave Indian anthropology its institutional base, an Indian reading of kinship and caste, and a place in world palaeoanthropology. Their racial typologies have been superseded by genetics, but their surveys, fieldwork and institutions endure.
free.upa-2025-an2-4a:
SanskritisationWesternisationPositional changeCaste associations

Caste mobility is the movement of a caste, a section of it, or its members up or down a local hierarchy. Classical writers saw caste as closed, but M.N. Srinivas, in his 1952 monograph on the Coorgs, showed that groups had always tried to rise, mainly through Sanskritisation. Such change was usually positional: a caste moved, but the hierarchy itself remained.

1. Types of caste mobility

  • Sanskritisation: a lower caste adopts the customs, rituals and beliefs of a higher caste and, after a generation or two, claims a higher rank; the model may be Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya or the locally dominant caste. Claims succeed only when backed by wealth or power.
  • Kshatriyisation: K.M. Panikkar argued that the Kshatriya category was repeatedly filled by successful rulers; tribal chiefs among the Bhumij, Gond and Munda built Rajput genealogies, and Shivaji's coronation (1674) followed a ritual claim to Kshatriya status.
  • Westernisation: Srinivas (Social Change in Modern India, 1966) described the adoption of British-period education, dress, technology and values; upper castes gained first, others followed.
  • De-Sanskritisation and backward status: the Self-Respect and Dravidian movements rejected Brahminical models; today Jats, Patidars and Marathas seek backward-class status, a mobility strategy that runs opposite to Sanskritisation.
  • Downward mobility: outcasting for breaking rules of marriage or food, ruin of artisan castes under factory competition and loss of land after zamindari abolition lowered the standing of groups and families.

2. Factors responsible

  • Economic opportunity: new wealth from trade, cash crops, liquor or migration is the usual first step. F.G. Bailey (Caste and the Economic Frontier, 1957) showed Distillers in Bisipara (Odisha) buying land and seeking higher rank, and Robert Hardgrave (The Nadars of Tamilnad, 1969) traced the Nadars' rise from palmyra-tapping to trade and Kshatriya claims.
  • Political power: historically, conquest and kingship turned chiefs into Kshatriyas; today numbers count in elections, dominant castes control panchayats and Mandal politics (1990) gave backward classes a share in power.
  • Education and new occupations: colonial schools, the army, railways, mills and the professions opened jobs that did not depend on caste.
  • Colonial census: when the 1901 Census ranked castes, many petitioned for higher varna titles; Srinivas likened census entries to old royal grants of rank.
  • Caste associations and reform movements: the SNDP Yogam (1903) under Sree Narayana Guru lifted the Ezhavas; the Rudolphs (The Modernity of Tradition, 1967) showed caste associations working as democratic pressure groups.
  • Constitution and law: abolition of untouchability (Article 17), reservation in education, jobs and legislatures, and the Prevention of Atrocities Act (1989) protect and promote mobility.
  • Urbanisation and migration: anonymity of cities and remittances weaken ritual barriers.

Resistance persists, from refusal of claims to violence against Dalit assertion. Louis Dumont called the present trend the substantialisation of caste: castes now act as competing interest groups rather than ranked parts of a ritual whole, and mobility is increasingly structural rather than merely positional.
free.upa-2025-an2-4b:
Demographic transitionPopulation momentumUniversal marriageSon preference

India's population rose from 36.1 crore in 1951 to 121.1 crore in Census 2011, and India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimates). Growth followed the demographic transition: deaths fell decades before births, and social institutions kept fertility high long after mortality declined. Census 2027, with 1 March 2027 as its reference date, will update the count.

1. Demographic factors

  • Mortality decline: famine relief, control of malaria, smallpox and cholera, antibiotics and immunisation cut deaths; the crude death rate is now 6.4 and infant mortality 24 per 1,000 (SRS 2024).
  • Lagging fertility: women had about six children in the 1950s; the total fertility rate fell to 2.0 in NFHS-5 (2019–21) and 1.9 in SRS 2024, but for decades births far outran deaths.
  • Natural increase: a crude birth rate of 18.3 against a death rate of 6.4 (SRS 2024) still adds about 1.2% a year.
  • Population momentum: past high fertility created a large cohort of young adults, so births stay numerous even at replacement fertility; growth will continue for several more decades.
  • Regional contrast: Bihar (TFR 2.9 in SRS 2024) and other north-central states drive future growth, while Delhi (TFR 1.2) and the southern states are below replacement.
  • Family planning gaps: use of any method is about 67% (NFHS-5), with heavy reliance on female sterilisation late in the reproductive span.

2. Social factors

  • Universal and early marriage: almost every woman marries, and 23.3% of women aged 20–24 married before 18 (NFHS-5), lengthening childbearing years.
  • Son preference: couples continue having children until a son is born, for lineage, old-age support and funeral rites; the sex ratio at birth remains skewed.
  • Economic value of children: Mahmood Mamdani (The Myth of Population Control, 1972) showed that in a Punjab village large families were rational for poor peasants who needed labour and security; John Caldwell's wealth-flows theory makes a similar point.
  • Status of women: Dyson and Moore (1983) linked the lower fertility of the south to greater female autonomy; schooling, delayed marriage and paid work reduce births.
  • Religion and community: NFHS-5 found total fertility of 1.94 for Hindus and 2.36 for Muslims; the gap is narrowing and reflects education and income more than doctrine.
  • Kinship pressure: joint households and the mother-in-law's authority limit women's reproductive choices.
  • High child mortality in the past: where infants often died, families had extra children as insurance, a habit that outlived the fall in deaths.

3. Policy responses

  • From targets to choice: coercion during the Emergency (1975–77) bred distrust; the target-free approach (1996) and the National Population Policy (2000) stress informed choice.
  • Social levers: the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (2006), girls' schooling and Mission Parivar Vikas (2016) in high-fertility districts address the social roots.

India's growth is now driven less by high fertility than by population momentum and regional gaps. Since fertility is embedded in marriage, kinship and gender, lasting change depends on women's education and autonomy rather than coercion.
free.upa-2025-an2-4c:
Article 342Lokur criteriaTribe as a social categorySelf-identification

The Constitution does not define a tribe. Article 366(25) defines Scheduled Tribes as communities deemed to be so under Article 342: the President notifies them for each state after consulting the Governor, and only Parliament can amend the list. The Lokur Committee (1965) framed the working tests used by administrators: primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact with the wider community, and backwardness.

1. The concept: anthropological views

  • Classical definitions: Lewis Henry Morgan (Ancient Society, 1877) saw the tribe as a stage of evolution; D.N. Majumdar stressed a common name, territory, language, marriage rules and mutual obligations.
  • Tribe or backward Hindu: G.S. Ghurye (1943) called tribes "backward Hindus", while N.K. Bose (1941) described the Hindu method of tribal absorption; Surajit Sinha saw a tribe–caste continuum.
  • No clear boundary: André Béteille (1986) argued that no single test separates tribe from caste in India; Virginius Xaxa stresses that tribes are distinct societies with their own identity, not merely backward groups.
  • Tribe as a product of the state: Morton Fried (The Notion of Tribe, 1975) argued that many tribes are secondary formations shaped by contact with states; Indian categories grew out of colonial censuses.
  • Indigeneity: India backed the UN declaration on indigenous peoples (2007) but treats all citizens as indigenous; many communities identify as Adivasi.

2. The administrative concept

  • Colonial lineage: "animists" (Census 1901), "hill and forest tribes" (1921), "primitive tribes" (1931) and "backward tribes" (Government of India Act, 1935) fed into the first ST Order of 1950.
  • State-specific lists: a community is scheduled only in particular states; Census 2011 counted 10.43 crore STs (8.6%) in about 705 notified communities.

3. Limitations of the administrator's criteria

  • Evolutionist and condescending: "primitive traits" and "shyness of contact" echo colonial evolutionism; the 2014 Task Force under Hrusikesh Panda called the criteria obsolete.
  • Vague and subjective: "primitive" or "distinctive" cannot be measured, and the Registrar General leans on old census ethnographies; self-identification plays no formal role.
  • Static view of culture: education, Christianity or Hindu practices and urban life mean that many listed groups, such as the Mizo, Khasi or Meena, no longer fit a literal reading, while other isolated groups remain outside the list.
  • Inconsistency across states: Santhal, Munda, Oraon and Gond workers in Assam's tea gardens are not STs there though they are in Jharkhand.
  • Political pressure: demands by strong groups, such as Gujjars in Rajasthan, six communities in Assam, the Paharis of Jammu and Kashmir (listed in 2024) and the Meitei claim before the Manipur violence of 2023, often outweigh criteria.
  • Blind to inequality: benefits concentrate among advanced STs while the 75 PVTGs lag, as the Xaxa Committee (2014) noted.
  • Reform stalled: the Task Force proposed socio-economic backwardness, historical isolation, a distinct language, a core culture and endogamy, but the Registrar General still applies the 1965 tests.

The ST category is a politico-administrative construct resting on dated anthropology. Transparent criteria that combine evidence of distinct identity with measurable deprivation, and that respect self-identification, would make scheduling fairer.
free.upa-2025-an2-5a:
IndustrialisationDevelopment-induced displacementProletarianisationIdentity assertion

Most of India's mines, steel plants and big dams stand on tribal land in the central and eastern belt, so industrialisation and the urbanisation that follows it reached tribes earlier and harder than most groups. Census 2011 still found about 90% of Scheduled Tribes in villages, but towns such as Jamshedpur, Rourkela, Bokaro and Ranchi have reshaped the lives of Santal, Ho, Munda and Oraon communities.

1. Economic impact

  • Land alienation and displacement: The Xaxa Committee (2014) notes the general agreement that about 40% of people displaced by development projects are tribals, though they form only 8.6% of the population. Cash compensation is soon spent, leaving families without land to fall back on.
  • Proletarianisation: Cultivators and gatherers become unskilled, often casual, wage workers who compete with migrants from outside. L.P. Vidyarthi's study of the Hatia industrial complex near Ranchi (Socio-cultural Implications of Industrialization in India, 1970) traced this shift from field to factory.
  • Distress migration: Seasonal migrants to brick kilns, construction sites and urban domestic work face debt, low wages and abuse, women and girls most of all.

2. Socio-cultural impact

  • Weakening of institutions: Clan elders, village councils and youth dormitories such as the Oraon dhumkuria lose their hold when people scatter to labour colonies and slums.
  • Cultural change: Language shift, new consumption habits and Hindu or Christian influence reshape ritual life. Martin Orans (The Santal: A Tribe in Search of a Great Tradition, 1965) showed Santals of the Jamshedpur belt adopting high-status Hindu practices to improve their rank in an industrial setting.
  • Health and environment: Mining dust, polluted streams and the loss of forest foods worsen health and nutrition.

3. Positive outcomes

  • Education and mobility: Schools, reserved jobs in public-sector units and urban exposure created an educated tribal middle class in Ranchi, Shillong and Aizawl.
  • Political consciousness: Educated leaders gave voice to the Jharkhand movement (State formed in 2000) and to resistance such as the Dongria Kondh rejection of bauxite mining in the Niyamgiri hills after the Supreme Court left the decision to gram sabhas (2013).

Industrialisation has given tribals wages and visibility but at the cost of land and autonomy. Honest implementation of PESA (1996), FRA (2006), the Samatha judgment (1997) and the consent and social impact assessment clauses of the 2013 land acquisition law, with mineral revenue shared through District Mineral Foundations, can turn displacement into inclusive development.
free.upa-2025-an2-5b:
RamapithecusSivapithecusMolecular clockPonginae

Ramapithecus is a Miocene hominoid from the Siwalik Hills. G. Edward Lewis collected its type upper jaw in the Siwaliks of Bilaspur State (present Himachal Pradesh) on the Yale North India Expedition of 1932 and named it Ramapithecus brevirostris ("short-snouted") in 1934. For two decades it was hailed as the earliest hominid; today it is merged with Sivapithecus (named by Guy Pilgrim in 1910), an Asian ape of the orangutan line.

1. The case for hominid status (1960s and early 1970s)

  • Simons and Pilbeam: From the 1960s Elwyn Simons, later joined by his student David Pilbeam, reassembled the fragmentary jaws and described a short face, small canines, a rounded (parabolic) dental arcade and thick molar enamel, all read as human-like traits.
  • An early split: Similar jaws from Fort Ternan in Kenya (Kenyapithecus, L.S.B. Leakey, 1962) seemed to show a hominid lineage about 14 million years old.
  • Ecological story: Thick enamel was read as adaptation to tough foods of open woodland.

2. The controversy

  • Molecular clock: Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson (1967), comparing blood albumins, placed the split of humans from African apes at about 5 million years ago (mya), far too late for a 14-million-year-old hominid.
  • New fossils: More complete jaws from the Potwar Plateau of Pakistan (1975–76) showed a V-shaped, ape-like arcade; Pilbeam himself gave up the hominid claim.
  • The orangutan link: Pilbeam's 1982 description of a Sivapithecus face (GSP 15000) showed a concave profile, narrow-set orbits and other orangutan features, and Peter Andrews and John Cronin (1982) placed both genera on the orangutan line.

3. Present taxonomic status

  • A junior synonym: Because Sivapithecus is the older name, specimens once called Ramapithecus are now placed in Sivapithecus; the smaller jaws are probably females of a strongly sexually dimorphic ape.
  • Pongine, not hominin: Sivapithecus (about 12.5–8.5 mya) is grouped with the orangutan in the subfamily Ponginae. Its limb bones, however, are unlike an orangutan's (Pilbeam and colleagues, 1990), so even this link is debated.
  • Range in India: A Sivapithecus upper jaw about 11 million years old, collected in Kutch (Gujarat) in 2011, extends the genus south of the Siwaliks.

The episode shows how fragmentary fossils can mislead and how molecular and fossil evidence correct each other. Ramapithecus is now an Asian ape of the orangutan lineage, not a human ancestor; the hominin lineage began in Africa about 7–6 mya.
free.upa-2025-an2-5c:
TribalismPseudo-tribalismEthnic boundaryST status claims

Tribalism is a strong sense of loyalty to one's own tribe or ethnic group, expressed in identity, solidarity and political action. Pseudo-tribalism is the attempt by groups without a tribal history or way of life to claim tribal identity, mainly to obtain Scheduled Tribe (ST) status and its benefits. Both show that tribal identity is also a political resource.

1. Tribalism: meanings and forms

  • Anthropological usage: Max Gluckman (1960) saw tribalism in Central African mining towns as a new urban form of grouping, not a rural survival, and Clyde Mitchell's The Kalela Dance (1956) showed tribe working as a category of interaction in Copperbelt towns.
  • Positive tribalism in India: Pride in land, language and custom drives the Jharkhand movement, pan-Adivasi solidarity and the demand for a separate Sarna religious code (Jharkhand Assembly resolution, 2020).
  • Negative tribalism: Exclusive loyalties can turn into inter-ethnic violence, as in the Naga–Kuki clashes of the 1990s and Bodo–Adivasi clashes in Assam (1996, 1998).
  • Critique of the term: Archie Mafeje ("The Ideology of Tribalism", 1971) argued that colonial writers used "tribalism" to hide class and political conflict; many scholars prefer "ethnicity".

2. Pseudo-tribalism: forms and causes

  • Contested claims for ST status: The Gujjars of Rajasthan agitated in 2007–08, but the Justice Jasraj Chopra Committee (2007) found that they did not meet ST criteria; six communities of Assam (Tai Ahom, Moran, Matak, Chutia, Koch-Rajbongshi and tea tribes) seek ST status against the opposition of existing STs.
  • False certificates and similar names: Groups sharing a name with a listed tribe, such as Koshti weavers claiming to be Halba, obtain certificates; in State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2000) the Supreme Court held that the ST list cannot be widened by courts, and in FCI v. Jagdish Balaram Bahira (2017) that benefits gained by false claims must be withdrawn.
