  • Causes: Reservation turns backwardness into a valued status, a process Marc Galanter analysed in Competing Equalities (1984); the vague Lokur criteria (1965) invite such claims.

3. Consequences

  • For genuine tribes: Benefits leak to better-off claimants, and fear of new entrants hardens boundaries, as in Assam and Manipur.
  • For policy: It calls for transparent, ethnographic criteria and verification by scrutiny committees, as laid down in Kumari Madhuri Patil (1994).

Tribalism as identity can serve self-determination, while pseudo-tribalism, though rooted in real deprivation, dilutes protections meant for the most marginal. Periodic, anthropologically grounded review of ST criteria and strict certificate checks can balance both.
free.upa-2025-an2-5d:
Varnashrama dharmaAshramaPurusharthaLife-course

Varnashrama dharma joins two Brahmanical schemes: varna, the fourfold ordering of society (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) first described in the Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda (X.90), and ashrama, the four stages of an individual's life set out in the Dharmasutras and the Manusmriti. Together they prescribed each person's duty (svadharma) according to social position and stage of life.

1. The scheme

  • Varna: an ideal allocation of work into learning and ritual, rule and protection, trade and agriculture, and service, each with its own dharma; in practice thousands of endogamous jatis were ranked by reference to it.
  • Ashrama: an ideal life of about a hundred years divided into four stages, each linked to the purusharthas (dharma, artha, kama, moksha) and to repaying the three debts (rinas) to gods, sages and ancestors.
  • Socio-psychological design: P.H. Prabhu (Hindu Social Organization, 1954) read the ashramas as a training of the person: discipline first, then worldly fulfilment, then gradual withdrawal.

2. Critique

  • Hierarchy and exclusion: The scheme applied fully only to men of the three twice-born varnas; Shudras and women were largely denied upanayana and the student stage.
  • Varna versus jati: M.N. Srinivas (Caste in Modern India, 1962) treated varna as a simplified all-India model of a regionally varied jati reality, and Irawati Karve (Hindu Society: An Interpretation, 1961) held jati, not varna, to be the real unit.
  • Ambedkar and Gandhi: Ambedkar's Annihilation of Caste (1936) rejected chaturvarnya as the root of graded inequality, while Gandhi defended varna as duty without privilege.

3. Contemporary relevance

  • Varna is constitutionally rejected: Articles 14, 15 and 17 deny any rank by birth, though varna labels survive in endogamy, Sanskritisation claims and caste associations.
  • Ashrama as life-course wisdom: Planning life in stages fits lifelong learning (NEP 2020), work–life balance and an ageing India, where people over 60 may form about a fifth of the population by 2050 (UNFPA India Ageing Report 2023); vanaprastha suggests active ageing and mentoring rather than isolation.
  • Ethics of restraint: The movement from acquisition to renunciation gives a cultural basis for mindful consumption, the idea behind Mission LiFE (2022).

As a hierarchy of birth, varna has no place in a constitutional democracy; as an ideal of stages of life and duties to society, the ashrama scheme still offers a humane framework for education, family, ageing and restraint.
free.upa-2025-an2-5e:
LothalHarappan dockyardMeluhhaMaritime trade

Lothal, in Saragwala village of Ahmedabad district near the Gulf of Khambhat, was excavated by S.R. Rao of the Archaeological Survey of India between 1955 and 1960. This small Harappan town, which flourished about 2400–1900 BCE, is famous for a large brick basin that Rao identified as the earliest known dockyard, and for clear evidence of trade with the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia.

1. The dockyard

  • Structure: a trapezoidal basin roughly 220 m long and 37 m wide on the eastern side of the town, lined with burnt bricks, with an inlet from an old river channel and a spillway to control the water level.
  • Linked facilities: a brick wharf along the basin led to a warehouse on a high platform; stone anchors and terracotta boat models support the idea of boats docking here.
  • Debate: Lawrence Leshnik (1968) argued that the basin was a freshwater reservoir for irrigation and drinking water. A 2024 study by IIT Gandhinagar, using satellite data, traced an old channel of the Sabarmati close to Lothal, strengthening the case for navigation.

2. Crafts that fed trade

  • Bead factory: workshops with furnaces and drills turned carnelian and agate, from sources such as Ratanpur, into long beads prized abroad.
  • Shell, copper and ivory: conch-shell bangles and inlays, copper tools and ivory objects were made for exchange.
  • Measures and seals: standard chert weights, a finely marked ivory scale and clay sealings with marks of cords and packing in the warehouse show that goods were measured, sealed and dispatched.

3. International trade relations

  • The Mesopotamian record: Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334–2279 BCE) boasted that ships from Meluhha, Magan (Oman) and Dilmun moored at his capital; Meluhha is generally identified with the Indus region.
  • Routes: Lothal linked the Indus heartland and Dholavira, through the Little Rann and the Saurashtra coast, to the Gulf of Khambhat and then along the Makran coast to Magan and Dilmun.
  • Goods: likely exports were beads, shell, ivory, cotton cloth and timber; imports probably included copper, silver and other raw materials.

Whether dock or reservoir, Lothal shows that the Harappans used maritime routes to reach the Gulf and Mesopotamia, making it India's earliest evidence of seaborne trade. The National Maritime Heritage Complex project at Lothal now builds on this legacy.
free.upa-2025-an2-6a:
André BéteilleVillage as a civilisational designHierarchy and interdependenceVillage studies

The statement is by André Béteille, in his essay "The Indian Village: Past and Present" (in Peasants in History, 1980). He argued that in Indian thought the village was not only a settlement but an ideological category: its layout, institutions and relations were seen as a miniature of Indian civilisation, which is why administrators, nationalists and anthropologists all made it their favourite unit.

1. The village as a design: values built into space and institutions

  • Hierarchy in space: Castes lived in separate streets ranked by ritual purity. In Sripuram, the Tanjore village of Béteille's Caste, Class and Power (1965), Brahmins lived in the agraharam, non-Brahmins in their own streets and Adi-Dravidas in the cheri outside the main settlement.
  • Holism and interdependence: The jajmani system, described by William Wiser (The Hindu Jajmani System, 1936), tied landowning patrons and service castes in hereditary exchange of grain for services, giving the village what Srinivas called vertical unity.
  • Purity and the sacred: Village deities, shrines and festivals made the village a ritual community; Louis Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus (1966) explains its ranking by the opposition of purity and pollution.
  • Authority and kinship: Caste and village panchayats settled disputes, and north Indian village exogamy made the village a kinship unit.
  • Link with the wider civilisation: Robert Redfield's little and great traditions (Peasant Society and Culture, 1956) and McKim Marriott's Kishan Garhi study (in Village India, 1955) showed the village where local and all-India traditions meet.

2. How this image was built

  • Colonial administrators: Charles Metcalfe's minute (1830) called villages "little republics", and Henry Maine (Village-Communities in the East and West, 1871) saw them as survivals of archaic communities.
  • Nationalists: Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909) and his ideal of gram swaraj made the self-reliant village the moral core of India. Ambedkar replied: "What is the village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism?" (Constituent Assembly, 4 November 1948).
  • Anthropologists: The 1950s village studies (Srinivas, S.C. Dube's Indian Village on Shamirpet, Marriott, D.N. Majumdar) used the village as a window on society.

3. Critical appraisal

  • Myth of the isolated republic: Srinivas ("The Indian Village: Myth and Reality", 1975) showed villages were tied to markets, towns and rulers.
  • Village or caste? Dumont and David Pocock ("Village Studies", 1957) argued that caste ties spreading across villages, not the village, form the real social unit.
  • Harmony hid domination: The design was largely an upper-caste ideal; for Dalits it meant segregation, the point of Ambedkar's critique.

4. The design today

  • Erosion: Decline of jajmani, land reforms, Dalit assertion, the Seventy-third Amendment (1992) with reserved panchayat seats, migration and rurbanisation have weakened the old design, though caste-wise settlement persists.
  • Continuity: Census 2011 counted 68.8% of Indians as rural; the village remains a base of identity, kinship and politics.

Béteille's remark explains why the village became the lens for understanding India: it embodied hierarchy, interdependence and sacred order. Yet it was as much an ideal as a reality, and the constitutional village of equal citizens and panchayat democracy is slowly redrawing it.
free.upa-2025-an2-6b:
NGOsWeaker sectionsEmpowermentIntermediary institutions

Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are voluntary, non-profit bodies registered as societies, trusts or not-for-profit companies. For the weaker sections (Scheduled Castes and Tribes, women, landless labourers, minorities and persons with disabilities) they act as intermediaries between communities and the state, market and courts, and often reach places where public services are thin.

1. Socio-economic development

  • Livelihoods and credit: SEWA (Ela Bhatt, 1972) organised self-employed women into a union and cooperatives; MYRADA's self-help groups inspired NABARD's SHG–Bank Linkage Programme (1992), the base of today's DAY-NRLM; PRADAN (1983) builds SHGs and farm livelihoods among tribals of Jharkhand and Odisha.
  • Health: SEARCH (Abhay and Rani Bang, Gadchiroli, 1986) showed that trained village women could deliver home-based newborn care, a model later taken up for ASHA workers.
  • Education and skills: Pratham's ASER surveys (since 2005) track children's learning, and Barefoot College, Tilonia (1972) trains rural women as solar engineers.

2. Political development and empowerment

  • Transparency and rights: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS, Rajasthan, 1990) held public hearings (jan sunwai) on village accounts, a campaign that led to the RTI Act (2005) and social audits under MGNREGA.
  • Dalit and tribal rights: Navsarjan Trust (Gujarat, 1989) and the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights (1998) document atrocities and press for use of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act; Ekta Parishad's land marches (Jan Satyagraha, 2012) pushed land reform onto the agenda.
  • Legal empowerment: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984) made the release and rehabilitation of bonded labourers a constitutional duty.
  • Grassroots leadership: Training women and SC/ST members elected to reserved panchayat seats deepens local democracy.

3. Facilitating other stakeholders

  • Bridge and translator: NGOs turn schemes into local language and practice and carry field realities back into policy; NITI Aayog's NGO Darpan portal registers them for partnerships.
  • Watchdog: Social audits, report cards and public hearings make officials and contractors answerable.

4. Limitations

  • Accountability: Donor dependence and weak transparency invite misuse; the FCRA amendment of 2020 capped administrative spending of foreign grants at 20% and barred passing them on to other NGOs.
  • Depoliticisation: James Ferguson (The Anti-Politics Machine, 1990) and Arturo Escobar (Encountering Development, 1995) warn that development agencies can turn questions of land and power into technical projects.
  • Uneven reach: NGOs cluster in accessible areas, and elite-led bodies may speak for, rather than with, the poor.

NGOs have become a third sector that extends the reach of the state and gives the weaker sections a voice. Transparent funding, community leadership and partnership with gram sabhas can make them catalysts of empowerment rather than substitutes for public action.
free.upa-2025-an2-6c:
Other Backward ClassesArticle 340Mandal CommissionArticle 342A

Other Backward Classes (OBCs) are the "socially and educationally backward classes" of Articles 15(4) and 340 that are neither Scheduled Castes nor Scheduled Tribes. There is a Central List for Union jobs and institutions and a separate State List in each State. Their identification has moved from colonial communal orders to commission-led, data-based methods under Article 342A.

1. History: before and after the Constitution

  • Precursors: Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur reserved half the posts for backward communities (1902); Mysore (Miller Committee, 1918) and the Madras Communal Government Order (1921) favoured non-Brahmins; the Starte Committee of Bombay (1930) used the term "other backward classes".
  • Constitution: Article 340 provided for a commission of inquiry, and the First Amendment (1951) added Article 15(4) after State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan.
  • Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953–55): listed 2,399 backward castes using caste rank, education and representation in services, trade and industry; the Centre did not accept it and in 1961 left the States to frame their own lists.

2. National level: from Mandal to the NCBC

  • Mandal Commission (1979–80): applied 11 indicators, social (3 points each), educational (2 each) and economic (1 each), to field surveys; castes scoring 11 of 22 points were backward. It listed 3,743 castes, estimated OBCs at 52% of the population and recommended 27% reservation, notified on 13 August 1990.
  • Indra Sawhney (1992): upheld the 27% quota with exclusion of the "creamy layer" and a 50% ceiling, and asked for a permanent body, leading to the National Commission for Backward Classes Act (1993).
  • Central List: the first list (1993) took castes common to the Mandal list and the State lists; later inclusions follow NCBC hearings and field enquiries.
  • Constitutional reform: The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave the NCBC constitutional status (Article 338B) and inserted Article 342A; after Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil (2021) read it as ending State power, the 105th Amendment (2021) restored the States' own lists.

3. State level: methods

  • State commissions: Anantharaman (Andhra Pradesh, 1970), Sattanathan (Tamil Nadu, 1970), Havanur (Karnataka, 1975) and Mungeri Lal (Bihar, 1976) used caste surveys, school and service data and hearings.
  • Sub-categories: Andhra Pradesh divides OBCs into BC-A to BC-E, Tamil Nadu has BC and MBC lists, and Bihar separates extremely backward classes (Karpoori Thakur formula, 1978).
  • Data requirement: Courts insist on current, quantifiable data, for example a dedicated commission for local-body quotas (Vikas Kishanrao Gawali, 2021); State caste surveys such as Bihar's (2023) try to supply it.

4. Current issues

  • Creamy layer: The income limit has stood at ₹8 lakh since 2017, and in Union of India v. Rohith Nathan (March 2026) the Supreme Court held that income alone cannot decide creamy-layer status; the parent's post must also count.
  • Data: Census 2027 (population count due February 2027) will enumerate caste, the first full caste count since 1931.

OBC listing has evolved from communal orders to commission-based, data-driven identification within a cooperative federal design. Reliable caste data, periodic review with exclusion of advanced groups and fair sub-categorisation are needed to keep the lists true to social justice.
free.upa-2025-an2-7a:
Tribal developmentTop-down planningApplied anthropologyCulturally appropriate development

Tribal development in India rests on Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, the Tribal Sub-Plan (1974–75), PESA (1996), FRA (2006) and missions such as PM-JANMAN (2023) and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024). Yet the Xaxa Committee (2014) found Scheduled Tribes still at the bottom of most indicators. Anthropology, which studies tribes from within, can narrow the gap between policy and people.

1. Contemporary limitations

  • Persistent gaps: ST literacy was 59% against 73% for all Indians (Census 2011), and 45.3% of rural STs were below the poverty line in 2011–12 against 25.7% of all rural people. Anaemia, malnutrition and sickle-cell disease remain high, which led to the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023).
  • Land and displacement: Mines, dams and protected areas still uproot tribals, who form about 40% of people displaced by projects (Xaxa Committee).
  • Weak implementation of protective laws: Several States framed PESA rules late; forest-rights claims, especially community forest resource rights, are often rejected or delayed; and gram sabha consent is bypassed.
  • Top-down, uniform schemes: Plans drawn up in capitals ignore local ecology and culture, as with houses unsuited to hill climates, schooling only in the State language, or cash crops that displace food crops.
  • Leakage and inequality within tribes: Tribal Sub-Plan funds are diverted or underused, and better-off groups capture benefits while PVTGs lag behind.
  • Conflict and distrust: Left-wing extremism in central India and ethnic conflict in the North-East disrupt services and weaken trust in the state.

2. How anthropological knowledge can contribute

  • Holistic baseline: Ethnography reveals livelihoods, kinship, land tenure and customary law, so that plans fit people. The Anthropological Survey of India's People of India project (led by K.S. Singh) and the State Tribal Research Institutes hold such knowledge.
  • The insider's (emic) view and participation: Participatory rural appraisal (Robert Chambers) and gram sabha planning, as in the Tribal Village Vision 2030 plans adopted by special gram sabhas in about one lakh tribal villages under the Adi Karmayogi Abhiyan (2025), build plans on community priorities.
  • Culturally appropriate delivery: Mother-tongue-based multilingual schooling, as in Odisha's tribal-language programme, cooperation with traditional healers and use of clan and village councils raise acceptance of schools and health care.
  • Predicting the costs of displacement: Michael Cernea's Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model (1997) and social impact assessment under the 2013 land acquisition law help anticipate and prevent impoverishment.
  • Policy and advocacy: Verrier Elwin's advice, reflected in the Panchsheel principle that tribes should develop "along the lines of their own genius", Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf's work among the Chenchus and Gonds and B.D. Sharma's role in shaping PESA show anthropologists influencing policy.

The core limitation is that tribal development is still largely done for tribes, not with them. Anthropology's holistic, participatory and comparative insight can make schemes culturally appropriate and rights-based, so that development strengthens rather than erodes tribal identity.
free.upa-2025-an2-7b:
EthnicityEthnic boundarySons of the soilConflict resolution

An ethnic group shares a sense of common descent, culture, language or religion and of difference from others. Ethnic conflict arises when such boundaries become lines of competition over land, jobs, power and recognition. Fredrik Barth (Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, 1969) showed that it is the boundary, more than the cultural content, that groups maintain and mobilise.

1. Rising ethnic conflicts: recent examples

  • Manipur: The worst recent case: besides 306 deaths and 49 missing to 31 August 2026 (State Home Minister in the Assembly), about 58,800 people had been displaced by March 2026 (State home department), and the hill–valley divide has hardened.
  • The North-East pattern: Older Naga–Kuki and Bodo–Adivasi conflicts show how demands for homelands pit neighbouring groups against each other.

2. Causes

  • Competition for scarce resources: Land, forests and jobs; Myron Weiner (Sons of the Soil, 1978) traced nativist movements to competition between local people and migrants in Assam and elsewhere.
  • Politics of recognition: Demands for ST status, territorial councils or new States turn identities into vote banks; Paul Brass (Ethnicity and Nationalism, 1991) stressed how elites manipulate ethnic symbols (instrumentalism).
  • Primordial attachments: Clifford Geertz (1963) saw ties of blood, language and religion as deeply felt givens that new states must accommodate.
  • Migration and demographic fear: Fear of being outnumbered, as in Tripura and Assam, and porous international borders.
  • Weak civic links and misinformation: Ashutosh Varshney (Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life, 2002) found that towns with associations cutting across communities stay peaceful; rumours on social media and armed groups magnify violence.

3. Remedial measures

  • Constitutional accommodation: Sixth Schedule councils, the special arrangements of Article 371 and negotiated accords (Bodo 2020, Karbi Anglong 2021) give autonomy without secession.
  • Dialogue and reconciliation: Inclusive peace talks with all groups, truth-telling and civil-society peace committees, like Mumbai's mohalla committees after the 1992–93 riots.
  • Impartial security and justice: Disarming militias, neutral forces, fast-track trials, and return and rehabilitation of displaced families.
  • Equitable development: Fair sharing of land, jobs and public investment; secure land and forest rights under PESA and FRA reduce zero-sum competition.
  • Shared civic spaces: Mixed schools, markets, cooperatives and associations, as Varshney suggests; anthropologists can map grievances and help mediate.

India's ethnic conflicts are products less of diversity itself than of competition, politicised identity and weak institutions. The Indian model of unity in diversity, with federal autonomy, dialogue and inclusive development, has settled several conflicts and remains the best remedy.
free.upa-2025-an2-7c:
Nation-stateImagined communitiesIndigenous peoplesState-nation

A nation-state is a sovereign state whose people are assumed to form one nation, sharing culture, language or history, so that political and cultural boundaries coincide. The model grew in Europe after the Peace of Westphalia (1648) and the French Revolution and, through decolonisation, became the world's standard political unit. For indigenous peoples it has meant both protection and loss.

1. The concept

2. Critical evaluation

  • Myth of homogeneity: Walker Connor ("Nation-Building or Nation-Destroying?", 1972) showed that very few states are ethnically homogeneous, so nation-building often meant suppressing minorities.
  • Simplifying people: James C. Scott (Seeing Like a State, 1998) shows how states make people "legible" through census, cadastral maps and fixed names; his The Art of Not Being Governed (2009) describes upland peoples of Southeast Asia (Zomia) who long kept states at a distance.
  • Order without the state: Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer (1940) and Pierre Clastres (Society Against the State, 1974) show stateless societies keeping order, questioning the state's universality.
  • Strengths: The nation-state provides citizenship, rights, a common market and the machinery for welfare and protection.
  • Alternative: India is better described as a state-nation (Stepan, Linz and Yadav, Crafting State-Nations, 2011), which accommodates many cultural nations within one state.

3. Impact on indigenous societies

  • Territory and resources: Eminent domain, forest laws (Indian Forest Acts of 1878 and 1927) and mining turned commons into state property; elsewhere the doctrine of terra nullius justified dispossession until Australia's Mabo judgment (1992).
  • Borders dividing peoples: Nagas and Kuki-Zo-Chin peoples live across the India–Myanmar border and Santals across the India–Bangladesh border; fencing and curbs on the Free Movement Regime (2024) strain their kinship and trade.
  • Assimilation: National languages, schools and religions press on indigenous cultures; Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) called its residential schools cultural genocide. In India, Verrier Elwin's early protectionism (The Loss of Nerve, 1941) contrasted with G.S. Ghurye's view of tribes as "backward Hindus" (1943).
  • Classification and citizenship: Census categories and ST lists fix fluid identities, and citizenship verification unsettles border communities.
  • Militarisation: Insurgency and laws such as AFSPA (1958) have shaped life in parts of the North-East.
  • Protection and recognition: The same state offers safeguards (Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA, FRA) and international norms such as ILO Convention 107 (ratified by India in 1958) and UNDRIP (2007); India voted for UNDRIP but holds that all its citizens are indigenous, using the category Scheduled Tribes instead.

The nation-state is a powerful but historically recent form that rarely fits the cultural map. For indigenous societies it has been a source of both dispossession and protection; plural, federal state-nation arrangements with self-governance and free, prior and informed consent offer a fairer balance.
free.upa-2025-an2-8a:
Nilgiri systemToda, Kota, Kurumba, IrulaJajmani-like exchangeCulture change

The Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu are a classic case of multi-ethnic interdependence: the pastoral Toda, artisan Kota and forest-dwelling Kurumba and Irula (all now PVTGs), with the farming Badaga, were bound by hereditary exchange of goods, services and rituals. W.H.R. Rivers (The Todas, 1906) and David Mandelbaum ("Culture Change among the Nilgiri Tribes", 1941) documented this jajmani-like system.

1. Ecological and occupational specialisation

  • Toda: buffalo herders of the high grassland, living in hamlets (mund) with sacred dairies; buffaloes and milk products were their wealth and ritual medium.
  • Kota: artisans and musicians living in seven villages, who made iron tools, pottery, baskets and woodwork and played music at ceremonies.
  • Kurumba: forest dwellers of the slopes, with sub-groups such as Alu, Palu, Betta, Jenu and Mullu Kurumba; they gathered honey and forest produce and were feared as sorcerers and valued as healers.
  • Irula: gatherers and cultivators of the lower slopes, credited with magical power, some serving as priests at local shrines.
  • Badaga: farmers who settled in the hills after the fall of Vijayanagara (1565) and supplied grain to all.

2. Nature of the interdependence

  • Economic reciprocity: Goods moved by barter and hereditary partnership; each Badaga family had its Kota associate and each Badaga village its Kurumba watchman, paid by a grain levy.
  • Ritual complementarity: Kota music was essential at Toda and Badaga funerals; a Kurumba acted as auxiliary priest at Badaga sowing and harvest festivals, and Todas sought Kurumba help against sorcery.
  • A ranked order: The system resembled caste: Todas claimed ritual purity, Kotas ranked low as meat-eating artisans, and Kurumbas and Irulas stood apart but were feared. A legend even made the Toda, Kota and Kurumba descendants of three brothers bound to serve each other.
  • Fear as social control: Belief in Kurumba sorcery kept exchanges going but also provoked 19th-century violence against them.

3. Changes in the interrelationships

  • Colonial settlement: After John Sullivan's entry (1819) and the growth of Ootacamund, tea and coffee plantations, roads and markets drew the hills into a cash economy.
  • Badaga ascendancy: Badaga numbers grew fast and they turned to tea, potatoes and vegetables, ending dependence on Toda ghee and Kota crafts.
  • Kota mobility: Reformers such as K. Sulli (Mandelbaum's informant) led Kotas to drop stigmatised customs such as buffalo sacrifice at funerals; many moved into schooling, government jobs and farming.
  • Toda transformation: Land allotment from 1843, shrinking pastures, conversion of some families to Christianity (from 1904), and new livelihoods such as potato farming and embroidery (Geographical Indication, 2013).
  • Kurumba and Irula: Most now work as plantation or forest labourers; protected areas such as Mudumalai and the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986) limit forest use, while plains Irulas earn from snake-catching through a cooperative (1978).
  • New links: Barter has given way to markets and State schemes, though ritual ties survive at some funerals and festivals.

The Nilgiri case shows how ecological niches and ritual bound distinct communities into one regional system. Market integration has replaced interdependence with independence, but also with marginality for the smaller groups; PVTG policy must secure their land, languages and heritage.
free.upa-2025-an2-8b:
MinorityNon-dominanceArticles 29 and 30Linguistic and religious diversity

Sociologically, a minority is a group set apart and treated unequally because of its religion, language, culture or physical traits. Louis Wirth (1945) defined it as "a group of people who, because of their physical or cultural characteristics, are singled out from the others in the society in which they live for differential and unequal treatment". The key test is non-dominance, not mere numbers.

1. Defining minority

  • Wagley and Harris (1958): unequal treatment, distinctive traits, ascribed membership, endogamy and awareness of shared disadvantage.
  • The UN view: Francesco Capotorti (1977) described a minority as numerically smaller and non-dominant, with distinct ethnic, religious or linguistic traits and a sense of solidarity to preserve them; Article 27 of the ICCPR (1966) protects such groups.
  • Indian Constitution: It does not define the term but protects religious and linguistic minorities (Articles 29, 30, 350A and 350B). Under the National Commission for Minorities Act (1992) the Centre notified Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Parsis (1993) and Jains (2014).
  • State-wise test: In T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002) the Supreme Court held that minority status is judged State by State; Hindus are thus a minority in States such as Punjab, Mizoram and Nagaland, and Maharashtra notified Jews as a minority in 2016.

2. Patterns of religious minorities

  • Regional concentration: Muslims are a majority in Jammu and Kashmir (68.3%) and Lakshadweep (96.6%) and a large share in Assam, West Bengal and Kerala; Christians are a majority in Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya; Sikhs in Punjab (57.7%). About three-quarters of Buddhists live in Maharashtra, mostly following the conversion led by Ambedkar at Nagpur in 1956.
  • Dispersed and tiny minorities: Jains are spread through western and central India and are highly urban; Parsis (about 57,000 in 2011) face decline, addressed by the Jiyo Parsi scheme.
  • Internal diversity: Caste-like ranking exists among Muslims (ashraf, ajlaf, arzal; Imtiaz Ahmad, Caste and Social Stratification among Muslims in India, 1973), and there are Dalit Christians and Mazhabi Sikhs.
  • Unequal status: The Sachar Committee (2006) found Muslims behind in education and formal jobs; Jains and Parsis are among the most advanced.

3. Patterns of linguistic minorities

  • Linguistic States and their minorities: The States Reorganisation Act (1956) made language the basis of States, so every State has linguistic minorities; the Seventh Amendment (1956) created the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (Article 350B).
  • Scale: Census 2011 grouped mother tongues into 121 languages, 22 scheduled and 99 non-scheduled; Hindi speakers were 43.6%, so even Hindi is a minority language in the national total.
  • Types: border minorities (Marathi speakers in Belagavi, Kannada speakers in Kasaragod), dispersed Urdu speakers, tribal-language communities (Bhili, Gondi; Santali and Bodo scheduled in 2003) and migrant groups in cities.
  • Vulnerability: The Census lists only languages with 10,000 or more speakers, so many small tribal languages stay invisible and endangered.

Minority in India is a relational and State-specific idea defined by non-dominance. Religious minorities are regionally concentrated and internally diverse, and linguistic minorities exist in every State; constitutional safeguards and inclusive citizenship keep this diversity a strength.
free.upa-2025-an2-8c:
PVTGsDhebar CommissionPre-agricultural technologyPM-JANMAN

Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) are the most marginal among Scheduled Tribes. The Dhebar Commission (1960–61) found wide inequality among tribes, and from the Fifth Five-Year Plan (1975) the Government of India identified the least developed as "Primitive Tribal Groups"; they were renamed PVTGs in 2006. The present list has 75 entries in 18 States and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

1. Identifying criteria

  • Pre-agricultural technology: hunting, gathering or shifting cultivation as the main livelihood, as among the Birhor, Jarawa and Cholanaickan.
  • Stagnant or declining population: for example the Great Andamanese and Onge.
  • Extremely low literacy and a subsistence economy with severe economic backwardness.
  • General ST markers: These are applied with the Lokur Committee's (1965) tests of distinctive culture, geographical isolation and shyness of contact. The criteria are administrative, set by the Government of India, not by the Constitution.

2. Nomenclature

  • From "primitive" to "vulnerable": The word primitive was criticised as evolutionist and demeaning, and the 2006 renaming stresses vulnerability instead.
  • One people, several entries: The 75 entries are counted State by State, so the Birhor (four entries), Lodha, Kolam, Koraga, Kattunayakan and Kurumbas appear more than once; distinct communities are fewer than 75.
  • Sections of larger tribes: Many PVTGs, such as the Dongria and Kutia Kondh, Hill Korwa and Abujh Maria, are sections of larger tribes that share one entry in the ST Orders, so Census figures for them are missing or unreliable.
  • Spelling variants: Saharia or Seharia, Dongria or Dungaria, and Kutia or Kuttiya differ across lists, which confuses data and delivery of benefits.

3. Distribution

  • Regional clusters: Most PVTGs live in the central and eastern tribal belt and the Eastern Ghats; others are island peoples (Great Andamanese, Jarawa, Onge, Sentinelese, Shompen) and Western Ghats and Nilgiri groups (Toda, Kota, Kurumba, Irula, Paniyan, Cholanaickan).
  • Size: They range from the Saharia, who number in lakhs, to Andamanese groups of a few dozen or a few hundred people; the government counted about 28 lakh PVTG people when PM-JANMAN was launched.

4. Current status

  • Development gaps: Poor housing, roads, water, health (anaemia, sickle-cell disease) and literacy well below the ST average.
  • Policy response: The central scheme for PVTG development funds conservation-cum-development plans, and PM-JANMAN (launched 15 November 2023; ₹24,104 crore; 11 interventions through 9 ministries) targets housing, roads, water, hostels, mobile medical units and Van Dhan centres.
  • Rights: Habitat rights under Section 3(1)(e) of the Forest Rights Act were first recognised for the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh in 2015; Odisha had recognised them for eight PVTGs by mid-2026.
  • Threats: Mining, relocation from protected areas and large projects such as the Great Nicobar development plan, which affects the Shompen, raise concerns about consent and survival.

PVTG policy has moved from the label "primitive" to recognition of vulnerability, and from welfare to saturation missions. A fresh, ethnographically grounded review of criteria and names, separate counting in the coming Census and habitat-based development are needed so that the smallest communities are counted and protected.
free.upa-2024-an1-1a:
CultureLearned and sharedSymbolicIntegrated and dynamic

Culture is the design for living that a people learn and share. E.B. Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) gave the classic definition: "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." Clifford Geertz (The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973) stressed its web of meanings. Both point to attributes found in every culture.

1. Attributes that define culture

  • Learned, not inherited: culture is acquired after birth through enculturation (M.J. Herskovits's term). An infant adopted across continents grows up with the speech, food habits and manners of the adoptive family, not of its biological parents.
  • Shared: culture belongs to a group, so members can predict one another's conduct. Ralph Linton (The Study of Man, 1936) showed that sharing is uneven: universals are held by all adults, specialties by particular groups (a potter caste, a priest), alternatives by a few.
  • Symbolic: meanings are fixed by convention, not by nature. Leslie White (The Science of Culture, 1949) treated the symbol as the basis of all culture; a mangalsutra, a national flag or a Toda sacred buffalo carries meaning only for those who share the code.
  • Transmitted and cumulative: language and writing store knowledge beyond any one lifetime; A.L. Kroeber called this level "superorganic" (1917).

2. Attributes that explain how culture works

  • Integrated: parts fit into a whole. Among the Todas of the Nilgiris (W.H.R. Rivers, 1906), buffalo herding links the economy, dairy temples, priesthood and kinship.
  • Adaptive: culture is the main human means of coping with environments, from Inuit snow houses to the stepwells and kunds of arid Rajasthan.
  • Dynamic: it changes through invention, diffusion and acculturation; W.F. Ogburn (Social Change, 1922) called the delay of beliefs and norms behind technology "cultural lag".

3. Universal yet particular

  • Universal: G.P. Murdock's "common denominator of cultures" (1945) lists family, language, religion and rules of property found everywhere.
  • Particular: each culture combines these differently, so it must be judged on its own terms (Boas's cultural relativism); Khasi inheritance through the youngest daughter differs sharply from the patrilineal norms of their neighbours.
  • Human in degree: chimpanzees at Gombe fish for termites with twigs (Jane Goodall), but only humans build cumulative, symbol-based culture.

These attributes make culture humanity's extra-somatic inheritance. They also warn against ranking cultures, which is why cultural relativism guides fieldwork and policy for tribal communities today.
free.upa-2024-an1-1b:
MeluhhaLothalDilmun and MaganPersian Gulf seals

The Harappan (Indus) Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) traded by sea with the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia. Cuneiform texts call a distant eastern land Meluhha, widely identified with the Indus region and Gujarat coast, whose ships moored at Akkad in the reign of Sargon (c. 2334–2279 BCE). Archaeology from Gujarat to Oman and Iraq confirms this exchange.

1. Evidence of maritime trade

  • Ports and coastal sites: Lothal on the Gulf of Khambhat (excavated by S.R. Rao, 1955–62) had a large brick-lined basin read as a dockyard, a warehouse and bead workshops. Sutkagen-dor and Sotka-koh on the Makran coast, Balakot, Kuntasi and Dholavira were other coastal or near-coastal nodes.
  • Boats: a seal from Mohenjo-daro depicts a flat-bottomed boat with a central cabin, and Lothal yielded a terracotta boat model and stone anchors.
  • Harappan goods abroad: etched carnelian beads in the royal cemetery at Ur and at Kish; Indus seals and cubical chert weights in Mesopotamia and the Gulf; black-slipped Harappan storage jars at Ras al-Jinz and other sites in Oman.
  • Foreign objects at home: a round "Persian Gulf" type seal at Lothal.
  • Texts: a cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu names him an interpreter of the Meluhhan language, and later Ur III texts mention a "Meluhha village" near Lagash, pointing to resident traders.

2. Routes and goods

  • Coastal voyaging: ships followed the Makran coast to Magan (Oman) and Dilmun (Bahrain and Failaka), which became middlemen for Mesopotamia.
  • Exports: carnelian and other beads, ivory, shell objects, timber and gold.
  • Imports: copper from Oman by sea; lapis lazuli from Badakhshan (through the Harappan outpost of Shortughai), tin and silver came mainly overland, and some lapis was shipped on to Mesopotamia.

3. Significance and debates

  • Economic organisation: a single weight standard, seals for marking consignments and craft centres such as the shell-working sites of Nageshwar and Gola Dhoro point to organised merchant networks.
  • Debates: Lawrence Leshnik (1968) argued that the Lothal basin was a reservoir, not a dock; overseas trade was small compared with internal exchange; and references to Meluhha fade after c. 1900 BCE as Indus cities declined.

Sea trade shows the Harappans as an early Indian Ocean people whose seals, weights and beads crossed the Arabian Sea. It is a classic case of culture contact through commerce, and anticipates the later monsoon trade of the region.
free.upa-2024-an1-1c:
Kinship usagesRadcliffe-BrownPermitted disrespectGender and power

Kinship usages are customary patterns of behaviour between particular relatives. Avoidance requires restraint or no contact between certain kin, usually in-laws, while a joking relationship is, in A.R. Radcliffe-Brown's words (1940), "a relation between two persons in which one is by custom permitted, and in some instances required, to tease or make fun of the other, who in turn is required to take no offence."

1. Forms and examples

  • Avoidance: a Navajo man and his mother-in-law traditionally avoid seeing each other; several Aboriginal Australian peoples, such as the Dyirbal, use a special speech style in the presence of a mother-in-law. In many north Indian Hindu households a bride veils her face before her husband's elder brother and father-in-law.
  • Joking: jija–sali and devar–bhabhi teasing in India; grandparents and grandchildren in many societies; a sister's son and mother's brother among the BaThonga (Radcliffe-Brown, "The Mother's Brother in South Africa", 1924); even whole groups, as in the Dogon–Bozo alliance of Mali.

2. Explanations offered

  • Structural-functional (Radcliffe-Brown, 1940 and 1949): marriage joins groups whose interests partly unite and partly diverge. Strict respect (avoidance) and friendly antagonism (joking) are two stable ways of managing such ambivalent ties without open conflict.
  • Earlier views: E.B. Tylor (1889) statistically linked mother-in-law avoidance with a husband living among his wife's kin; Sigmund Freud (Totem and Taboo, 1913) saw avoidance as a guard against incestuous attraction; G.P. Murdock (Social Structure, 1949) noted that joking often links potential spouses, as in devar–bhabhi joking where levirate is practised.

3. Critical perspective

  • Circular and static: explaining a custom by the conflict it is said to prevent is hard to test; the model cannot say why one society chooses joking where another chooses avoidance, or why these usages fade in urban, nuclear families.
  • Gender and power: the burden of avoidance falls mostly on women (ghunghat, silence before elders), sustaining patriarchal authority; licensed joking can mask hierarchy or slide into harassment, so feminist scholars read power where Radcliffe-Brown saw harmony.
  • Other readings: Marcel Griaule (1948) saw Dogon joking alliances as a "cathartic alliance" rooted in myth; Mary Douglas (1968) treated jokes as brief challenges to social order; Claude Lévi-Strauss (1945) showed that familiarity and reserve form a balanced system of attitudes within the "atom of kinship".

Avoidance and joking are two answers to one problem, the ambivalence of relations created by marriage. Radcliffe-Brown's insight endures, but present-day anthropology reads these usages through power, gender and change as well.
free.upa-2024-an1-1d:
Lethal alleleLucien Cuénot (1905)Sublethal genesGenetic load

A lethal gene is an allele whose expression kills its carrier, usually before reproductive age, so the individual leaves no offspring. Lucien Cuénot (1905) first detected one in yellow mice: crosses of two yellow mice gave a 2:1 instead of the expected 3:1 ratio; Castle and Little (1910) showed that the homozygotes die as embryos. Sublethal (semilethal) genes kill only a part of their carriers or shorten life.

1. Types of lethal genes

  • Dominant lethal: kills in a single dose, so it vanishes in one generation unless it acts late. Huntington's disease (HTT gene, chromosome 4) usually appears after the reproductive years and therefore persists.
  • Recessive lethal: kills only homozygotes; healthy carriers keep the allele hidden in the population. Tay–Sachs disease (HEXA) causes death in early childhood.
  • Dominant visible, recessive lethal: one copy changes the phenotype, two copies kill, as with the yellow allele in mice and achondroplasia in humans, where homozygous infants rarely survive.
  • Conditional lethal: deadly only in a particular environment; G6PD deficiency causes a haemolytic crisis after fava beans or drugs such as primaquine.
  • Synthetic lethal: two mutations harmless singly kill a cell together; PARP-inhibitor drugs exploit this against BRCA-mutant cancers.
  • By time of action: gametic, embryonic (a cause of early miscarriage), infantile or juvenile lethals.

2. Sublethal genes

  • Partial lethality: some affected individuals die early while others survive with disease, as in haemophilia A before clotting-factor therapy and sickle-cell anaemia in malarial regions.
  • Category depends on care: transfusions for thalassaemia, factor VIII for haemophilia and a low-phenylalanine diet for phenylketonuria move conditions from lethal towards sublethal, showing that fitness depends on environment and culture.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Genetic load: H.J. Muller ("Our Load of Mutations", 1950) and Morton, Crow and Muller (1956) estimated hidden recessive lethals as "lethal equivalents", using data on consanguineous marriages.
  • Consanguinity: cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriages in parts of South India raise homozygosity and expose recessive lethals, a key concern of genetic counselling.
  • Balanced polymorphism: a lethal can persist when carriers gain an advantage; the sickle-cell allele protects heterozygotes against falciparum malaria (A.C. Allison, 1954), which explains its high frequency in parts of central India.

Lethal and sublethal genes show that fitness results from genotype and environment together. Medicine, diet and marriage rules change their effect, which is why carrier screening and genetic counselling matter in India.
free.upa-2024-an1-1e:
HaemoglobinHbA, HbA2, HbFHaemoglobinopathiesBalanced polymorphism

Haemoglobin (Hb) is the iron-containing protein of red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. Each molecule is a tetramer of four globin chains, each holding a haem group with ferrous iron, so it binds four oxygen molecules. The α-globin genes lie on chromosome 16 and the β-globin cluster on chromosome 11, which makes Hb a classic genetic marker in anthropology.

1. Haemoglobin in health

  • Developmental switching: embryonic haemoglobins (Gower, Portland) give way to foetal HbF, whose higher oxygen affinity draws oxygen across the placenta; within the first year adult HbA becomes dominant, with a small HbA2 fraction.
  • Functions: besides oxygen transport, Hb carries part of the carbon dioxide and buffers blood pH. Cooperative binding gives an S-shaped dissociation curve, and the Bohr effect releases more oxygen in active tissues.
  • Normal levels and adaptation: WHO defines anaemia below 13 g/dL in men and 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women. At high altitude Andean highlanders raise their Hb, while Tibetans keep near sea-level values, a trait linked to an EPAS1 variant inherited from Denisovans (Huerta-Sánchez and colleagues, Nature, 2014).
  • Diagnostic marker: glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) of 6.5% or more indicates diabetes.

2. Haemoglobin in disease

  • Structural variants: a single amino-acid change alters the molecule; HbS polymerises at low oxygen, sickling red cells and causing pain crises, anaemia and organ damage.
  • Thalassaemias: reduced output of α or β chains; β-thalassaemia major needs lifelong transfusion, and carrier rates are higher in some communities of western and northern India.
  • Acquired disorders: iron-deficiency anaemia is widespread: NFHS-5 (2019–21) found 57% of women aged 15–49 and 67.1% of children aged 6–59 months anaemic. Carbon monoxide binds Hb about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, causing poisoning.

3. Anthropological and public-health significance

  • Balanced polymorphism: sickle-cell carriers resist falciparum malaria (A.C. Allison, 1954), which explains high HbS frequencies among tribal communities such as the Gond and Bhil in malarial central and western India.
  • Policy: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched July 2023, Shahdol) targets elimination by 2047; by June 2026 it had screened over 7.19 crore people, diagnosing about 2.46 lakh patients and over 20 lakh carriers. Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018) tackles nutritional anaemia.

Haemoglobin links biology, environment and culture: it reveals human adaptation to altitude and malaria and remains central to India's fight against anaemia and sickle-cell disease.
free.upa-2024-an1-2a:
Historical particularismFranz BoasCritique of the comparative methodCultural relativism

Classical evolutionism (E.B. Tylor's Primitive Culture, 1871; L.H. Morgan's Ancient Society, 1877; J.G. Frazer's The Golden Bough, 1890) placed all societies on one ladder from "savagery" to "civilisation". Franz Boas and his students rejected this ladder; Marvin Harris (The Rise of Anthropological Theory, 1968) later named their approach historical particularism: every culture is the product of its own particular history.

1. What classical evolutionism assumed

  • Psychic unity and fixed stages: similar minds everywhere would produce the same institutions in the same order, such as Morgan's seven ethnical periods and Frazer's magic, religion and science.
  • Comparative method and survivals: traits were lifted out of context and compared worldwide, and Tylor's "survivals" were used to reconstruct earlier stages.
  • Armchair data and ethnocentrism: evidence came from missionaries and travellers, with Victorian Europe at the top.

2. Boas's critique

  • "The Limitations of the Comparative Method of Anthropology" (1896): like traits can arise from different causes; masks, for instance, serve different purposes in different societies, so similarity does not prove a common stage.
  • Diffusion and borrowing: by mapping folktales on the North Pacific Coast he showed that many traits spread through contact.
  • Context over type: in his 1887 debate with Otis Mason he urged museums to display objects by tribe and setting, not in evolutionary series.
  • Race, language and culture are independent: The Mind of Primitive Man (1911) and his study of immigrants' children (1912), whose head form changed in America, undermined racial explanations of culture.

3. Core tenets of historical particularism

  • Unique histories: environment, contact, borrowing and creativity combine differently in each culture; explanation must be historical and regional before it is general.
  • Intensive fieldwork in the local language: Boas worked among the Inuit of Baffin Island (1883–84) and, for decades, among the Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) with George Hunt, recording texts in their own language.
  • Cultural relativism and the four fields: each culture is judged by its own standards; his students Kroeber, Lowie, Sapir, Benedict, Mead and Herskovits built American anthropology on this base.
  • Testing the schemes: Robert Lowie (Primitive Society, 1920) showed that clans are absent in many simple societies and that matriliny does not always precede patriliny.

4. Why it was a critical advance

  • Evidence over speculation: fieldwork replaced conjectural stages.
  • Against racism: cultural differences were explained by history, not race.
  • An Indian illustration: the matrilineal Khasi of Meghalaya and Nayars of Kerala developed matriliny through separate histories beside patrilineal neighbours, not as survivals of a universal "mother-right" stage.

5. Limitations

  • Inductivism: Harris accused the school of collecting facts without theory; Leslie White branded it "anti-evolutionist".
  • Fragmentation: trait lists neglected social structure, a gap British structural-functionalism filled.
  • Evolution revived: White (The Science of Culture, 1949), Julian Steward's multilinear evolution (Theory of Culture Change, 1955) and Sahlins and Service (Evolution and Culture, 1960) restored evolution in a careful, non-racial form.

Historical particularism turned anthropology from speculative history into an empirical science grounded in fieldwork and relativism. Its anti-racist, context-sensitive outlook still guides ethnography, while later neo-evolutionists took up the generalisations it had postponed.
free.upa-2024-an1-2b:
MehrgarhNeolithic food productionZebu domesticationRoots of the Harappan civilization

Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass on the Kachi plain of Balochistan (Pakistan), was excavated from 1974 by Jean-François Jarrige and the French Archaeological Mission. Its aceramic Neolithic level (Period I, placed by the excavators around 7000 BCE, though some scholars prefer a later date) offers the oldest well-documented evidence of farming and herding in South Asia.

1. Evidence of food production

  • Cereals: grain impressions in mud bricks and charred seeds show domesticated barley, with naked six-row barley as the main crop, alongside smaller amounts of hulled and naked wheats.
  • Tools and storage: flint sickle blades set in bitumen, grinding stones and, from the later Neolithic levels, compartmented mud-brick buildings interpreted as granaries.
  • Other plants: jujube (Zizyphus), dates and grapes; cotton seeds, and mineralised cotton fibres preserved inside a copper bead from a Neolithic burial (Moulherat and colleagues, 2002), among the earliest evidence of cotton anywhere.
  • Settled villages: multi-roomed rectangular houses of hand-moulded mud bricks bearing finger impressions show year-round settlement.

2. Evidence of animal domestication

  • From hunting to herding: the lowest levels are dominated by wild game such as gazelle, nilgai, onager, chital, wild pig and even elephant; through Period I gazelle declines while sheep, goat and cattle rise (Richard Meadow's faunal studies).
  • Zebu cattle: humped cattle (Bos indicus) become the leading animal, and a reduction in the body size of cattle, sheep and goats, a classic marker of domestication, suggests that zebu were domesticated in the region itself.
  • Ritual value of herds: young goats were placed in some human graves.

3. Burials, crafts and exchange

  • Rich burials: flexed bodies with red ochre, shell, bone and stone ornaments, and bitumen-coated baskets.
  • Long-distance contacts: turquoise from Iran or Central Asia, lapis lazuli from northern Afghanistan and marine shell from the Arabian Sea coast.
  • Early dentistry: eleven drilled molar crowns from nine adults, 7,500–9,000 years old (Coppa and colleagues, Nature, 2006).

4. Significance

  • Earliest food production in South Asia: it pushes farming back to about the seventh millennium BCE, thousands of years before Neolithic sites such as Burzahom in Kashmir; claims of very early rice at Lahuradewa in the Ganga plain remain debated.
  • Local development, not mere diffusion: barley and wheat link it to the wider farming zone of the Iranian plateau, but local zebu domestication and indigenous crafts show regional innovation rather than a simple transplant from the Fertile Crescent.
  • A gradual transition: the slow move from broad-spectrum hunting to herding qualifies V. Gordon Childe's image of a sudden "Neolithic Revolution" (Man Makes Himself, 1936).
  • Roots of the Indus civilization: an unbroken sequence through Chalcolithic levels, with copper, wheel-made pottery, seals and figurines, continued at nearby Nausharo, showing that Harappan urbanism grew from local village farming.

Mehrgarh shows South Asia as an independent centre of early food production, where farming, herding, crafts and trade grew together over millennia and laid the foundations of the Harappan civilization.
free.upa-2024-an1-2c:
Non-communicable diseasesEpidemiological transitionThrifty genotypeStructural determinants

Lifestyle diseases are chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, many cancers and chronic lung disease, linked to diet, physical inactivity, tobacco, alcohol and stress. Abdel Omran's epidemiological transition (1971) describes how, as societies modernise, these degenerative and man-made diseases replace infections as the main killers.

1. Magnitude of the problem

  • Global: according to WHO (fact sheet, September 2025), NCDs killed at least 43 million people in 2021, about 75% of non-pandemic deaths; 18 million of them died before 70, and 82% of these premature deaths were in low- and middle-income countries.
  • India: the ICMR–INDIAB study (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, 2023; surveys from 2008 to 2020) found diabetes in 11.4% of adults, prediabetes in 15.3%, hypertension in 35.5% and generalised obesity in 28.6%.

2. Causes: an anthropological reading

  • Evolutionary mismatch: bodies shaped by active foraging and fibre-rich food now meet sedentary work and energy-dense diets. James Neel's thrifty genotype (1962) and Hales and Barker's thrifty phenotype (1992) explain why populations that faced scarcity, or babies undernourished in the womb, are more prone to diabetes.
  • Nutrition transition (Barry Popkin): millets, pulses and vegetables give way to refined grains, sugar, oils and packaged food as incomes and urbanisation rise.
  • Body build: the "Y-Y paradox" (Yajnik and Yudkin, 2004) shows that Indians carry more body fat at a given weight, which is why lower BMI cut-offs are used for South Asians.
  • Acculturation: the Pima of Arizona, after losing their farming water and adopting a market diet, developed one of the world's highest diabetes rates, far above their relatives in Mexico who still farm.

3. Impact on human health

  • Physical: heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure, blindness and amputations, often together as multimorbidity, and earlier in Indians than in Europeans.
  • Economic: lifelong treatment drives out-of-pocket and catastrophic health spending and removes adults in their working prime.
  • Psychosocial and syndemic: depression, stigma and caregiver strain; Merrill Singer's concept of "syndemic" captures how diabetes worsens tuberculosis and COVID-19.
  • Double burden: undernutrition and obesity now coexist in the same districts and even households.

4. Critical comment

  • "Lifestyle" blames the individual: poverty, long working hours, unsafe streets, aggressive marketing of processed food and tobacco, and air pollution are not personal choices.
  • Not only diseases of affluence: NCDs are spreading to the rural poor and to tribal communities whose diets are changing.
  • Medicalisation: pills often replace prevention, and traditional diets and active livelihoods are undervalued.
  • Responses: the National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs screens adults over 30 for hypertension, diabetes and common cancers; the Fit India Movement (2019) and Eat Right India (FSSAI) promote prevention.

Lifestyle diseases are the price of a rapid transition that our biology has not caught up with. Effective control needs more than individual advice: it needs culturally sensitive, structural action on food, work and environment.
free.upa-2024-an1-3a:
KaryotypeTjio and Levan (1956)G-bandingChromosomal aberrations

A karyotype is the complete chromosome complement of a cell or individual, described by number, size, centromere position and banding pattern; arranged in standard order it forms a karyogram (a drawn version is an idiogram). Tjio and Levan (1956) established that humans have 46 chromosomes, and the Denver Conference (1960) sorted the 23 pairs into seven groups, A to G. A normal karyotype is written 46,XX or 46,XY.

1. Preparing a karyotype

  • Sources of cells: usually lymphocytes from peripheral blood, stimulated to divide with phytohaemagglutinin (PHA); for prenatal diagnosis, chorionic villi (about 10–13 weeks) or amniotic fluid cells (about 15–20 weeks); bone marrow in leukaemia.
  • Banding: Giemsa (G) banding gives about 400–550 bands per haploid set; Q-banding (quinacrine), R-banding, C-banding of heterochromatin and NOR staining answer special questions.
  • Classification and nomenclature: chromosomes are paired as metacentric, submetacentric or acrocentric and reported in the International System for Human Cytogenomic Nomenclature (ISCN), for example 47,XY,+21.

2. Kinds of chromosomal aberration

  • Numerical: aneuploidy (trisomy, monosomy) mostly from non-disjunction in meiosis; polyploidy such as triploidy, usually lethal; mosaicism from errors after fertilisation.
  • Structural: deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation (reciprocal or Robertsonian), ring chromosome and isochromosome.

3. How karyotype analysis aids diagnosis

  • Confirming syndromes: it confirmed trisomy 21 in Down syndrome (Lejeune and colleagues, 1959), trisomies 18 and 13 (Edwards and Patau, 1960), 45,X in Turner syndrome and 47,XXY in Klinefelter syndrome (both 1959).
  • Mechanism and recurrence risk: about 95% of Down syndrome is free trisomy, but a few per cent arise from a Robertsonian translocation; finding a balanced translocation in a parent changes the recurrence risk and guides the counselling of relatives.
  • Reproductive problems: balanced rearrangements in couples with recurrent miscarriage, and 47,XXY or Y-chromosome changes in male infertility.
  • Prenatal diagnosis: indicated for advanced maternal age, abnormal screening results or a previous affected child.
  • Cancer: the Philadelphia chromosome (Nowell and Hungerford, 1960), shown by Janet Rowley (1973) to be a 9;22 translocation, diagnoses chronic myeloid leukaemia and guides targeted therapy.

4. Limitations and newer methods

  • Resolution: banding cannot see changes smaller than about 5–10 million base pairs, nor single-gene mutations, and it needs living, dividing cells.
  • Molecular cytogenetics: FISH, spectral karyotyping, chromosomal microarray and non-invasive prenatal testing on cell-free foetal DNA now detect smaller changes, faster.

5. Anthropological relevance

  • Evolution: comparing karyotypes shows that human chromosome 2 arose from the fusion of two ancestral chromosomes still separate in the great apes, which have 48.
  • Indian context: high consanguinity in some communities and the PC-PNDT Act, 1994, which permits prenatal tests only for genetic abnormalities, make karyotyping central to ethical genetic counselling.

Karyotyping remains the first-line, genome-wide view of chromosomes. Combined with molecular tools and sensitive genetic counselling, it allows early diagnosis, informed reproductive choices and better care.
free.upa-2024-an1-3b:
UrbanizationUrbanism as a way of lifeJoint and nuclear familyFunctional jointness

Urbanization is the process by which a growing share of a population comes to live in towns and cities, moving from farming to industry and services. Louis Wirth ("Urbanism as a Way of Life", 1938) added that the size, density and heterogeneity of cities produce a more impersonal urbanism. India was about 31% urban at the 2011 Census, and the share continues to rise.

1. Changes in family structure

  • Smaller households: migration for work, costly housing and small flats separate married sons from parents and favour neolocal, nuclear households.
  • Household is not family: A.M. Shah (The Household Dimension of the Family in India, 1973) showed that a nuclear household often remains part of a wider joint family. I.P. Desai's study of Mahuva in Gujarat (1964) found that many families remained joint in obligations though living apart.
  • Jointness that adapts: M.S. Gore (Urbanization and Family Change, 1968) found Aggarwal families around Delhi keeping joint-family values, and Milton Singer (1968) showed Madras industrialists using the joint family as a business asset.
  • Fewer children: NFHS-5 (2019–21) recorded a total fertility rate of 1.6 in urban India against 2.1 in rural areas.

2. Changes in roles and relationships

  • Women: education and paid work, as in the dual-earner IT families of Bengaluru and Hyderabad, give wives more voice, but also a double burden of office and housework.
  • Conjugal bond: the husband–wife tie gains over the father–son tie; choice in marriage, inter-caste unions, later marriage and matrimonial websites grow.
  • Elders: some old parents live alone or in old-age homes, prompting the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; elsewhere grandparents move to cities to raise grandchildren.
  • New forms: single-parent, single-person and live-in households; split migrant families, with men in cities and wives in villages; and Kerala's Gulf households headed by women (Leela Gulati, In the Absence of Their Men, 1993).

3. Changes in functions

  • Functions shared: schools, hospitals, crèches, insurance and the state take over education, health and security; the family keeps emotional support and early socialisation.
  • Kin networks as urban capital: relatives and caste fellows help migrants find jobs and housing in cities such as Mumbai and Surat.
  • Tribal families: young Adivasi migrants from Jharkhand and Odisha working in cities live beyond clan elders' control, which often loosens customary marriage rules.

4. Assessment

  • Not a simple joint-to-nuclear shift: Indian families show adaptation, close to Eugene Litwak's "modified extended family" (1960), linked by phones, remittances and festivals.
  • Strains: loneliness, conflicts and domestic violence, addressed partly by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

Urbanization has made the Indian family smaller and more egalitarian but not individualistic in the Western sense. Its resilient, functionally joint character needs policy support for elder care, child care and women's work.
free.upa-2024-an1-3c:
FieldworkParticipant observationReflexivityResearch ethics

Fieldwork, long-term first-hand study of a community through participant observation, interviews and genealogies, became anthropology's hallmark after Bronisław Malinowski's Trobriand research (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922). The classic model assumed a bounded village, an outsider researcher and a long continuous stay; today each of these assumptions is under strain.

1. Who represents whom

  • Crisis of representation: Writing Culture (James Clifford and George Marcus, 1986) showed that ethnographies are partial, authored texts, so researchers must reflect on their own position and include local voices.
  • Insider and outsider: "native" anthropologists bring access but risk blind spots. M.N. Srinivas contrasted the "field view" with the "book view"; when his Rampura field notes burned in a 1970 fire at Stanford, he wrote The Remembered Village (1976) from memory, a reminder of how fragile field data are.
  • Decolonising research: communities question one-way extraction of knowledge and ask for co-authorship and a say in how they are portrayed.

2. The changing "field"

  • Global and mobile lives: migrants, diasporas and commodities cross borders, so George Marcus proposed multi-sited ethnography (1995) that follows people, things and conflicts.
  • Online worlds: social media and virtual communities are now field sites, as in Tom Boellstorff's Coming of Age in Second Life (2008), raising new doubts about consent and what counts as public.
  • Pandemic disruption: COVID-19 lockdowns (2020–21) stopped travel; "patchwork ethnography" (Günel, Varma and Watanabe, 2020) combines short visits, remote interviews and the researcher's own constraints.
  • Studying up: Laura Nader (1972) urged the study of corporations, bureaucracies and elites, where access is guarded.

3. Ethical and legal challenges

  • Consent and harm: codes such as the American Anthropological Association's Principles of Professional Responsibility (2012) and India's ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017) require informed consent and protection of vulnerable groups.
  • Controversies: Darkness in El Dorado (2000) on research among the Yanomami; the Havasupai blood samples reused beyond consent (settled 2010); and the US Army's Human Terrain System, which the AAA opposed in 2007.
  • Benefit-sharing and data: the Kani of Kerala shared licence fees for the herbal drug Jeevani; Indigenous data sovereignty and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 govern how data are stored.

4. Practical challenges in India

  • Restricted access: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Protection of Aboriginal Tribes) Regulation, 1956 protects the Jarawa and Sentinelese; Inner Line Permits apply in parts of the North-East; conflict zones need security clearance.
  • Research fatigue: much-studied communities grow weary of surveys that bring no benefit.
  • Time, money and safety: short doctoral timelines and grants squeeze long stays, and women researchers face added safety risks.

Fieldwork survives because it remains the best way to grasp lived reality. Its future lies in reflexive, collaborative and ethically accountable research that combines long immersion with digital and multi-sited tools.
free.upa-2024-an1-4a:
Ruth BenedictApollonian and DionysianConfigurationalismZuni Pueblo

Ruth Benedict, a student of Boas, set out this idea in "Psychological Types in the Cultures of the Southwest" (International Congress of Americanists, 1928; published 1930) and developed it in Patterns of Culture (1934). Borrowing Nietzsche's contrast in The Birth of Tragedy (1872), she called the Pueblo cultures Apollonian and most of their neighbours Dionysian.

1. The configurational approach

  • Culture as a pattern: for Benedict, "A culture, like an individual, is a more or less consistent pattern of thought and action." Each culture selects a few possibilities from a "great arc" of human potential and organises institutions around a dominant ethos.
  • Personality writ large: child rearing and institutions mould individuals to the pattern; whoever does not fit is "abnormal" only by that culture's standard ("Anthropology and the Abnormal", 1934).
  • Field base: she worked at Zuni (1924–25), Cochiti and among the Pima, and used others' data for the Kwakiutl (Boas) and Dobu (Reo Fortune).

2. The Apollonian type: the Pueblos (Zuni, Hopi)

  • Measure and sobriety: in her account the Pueblos distrust excess and do not use drugs, alcohol or self-torture to reach ecstatic states; their dances are collective, repetitive and exact.
  • Ritual as group work: priesthoods, masked katcina societies and medicine societies perform rain and fertility rites where correct performance, not personal ecstasy, matters.
  • Self-effacement: the ideal man is dignified, affable and never seeks to lead; one hungry for power risks suspicion of sorcery.
  • Mild life crises: katcina initiation whipping is purifying rather than an ordeal; marriage and divorce in the matrilocal household are simple, a wife ending the marriage by placing her husband's belongings outside; mourning is short and restrained.

3. The Dionysian type: the neighbours

  • Pursuit of excess: Plains peoples sought a guardian spirit through fasting and self-torture, as in the Sun Dance.
  • Intoxication and frenzy: the Pima, whom she visited, drank fermented cactus liquor in rain ceremonies, and peyote spread among many surrounding tribes.
  • Individualism: personal power, display and violent expressions of grief were valued. Outside the Southwest she called the Kwakiutl Dionysian and megalomaniac, and the Dobuans paranoid.

4. Critical evaluation

  • Contributions: cultural relativism, the cultural definition of normality and the link between culture and personality; the method fed national character studies (The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, 1946) and Indian work such as G. Morris Carstairs's The Twice-Born (1957).
  • An idealised Zuni: Li An-Che (1937), after fieldwork at Zuni, found anxiety, quarrels and strong individuals; Esther Goldfrank (1945) stressed harsh discipline and factionalism; John W. Bennett (1946) set Benedict's harmonious "organic" picture against a "repressive" one.
  • Stereotyping: one label for a whole people ignores differences of age, gender and status.
  • Ahistorical: Spanish rule, the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, missions and American control shaped Pueblo restraint and secrecy.
  • Method: labels taken from Greek drama and psychiatry are impressionistic and untestable; Helen Codere (1956) described "the amiable side" of Kwakiutl life.

Benedict's portrait is too neat, yet it showed that cultures have a recognisable ethos that shapes personality and the very idea of normality, an insight that still informs psychological anthropology.
free.upa-2024-an1-4b:
Lower PalaeolithicSoanian pebble toolsAcheulian handaxes and cleaversAttirampakkam

India's Lower Palaeolithic shows two technological traditions: a pebble-tool (chopper-chopping) tradition comparable to the African Oldowan (Mode 1), called Soanian after the Soan valley, and the Acheulian handaxe-cleaver tradition (Mode 2), once called "Madrasian". Indian prehistory began when Robert Bruce Foote found a handaxe at Pallavaram near Chennai in 1863.

1. The two-tradition model and its reassessment

  • Soan culture: the Yale–Cambridge expedition of Helmut de Terra and T.T. Paterson (1935; Studies on the Ice Age in India, 1939) described pebble tools from river terraces of the Potwar plateau in Pakistan in a Pre-Soan, Early Soan and Late Soan sequence tied to Himalayan glacial stages.
  • Madras culture: handaxes and cleavers from the Kortallayar valley (Attirampakkam) and other southern sites.
  • Movius Line: Hallam Movius (1940s) set a chopper-chopping eastern Asia against a handaxe zone that included India.
  • Reassessment: handaxes also occur in the Potwar and Siwaliks, and choppers within southern Acheulian sites, so H.D. Sankalia and later workers treat the "two cultures" as overlapping traditions.

2. The Oldowan or pebble-tool tradition (Mode 1)

  • Origin: named after Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania (classified by Mary Leakey, 1971); it dates to about 2.6 million years at Gona, Ethiopia, perhaps nearly 3 million at Nyayanga, Kenya (Plummer and colleagues, Science, 2023), and was made mainly by early Homo, possibly also by Paranthropus.
  • Tools and technique: choppers flaked on one face, chopping tools on both faces, polyhedrons and sharp flakes, made by a few hammerstone blows on river pebbles.
  • Indian evidence: Soanian assemblages in the Potwar, the Siwalik foothills and the Beas–Banganga valleys of Himachal Pradesh; artefacts at Riwat (Pakistan) have been claimed at about 1.9 million years, and cut-marked bones at Masol near Chandigarh at about 2.6 million years (2016).
  • Doubts: many pebble-tool finds are undated surface collections, and the Riwat and Masol claims remain contested.

3. The Acheulian tradition (Mode 2)

  • Origin: named after Saint-Acheul in France; it appears in East Africa about 1.76 million years ago and is linked to Homo erectus and later archaic humans.
  • Tools and technique: symmetrical bifacial handaxes (ovate, cordiform, lanceolate), cleavers with a straight cutting edge (very common in India) and picks, shaped from large flakes and thinned with soft hammers.
  • Key Indian sites: Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu, about 1.5 million years (Pappu and colleagues, Science, 2011); Isampur in the Hunsgi–Baichbal valleys, Karnataka (K. Paddayya), a limestone quarry-workshop of about 1.2 million years; Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), Didwana (Rajasthan), Chirki-Nevasa (Maharashtra) and Hathnora on the Narmada, where Arun Sonakia found the Narmada hominin (1982).
  • Raw materials: quartzite in most regions, limestone at Isampur, basalt or dolerite in the Deccan.

4. Significance

  • Early arrival: Acheulian toolmakers reached South Asia soon after the tradition appeared in Africa.
  • Continuity: at Attirampakkam, Acheulian levels give way to Middle Palaeolithic prepared-core tools by about 385,000 years ago (Akhilesh and colleagues, Nature, 2018).

Indian evidence shows a long, diverse Lower Palaeolithic in which pebble-tool and Acheulian technologies overlapped, and places South Asia among the earliest regions colonised by Acheulian hominins outside Africa.
free.upa-2024-an1-4c:
Genetic counsellingSheldon Reed (1947)Pedigree and recurrence riskNon-directive counselling

Genetic counselling is "the process of helping people understand and adapt to the medical, psychological and familial implications of genetic contributions to disease" (National Society of Genetic Counselors, 2006). The term was coined by Sheldon Reed in 1947, who wanted the service to respect families' own decisions. It is the applied face of human genetics and physical anthropology.

1. Who needs it

  • Family history: a child or relative with a genetic disorder such as thalassaemia, sickle-cell disease, haemophilia or Duchenne muscular dystrophy, or with birth defects or intellectual disability.
  • Reproductive concerns: mother aged 35 or more, recurrent miscarriage, infertility or an abnormal prenatal screening result.
  • Population risk: consanguineous marriages, common in parts of South India, and communities with high carrier rates, such as sickle-cell among tribal groups of central India.
  • Adult-onset disease: Huntington's disease or inherited cancers (BRCA1 and BRCA2).

2. Steps: assessment

  • Intake and rapport: the counsellor learns the family's concerns, language and beliefs before giving any facts.
  • Family history and pedigree: a three-generation pedigree records affected members, consanguinity, miscarriages and ancestry.
  • Confirming the diagnosis: clinical examination and tests such as karyotyping, HPLC for haemoglobin variants or DNA analysis; every later step depends on an accurate diagnosis.
  • Estimating risk: Mendelian rules give exact recurrence risks, while chromosomal and multifactorial conditions use empirical figures; for example, the risk of Down syndrome is about 1 in 350 at a maternal age of 35 and about 1 in 100 at 40.

3. Steps: communication and support

  • Explaining the condition: its course, treatment and the meaning of being a carrier, in simple local terms.
  • Laying out options: prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis), preimplantation genetic testing, donor gametes, adoption or accepting the risk, and carrier testing of relatives (cascade screening).
  • Non-directive decision-making: the counsellor informs but the family decides, in line with its own values.
  • Psychosocial support and follow-up: guilt, blame (often directed at the mother), stigma and grief are addressed, with referral to support groups and later review as tests improve.

4. Indian context and the anthropologist's role
