  • Programmes and law: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission issues genetic status cards and counsels carriers; the UMMID initiative (DBT, 2019) set up NIDAN Kendras; the PC-PNDT Act, 1994 allows prenatal diagnosis for genetic abnormalities but bans sex selection.
  • Ethics: confidentiality, unexpected findings such as misattributed paternity, stigma of carriers in marriage, pressure on women and the risk of drifting into eugenics need care; Cyprus cut thalassaemia births through premarital screening with counselling.
  • Cultural competence: F. Clarke Fraser (1974) set the aim as helping families choose a course suited to their risk, family goals and ethical and religious standards; knowing kinship rules, ideas of fate and karma and local terms for illness makes this possible.

Genetic counselling turns genetic knowledge into informed, autonomous choice. In a country with high consanguinity and many carrier communities, culturally sensitive counselling is as important as the laboratory test.
free.upa-2024-an1-5a:
Chronometric datingRadioactive decayHalf-lifeCalibration

Chronometric (absolute) dating gives a fossil, artefact or deposit an age in years, with a stated error range, whereas relative dating (stratigraphy, typology, the fluorine test) only says whether something is older or younger than something else. Most chronometric methods read a natural "clock" that runs at a known rate, above all radioactive decay. Willard Libby's radiocarbon method (1949) began this revolution in prehistory.

1. Principles

  • Constant rate: a radioactive isotope breaks down at a fixed rate, expressed as its half-life, which heat or pressure do not alter; the ratio of parent to daughter isotope measures the time elapsed.
  • A starting event: the clock must be set to zero by a known event: the death of an organism (radiocarbon), the cooling of lava (potassium–argon), or the last heating or exposure to sunlight of a crystal (luminescence).
  • Closed system and error: the sample must neither gain nor lose atoms after that event; results are given as a range (for example 4,500 ± 40 years BP) and radiocarbon ages are calibrated against tree-ring and other records (the IntCal20 curve).

2. Applications in human evolution and prehistory

  • Potassium–argon at Olduvai: in 1961 it gave Bed I at Olduvai Gorge an age of about 1.75 million years, stretching the time scale of human evolution far beyond earlier guesses.
  • Indian examples: luminescence (OSL) dates at Jwalapuram, Kurnool district, placed Middle Palaeolithic tools both below and above the Toba volcanic ash of about 74,000 years ago (Petraglia et al., 2007); cosmogenic nuclide burial dating gave about 1.5 million years for Acheulean tools at Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu (Pappu et al., 2011).
  • Cross-checking: using several methods together builds confidence; Homo naledi from the Rising Star cave was dated by uranium series and ESR to about 335,000–236,000 years ago.

3. Limitations

  • Contamination and leakage: modern carbon, uranium uptake or argon loss can make dates too young or too old.
  • Material and association: each method needs suitable material, and a date belongs to the sample, not automatically to the fossil next to it, so careful stratigraphy is still essential.

Chronometric methods turned prehistory into a dated science. Combined with relative dating and Bayesian modelling of many dates, they now give ever sharper chronologies of human evolution and culture.
free.upa-2024-an1-5b:
Kula ringReciprocityTrobriand IslandersGift and prestige

The Kula is a ceremonial exchange of shell valuables among the islands of the Massim region of eastern Papua New Guinea. It was made famous by Bronislaw Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), based on his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands (1915–18). Its valuables are never used up but circulate endlessly, so the Kula shows exchange as a total social institution rather than mere trade.

1. The institution

  • Two valuables, two directions: red shell-disc necklaces (soulava) move clockwise round the ring of islands and white armshells (mwali) move anticlockwise; each famous piece carries a name and a remembered history of its holders.
  • Lifelong partnerships: a man has fixed Kula partners on other islands; an opening gift (vaga) is answered later by an equivalent return gift (yotile), and haggling is considered shameful.
  • Voyages and magic: overseas expeditions involve canoe building, canoe and beauty magic and myths of Kula heroes; ordinary goods are bartered separately (gimwali) during the same visits.

2. Cultural relevance

  • Social integration: the ring links islands with different languages and resources into a web of peace, hospitality and alliance; a partner is a host and protector in a foreign place.
  • Prestige, not profit: a man gains renown by holding famous valuables for a while and passing them on generously, which contradicts the idea of a universal profit-seeking "economic man".
  • Economy embedded in society: ceremonial and utilitarian exchange go together, a point Karl Polanyi later used to argue that economies are embedded in social institutions.
  • Theory of the gift: Marcel Mauss (The Gift, 1925) read the Kula as a "total social fact" built on three obligations: to give, to receive and to repay.
  • Indian parallels: recorded wedding gifts that must be returned with an increase (moi in Tamil Nadu, neota in north India) follow the same logic of delayed, obligatory return.

3. Later reassessments

  • Gender: Annette Weiner's restudy showed that Malinowski's male-centred account ignored women's banana-leaf bundles and skirts, central to Trobriand value; she later developed the idea of "keeping-while-giving" (Inalienable Possessions, 1992).
  • Continuity and change: studies collected by Jerry and Edmund Leach (The Kula, 1983) showed the system still working, adapted to cash, schooling and local politics.

The Kula shows that exchange creates relationships, fame and moral obligation. Its study founded economic anthropology and still guides analyses of gift economies, from wedding gifts to modern reputation networks.
free.upa-2024-an1-5c:
HeritabilityPhenotypic varianceTwin methodFalconer's formula

Heritability is the proportion of phenotypic variance in a trait, within a particular population and environment, that is due to genetic differences between individuals. It is a population statistic, not a statement about any one person. The idea came from animal breeding (Jay Lush, 1930s) and was formalised by D.S. Falconer in Introduction to Quantitative Genetics (1960); its value lies between 0 and 1.

1. The concept

  • Partitioning variance: total variance VP = VG + VE (plus gene–environment interaction and correlation); VG itself has additive (VA), dominance and epistatic parts.
  • Broad and narrow sense: broad-sense heritability H² = VG/VP covers all genetic effects; narrow-sense h² = VA/VP covers the additive part that makes children resemble parents and predicts response to selection (R = h²S).
  • Context-bound: the same trait can show different heritability in another population or period; height is highly heritable where nutrition is uniformly good, less so where it varies.

2. Methods of estimation

  • Twin method: pioneered by Francis Galton (1875). Identical (MZ) twins share all their genes and fraternal (DZ) twins about half, so Falconer's formula estimates H² ≈ 2(rMZ − rDZ); for present/absent traits, concordance rates are compared (Holzinger's formula).
  • Adoption and foster-child studies: a child's resemblance to biological versus adoptive parents separates heredity from rearing.
  • Family regression: the slope of offspring values on the mid-parent value estimates h²; sibling correlations add evidence.
  • Genomic methods: SNP-based heritability from large samples of unrelated people (GCTA, LD-score regression) gives lower figures than twin studies, the "missing heritability" problem.

3. Examples and limitations

  • Examples: total finger ridge count is among the most heritable human traits (about 0.9; Sarah Holt, 1968); stature is about 0.8 in well-fed populations; a meta-analysis of fifty years of twin studies across 17,804 traits found an average heritability of about 49% (Polderman et al., 2015).
  • Misreadings: high heritability does not mean a trait is fixed, nor that differences between groups are genetic; Richard Lewontin (1970) showed this with seeds from one genetically varied stock grown in rich and poor soil: differences within each plot are genetic, but the gap between plots is wholly environmental.
  • Environment still matters: the rapid gain in height in post-war Japan, with little genetic change, shows environment shifting the average.

Heritability is a useful population-level guide in studies of growth, disease risk and selection, but it must be read together with the environment, since genes act through gene–environment interaction.
free.upa-2024-an1-5d:
Power and authorityLegitimacyBand, tribe, chiefdom, stateMax Weber

Power is the ability to make others act as one wishes, even against resistance; authority is power that people accept as rightful because it carries legitimacy. Max Weber (Economy and Society, 1922) described three ideal types of legitimate rule. Where authority resides, in persons, kin groups or offices, distinguishes the forms of political organisation classified by Elman Service (Primitive Social Organization, 1962).

1. Weber's types of authority

  • Traditional: rests on custom and inherited position; hereditary chiefs such as the Konyak Naga Angh rule because custom has always placed their lineage in office.
  • Charismatic: springs from extraordinary personal qualities and often arises in crisis; Birsa Munda, hailed as Dharti Aba, led the Munda Ulgulan (1899–1900). Such authority is unstable and tends to become routinised after the leader.
  • Rational-legal: obedience is owed to impersonal rules and offices, as in bureaucracy or the gram sabha empowered by PESA, 1996.
  • In practice the types mix: a tribal headman may now also be an elected panchayat member.

2. Forms of political organisation

  • Uncentralised and centralised: Fortes and Evans-Pritchard (African Political Systems, 1940) contrasted stateless societies (Nuer, Tallensi, Logoli) with centralised ones (Zulu, Ngwato, Bemba); Morton Fried (1967) added a sequence of egalitarian, rank, stratified and state societies.
  • Band and tribe: in foraging bands leadership is informal and levelling is strong (Richard Lee's !Kung San "insulting the meat"); tribes rely on lineages, age-sets and councils, as in the Nuer segmentary system, or on the Melanesian big man who earns influence by generosity (Sahlins, 1963).
  • Chiefdom and state: chiefdoms have permanent, often hereditary offices, ranked lineages and redistribution (Polynesia; the Khasi syiem of a hima, chosen from a royal clan by the dorbar); the state claims a monopoly of legitimate force over a territory through a bureaucracy (Weber).

3. Indian tribal illustrations

  • Village and inter-village councils: the Munda village head (munda) and the parha council of a group of villages, and the Santal village manjhi and the parganait over a cluster of villages, combine traditional authority with consensus.
  • Contrasts among the Nagas: Angami villages were run by councils of elders, while Konyak villages were ruled by powerful hereditary chiefs.

Political organisation is a continuum rather than a ladder. In India, customary authority now coexists with rational-legal institutions such as PESA gram sabhas and Sixth Schedule district councils, a form of legal pluralism.

Mendelian disordersPoint mutationPatterns of inheritanceSickle cell disease

Single-gene (monogenic or Mendelian) disorders arise when a mutation in one gene changes the amount or working of its protein enough to cause disease; they pass through families in Mendelian ratios. Archibald Garrod (1902) first showed this for alkaptonuria, an "inborn error of metabolism", and Linus Pauling (1949) called sickle-cell anaemia a "molecular disease". Each is rare, but together they number several thousand.

1. Kinds of mutation

  • Missense: one base change alters one amino acid; in sickle-cell disease GAG becomes GTG in the β-globin gene (HBB, chromosome 11), putting valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6.
  • Deletions, insertions and stop codons: the commonest cystic fibrosis mutation (ΔF508) removes three bases and one amino acid of the CFTR protein; nonsense and frameshift mutations cause many β-thalassaemias.
  • Expanding triplet repeats: extra CAG repeats in the HTT gene cause Huntington's disease, and CGG repeats in FMR1 cause fragile X syndrome; repeats can lengthen in successive generations (anticipation).

2. Patterns of inheritance

  • A historical pedigree: haemophilia spread from Queen Victoria into several European royal houses; DNA from the Russian royal family showed in 2009 that it was haemophilia B.

3. Anthropological and Indian significance

  • Balanced polymorphism: carriers of the sickle-cell allele resist severe falciparum malaria (A.C. Allison, 1954), so the allele is common in malarial belts of Africa and in many tribal communities of central, western and southern India.
  • Endogamy and founder effect: Tay–Sachs disease among Ashkenazi Jews, and recessive disorders concentrated in particular endogamous or consanguineous communities in India, show how marriage rules shape disease frequencies.
  • Public health: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched at Shahdol, Madhya Pradesh, on 1 July 2023) aims at elimination by 2047; its target of screening 7 crore people aged 0–40 in 17 states with large tribal populations has been met, with about 7.19 crore screened by June 2026, about 2.5 lakh people diagnosed and over 20 lakh carriers identified, backed by genetic status cards and counselling. Gene therapy (CRISPR-based Casgevy, approved in the UK and USA in 2023) offers new hope.

Monogenic disorders show how one change in DNA, filtered through selection, endogamy and culture, shapes the health of whole communities; genetic counselling sensitive to marriage customs is where anthropology helps most.
free.upa-2024-an1-6a:
Homo erectusOut of Africa IAcheuleanErgaster–erectus debate

Homo erectus lived from about 2 million to about 110,000 years ago, longer than any other human species; it was the first hominin with a near-modern body and the first to spread far beyond Africa. Eugène Dubois found the first fossil, Pithecanthropus erectus, at Trinil, Java, in 1891; Chinese "Peking Man" (Davidson Black, 1927) and the Javanese finds were later united as Homo erectus.

1. Geographical distribution

  • Africa, the homeland: the oldest cranium is from Drimolen, South Africa (about 2 million years); Kenya has Koobi Fora and the near-complete "Turkana Boy" of Nariokotome (about 1.5 million years); Ethiopia has Daka (about 1 million years). Early African fossils are often called Homo ergaster.
  • The Caucasus: Dmanisi, Georgia (about 1.8 million years) yielded five small-brained skulls (about 550–775 cc), showing that hominins left Africa very soon after the species arose.
  • Java: Trinil, Sangiran and Ngandong on the Solo river, whose fossils of 117,000–108,000 years ago are the last known H. erectus (Rizal et al., 2020).
  • China: Gongwangling in Lantian (about 1.6 million years), Zhoukoudian ("Peking Man") and Hexian.
  • Europe and India: classic H. erectus is absent from Europe, where Atapuerca's H. antecessor is treated as a separate species. In India the Hathnora (Narmada) skull found by Arun Sonakia (1982) was first named Homo erectus narmadensis but is now mostly classed as archaic Homo; Acheulean tools at Attirampakkam (about 1.5 million years) and Isampur still point to erectus-grade toolmakers.

2. Physical features

  • Skull: cranial capacity about 550–1,250 cc, rising over time; long, low, thick-walled vault; massive brow ridge with constriction behind it; sagittal keel; angular occipital with a torus; greatest breadth low on the skull; no chin.
  • Face and teeth: a large face but smaller teeth and jaws than H. habilis.
  • Body: tall, long-legged, narrow-hipped, with modern limb proportions (Turkana Boy about 1.6 m at death), suited to long-distance walking and running in hot, open country.

3. Place in the human evolutionary line

  • Between habilis and later Homo: its body plan, larger brain, Acheulean tools and possible fire use (Wonderwerk Cave, about 1 million years) place it at the base of later human evolution.
  • Ergaster or erectus? Splitters (Groves and Mazák, 1975) separate African H. ergaster, our likely ancestor, from Asian H. erectus, a specialised side branch; the wide variation within the single Dmanisi group supports lumpers who keep one variable species.
  • Asian populations: the multiregional model (Wolpoff, Wu Xinzhi and Thorne, 1984) saw continuity from Asian H. erectus to living East Asians, but genetic evidence (Cann, Stoneking and Wilson, 1987) favours a recent African origin of H. sapiens with only limited archaic admixture.
  • Descendants: African H. erectus probably gave rise to H. heidelbergensis, the likely ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans; H. floresiensis may descend from dwarfed Javanese H. erectus.

Homo erectus was a widespread, variable species: African populations led towards Homo sapiens, while Asian ones survived as regional branches until about 110,000 years ago, after humanity's first "Out of Africa".
free.upa-2024-an1-6b:
Forensic anthropologyBiological profileDisaster victim identificationHuman rights investigation

Forensic anthropology applies physical anthropology and archaeology to questions of law, chiefly the identification of human remains and the reconstruction of what happened to them. Wilton Krogman (The Human Skeleton in Forensic Medicine, 1962) systematised its methods, and T. Dale Stewart (Essentials of Forensic Anthropology, 1979) defined its field as skeletonised remains. It now extends to disasters, human rights cases and the living.

1. Identification: building the biological profile

  • Human or animal, how many people: bone shape and microstructure separate human from animal bone; duplicated bones give the minimum number of individuals.
  • Sex and age: the pelvis (sciatic notch, subpubic region) and skull indicate sex; tooth eruption and fusion of epiphyses give age in the young, while the pubic symphysis (Todd, 1920; Suchey–Brooks phases) and auricular surface give age in adults.
  • Stature and ancestry: regression formulae on long bones (Trotter and Gleser, 1952; population-specific Indian formulae) estimate height; skull and tooth traits give a cautious estimate of population affinity.
  • Individual identity: healed fractures, dental work, implants, DNA (STR profiles, mitochondrial DNA), and facial approximation or skull–photo superimposition narrow the search to one person.

2. Crime scene and trauma analysis

  • Recovery: forensic archaeology locates clandestine graves, excavates them layer by layer and keeps the chain of custody so that evidence stands in court.
  • Trauma and time since death: the anthropologist separates injuries made before, around and after death (blunt, sharp, gunshot) and uses taphonomy to estimate how long the body has lain.

3. Mass disasters and human rights

  • Disaster victim identification: after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, teams from many countries in Thailand identified most foreign victims through dental records and fingerprints, supported by DNA, following Interpol's protocol.
  • Human rights: Clyde Snow helped train the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team (1984) to identify people "disappeared" under military rule; DNA-led identification of the Srebrenica (1995) victims supplied evidence to the international tribunal.

4. Historical and Indian cases

  • Ajnala, Punjab: skeletons found in an old well in 2014 were shown by mitochondrial DNA and oxygen isotopes (Sehrawat et al., 2022) to belong to people from the Gangetic plain and eastern India, consistent with soldiers of the 26th Native Bengal Infantry killed in 1857.
  • Roopkund, Uttarakhand: ancient DNA (Harney et al., 2019) revealed genetically distinct groups who died in separate events roughly a thousand years apart, one of them of eastern Mediterranean ancestry.
  • Richard III: the English king's remains, found in Leicester in 2012, were identified by scoliosis, battle wounds, radiocarbon dating and a mitochondrial DNA match with living maternal-line relatives.

5. The living

  • Age estimation: where no birth or school record exists, the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 (Section 94) allows an ossification test to decide whether a person, including an accused, is a child.
  • Identification of the living: comparison of faces and gait in CCTV images, and fingerprint classification, developed in Bengal by Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose under Edward Henry (1897).

Forensic anthropology turns knowledge of human variation into justice, closure for families and historical truth. India needs more trained forensic anthropologists and population-specific standards for its diverse communities.
free.upa-2024-an1-6c:
StructuralismThe Story of Asdiwal (1958)Binary oppositionsMediation of contradictions

Claude Lévi-Strauss treated myth like language: its meaning lies not in single episodes but in the relations between them. In "La Geste d'Asdiwal" (1958), translated as "The Story of Asdiwal" (1967), he analysed a myth of the Tsimshian of the Skeena and Nass rivers in British Columbia, using Franz Boas's versions, the main one written down by the Tsimshian Henry Tate (Tsimshian Texts, 1912; Tsimshian Mythology, 1916).

1. The myth in brief

  • Famine: in a winter famine on the frozen Skeena, a widowed mother from downstream and her widowed daughter from upstream meet halfway; a supernatural visitor feeds them and fathers Asdiwal.
  • Sky: Asdiwal follows a white she-bear to the sky, marries Evening Star, daughter of the Sun, survives his father-in-law's tests, but grows homesick and loses her.
  • Sea and death: he marries mortal women, quarrels with his brothers-in-law, is abandoned on a reef and taken to the sea lions' underground home, where he heals them; finally, hunting on a mountain without his snowshoes, he is turned to stone.

2. Lévi-Strauss's reading

  • Sequences and schemata: beneath the order of events lie four codes, geographic, economic, sociological and cosmological, repeating one pattern of oppositions.
  • Matrilocal marriage tested: the Tsimshian were matrilineal and preferred residence with the husband's kin, yet every marriage of Asdiwal is matrilocal and each one fails. The myth imagines the opposite of real practice in order to show that it cannot work, and so justifies the actual order.
  • Transformations: the Nass river version inverts many elements; variants of a myth are logical transformations of one another.

3. Structuralism in his study of mythology

  • Mythemes: "The Structural Study of Myth" (1955) broke the Oedipus story into units arranged in columns, showing how myth mediates contradictions such as autochthony versus birth from two parents.
  • Mythologiques (1964–71): four volumes, from The Raw and the Cooked, trace transformations across more than 800 American myths around oppositions like raw–cooked and nature–culture.
  • Universal mind: myths are a "bricolage" of available materials worked by the mind's binary logic (The Savage Mind, 1962); he aimed to show "how myths operate in men's minds without their being aware of the fact".

4. Critical evaluation

  • Contributions: revealed order beneath seemingly absurd stories, inspiring Edmund Leach's "Genesis as Myth" and, in India, Veena Das's Structure and Cognition (1977).
  • Unverifiable and reductive: Mary Douglas (1967), commenting on Asdiwal, admired the analysis but doubted that the structure it reveals is the meaning of a myth, and noted that such analyses are hard to test.
  • Mind without people: Geertz ("The Cerebral Savage", 1967) attacked its intellectualism, and Ricoeur called it "Kantianism without a transcendental subject"; it ignores narrators, performance, emotion and power.
  • Ahistorical and imposed: binary pairs may reflect the analyst more than the culture; he worked from translated texts, and his reading of Tsimshian kinship has been debated; Derrida (1966) rejected a fixed structural centre.

The Asdiwal study remains the clearest demonstration of structural analysis: myth as a logical tool for living with contradictions. Though abstract and hard to verify, it deeply shaped symbolic anthropology.
free.upa-2024-an1-7a:
DeconstructionLogocentrismDifféranceWriting Culture (1986)

Deconstruction is a practice of close reading developed by Jacques Derrida in Of Grammatology and Writing and Difference (both 1967). It shows that texts built on binary oppositions (speech/writing, nature/culture, presence/absence) quietly privilege one term, and that meaning is never fully present or final. It fed the postmodern critique of representation that reshaped anthropology in the 1980s.

1. The notion of deconstruction

  • Against logocentrism: Western thought, Derrida argued, seeks a fixed centre or origin (truth, presence, the spoken word); this "metaphysics of presence" treats speech as closer to truth than writing.
  • Différance: his coinage joins "to differ" and "to defer"; following Saussure, a sign means only through its difference from other signs, so meaning is endlessly postponed along a chain of traces.
  • Reversal and displacement: a reading first overturns a hierarchical pair, then shows that each term depends on the other, so the opposition itself becomes unstable; Rousseau's view of writing as a mere "supplement" to speech is his classic case.
  • "There is no outside-text": the phrase does not deny the world; it says we never reach reality free of language and interpretation.
  • Not a method: deconstruction is not applied from outside; it brings out tensions already at work within a text.

2. Derrida's engagement with anthropology

  • Critique of Lévi-Strauss: in "Structure, Sign and Play" (1966) he argued that structuralism still assumes a fixed centre, and that the nature/culture divide collapses at the incest prohibition, which Lévi-Strauss himself called a "scandal" because it is both universal and a rule.
  • "The Violence of the Letter": reading Lévi-Strauss's "Writing Lesson" among the Nambikwara (Tristes Tropiques, 1955), he argued that picturing an innocent people without writing repeats Rousseau's romanticism.
  • Ethnography as text: Writing Culture (Clifford and Marcus, 1986) treated ethnographies as rhetorical constructions offering "partial truths"; Geertz (Works and Lives, 1988) examined the anthropologist as author; dialogic accounts such as Crapanzano's Tuhami (1980) gave informants a voice.
  • Indian connection: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak translated Of Grammatology (1976) and in "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) showed how colonial and elite discourses spoke for the Indian woman in the sati debate.

3. Critical evaluation

  • Gains: reflexivity about power in representation, attention to silenced voices, and suspicion of colonial categories such as "tribe" and "primitive".
  • Relativism: if all meaning is undecidable, comparison and empirical knowledge suffer; Ernest Gellner (1992), Melford Spiro (1996) and Roy D'Andrade (1995) defended anthropology as a science.
  • Textualism: treating culture as text can neglect hunger, violence and political economy; Nancy Scheper-Hughes (1995) argued for the "primacy of the ethical".
  • Style and exclusions: its language is often obscure, and Women Writing Culture (Behar and Gordon, 1995) noted that the 1986 volume largely left out feminist ethnographers.
  • Later ethics: Derrida's later writing on justice ("Force of Law", 1990) shows deconstruction need not be politically empty.

Deconstruction offered no new theory of society, but it made anthropologists reflexive about the texts they write and the categories they use; good practice joins that critical awareness with rigorous fieldwork and attention to material conditions.
free.upa-2024-an1-7b:
Multifactorial traitPolygenic inheritanceLiability–threshold modelGene–environment interaction

A multifactorial trait is produced by many genes of small, additive effect (polygenes) acting together with environmental factors, so it shows no simple Mendelian ratios. Such traits vary continuously, like stature, or appear as a disease only when combined risk passes a threshold, like cleft lip or diabetes. R.A. Fisher (1918) showed that many Mendelian genes acting together explain continuous variation and the resemblance of relatives.

1. Characteristics

  • Continuous variation: values form a bell-shaped curve in the population; Nilsson-Ehle's wheat crosses (1909) showed how several additive genes produce such grading.
  • Environmental modification: nutrition, climate, disease and lifestyle shift the expression of the same genotype, so heritability is less than one.
  • Familial clustering without ratios: relatives of an affected person are at higher risk than the general population, the risk falls steeply with more distant relationship, and it rises with the number of affected relatives and the severity of the case.
  • Sex differences: when one sex has a higher threshold, affected members of that sex carry more liability; in pyloric stenosis, commoner in boys, the children of affected women run a higher risk (the Carter effect).

2. Continuous traits in humans

  • Stature: heritability is about 0.8 in well-fed populations, and a 2022 study of 5.4 million people (Yengo et al.) linked 12,111 common variants to height; yet height rose sharply in post-war Japan through better diet and health.
  • Skin colour: genes such as SLC24A5, SLC45A2, MC1R and OCA2 combine with sun exposure and tanning; in South Asia a lighter-skin allele of SLC24A5 explains part of the regional variation (Basu Mallick et al., 2013).
  • Others: blood pressure, body mass, finger ridge count and cognitive ability are all shaped by many genes plus environment.

3. Multifactorial disorders

  • Birth defects: cleft lip and palate, and neural tube defects such as spina bifida; folic acid taken around conception cut recurrence of neural tube defects by about 72% in the MRC Vitamin Study (1991).
  • Developmental dysplasia of the hip: familial and commoner in girls, but culture matters: tight swaddling with the legs straight raises risk, and Japan reduced cases after a campaign against it from 1975, while carrying infants astride the hip lowers risk.
  • Adult complex diseases: type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, hypertension and schizophrenia. The ICMR–INDIAB study (2023) estimated about 101 million Indians with diabetes; C.S. Yajnik's "thin-fat" Indian baby and the thrifty phenotype (Hales and Barker, 1992) show early nutrition interacting with genes.

Most normal human variation and the commonest diseases are multifactorial: heredity sets a range of possibilities, while environment and culture decide where people fall. Prevention through nutrition, lifestyle and screening therefore works even for highly heritable conditions.
free.upa-2024-an1-7c:
SamplingProbability and non-probability samplingRepresentativenessTheoretical saturation

Sampling means selecting a part of a population (the universe) so that what is learnt from it can be applied to the whole. In anthropology the right technique depends on the question: probability sampling suits surveys that must be statistically representative, while non-probability sampling suits intensive fieldwork that seeks depth of meaning rather than frequencies (H. Russell Bernard, Research Methods in Anthropology).

1. Before choosing: defining the study group

  • Universe and unit: decide whether the unit is the individual, household, lineage, hamlet or village.
  • Sampling frame: a list from which to draw (census or voter lists, a village house-listing, or genealogies collected by Rivers's genealogical method, 1910); its absence in remote areas limits random methods.
  • Size: depends on the population's variability, the precision needed and resources; in qualitative work, sampling continues until new cases add nothing new (saturation).

2. Probability techniques and where they fit

  • Simple random: every unit has an equal chance, by lottery or random numbers; suitable for a nutrition or anthropometric survey of households in one village with a full list.
  • Systematic: every k-th unit after a random start from a list; easy in a house-listed village, but biased if the list has a hidden pattern.
  • Stratified random: the population is divided into strata such as caste, clan, sex, age or landholding, and each is sampled; essential in a multi-caste Indian village so that Dalit, tribal and minority households are not missed.
  • Cluster and multistage: villages or hamlets are chosen first and households within them later; economical for scattered tribal populations. The National Family Health Survey uses a stratified two-stage design, selecting villages with probability proportional to size and then households systematically.
  • Biological studies: allele frequencies and growth standards need unrelated, randomly chosen individuals within each population; GenomeIndia sequenced about 10,000 healthy, unrelated Indians from 83 populations (2025).

3. Non-probability techniques

  • Purposive (judgment): cases are chosen for their relevance, as in single-village studies like M.N. Srinivas's Rampura.
  • Key informants: ritual specialists, elders and headmen give expert knowledge; cultural consensus analysis (Romney, Weller and Batchelder, 1986) shows that a few highly competent informants can reliably reveal shared knowledge.
  • Snowball and respondent-driven sampling: each respondent leads to others; the only practical route to hidden or stigmatised groups such as sex workers, drug users, transgender communities or circular migrants (Heckathorn, 1997).
  • Quota and convenience: fixed numbers per category, or whoever is available; quick for pilot studies but weak for generalisation.
  • Theoretical sampling: in grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss, 1967) new cases are chosen to test emerging concepts until saturation.

4. Limitations in the field

  • Frames and mobility: pastoralists, shifting cultivators and migrants rarely fit fixed lists; in very small communities such as many PVTGs, a complete enumeration is better than a sample.
  • Gatekeepers and bias: headmen or elite men may steer the anthropologist, silencing women and the poor; ethics demands informed individual and community consent.

No single technique is best. Good anthropology matches the sampling design to the research question and often combines the representativeness of probability methods with the depth of purposive ones.
free.upa-2024-an1-8a:
Social stratificationStructured inequalityCaste, class and genderFunctionalist and conflict views

Social stratification is the ranking of people into layers (strata) with unequal access to wealth, power and prestige, built into institutions and passed on across generations. Unlike individual differences of skill or luck, it is structured inequality, embedded in rules of descent, property, marriage and belief. Morton Fried (1967) separated egalitarian, rank and stratified societies; only in the last do groups have unequal access to basic resources.

1. How stratification sustains inequality

  • Ascription and closure: where position is fixed by birth (caste, race, estate), mobility is blocked; G.S. Ghurye (Caste and Race in India, 1932) listed hereditary occupation, endogamy and restrictions on food and contact as features that guard caste boundaries.
  • Control of resources: for Marx, classes arise from ownership of the means of production; inherited land and capital let advantage pass to the next generation.
  • Ideology and legitimation: beliefs make inequality look natural or deserved, such as karma and the purity–pollution scale analysed by Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966), racial theories, or claims of pure merit.
  • Power and sanction: M.N. Srinivas's dominant caste combines land, numbers and political weight; untouchability was enforced by boycott and violence.
  • Cultural capital: Pierre Bourdieu (Distinction, 1979) showed how taste, language and schooling reproduce class advantage, as English-medium education does in India today.

2. Theoretical perspectives

3. Critical examination

  • Not universal or natural: egalitarian foragers such as the Hadza and !Kung (James Woodburn, 1982; Christopher Boehm's "reverse dominance hierarchy", 1993) show that stratification arose historically with surplus, sedentary life and the state; many Indian tribal communities remain relatively egalitarian, though inequality is growing.
  • Mobility and change: Sanskritisation, Westernisation, education, migration and reservations (Articles 15(4), 16(4), 46) show strata are not frozen; André Béteille (Caste, Class and Power, 1965) found in Sripuram that caste, class and power were drifting apart.
  • Resistance and agency: lower strata rarely accept their rank; the Dalit movement inspired by Ambedkar and tribal movements challenge both hierarchy and its justifying ideology.
  • Intersectionality: gender cuts across caste and class (Kimberlé Crenshaw, 1989); Uma Chakravarti (1993) showed how "Brahmanical patriarchy" controls women's sexuality to preserve caste purity.
  • Order versus justice: functionalists stress coordination, but the Constitution treats inherited inequality as unjust: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, backed by the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. New divides of wealth and digital access show stratification also takes new forms.

Stratification is therefore not mere difference but organised, inherited inequality, upheld by property, ideology and power. Comparative evidence shows it is historically made and changeable, and India's experience shows both its persistence and its erosion.
free.upa-2024-an1-8b:
ABO blood groupMultiple alleles and codominanceRh (D) antigenHaemolytic disease of the newborn

Blood groups are inherited antigens on red cells. Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO system in 1900–01; the Rh system emerged when Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener (1940) raised antibodies against rhesus monkey cells, after Levine and Stetson (1939) had described a mother's reaction to her baby's blood. Simply inherited and easy to test, they became the first genetic markers in population studies (the Hirszfelds, 1919).

1. Genetics of the ABO system

  • One gene, an enzyme: the ABO gene on chromosome 9 (9q34) codes a glycosyltransferase that adds a sugar to the H substance: the A form adds N-acetylgalactosamine, the B form adds galactose, and the common O allele carries a one-base deletion that makes the enzyme inactive, leaving H unchanged.
  • Multiple alleles (Felix Bernstein, 1924): three main alleles, IA, IB and i; A and B are codominant and both are dominant over O; subgroups such as A1 and A2 exist.
  • Six genotypes, four phenotypes: AA or AO gives A, BB or BO gives B, AB gives AB, OO gives O.
  • Natural antibodies: people carry anti-A or anti-B against the antigens they lack, without prior exposure; this decides transfusion compatibility.
  • Bombay phenotype: described in Bombay by Bhende and colleagues (1952), people homozygous for a non-working H gene (FUT1, chromosome 19) cannot make H substance and type as O even when they carry A or B alleles, a classic case of epistasis.

2. Genetics of the Rh system

  • Two genes: RHD (D antigen) and RHCE (C/c and E/e antigens) lie side by side on chromosome 1 (1p36).
  • Rh positive and negative: a person with the D antigen is Rh positive (DD or Dd); Rh negative people are dd, in Europeans usually because RHD is deleted, so D behaves as a dominant trait.
  • Notation: Fisher and Race proposed three closely linked loci (C, D, E; haplotypes such as CDe and cde), while Wiener proposed one locus with many alleles; molecular work has confirmed two genes.
  • No natural anti-D: antibodies form only after exposure through transfusion or pregnancy.
  • Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin given to Rh-negative mothers (in use since the late 1960s) destroys foetal cells before she is sensitised; ABO incompatibility between mother and foetus also gives partial protection.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Distribution: O is the commonest group worldwide and very high among many Native American peoples; B reaches its highest frequencies in Central and South Asia, including India; Rh-negative people are about 15% in Europe, most among the Basques, and very rare in East Asia.
  • Selection: group O is linked with severe cholera (Bangladesh, 1985) but with protection against severe falciparum malaria (Rowe et al., 2007), and group A with stomach cancer (Aird et al., 1953), suggesting that natural selection shaped these frequencies.
  • Uses: safe transfusion, antenatal care, early population-affinity studies (A.E. Mourant) and, before DNA testing, paternity exclusion.

ABO and Rh show classic Mendelian inheritance with multiple alleles, codominance and epistasis, and their varied distribution makes them a window on human population history and selection.
free.upa-2024-an1-8c:
Biocultural evolutionPositive feedbackGene–culture coevolutionNiche construction

Human evolution is biocultural: biological changes made culture possible, and culture in turn altered the pressures of natural selection on the body. Darwin (The Descent of Man, 1871) already linked upright posture, free hands, tools and a larger brain, and Sherwood Washburn ("Tools and Human Evolution", 1960) argued that tools shaped the human body as much as the body shaped tools. This mutually reinforcing feedback is the synergy.

1. Biology that made culture possible

  • Bipedalism: walking upright, clear in the Laetoli footprints (about 3.66 million years ago), freed the hands for carrying and making tools.
  • Hand and brain: a strong opposable thumb with a precision grip, and a brain that grew from about 450 cc in australopithecines to about 1,350 cc in modern humans, allowed planning, imitation and teaching.
  • Long childhood and language: slow growth gave years for learning, and changes in the vocal tract and brain made symbolic communication possible, so knowledge could pass across generations.

2. Culture that reshaped biology

  • Tools and meat: stone tools from Lomekwi (about 3.3 million years) and the Oldowan (from about 2.6 million years) opened access to meat and marrow; the "expensive tissue" hypothesis (Aiello and Wheeler, 1995) links this rich diet to a bigger brain and a smaller gut.
  • Fire and cooking: Richard Wrangham (Catching Fire, 2009) argued that cooking shrank teeth, jaws and gut in Homo erectus; burnt material at Wonderwerk Cave shows fire use by about 1 million years ago, though the start of habitual cooking is debated.
  • Gene–culture coevolution: cultural practices created new selection pressures (see table); dual inheritance theory (Boyd and Richerson, 1985) and niche construction theory (Odling-Smee, Laland and Feldman, 2003) model this two-track inheritance.
  • Social learning: cumulative culture rewarded better social cognition, cooperation and longer childhood, which in turn made culture richer.

3. Critical discussion

  • Synergy, not a single cause: earlier "brain-first" and "Man the Hunter" views (Washburn and Lancaster, 1968) gave way to mosaic models; Sally Slocum's "Woman the Gatherer" (1975) argued that gathering, food sharing and childcare were equally important.
  • Uneven evidence: dates for fire, language and cooking remain uncertain, and correlations between tools and anatomy do not prove cause.
  • Buffering and mismatch: clothing, shelter and medicine relax some selection, while rapid cultural change creates mismatches such as obesity and type 2 diabetes (Neel's "thrifty genotype", 1962).
  • Indian illustrations: the main European lactase-persistence allele also occurs in India, more often in the north-west and among some herding groups (Gallego Romero et al., 2012), and the sickle-cell allele is frequent in malarial tribal belts of central India.

Humans are products of biocultural evolution; neither biology nor culture alone explains us. As agriculture, cities, medicine and now gene editing accelerate change, this coevolution continues.
free.upa-2024-an2-1a:
DigitisationJAM trinityDigital divideTechnoscapes

Digitisation of the rural economy is the shift of village credit, payments, markets, land records and welfare delivery onto digital platforms. Since Digital India (2015) and the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and mobile phones), the Indian village has entered what Arjun Appadurai (1990) called global technoscapes, which are reshaping old patron–client ties and creating new divides.

1. Instruments of digitisation

  • Money and welfare: Jan Dhan accounts (2014), Aadhaar-based Direct Benefit Transfer and UPI (2016) now carry MGNREGA wages, pensions and PM-KISAN instalments (₹6,000 a year since 2019) straight to rural households.
  • Markets and farming: e-NAM (2016) links agricultural mandis online, and the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) is building an Agri Stack of farmer IDs and digital crop surveys.
  • Land and governance: SVAMITVA (2020) maps village house sites by drone and gives owners property cards usable as collateral; Common Service Centres and BharatNet take e-governance to gram panchayats.

2. Changes in village society and economy

  • Fewer middlemen: direct transfers reduce leakages and weaken the hold of the moneylender, ration dealer and trader; Robin Jeffrey and Assa Doron's Cell Phone Nation (2013) shows how the mobile phone gave farmers, fishers and small traders price information and new bargaining power.
  • New roles for women: women of self-help groups work as banking correspondents and, under the Namo Drone Didi scheme (2023), as drone operators for spraying crops, entering public economic roles once closed to them.
  • Translocal households: instant transfers tie migrant workers in cities to families in the village, so the village economy now extends far beyond its boundary.

3. Concerns from an anthropological view

  • Digital divide: women who had ever used the internet rose from 33% in NFHS-5 (2019–21) to 64% in NFHS-6 (2023–24), yet over a third had never gone online; older, poorer and remote Adivasi households lag further behind.
  • Exclusion errors: failed biometric authentication or unlinked records can cut off rations and wages; the death of eleven-year-old Santoshi Kumari in Simdega, Jharkhand (2017), after her family's ration card was cancelled for want of Aadhaar linking, became a symbol of this risk.
  • New dependencies: kiosk operators and agents emerge as fresh intermediaries, while the collection of personal data raises issues of privacy and surveillance.

Digitisation is turning the village as a social system from a face-to-face, patron-based economy into a networked one. Its gains will be inclusive only if digital literacy (PMGDISHA), local-language platforms and offline grievance options reach women, the elderly and remote Adivasi hamlets.
free.upa-2024-an2-1b:
State formationChiefdom to stateCircumscription theoryRajput myth

A state society has a centralised government that claims, in Max Weber's sense, a monopoly of legitimate force over a territory, supported by taxation, a bureaucracy, law and class stratification. In Elman Service's sequence of band, tribe, chiefdom and state (Primitive Social Organization, 1962) and Morton Fried's sequence of egalitarian, rank, stratified and state societies (1967), the state is the most complex form of political organisation.

1. Theories of the origin of the state

  • Integrative theories: Karl Wittfogel (Oriental Despotism, 1957) linked early states to the management of large irrigation works; others stress the control of long-distance trade and the redistribution of surplus.
  • Conflict theories: Friedrich Engels (The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, 1884) saw the state as the instrument of a propertied class; Robert Carneiro (1970) argued that population growth in circumscribed land, such as the narrow coastal valleys of Peru, led to warfare, conquest and centralised rule.
  • Urban revolution: V. Gordon Childe (1950) tied the state to food surplus, full-time specialists, writing and monumental building in the first cities.

2. How archaeology recognises a state

  • Settlement hierarchy: three or more tiers of settlement (capital, towns, villages) point to administrative control, as Henry Wright and Gregory Johnson (1975) argued for early south-western Iran.
  • Material markers: palaces, temples, standard weights, seals, writing, fortifications and differences in burial wealth reveal central authority and inequality.

3. State formation in India

  • Harappan civilisation: planned cities, uniform weights and seals suggest strong authority, yet the lack of palaces and royal tombs led Gregory Possehl to describe a complex society without a clear state, while others speak of city-states.
  • Ganga valley: Romila Thapar's From Lineage to State (1984) traces how iron-age surplus and ranked clans turned gana-sanghas into monarchies, leading to the Mahajanapadas (c. 6th century BCE) and the rise of Magadha.
  • Tribal states: Surajit Sinha (1962) showed how chiefs in tribal central India, such as those of the Bhumij, claimed Rajput descent to legitimise kingship; the Nagvanshis of Chotanagpur and the Ahom kingdom of Assam are other cases of tribal state formation.

The state thus arose from multiple causes working together: surplus, population pressure, war, trade and ritual legitimation. Indian evidence, from Harappa to the kingdoms of Chotanagpur, also explains present-day tribe–state relations.
free.upa-2024-an2-1c:
St Thomas ChristiansEast Syriac riteSynod of DiamperCaste-like status

The Syro-Malabar Christians are the largest section of Kerala's St Thomas Christians (Nasranis), who trace their faith to the apostle Thomas, believed by tradition to have landed at Kodungallur in 52 CE. Their church is an Eastern Catholic Church in full communion with Rome but with its own East Syriac liturgy; it became a Major Archiepiscopal Church in 1992 and has been headed by Major Archbishop Mar Raphael Thattil since 2024.

1. Historical formation

  • Persian links: for centuries the community received bishops from the Church of the East and worshipped in Syriac; the Tharisapalli copper plates (c. 849 CE) record privileges granted to a church at Kollam and show the Christians' standing among Kerala's trading groups.
  • Latinisation: after the Portuguese arrived, the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperur, 1599), led by Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa, imposed Latin rites and Roman control.
  • Split: resentment culminated in the Coonan Cross Oath (1653); those who stayed with Rome (Pazhayakoottukar) became today's Syro-Malabar Church, while the Puthenkoottukar adopted the West Syriac (Jacobite and Orthodox) tradition.

2. Socio-cultural features: Christianity in an Indian idiom

  • Caste-like status: Syrian Christians traditionally claimed high-caste origin, kept rules of ritual distance from lower castes and married within the community; L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer recorded these patterns in Anthropology of the Syrian Christians (1926). Later Dalit converts were often kept in separate congregations.
  • Endogamous sub-group: the Knanaya (Southists), who trace descent from the merchant Thomas of Cana, still practise strict endogamy within the church.
  • Shared Kerala customs: at marriage the groom ties a minnu (a tali bearing a cross) and gives a mantrakodi sari; the oil lamp, the Margamkali dance and the traditional chatta and mundu dress show a common regional culture.

3. Contemporary profile

  • Agrarian migration: from the 1920s to the 1970s, Syrian Christian farmers from Travancore settled the Malabar highlands, turning forests into plantations but also adding to pressure on Adivasi land in areas such as Wayanad.
  • Diaspora and internal debate: migration to the Gulf, Europe and North America, and the recent dispute over a uniform mode of celebrating the Holy Qurbana, show a community negotiating tradition and change.

The Syro-Malabar Christians illustrate the Indianisation of Christianity: a universal faith rooted in local caste, kinship and ritual idioms, which adapted to Kerala society instead of replacing it.
free.upa-2024-an2-1d:
Simple artisan tribesAsur iron-smeltingInter-tribal exchangeCraft revival

In Census 2011, Jharkhand's 32 Scheduled Tribes formed 26.2% of its population (the list was widened in 2022, adding the Puran). Besides large cultivating tribes such as the Santhal, Munda, Oraon and Ho, some small communities specialised in crafts. L.P. Vidyarthi and B.K. Rai (The Tribal Culture of India, 1977) placed such groups in a separate simple artisan type of tribal economy, which shows that tribal economies were never purely subsistence-based.

1. Features of the artisan economy

  • Symbiotic exchange: artisan families lived in or near Munda and Oraon villages and exchanged tools, cloth and baskets for grain at harvest, a customary system resembling jajmani ties.
  • Myth and memory: Munda origin myths speak of the sun-god Singbonga overcoming the Asur iron-smelters, which hints at old links between iron-working and cultivating peoples.
  • Technical knowledge: they hold specialised knowledge of ores, charcoal, bamboo and fibres, passed down within families; the Birhor of S.C. Roy's The Birhors (1925) combined hunting with rope-making for sale in markets.

2. Problems and change

  • Decline of crafts: colonial forest laws restricted charcoal-making and bamboo cutting, while cheap factory iron and, later, plastic goods destroyed markets for smelted iron and baskets.
  • Shift to wage work: many artisans have become cultivators, mine and construction labourers or seasonal migrants; bauxite mining in the Asur hill country adds pressure on their land.
  • Marginality: small numbers, low literacy and weak bargaining power keep them dependent on traders and middlemen.

3. Efforts at revival

  • Markets and design: Jharcraft (a State undertaking), TRIFED's Tribes India outlets and Van Dhan Vikas Kendras help artisans reach urban buyers.
  • Skills and credit: PM Vishwakarma (2023) supports trades such as blacksmithy and basket-making with training, tool kits and loans, and PM-JANMAN covers the PVTGs among them.

The artisan tribes of Jharkhand show occupational specialisation and exchange within tribal society. Protecting their traditional knowledge through design support, fair markets and recognition of their crafts can turn heritage into a secure livelihood.
free.upa-2024-an2-1e:
Stunting and wastingIntergenerational undernutritionUNICEF causal frameworkFood insecurity

Stunting (low height-for-age, below –2 SD of the WHO growth standard) reflects long-term undernutrition, while wasting (low weight-for-height) reflects recent hunger or illness. NFHS-6 (2023–24) found 29.3% of Indian children under five stunted (35.5% in NFHS-5) and wasting almost unchanged at 19.0%, with Scheduled Tribe children faring worse. The UNICEF conceptual framework (1990) groups the causes into three levels.

1. Immediate causes

  • Poor diet: low intake of protein, fats and micronutrients, seasonal hunger before the harvest, and a shift from millets, pulses, tubers and forest foods to polished rice alone.
  • Disease burden: repeated diarrhoea, malaria (common in the forested belt of Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand) and worm infestations reduce absorption and cause sudden weight loss.
  • Low birth weight: early marriage and pregnancy, and anaemic, underweight mothers, produce small babies, so undernutrition passes from one generation to the next.

2. Underlying causes

  • Household food insecurity: land alienation, displacement and restricted access to forests have cut food from gathering, hunting and fishing, increasing dependence on markets and the PDS.
  • Care practices: long hours of work in fields, forest collection or migrant labour leave mothers little time for frequent feeding; delayed complementary feeding and some pregnancy food taboos play a part, though culture should not be blamed in isolation.
  • Water, sanitation and services: unsafe water and open defecation cause gut infections that stunt growth, and scattered hamlets often lack functioning anganwadis and health centres.

3. Basic causes

  • Poverty and isolation: remote hill settlements, poor roads and low incomes limit both food and care; Meghalaya (36.8%), a tribal-majority State, and Jharkhand (35.0%) are among the States with the most stunting (NFHS-6), and in NFHS-5 the tribal-majority district of West Singhbhum had India's highest district figure, 60.6%.
  • Low education and voice: low female literacy and weak participation in planning keep nutrition low on the local agenda.
  • Migration and conflict: seasonal migration interrupts ICDS services, and insecurity in some districts disrupts delivery. Repeated child deaths among the Korku of Melghat (Maharashtra) showed how seasonal hunger, illness and distance from care combine.

Child undernutrition among tribes is intergenerational and has many causes. Along with POSHAN 2.0, ICDS and PM-JANMAN anganwadis, it needs secure forest and land rights, the revival of millets and forest foods, clean water and counselling by local tribal health workers.
free.upa-2024-an2-2a:
PVTGsPM-JANMANHabitat rightsCritique of "primitive"

Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) are the most marginalised among the Scheduled Tribes: 75 communities in 18 States and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. After the Dhebar Commission (1960–61) noted wide inequality within the STs, the government began from 1975 to identify Primitive Tribal Groups (PTGs) on four criteria: pre-agricultural technology, very low literacy, economic backwardness and a stagnant or declining population. The term was changed to PVTG in 2006.

1. Recent welfare measures

  • PM-JANMAN (launched at Khunti, 15 November 2023): a ₹24,104 crore mission (Centre ₹15,336 crore) planned for 2023–24 to 2025–26, with works continuing in 2026, that brings 11 interventions of nine ministries to PVTG habitations: pucca houses, roads, piped water, electricity, mobile medical units, anganwadis, hostels, multipurpose centres and Van Dhan Vikas Kendras.
  • Development of PVTGs scheme: central funds for State Conservation-cum-Development plans on housing, livelihood, education and culture.
  • Health: the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) screens tribal populations, including PVTGs.
  • Rights: the Forest Rights Act, 2006 provides habitat rights for PVTGs (Section 3(1)(e)), first granted to the Baigas of Madhya Pradesh (2015) and since to groups such as the Kamar of Chhattisgarh and eight PVTGs of Odisha, still a small share of the 75.

2. Critical assessment

  • Strengths: the first time-bound, habitation-level plan with dedicated funds and convergence of ministries, reaching hamlets never served before.
  • Slow delivery: official figures show only about half the houses, a seventh of the road length and almost none of the hostels completed by December 2025, in the plan's final year.
  • Infrastructure over culture: a uniform "saturation" model can ignore each group's ecology and choices; roads also bring traders and tourists into fragile habitats, as the Andaman Trunk Road did for the Jarawa.
  • Data and identification: there is no reliable PVTG census, the list is unrevised since 1993, and States identify groups differently, so needy groups may be missed.
  • Rights deficit: few habitat claims are settled, while mining and conservation projects threaten PVTG lands.

3. Why "Primitive Tribal Group" was a misnomer

  • Evolutionist baggage: "primitive" comes from nineteenth-century unilinear evolutionism, such as L.H. Morgan's Ancient Society (1877), which ranked peoples from savagery to civilisation; Adam Kuper's The Invention of Primitive Society (1988) showed the category to be a Western construct.
  • Wrong basis: the criteria mostly measured vulnerability (stagnant numbers, low literacy, economic backwardness), not cultural simplicity. Toda pastoralists, Kota artisans and the Siddis of Gujarat, of African descent, are all on the list but none is "primitive".
  • Stigma and paternalism: the label portrayed these groups as living fossils to be "civilised", ignoring their sophisticated ecological knowledge, such as the Dongria Kondh's stewardship of the Niyamgiri hills.
  • Rights-based shift: "vulnerable" locates the problem in historical marginalisation, in line with the State's duty under Article 46 to protect weaker sections from injustice.

PVTG policy has moved from labelling to targeted investment, but success depends on consent-based, culturally sensitive development that joins services with secure habitat rights, in the spirit of Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel: development along the lines of the people's own genius.
free.upa-2024-an2-2b:
PESA 1996Gram SabhaFifth ScheduleWomen's representation

The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA), based on the Bhuria Committee report (1995), extends Part IX of the Constitution, with modifications, to the Fifth Schedule Areas of ten States. It makes the Gram Sabha the core of self-rule and requires State laws to be in consonance with customary law, social and religious practices and traditional management of community resources, a form of legal pluralism long advocated by anthropologists.

1. How PESA empowers local self-governance

  • Gram Sabha at the centre: every habitation or group of habitations managing its affairs by custom can have its own Gram Sabha, which approves plans, selects beneficiaries and certifies the use of funds.
  • Control over resources: ownership of minor forest produce, prior recommendation for minor-mineral leases, management of minor water bodies and consultation before land acquisition.
  • Protection from exploitation: powers to prevent land alienation and restore illegally alienated land, regulate money-lending and the sale of liquor, and manage village markets.
  • Tribal leadership: at least half the seats are reserved for STs, and all chairperson posts are reserved for STs, so traditional leaders and new elites enter the formal system.
  • Example: Jharkhand's rules, notified on 2 January 2026, require the Gram Sabha's prior consent for land acquisition and allow it to keep a village fund from forest produce, market fees and ponds; MP and Chhattisgarh framed their rules in 2022, while Odisha's are still pending.

2. Impact on women's political participation

  • Numbers: Article 243D's one-third reservation for women applies in Scheduled Areas, and several PESA States, such as Jharkhand, Odisha, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, reserve half the seats; Adivasi women now serve as ward members, sarpanches and Zila Parishad chairpersons.
  • An open forum: every adult voter is a Gram Sabha member, so women can speak directly on liquor, forest produce, rations and schools; some villages, like Khamdhogi in Kanker (Chhattisgarh), require one woman and one man from each household at decision meetings.
  • Issue-based leadership: women have led Gram Sabha resolutions against liquor shops and for forest protection, and Dongria Kondh women spoke at the Niyamgiri Gram Sabhas (2013) that rejected bauxite mining.

3. Limitations

  • Custom versus equality: customary councils such as the Manki-Munda of the Ho and Munda or the Majhi-Pargana of the Santhal rarely admit women; in Madhu Kishwar v. State of Bihar (1996) the Supreme Court declined to strike down male-only succession to land among Chotanagpur tribes.
  • Proxy representation: husbands acting for elected women ("sarpanch-pati"), low literacy and heavy work burdens limit real voice.
  • Weak implementation: delayed rules, bureaucratic control and Gram Sabha consent treated as a formality in mining and land deals.

PESA is a charter of self-rule, and reservation has brought Adivasi women into public life; turning presence into power needs timely rules, training in tribal languages, women's meetings before each Gram Sabha and joint land titles under the Forest Rights Act.
free.upa-2024-an2-2c:
Colonial ethnographyCensus and casteIndigenisationField view

Anthropology in India began as colonial knowledge: administrators, missionaries and census officers described "tribes and castes" in order to govern them. Bernard Cohn (Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge, 1996) and Nicholas Dirks (Castes of Mind, 2001) showed how this "ethnographic state" fixed fluid identities into rigid categories. Indian anthropologists, from S.C. Roy to M.N. Srinivas, gradually made the discipline an autonomous, field-based science.

1. Deconstructing the colonial phase

  • Orientalist beginnings: the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, William Jones) studied India mainly through Sanskrit texts, producing a "book view" of a timeless, caste-bound society.
  • Ethnography for rule: works such as E.T. Dalton's Descriptive Ethnology of Bengal (1872), H.H. Risley's The Tribes and Castes of Bengal (1891) and Edgar Thurston's Castes and Tribes of Southern India (1909) served revenue, army recruitment and policing.
  • Racial theory of caste: Risley used the nasal index to argue that caste rank reflected race (The People of India, 1908), and his 1901 Census ranked castes by social precedence, prompting caste associations to petition for higher rank.
  • Policies built on labels: the Criminal Tribes Act (1871), "martial races" recruitment and the isolation of Excluded Areas (1935) applied these categories to whole communities.

2. Indian anthropologists and the autonomy of the discipline

  • S.C. Roy (1871–1942): a Ranchi lawyer who wrote the pioneering monograph The Mundas and their Country (1912), used his knowledge to defend Munda land rights, and founded Man in India (1921) as an Indian platform.
  • G.S. Ghurye: questioned Risley's racial theory in Caste and Race in India (1932) and the colonial isolation policy in The Aborigines—"So-called"—and Their Future (1943), though he himself saw tribes as backward Hindus.
  • N.K. Bose and D.N. Majumdar: Bose's "Hindu method of tribal absorption" (1941) offered an Indian civilisational model of tribe–caste interaction; Majumdar studied culture contact (A Tribe in Transition, 1937) and founded The Eastern Anthropologist (1947).
  • Iravati Karve and M.N. Srinivas: Karve's Kinship Organisation in India (1953) joined textual and field evidence; Srinivas's "field view", with concepts such as Sanskritisation and dominant caste, replaced the colonial and Indological "book view".

3. Institutions and policy voice

  • Indian institutions: the first university department of anthropology at Calcutta, the Anthropological Survey of India (1945) and Tribal Research Institutes built research capacity at home.
  • Influence on policy: the debate between Ghurye's assimilation and Verrier Elwin's protection led to the middle path of integration in Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel.
  • Self-reflection: L.P. Vidyarthi traced formative, constructive and analytical phases of Indian anthropology, and K.S. Singh's People of India project documented 4,635 communities.

4. Limits of autonomy

  • Colonial categories such as "tribe" and fixed caste lists still shape research and policy, and upper-caste perspectives long dominated; Adivasi and Dalit scholars, such as Virginius Xaxa, now call for views from within the communities studied.

Indian anthropology has moved from colonial ethnography to an independent, field-based discipline; making it fully decolonised requires reflexive, community-centred research that serves the people it studies.
free.upa-2024-an2-3a:
RakhigarhiSothi-Siswal cultureAncient DNAIndigenous origins

Rakhigarhi (Hisar district, Haryana), on the plain of the now-dry Ghaggar–Chautang river system, is one of the largest sites of the Harappan civilisation (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE). Excavated by Amarendra Nath of the ASI (1997–2000), by Vasant Shinde of Deccan College in the 2010s and again by the ASI in recent years, its mounds record the growth of a farming village into a Harappan town and have yielded the first ancient genome from a Harappan site.

1. Evidence from Rakhigarhi

  • Cultural sequence: excavators report an early phase with Hakra-related pottery, an Early Harappan phase with Sothi-Siswal ware, and a Mature Harappan phase, a continuous local development.
  • Urban features: planned streets and lanes, drains, houses of mud brick and burnt brick, platforms and enclosure walls follow familiar Harappan norms.
  • Crafts and exchange: bead-making of carnelian, agate and other stones, shell bangles, copper and gold ornaments, terracotta, weights and inscribed seals show full integration into Harappan technology and trade.
  • Cemetery: extended burials, mostly laid north–south with pots and ornaments as grave goods, follow Harappan custom; a joint burial of a man and a woman was reported in 2018.
  • Ancient DNA: the genome of a woman from the Harappan cemetery, in a settlement dated c. 2800–2300 BCE (Shinde and colleagues, Cell, 2019), carried a mix of Iranian-related and Ancient Ancestral South Indian (AASI) ancestry and no steppe pastoralist ancestry; her Iranian-related lineage had separated from that of Iranian plateau farmers before farming began there.

2. Linkages to the Harappan civilisation

  • An eastern core: together with Kalibangan, Banawali and Bhirrana, Rakhigarhi shows that the Ghaggar basin was a heartland of the civilisation, not a periphery.
  • Indigenous roots: continuity of pottery and settlement supports a home-grown transition from village farming to urban life, rather than colonisation from the west.
  • Genetic links: the Rakhigarhi genome resembles the "Indus Periphery" individuals found at Gonur (Turkmenistan) and Shahr-i-Sokhta (Iran), confirming long-distance contact; populations of this kind are the largest source of ancestry in present-day South Asians.
  • Heritage: the Union Budget 2020–21 named Rakhigarhi one of five iconic archaeological sites to be developed with an on-site museum.

3. Critical appraisal

  • One genome, large claims: conclusions about a whole civilisation rest on a single, poorly preserved genome; more samples from several sites are needed.
  • Politicised readings: the result was publicised as settling the "Aryan" question, but the authors argued that steppe ancestry, and probably Indo-European languages, arrived after the Harappan period; it neither proves nor disproves a Vedic Harappa.
  • Size and dating: claims that Rakhigarhi was larger than Mohenjo-daro assume that all mounds were occupied together, and a very early beginning rests on a few radiocarbon dates.
  • Protection: the modern villages of Rakhi Khas and Rakhi Shahpur sit on parts of the site, and full excavation reports are still awaited.

Rakhigarhi has shifted the Harappan story eastward and given bio-archaeology a central place. Its evidence is best read critically and in combination with archaeology, genetics and linguistics, not used to settle present-day identity debates.
free.upa-2024-an2-3b:
SanskritisationDominant casteSacred complexNature-Man-Spirit complex

Two influential lenses shaped the study of change in village India. M.N. Srinivas, trained under G.S. Ghurye at Bombay and at Oxford in structural-functionalism, explained change through caste mobility in a single village, Rampura. L.P. Vidyarthi, trained at Lucknow and at Chicago under Robert Redfield, used a civilisational and holistic approach that linked villages and tribes to sacred centres, ecology and industry.

1. Srinivas's approach

  • Field view: he held that intensive fieldwork, not texts (the "book view"), reveals how caste actually works; his Rampura fieldwork is recalled in The Remembered Village (1976).
  • Sanskritisation: introduced in Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India, published in 1952: a lower caste or tribe adopts the rituals, diet and beliefs of a higher caste to claim higher rank, bringing positional change without structural change.
  • Dominant caste: a caste with numerical strength, land, and economic and political power, such as the Okkaligas of Rampura ("The Dominant Caste in Rampura", 1959), sets local models and settles disputes.
  • Westernisation and secularisation: Social Change in Modern India (1966) traced the effects of British rule, education, law and technology on caste and ritual.

2. Vidyarthi's approach

  • Sacred complex: in The Sacred Complex in Hindu Gaya (1961) he showed how sacred geography, sacred performances and sacred specialists (the Gayawal priests) tie pilgrims from countless villages to a centre of the great tradition.
  • Nature-Man-Spirit complex: in The Maler (1963), on the Sauria Paharia of the Rajmahal hills, ecology, social life and the spirit world form one interdependent whole, so a change in one, such as forest loss, transforms the others.
  • Industrialisation and planned change: his study of tribal villages around the Hatia industrial area near Ranchi (Socio-cultural Implications of Industrialisation in India, 1970) traced land loss, migration and wage labour; he argued for an applied, problem-solving anthropology in tribal development.

3. Points of convergence

  • Fieldwork: both relied on long, first-hand fieldwork rather than texts alone.
  • Village and civilisation: both saw the village as linked to a wider civilisation; Sanskritisation and the sacred complex are both channels between the little and great traditions of Robert Redfield, applied to India also by McKim Marriott.
  • Continuity: both treated change as adaptive and gradual rather than a break with tradition.

4. Critical evaluation

  • Srinivas: Yogendra Singh (Modernization of Indian Tradition, 1973) and others noted that his concepts are cultural and say little about class, conflict or structural change; Sanskritisation takes a Brahmanical model as the norm and does not explain Dalit assertion against the caste order.
  • Vidyarthi: richer on ecology and applied concerns, but largely descriptive; the sacred complex stresses integration and harmony more than power and inequality.

Srinivas explained who moves up and how within the caste order, while Vidyarthi showed how villages and tribes are bound to civilisation, ecology and industry; read together, they offer a fuller picture of social change in village India.
free.upa-2024-an2-3c:
Indian Forest Act 1878State monopolyLand alienationHistorical injustice

For Adivasis the forest is land, food, medicine and sacred space. Colonial forestry, beginning with the Indian Forest Act, 1878, turned customary rights into privileges granted by the State, and post-colonial policy largely continued this monopoly until the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, which admitted in its preamble a historical injustice to forest-dwelling communities.

1. Colonial phase (1878–1947)

  • Indian Forest Act, 1878: divided forests into reserved, protected and village forests; in reserved forests local rights could be extinguished or commuted, and shifting cultivation, grazing and collection without permission became offences.
  • Forest Policy, 1894: declared that State forests existed for the public benefit, subordinated users' claims, and released forest land for permanent cultivation, which opened tribal tracts to non-tribal settlers.
  • Indian Forest Act, 1927: consolidated these powers and is still the basic forest law; forest villages, grazing fees and forced labour for forest staff became common.
  • Impact: shifting cultivation (bewar of the Baiga, podu of the Konda Reddi) was banned or confined, and forest grievances fed the Rampa rebellion of Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922–24) and the Gond struggle of Komaram Bheem (1940).

2. After Independence (1947–2006)

  • National Forest Policy, 1952: put national needs above local ones, set a goal of one-third of land under forest, and treated local use as concessions to be regulated rather than rights.
  • Conservation laws: the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and Project Tiger (1973) created parks and sanctuaries that displaced forest villages; the 42nd Amendment (1976) moved forests to the Concurrent List.
  • Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980: central approval for diverting forest land slowed deforestation but froze the regularisation of tribal cultivation, so long-settled cultivators became "encroachers".
  • National Forest Policy, 1988: a turning point that recognised the symbiotic bond of tribals with forests and made their domestic needs the first charge on forest produce; Joint Forest Management (1990) followed, though as a partnership on the department's terms.
  • PESA and the courts: PESA (1996) gave Gram Sabhas ownership of minor forest produce, but a 2002 drive to evict "encroachers", following Supreme Court orders in the Godavarman case, uprooted many families and spurred the campaign for the FRA.

3. FRA 2006 as a corrective

  • Rights recognised: individual rights to land cultivated before 13 December 2005 (up to 4 ha), community forest resource rights and habitat rights of PVTGs, with the Gram Sabha starting the process.
  • Persisting gaps: high rejection of claims, few community rights and the Supreme Court's 2019 eviction order for rejected claimants (soon stayed) show that insecurity continues.

Between 1878 and 1988 policy treated forests as State property and Adivasis as a problem; the FRA reversed this logic towards community rights. Verrier Elwin (The Baiga, 1939) and Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf documented the costs; implementing the FRA in letter and spirit is now the real test.
free.upa-2024-an2-4a:
Informed consentIndigenous data sovereigntyAlgorithmic biasGenetic essentialism

Anthropological ethics rest on doing no harm, informed consent and respect for the people studied, as set out in the American Anthropological Association's Principles of Professional Responsibility (2012). Rapid advances in ancient and population genomics, gene editing and artificial intelligence (AI), which can analyse images, texts and DNA at scale, have sharpened old dilemmas of consent, ownership, privacy and power.

1. Biological anthropology and genetic research

  • Consent and secondary use: blood samples given by the Havasupai of Arizona for diabetes research were later used for studies of inbreeding, migration and schizophrenia without consent; the tribe's lawsuit was settled in 2010.
  • Biocolonialism: the Human Genome Diversity Project (proposed 1991) was criticised by indigenous groups for collecting their DNA for global science and possible patents without benefit-sharing; the Nagoya Protocol (2010) and India's Biological Diversity Act (2002) now require fair benefit-sharing.
  • Ancient DNA and the dead: sampling skeletons, as at Rakhigarhi, raises the question of who speaks for the dead; researchers proposed five global guidelines for such work in Nature (2021), including early engagement with communities and other stakeholders.
  • Genetic essentialism: ancestry findings can be misused to revive racial typologies, rank groups or fuel identity politics over "Aryan" or "indigenous" origins.
