  • Stigma and limits: screening of tribal populations under the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023) is vital but needs counselling and confidentiality to avoid stigma in marriage and work; He Jiankui's gene-edited babies (2018) showed how easily ethical lines can be crossed.

2. Socio-cultural anthropology and AI

  • Culture as data: AI systems trained on scraped posts, folk songs, oral narratives and images of Adivasi communities turn living culture into corporate property, which Nick Couldry and Ulises Mejias (2019) call data colonialism.
  • Algorithmic bias: commercial facial-analysis systems misclassified darker-skinned women far more often than lighter-skinned men (Buolamwini and Gebru, "Gender Shades", 2018); in India, predictive policing could reproduce the colonial "criminal tribe" stigma against Denotified Tribes.
  • Privacy in digital fieldwork: online ethnography blurs public and private, and AI can re-identify people even from anonymised interviews or photographs.
  • Representation: AI-generated "tribal" images and deepfakes can exoticise communities, while tribal languages are barely represented in AI tools, deepening exclusion.

3. Indian context and the way forward

  • Genome India: the Genome India Project (2020) released data on about 10,000 genomes in January 2025 through the Indian Biological Data Centre; its promise for precision medicine depends on strict access rules and feedback to the communities sampled.
  • Frameworks: ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research (2017) and its AI guidelines for health research (2023), the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) and UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021).
  • Anthropology's contribution: participatory research, return of results in local languages, prior consent of Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas, and indigenous data sovereignty under the CARE principles (collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, ethics).

AI and genomics can deepen understanding of human diversity and improve health, but without consent, equity and accountability they risk a new extractive research. Anthropology's insistence on the voice of the people studied should guide both.
free.upa-2024-an2-4b:
Birsa MundaUlgulanKhuntkattiRevitalisation movement

Birsa Munda (1875–1900), revered as Dharti Aba (father of the earth), led the Ulgulan (great tumult) of the Mundas of Chotanagpur. His movement joined religious reform, agrarian protest and political assertion against dikus (outside landlords and moneylenders), missionaries and British rule. K.S. Singh's The Dust-Storm and the Hanging Mist (1966) remains its classic study.

1. Early life

  • Birth: born on 15 November 1875 at Ulihatu (now in Khunti district, Jharkhand) into a poor Munda family that moved from village to village in search of work.
  • Education: studied at the German Lutheran mission school at Chaibasa and briefly became a Christian, but broke with the missionaries over their attitude to the Munda land struggle.
  • Influences: learnt Vaishnava ideas from Anand Panre and came into contact with the Sardar agitation (mulkai larai), which since the mid-nineteenth century had sought Munda land rights through petitions and courts.

2. Prophet and reformer (1895)

  • New faith: in 1895 he declared himself a messenger of Singbonga, the supreme god, and gathered followers known as Birsaites.
  • Teachings: belief in one god, giving up liquor, animal sacrifice and fear of witchcraft, cleanliness and wearing the sacred thread, a blend of Munda, Hindu and Christian ideas.
  • Politics: he called for an end to the rule of the dikus and the British and the return of the Mundas' own rule; arrested in 1895, he spent two years in jail.

3. The Ulgulan (1899–1900)

  • Causes: the breakdown of khuntkatti, the joint ownership of land by the lineage of the original clearers, as jagirdars and thikadars took over villages; forced labour (beth-begari), rising rents, moneylenders and forest restrictions.
  • Course: around Christmas Eve 1899 his followers attacked churches, police stations and landlords' property around Khunti, Ranchi and Singhbhum; in January 1900 troops fired on Mundas gathered at Dombari Buru.
  • End: captured in February 1900, Birsa died in Ranchi jail on 9 June 1900, aged about twenty-five.

4. Impact of his sacrifice on tribal society

  • Land protection: survey and settlement operations recorded khuntkatti rights, and the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908 restricted the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals; it remains a key shield for Adivasi land.
  • Identity and pride: the Birsaite faith survives, the movement anticipated later reformist movements such as the Tana Bhagats (1914), and it inspired the Jharkhand movement; the State was created on his birth anniversary in 2000.
  • National recognition: his portrait hangs in Parliament, 15 November is observed as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, and his 150th birth anniversary year (2024–25) was celebrated as Janjatiya Gaurav Varsh; PM-JANMAN was launched at Khunti on 15 November 2023.
  • Anthropological meaning: a revitalisation movement in Anthony Wallace's sense (1956) and a messianic one in Stephen Fuchs's Rebellious Prophets (1965), it shows tribal religion becoming a vehicle of reform and resistance.

Birsa's short life turned Munda grievances into a movement for land, dignity and self-rule. The CNT Act and Jharkhand's statehood are his living legacy, and today's debates over land and forest rights keep his call for abua raj (our own rule) relevant.
free.upa-2024-an2-4c:
Demographic transitionPopulation ageingDemographic dividendRegional divergence

India became the world's most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate) and is in the late stage of the demographic transition. NFHS-6 (2023–24) put its total fertility rate (TFR) at 2.0 and the Sample Registration System at 1.9 for 2024, below the replacement level of 2.1, and the UN's World Population Prospects 2024 projects a peak of about 1.7 billion in the early 2060s followed by decline. The next fifty years will therefore bring ageing and uneven change rather than runaway growth.

1. A closing demographic dividend

  • Peak and decline: the share of the working-age population is expected to peak around 2041 (Economic Survey 2018–19); unless jobs, skills and health keep pace, the dividend can become a burden of unemployment.
  • Unused potential: low female work participation and a large informal sector limit the gains from a young workforce.

2. Rapid ageing

  • Scale: the UNFPA India Ageing Report 2023 projects the share of people aged 60 and above to rise from 10.5% in 2022 to 20.8% by 2050, with the elderly outnumbering children by about 2046.
  • Care deficit: more widows (feminisation of ageing), smaller and nuclear families, migration of the young and weak pension coverage will strain family care, while chronic diseases and dementia rise.

3. Regional and federal divergence

  • Two demographic Indias: southern and western States reached low fertility early, while Bihar (2.7) and Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Meghalaya (2.2 each) remain above replacement in NFHS-6, so future young workers will be concentrated in the north and east.
  • Federal balance: Lok Sabha seats are frozen until the first Census after 2026 (84th Amendment, 2001); delimitation after Census 2027 could shift seats towards high-growth States and strain Centre–State relations.
  • Migration: large flows from north to south and from village to city will reshape cities and may provoke nativist demands for local jobs.

4. Gender and social structure

  • Skewed sex ratio at birth: 929 girls per 1,000 boys (NFHS-5, 2019–21; not reported in the NFHS-6 fact sheets) reflects son preference, creating marriage squeezes and long-distance brides in parts of the north.
  • Changing family: later marriage, fewer children and more elderly living alone mark what Ron Lesthaeghe and Dirk van de Kaa (1986) called the second demographic transition, weakening kin-based care.
  • Vulnerable groups: very small communities such as the Great Andamanese and Onge face fragile numbers, while Scheduled Tribes, with higher fertility and poor health services, need tailored policies.

India's task is shifting from population control to population management: jobs and skills for the young, more women in work, universal health and pensions for the old, and fair federal arrangements. Anthropology can help by studying how families, kinship care and migration adapt to these changes.
free.upa-2024-an2-5a:
Bridge and bufferTribal frontiersMeeting points of regionsRoy Burman

B.K. Roy Burman, Census anthropologist and later professor at Visva-Bharati, argued that India's tribal homelands form a buffer zone. They lie at the meeting points of the dominant linguistic-political regions and along international frontiers, so tribal peoples historically played a double "bridge and buffer" role between civilisations, a theme he restated in his paper "Tribal and Indigenous Rights and Wrongs" (1996).

1. The concept

  • Location: tribal tracts form an almost unbroken belt of hills and forests from the north-west to the north-east of the subcontinent, wedged between plains-based states and language regions. The Gond and Bhil country, for instance, spans the borderlands of the Hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Odia and Telugu regions.
  • Bridge role: tribes carried goods, people and ideas across these frontiers. The Bhotias of the Kumaon–Garhwal Himalaya ran the trade with Tibet, and hill peoples of the North-East exchanged produce at foothill markets of the Assam plains.
  • Buffer role: by occupying the spaces between powerful neighbours, tribes kept them apart and absorbed their friction. Dominant states therefore had an interest in leaving tribal identity and autonomy intact. Roy Burman's own doctoral fieldwork was among the Toto, near the Bhutan border.

2. Colonial disruption and policy

  • Dysfunction: colonial armies, roads, trade and resource extraction pierced the buffer and made this role largely dysfunctional, which he linked to tribal unrest. After the Kol rising (1831–32), Chotanagpur was made a non-regulation area under Regulation XIII of 1833.
  • Protective administration: the Inner Line (Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873), the Scheduled Districts Act (1874) and, after 1950, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules partly preserved the buffer by limiting outside penetration.
  • Present relevance: frontier communities of Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh and the Indo-Myanmar border remain strategic, so their rights and goodwill matter for national integration as well as security.

3. Evaluation

  • Strength: the idea joins ecology, geography and politics and explains why tribal identities survived beside large civilisations, complementing Surajit Sinha's tribe–caste continuum (1965).
  • Criticism: it values tribes for the service they render to states; a buffer can also become a militarised zone, or a contact zone where traders and moneylenders exploit tribal people. Many writers therefore read the buffer zone as this transitional interface of exchange and exploitation.

Roy Burman thus turned the "periphery" into a frontier of interaction. Secure land rights and real autonomy allow these communities to remain bridges of national integration rather than zones of conflict.
free.upa-2024-an2-5b:
ILO Convention No. 169Self-identificationConsultationConvention No. 107

The Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169) of the International Labour Organization was adopted on 27 June 1989 and came into force on 5 September 1991. It revised Convention No. 107 (1957), replacing its goal of integration with respect for the distinct identity, institutions and land rights of these peoples.

1. Main provisions

  • Coverage and self-identification: it applies to tribal peoples whose social, cultural and economic conditions set them apart, and to indigenous peoples descended from populations present at conquest or colonisation. Self-identification is a fundamental criterion (Article 1).
  • Consultation and participation: governments must consult these peoples through their own representative institutions, in good faith and with the aim of reaching agreement or consent (Article 6); they may set their own development priorities (Article 7).
  • Customs and institutions: customary law and institutions are respected where compatible with human rights (Articles 8–10).
  • Land and resources: ownership and possession of traditionally occupied lands, rights in natural resources, consultation before mineral exploration and a share in benefits (Articles 14–15); relocation only with free and informed consent, with a right to return or compensation (Article 16).
  • Welfare: fair employment, vocational training, community-based health services using traditional medicine, mother-tongue education and cross-border contacts.

2. Is India a signatory?

  • No. ILO conventions are ratified rather than signed, and India has not ratified No. 169. It remains bound by No. 107, which it ratified on 29 September 1958 and which continues for states that have not moved to No. 169.
  • Reasons: the Government holds that all Indians are indigenous and prefers the constitutional category of Scheduled Tribes, notified under Article 342, to self-identification. Provisions on land ownership, subsurface resources and consent also sit uneasily with eminent domain and State ownership of minerals.
  • Few takers: only about two dozen states have ratified it, mostly in Latin America; Nepal (2007) is the only South Asian party.
  • Related stand: India voted for the non-binding UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) on the same understanding.

3. Indian parallels

  • Domestic equivalents: the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA 1996, the Forest Rights Act 2006 and gram sabha consent under the land acquisition law of 2013 echo the Convention; in the Niyamgiri case (2013) the Supreme Court let gram sabhas decide on bauxite mining.

India's non-ratification reflects its reservations about "indigeneity" and resource sovereignty rather than a lack of safeguards; faithful implementation of PESA and FRA would deliver much of the Convention's promise of consent-based development.
free.upa-2024-an2-5c:
ApataniWet-rice cultivationRice–fish cultureZiro valley

The Apatani, a Tani-speaking (Tibeto-Burman) people of the Ziro valley in Lower Subansiri district, Arunachal Pradesh (about 1,500–1,600 m), practise settled, highly productive wet-rice cultivation amid neighbours who traditionally relied on shifting cultivation. C. von Fürer-Haimendorf (The Apa Tanis and Their Neighbours, 1962) described their valley as a striking pocket of intensive farming in the eastern Himalaya.

1. Rice–fish–millet integration

  • Wet-rice plots: the flat valley floor is divided into levelled plots enclosed by raised earthen bunds that hold water through the season; early- and late-ripening local rice varieties are transplanted.
  • Rice–fish culture: fingerlings, today mainly common carp, are released into the flooded plots soon after transplanting. Deeper trenches inside each plot shelter the fish in hot spells, and fish are harvested with the paddy, adding protein and cash.
  • Millet on bunds: finger millet is grown on the partition bunds, so no land is wasted.

2. Water, soil and labour

  • Irrigation: streams from the forested hills are diverted into main and branch channels; bamboo or wooden pipes pass water from plot to plot, and bamboo screens at the outlets stop fish escaping.
  • Community control: channels are repaired by collective labour, and water is shared by customary rules under village elders and the traditional council (bulyang).
  • Organic fertility: crop residues, village organic waste and nutrient-rich runoff from the slopes keep fields fertile without chemical fertiliser.
  • Human labour: there are no ploughs or draught animals; men and women work with hoes and simple tools, often in cooperative groups.

3. A managed landscape

  • Zoned land use: rice fields, dry gardens, bamboo and pine groves, community forests and sacred groves are kept apart, protecting the watersheds that feed the fields.
  • Exchange and ritual: surplus rice has long been traded to neighbouring Nyishi and hill Miri groups; festivals such as Myoko (March) and Dree (July, for a healthy crop) tie farming to ritual.
  • Recognition and pressures: the Apatani Cultural Landscape is on India's Tentative List for UNESCO World Heritage (2014), but the growth of Ziro town and the shift of youth to other occupations put the system under pressure.

Apatani farming shows that sustainable intensification is possible through indigenous knowledge, community institutions and ecological balance, a lesson for climate-resilient agriculture in the hills.
free.upa-2024-an2-5d:
Sixth ScheduleArticle 244(2)Autonomous District Councils125th Amendment Bill

The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) provides self-government for tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram through Autonomous District Councils (ADCs). It grew out of the Constituent Assembly's sub-committee on the North-East tribal areas chaired by Gopinath Bordoloi (1947), which preferred autonomy to the colonial policy of exclusion.

1. Present structure and powers

  • Ten councils function today (see table); the Governor can create, merge or alter autonomous districts and regional councils.
  • Composition: a council has up to 30 members, of whom up to four are nominated by the Governor, for a five-year term; the Bodoland Territorial Council is larger.
  • Legislative powers: land, forests other than reserved forests, jhum, village and town administration, inheritance, marriage, divorce and social customs, with the Governor's assent.
  • Judicial and fiscal powers: village and council courts try cases among tribal people; councils levy taxes on land, professions and markets, share mineral royalties and regulate money-lending and trade by non-tribals. Acts of Parliament and the State can be applied with modifications or withheld.

2. Status: gains

  • Protection: restrictions on land transfer and recognition of customary law (Khasi, Garo, Mizo, Karbi, Bodo) have slowed land alienation and preserved identity.
  • Instrument of peace: accords have used the Schedule to end insurgencies. The Bodo Accord of 2003 created the Bodoland Territorial Council, and the Bodo Accord (2020) and Karbi Anglong Agreement (2021) promised more powers and funds.

3. Status: problems and reform

  • Fiscal dependence: councils rely on State grants that are often delayed, and parallel State departments blur accountability.
  • Weak grassroots democracy: below the council, traditional chiefs and village bodies are often unelected and exclude women; non-tribals and smaller tribes within a council area feel unrepresented.
  • Pending reform: the Constitution (125th Amendment) Bill, introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 6 February 2019, would add elected village and municipal councils, State Finance Commissions and elections by State Election Commissions. The Standing Committee reported in March 2020, but the Bill was still pending in 2026.
  • Demands for extension: Ladakh (a Union Territory since 2019) and the hill areas of Manipur seek Sixth Schedule status; Ladakh's talks with the Centre were still unresolved in October 2026.

The Sixth Schedule remains India's most far-reaching model of tribal self-rule. Passing the 125th Amendment, assured finances and elected, inclusive village councils would turn it into genuine participatory democracy.
free.upa-2024-an2-5e:
Backward classesProtective discriminationArticles 15(4) and 16(4)Indra Sawhney

The Constitution does not define "backward classes" as such; in practice the term covers Scheduled Castes (Article 341), Scheduled Tribes (Article 342) and socially and educationally backward classes (SEBCs, Article 342A), commonly called OBCs. Their safeguards rest on substantive equality: special measures for the disadvantaged are a facet of equality, not an exception to it, as the Supreme Court affirmed in Indra Sawhney (1992).

1. Social and educational safeguards

  • Article 15(4): special provisions for SEBCs, SCs and STs, added by the First Amendment (1951) after the Champakam Dorairajan judgment.
  • Article 15(5): reservation in admissions to educational institutions, including private unaided ones but not minority institutions (93rd Amendment, 2005).
  • Articles 17 and 46: abolition of untouchability, and a directive to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially SCs and STs, and protect them from injustice and exploitation.
  • Articles 19(5), 23 and 244: reasonable restrictions on outsiders' movement and property rights to protect STs, a ban on forced and bonded labour, and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules for Scheduled and Tribal Areas.

2. Safeguards in public employment

  • Article 16(4): reservation in posts for any backward class not adequately represented in the services.
  • Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B): reservation in promotion for SCs and STs (77th Amendment, 1995) and carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies (81st Amendment, 2000); Article 335 balances these claims with efficiency of administration.
  • Judicial limits: Indra Sawhney upheld the 27% OBC quota but excluded the creamy layer and set a 50% ceiling; State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024) allowed sub-classification of SCs.

3. Political and institutional safeguards

  • Representation: reserved seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies (Articles 330 and 332, extended to 2030 by the 104th Amendment), and in panchayats and municipalities (Articles 243D and 243T), where States may also reserve seats for backward classes.
  • Commissions: Article 340 lets the President appoint a commission on backward classes (Kalelkar, Mandal). The National Commissions for SCs (Article 338), STs (Article 338A, 89th Amendment, 2003) and Backward Classes (Article 338B, 102nd Amendment, 2018) monitor safeguards.
  • Federal balance: the 105th Amendment (2021) restored the States' power to prepare their own SEBC lists.

These provisions make protective discrimination a constitutional tool of social justice; their future lies in better data, sub-categorisation so that benefits reach the most backward, and effective enforcement.
free.upa-2024-an2-6a:
Custodians of natureClimate vulnerabilityTraditional ecological knowledgeClimate justice

India's Scheduled Tribes (10.43 crore, 8.6% of the population, Census 2011) live mostly in forests, hills, drylands and islands, where sacred groves, rotational farming and community rules have conserved the landscape. Yet they lag on almost every indicator of well-being: in 2011–12, 45.3% of rural STs were below the poverty line (Tendulkar method). This paradox of custodianship leaves them highly exposed to climate change, which they did little to cause.

1. Custodians, yet deprived

  • Conservation ethic: the Dongria Kondh revere the Niyamgiri hills as the domain of Niyam Raja; Khasi villages protect sacred forests such as Mawphlang; the Baiga refused to plough "Mother Earth" (Verrier Elwin, The Baiga, 1939).
  • Dispossession: colonial forest laws turned commons into State property, and dams and mines displaced tribal people; Amita Baviskar's In the Belly of the River (1995) traced this for the Bhilala of the Narmada valley.
  • Unfinished recognition: the Forest Rights Act 2006 admitted a "historical injustice", but community forest rights remain far from fully recognised.

2. How climate change threatens survival

  • Food and livelihood: tribal farming is largely rain-fed; erratic monsoons, droughts and heatwaves cut yields of millets, pulses and paddy.
  • Forest produce: shifts in the flowering and fruiting of mahua, sal and tendu, and more frequent forest fires (Similipal, 2021), shrink incomes and diets.
  • Water and pastures: drying springs in the Himalaya and north-eastern hills, and erratic snowfall and shrinking pastures for pastoralists such as the Changpa of Ladakh and the Gaddi.
  • Health: heat stress and the spread of malaria and other vector-borne diseases in belts already burdened by anaemia, sickle cell disease and undernutrition.
  • Islands and coasts: sea-level rise and cyclones threaten the Nicobarese and other island communities, as the 2004 tsunami showed.
  • Culture: distress migration to brick kilns and cities loosens ties with sacred sites, language and ecological knowledge.

3. The added risk of climate "solutions"

  • Green grabbing: compensatory plantations, large hydropower dams, solar parks and mining of critical minerals can take tribal commons in the name of mitigation, and carbon projects may bypass gram sabhas.

4. Critical appraisal

  • Not passive victims: traditional ecological knowledge — diverse seeds and millets, Apatani rice–fish farming, community fire lines — is recognised by the IPCC (Sixth Assessment, 2022) as vital for adaptation.
  • Against romanticism: Kent Redford's critique of the "ecologically noble savage" (1991) warns that conservation is livelihood-based, not innate; Guha and Martinez-Alier call it an "environmentalism of the poor".
  • Structural roots: vulnerability springs as much from insecure land rights, poor services and exclusion from decisions as from climate itself; infrastructure schemes such as PM-JANMAN (2023, ₹24,104 crore for PVTGs) and DAJGUA (2024, ₹79,156 crore) need a climate-adaptation lens.

Tribal people are front-line victims but also knowledge holders. Securing community forest rights, gram sabha consent under PESA and tribal-led adaptation would turn custodianship into climate justice.
free.upa-2024-an2-6b:
SecularisationReligiosityFundamentalismSpirituality

Anthropology treats religion as a cultural system of symbols (Clifford Geertz, 1966) and the sacred as things set apart from the profane (Émile Durkheim, The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, 1912). In this frame, secularism, religiosity, religious fundamentalism and spiritualism are different orientations to the sacred: the place of religion in public life, the intensity of personal commitment, a militant return to "fundamentals", and an inward search for the transcendent.

1. Secularism

  • Meaning: a political principle that separates religion from State power; secularisation is the social process by which religion loses public authority, what Max Weber called the "disenchantment of the world" (1917 lecture).
  • Contested thesis: Peter Berger's The Sacred Canopy (1967) predicted religious decline, but he later spoke of the "desecularisation" of the world (1999).
  • Indian form: equal respect and "principled distance" (Rajeev Bhargava) rather than a wall of separation; "secular" entered the Preamble through the 42nd Amendment (1976), and S.R. Bommai (1994) made it part of the basic structure.
  • Anthropological critique: Talal Asad (Formations of the Secular, 2003) shows the secular is itself a historically made Western category; T.N. Madan (1987) argued it sits uneasily with South Asian religious life.

2. Religiosity

  • Meaning: the degree of religious involvement, with belief, ritual, experience, knowledge and consequences as its dimensions (Charles Glock, 1962).
  • Ethnography: popular religiosity lives in pilgrimage, vows and festivals, as in L.P. Vidyarthi's sacred complex of Gaya (1961); tribal religiosity is woven into daily life, as in sarna (sacred grove) worship of the Munda and Oraon and the Ho belief in bonga spirits described by D.N. Majumdar.
  • Point: high religiosity is compatible with a secular State, as India shows.

3. Religious fundamentalism

  • Origin: the term comes from The Fundamentals (1910–15), pamphlets of American Protestants defending the literal truth of scripture.
  • Features: literal reading of sacred texts, an imagined pure past, sharp boundaries between believers and others, selective use of modern technology and a drive to shape State and law; the Fundamentalism Project of Martin Marty and Scott Appleby (1990s) saw it as a reaction to secular modernity.
  • Anthropological reading: it is a modern identity politics, not "tradition"; Arjun Appadurai (Fear of Small Numbers, 2006) links such movements to the insecurities of globalisation. Taliban rule in Afghanistan is an example.

4. Spiritualism

  • Two senses: narrowly, belief in communication with spirits of the dead, a Western movement of the nineteenth century; broadly, spirituality as a personal, experiential quest for meaning, often outside institutions. E.B. Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) defined religion minimally as "the belief in Spiritual Beings" (animism).
  • Ethnography: Saora shamans marry spirit spouses of the underworld (Verrier Elwin, The Religion of an Indian Tribe, 1955); Vidyarthi's nature–man–spirit complex among the Maler (1963); Bhakti and Sufi mysticism; modern yoga and meditation movements.

The categories overlap: a deeply religious society can be secular, spirituality may reject institutions, and fundamentalism is itself a product of modernity. Anthropology's comparative, emic view shows each as a way of seeking meaning and identity in a plural society.
free.upa-2024-an2-6c:
LodhaCriminal Tribes ActDenotificationAction anthropology

The Lodha are a small forest community of the old Midnapore district (now Paschim Medinipur and Jhargram) of West Bengal, listed as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group. Branded a "criminal tribe" under the colonial Criminal Tribes Act (1871), they carried that stigma long after denotification in 1952. P.K. Bhowmick (1926–2003) of the University of Calcutta, a student of N.K. Bose, through his doctoral study The Lodhas of West Bengal (1963) and decades of fieldwork and welfare work, helped turn this label into a story of rehabilitation.

1. How the Lodha came to be "criminalised"

  • Loss of the forest: hunters, gatherers and collectors of forest produce, they lost access as forests were reserved by the colonial State or cleared for cultivation; landlessness and hunger pushed some into petty theft.
  • Colonial labelling: the Act treated whole communities as hereditary criminals, with registration, roll-calls and curbs on movement, so police and neighbours suspected every Lodha.
  • Persistent stigma: even after 1952, "habitual offender" laws, police suspicion and social boycott continued; the death of Chuni Kotal (1992), the first woman graduate among the Lodhas, after harassment at her university showed how deep the prejudice ran.

2. Bhowmick's ethnographic contribution

  • Ethnography against stereotype: his long fieldwork described Lodha clans, kinship, economy and beliefs, and showed that their "criminality" was a product of dispossession and poverty, not of birth or culture — a direct challenge to the colonial theory of hereditary crime.
  • Identity in transition: he recorded their claim to Savara (Sabar) descent and their shift from foraging to wage labour and settled farming, situating them as a changing community rather than a fixed "criminal type".
  • Voice in policy: his writings made the Lodha a model case for rehabilitating, not policing, ex-criminal tribes.

3. Action anthropology in the field

  • Institution-building: encouraged by N.K. Bose, he founded a voluntary body, the Samaj Sevak Sangha (1955), and later the Institute of Social Research and Applied Anthropology; their centre at Bidisa, near Narayangarh in Paschim Medinipur, opened an ashram hostel for Lodha boys in 1964 and schools at Daharpur.
  • Rehabilitation: with support from the district administration and police, Lodha families were settled on farmland at Daharpur; the work combined settled agriculture, schooling, vocational skills and access to government schemes, so that the community could earn a living with dignity.
  • Building trust: the approach rested on long-term rapport, working with the people rather than only studying them, in the spirit of what Sol Tax called "action anthropology".

4. Wider significance and limits

  • A model for denotified tribes: his work anticipated the national campaign of Mahasweta Devi and Ganesh Devy for denotified communities, the Renke (2008) and Idate (2018) commissions and the welfare board for DNTs (2019).
  • Limits: rehabilitation by welfare could not by itself undo police prejudice, landlessness or poor schooling; lasting change needs repeal of habitual-offender laws, land rights and sensitised police.

Bhowmick showed that anthropology can be a tool of social justice: by replacing a colonial stereotype with ethnographic understanding and patient rehabilitation, he helped the Lodha move from stigma towards citizenship.
free.upa-2024-an2-7a:
Holistic healthSocial determinantsMedical pluralismSyndemic

Holistic health treats well-being as physical, mental, social and spiritual, shaped by culture, economy and environment; the WHO Constitution (1948) defines health as "a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity". For marginalised sections — tribal people, Dalits, migrant workers, slum dwellers, women and the elderly poor — COVID-19 tested how far existing paradigms deliver this ideal.

1. Existing paradigms

  • Biomedical model: disease as bodily malfunction, treated by drugs and hospitals; powerful but narrow, and still dominant in health spending.
  • Biopsychosocial model: George Engel (Science, 1977) added psychological and social factors to diagnosis and care.
  • Primary health care and social determinants: the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) called for "Health for All", and the WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (2008, chaired by Michael Marmot) tied health to income, housing, education and gender.
  • Medical pluralism: Charles Leslie (Asian Medical Systems, 1976) and Arthur Kleinman's "explanatory models" (1980) show that people combine biomedicine, AYUSH and folk healers; tribal healing links nature, humans and spirits.
  • Critical medical anthropology: Paul Farmer's "structural violence" and Merrill Singer's "syndemic" (1990s) show diseases clustering with poverty and exclusion; One Health links human, animal and environmental health.

2. Inferences from COVID-19

  • Distancing as privilege: crowded slums, shared toilets and daily-wage work made isolation impossible; the 2020 lockdown sent lakhs of migrant workers walking home.
  • A syndemic, not just a pandemic: Richard Horton (The Lancet, 2020) argued that the virus interacted with chronic disease and inequality.
  • Small, isolated groups at risk: infection reached the Great Andamanese (2020), showing the danger to communities with little immunity and access.
  • Digital divide: online vaccine registration and online schooling excluded the poor; vaccine hesitancy in tribal areas eased where local leaders, ASHAs and tribal languages were used.
  • Community as frontline: ASHAs, self-help groups such as Kerala's Kudumbashree and village councils carried the response; free grain under PMGKAY for about 80 crore people protected nutrition.

3. Critical examination

  • Biomedical, hospital bias: public health spending stayed far below the National Health Policy 2017 target of 2.5% of GDP by 2025, and hospital insurance under PM-JAY does not cover outpatient care, nutrition or sanitation.
  • Holism on paper: mental health and social determinants remain under-funded; the Expert Committee on Tribal Health (Abhay Bang, report 2018) found tribal health lagging and sought a separate tribal health plan.
  • Pluralism needs evidence: traditional systems carry cultural trust, but unproven cures also spread during the pandemic.

4. Way forward

  • Integrated primary care: strengthen Ayushman Arogya Mandirs in tribal and slum areas with local health workers, as Chhattisgarh's Mitanins did.
  • Culturally competent care: use tribal languages, involve healers in referral and target diseases such as sickle cell anaemia (National Mission, 2023).

COVID-19 proved that health is social before it is clinical. A rights-based, community-led and culturally sensitive model is the true test of holistic health for the marginalised.
free.upa-2024-an2-7b:
Origin of casteRacial theoryEndogamyCaste, class and race

Caste (jati) is a hereditary, endogamous and ranked group linked to occupation and to ideas of purity and pollution. G.S. Ghurye (Caste and Race in India, 1932) listed its six features: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities and privileges, restricted choice of occupation and restrictions on marriage. Its origin is debated, and no single theory explains it.

1. Theories of origin and their criticism

  • Traditional (varna) theory: the Purusha Sukta (Rig Veda X.90) derives four varnas from the cosmic being. Criticism: it explains varna, not thousands of jatis, and legitimises hierarchy.
  • Racial theory: H.H. Risley (The People of India, 1908) used the nasal index to argue that caste ranks followed an Aryan–non-Aryan racial gradient; Ghurye traced caste to Indo-Aryan Brahmins' concern with purity. Criticism: Ghurye found the correlation only in the north, and Iravati Karve's measurements in Maharashtra found castes closer to regional neighbours than to equally ranked castes elsewhere; the nasal index is no measure of race. Genome studies (Reich et al., 2009; Moorjani et al., 2013) show mixed ancestry followed by long endogamy, not separate races.
  • Occupational theory: John Nesfield (1885) saw castes as occupational groups ranked by the prestige of their work. Criticism: castes of different rank share occupations, and occupation cannot explain endogamy or untouchability.
  • Ritual theories: A.M. Hocart (Caste, 1950) traced caste to hereditary roles in royal sacrifice; Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966) built it on the opposition of pure and impure. Criticism: Gerald Berreman saw in it a Brahmanical view from above that ignores power and exploitation.
  • Mana theory: J.H. Hutton (Caste in India, 1946) linked caste to tribal taboos on food and marriage and belief in mana. Criticism: mana is a Melanesian idea, and such taboos exist without caste elsewhere.
  • Endogamy theory: B.R. Ambedkar ("Castes in India", 1916) argued that caste arose when endogamy was superimposed on exogamy, enforced through sati, enforced widowhood and child marriage. Criticism: it explains how caste was maintained better than how it began.
  • Other and multi-factor views: Émile Senart (1896) traced caste to ancient family and marriage rules, and Denzil Ibbetson (1883) to tribes and guilds hardened by Brahmin influence; Hutton and Karve (Hindu Society: An Interpretation, 1961) conclude that race, occupation, ritual, politics and the absorption of tribes worked together over centuries.

2. Caste, class and race distinguished

  • Comparisons: Oliver C. Cox (Caste, Class and Race, 1948) treated them as distinct systems; Gerald Berreman (1960) found caste in India and race in the American South alike: rigid and birth-ascribed.
  • Changing caste: groups rise through Sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas, 1952), and caste, class and power, once aligned, drift apart, as André Béteille found in a Tanjore village (Caste, Class and Power, 1965).
  • Race today: biological anthropology treats race as a social construct, not a valid biological division.

Caste is best seen as the product of multiple historical processes, hardened by endogamy. Today it adapts to class and politics rather than vanishing, which is why constitutional safeguards against caste discrimination remain essential.
free.upa-2024-an2-7c:
Ethno-nationalismEthnic boundariesImagined communitiesIdentity politics

Ethno-nationalism is the claim that a people defined by shared descent, language, religion or culture should have its own political community — autonomy, statehood or dominance within a State. Modernisation was expected to dissolve such loyalties, yet from the break-up of Yugoslavia and the Rwandan genocide (1990s) to the Catalan referendum (2017) and conflicts in India's North-East, it has seen a resurgence. Anthropology explains it through ethnicity as a socially maintained boundary (Fredrik Barth, Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, 1969).

1. Anthropological lenses

  • Primordialism: Clifford Geertz ("The Integrative Revolution", 1963) described attachments to blood, language, religion and custom as deeply felt "givens" that new States struggle to integrate; this explains the emotional intensity of ethnic claims.
  • Instrumentalism: Abner Cohen (Custom and Politics in Urban Africa, 1969) and Paul Brass (Ethnicity and Nationalism, 1991) show elites mobilising ethnicity to compete for land, jobs and power.
  • Constructivism: Benedict Anderson's "imagined communities" (1983), Ernest Gellner's Nations and Nationalism (1983) and Hobsbawm and Ranger's The Invention of Tradition (1983) show nations being made through print, schooling and symbols.
  • Ethno-symbolism: Anthony D. Smith (The Ethnic Origins of Nations, 1986) argues that modern nations rework older myths, memories and homelands, which is why some identities resonate.
  • Boundary approach: for Barth, the boundary matters more than the "cultural stuff" inside it; boundaries harden when groups compete for scarce resources.

2. Why the resurgence?

  • Globalisation and insecurity: Arjun Appadurai (Fear of Small Numbers, 2006) argues that global flows breed uncertainty, turning majorities against minorities; Thomas Hylland Eriksen sees identity politics as a response to rapid change.
  • Migration and demography: fear of outsiders over land, jobs and culture drives "sons of the soil" movements (Myron Weiner, 1978), such as the Assam movement (1979–85); the final NRC list in Assam (2019) left out about 19 lakh people.
  • Uneven development: relative deprivation fuels demands for autonomy, as in the Jharkhand movement (State formed 2000) and Bodoland.
  • Recognition politics: contests over ST status and territory, as in Manipur's Meitei–Kuki-Zo conflict since May 2023, and the Pathalgadi movement in Jharkhand (2017–18) asserting gram sabha authority.
  • Digital media and elections: social media spreads myths of origin and grievance, and electoral competition rewards ethnic appeals.

3. Evaluation

  • Constructive side: recognition through linguistic States, the Sixth Schedule and peace accords has accommodated many movements, as Mizoram's lasting peace shows.
  • Destructive side: exclusive identities can lead to majoritarianism, ethnic cleansing and displacement of minorities.
  • Anthropological lesson: identities are multiple and situational; essentialising them, by States or movements, deepens conflict.

Ethno-nationalism is thus a modern response to insecurity, not a survival of the past. Federal accommodation, dialogue and equal citizenship, rather than suppression, are the anthropologically informed answer.
free.upa-2024-an2-8a:
Madras handaxe industryAcheulianAttirampakkamJwalapuram

South India holds some of the oldest and best-dated Palaeolithic evidence in Asia. Indian prehistory itself began here when Robert Bruce Foote found a handaxe at Pallavaram, near Chennai, on 30 May 1863 — the first Palaeolithic tool recognised in India. Sites in the Kortallayar, Hunsgi–Baichbal, Krishna and Kurnool regions span the Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic.

1. Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian) sites

  • Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu): in the Kortallayar valley, Shanti Pappu and colleagues dated Acheulian handaxes and cleavers to about 1.5 million years ago by cosmogenic burial dating (Science, 2011), among the oldest Acheulian outside Africa.
  • Pallavaram and Vadamadurai (near Chennai): quartzite handaxes and cleavers formed the "Madras handaxe industry", which de Terra and Paterson (1939) contrasted with the chopper-dominated Soanian of the north-west.
  • Isampur, Hunsgi valley (Karnataka): K. Paddayya excavated an Acheulian quarry-cum-workshop on limestone, tentatively dated by ESR on herbivore teeth to about 1.27 million years ago (2002); nearby Hunsgi localities preserve camp sites with tools in place.
  • Andhra Pradesh and Telangana: Acheulian tools occur along the Krishna (Nagarjunakonda, Nalgonda) and in the Kurnool and Prakasam (Giddalur) basins.

2. Middle Palaeolithic sites

  • Attirampakkam: Levallois flakes and points dated to about 385,000–172,000 years ago (Akhilesh and colleagues, Nature, 2018) reveal an early Middle Palaeolithic in India.
  • Jwalapuram (Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh): Middle Palaeolithic tools lie just below and above the Youngest Toba Tuff ash (about 74,000 years); Michael Petraglia's team (Science, 2007) argued that toolmakers survived the eruption. A long microlithic sequence from about 35,000 years ago follows at the Locality 9 rock shelter (Clarkson and colleagues, 2009).

3. Upper Palaeolithic sites

  • Kurnool caves (Andhra Pradesh): Robert Bruce Foote and his son Henry explored the Billa Surgam caves in 1884; Muchchatla Chintamanu Gavi, studied by M.L.K. Murty in the 1970s, yielded rare bone tools with late Pleistocene fauna.
  • Renigunta (Andhra Pradesh): M.L.K. Murty (1968) reported a blade-and-burin industry.

4. Significance of South Indian Palaeolithic cultures

  • Early dispersal: an Acheulian about 1.5 million years old shows that early humans, probably Homo erectus, reached peninsular India soon after this technology appeared in Africa, not as late, marginal newcomers.
  • Local evolution: the early Levallois industry at Attirampakkam suggests a gradual local transition, long before the generally accepted spread of modern humans; who made these tools is still debated.
  • Out-of-Africa and Toba: Jwalapuram is central to debates on when Homo sapiens reached India and how the Toba super-eruption affected life.
  • Behaviour and ecology: quarries, workshops and camps (Isampur, Hunsgi) show planning and raw-material choice; caves preserve fauna and bone tools.
  • History of the discipline: Foote's finds launched Indian prehistory, and southern data tested the two-culture (Soan versus Madras) model.
  • Gaps: no fossil of the Acheulian or Middle Palaeolithic toolmakers has come from these sites (India's best-known Middle Pleistocene hominin is the Narmada cranium, Hathnora, 1982), and many sites remain undated.

South India thus offers a nearly continuous record of hominin adaptation over 1.5 million years, making it vital for understanding human dispersal across Asia.
free.upa-2024-an2-8b:
TheocracySecular stateSacred kingshipLegal-rational authority

A theocratic state claims that sovereignty belongs to God and is exercised by religious authorities or by a ruler sanctified by religion, with law drawn from scripture. A secular, liberal, democratic state places sovereignty in the people, keeps the State neutral or at a principled distance from all faiths and guarantees individual rights under a constitution. Max Weber's types of authority (Economy and Society, 1922) frame the contrast: traditional and charismatic authority, often sacralised, versus legal-rational authority.

1. Distinguishing features

  • Legitimacy: a theocracy justifies power by divine will; a democracy by consent expressed in free elections.
  • Pluralism: the secular State protects religious minorities and non-believers, while a theocracy privileges one faith.
  • Change: in a theocracy law is fixed by revelation and interpreted by clerics; in a democracy it can be amended through deliberation.

2. Illustrations from tribal and pre-modern societies

  • Divine kingship: the Shilluk king (reth) embodied the founding hero Nyikang; E.E. Evans-Pritchard (1948) showed him to be more a ritual centre than a ruler, following J.G. Frazer's The Golden Bough (1890) on sacred kings.
  • Sacred chiefs: Polynesian chiefs held authority through mana, guarded by tapu, fusing ritual and political rank.
  • Sacred authority without a State: the Nuer leopard-skin chief (Evans-Pritchard, The Nuer, 1940) settled feuds through ritual status but had no power to coerce.
  • Separation in Indian tribes: among the Munda the headman (munda) and the priest (pahan) hold distinct offices (S.C. Roy, The Mundas and Their Country, 1912), as do the manjhi and naeke among the Santal, a built-in separation of secular and sacred roles.
  • Sacral kingship in India: the Gajapati king of Puri ritually sweeps the chariots of Jagannath as the deity's servant, drawing legitimacy from the god (Hermann Kulke); tribal chiefs of central India adopted Rajput origin myths to sanctify rule (Surajit Sinha, 1962).

3. Contemporary societies

  • Theocracies: Iran since 1979, where elected bodies work under a Supreme Leader and a Guardian Council that vets candidates and laws; Vatican City under the Pope; Afghanistan under the Taliban since 2021.
  • Hybrids: democracies with an established or official religion, such as the United Kingdom (Church of England) and Pakistan (an Islamic Republic).
  • Secular democracies: France's laïcité (law of 1905), the separation of church and State in the USA, and India's Articles 25–28, with "secular" added to the Preamble in 1976 and held part of the basic structure in S.R. Bommai (1994).

4. Anthropological evaluation

  • A continuum, not a binary: secular States keep religious symbols, oaths and holidays; theocracies hold elections.
  • Culturally specific secularism: Talal Asad shows the secular is itself historically made; Indian secularism accommodates community personal laws.

The contrast is between divine and popular sovereignty. The anthropological record shows that even many small-scale societies separated priestly and political roles, and that freedom of conscience is best protected where authority rests on law and consent.
free.upa-2024-an2-8c:
Resource curseDisplacementFifth ScheduleBenefit sharing

India's coal, iron ore and bauxite belts overlap heavily with the Fifth Schedule tribal areas of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. Mining brings revenue to the nation but often displacement and dispossession to the tribal communities who live on the land, a paradox called the resource curse. Walter Fernandes estimated that about 40% of the roughly 60 million people displaced or affected by development projects between 1947 and 2004 are tribal.

1. Economic impacts

  • Loss of land and commons: acquisition of fields, forests and grazing land destroys a mixed economy of farming, forest produce and hunting; cash compensation is soon spent, and landless users of the commons often get nothing.
  • Insecure wage work: few tribal people get skilled mining jobs; most become casual, contract or migrant labourers, and women lose forest-based livelihoods.
  • Inflation and debt: the inflow of outsiders, money and markets raises prices and strengthens traders and moneylenders.
  • Gains: roads, markets, some jobs and the District Mineral Foundation, created by the MMDR Amendment Act (2015) to spend a share of royalty on mining-affected people through PMKKKY.

2. Social and cultural impacts

  • Impoverishment risks: Michael Cernea's model (1997) lists landlessness, joblessness, homelessness, marginalisation, food insecurity, ill health, loss of common property and social disarticulation, all visible in mining displacement.
  • Broken kinship and institutions: resettlement scatters clans and villages and weakens customary councils and mutual aid.
  • Loss of the sacred: hills, sarna groves and burial grounds anchor identity; the Dongria Kondh revere Niyamgiri as the domain of Niyam Raja.
  • Health and gender: dust, silicosis and tuberculosis among quarry workers, polluted water and alcoholism; women face harassment and loss of control over resources.
  • Industrial transition: L.P. Vidyarthi's study of industrialisation in tribal Bihar (1970) recorded new wage work alongside land loss and cultural strain around Chotanagpur's new industrial centres.
  • Conflict: resistance at Niyamgiri and Hasdeo Arand (Chhattisgarh); the Planning Commission's Expert Group (2008) linked such alienation to the spread of Left-wing extremism.

3. Developmental impacts

  • Wealth without welfare: mineral districts such as West Singhbhum (Jharkhand) and Dantewada (Chhattisgarh) remain Aspirational Districts despite large revenues.
  • Ecological costs: deforestation, falling water tables and polluted rivers erode the base of future development.
  • Legal correctives: Samatha (1997) barred the lease of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private non-tribal mining firms; in Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (2013) the Supreme Court let gram sabhas decide on Niyamgiri, and all twelve rejected bauxite mining.
  • Anthropological critique: Felix Padel and Samarendra Das (Out of This Earth, 2010) show how mining for global markets reshapes tribal landscapes, while the Xaxa Committee (2014) identified displacement and land alienation as central causes of tribal deprivation.

Mining can aid tribal development only if it moves from extraction to benefit sharing: prior informed consent of gram sabhas, land-for-land rehabilitation, tribal control of DMF funds and mine-closure restoration would make it inclusive development.
free.upa-2023-an1-1a:
Social anthropologyCultural anthropologyHolism and fieldworkApplied relevance

Social-cultural anthropology studies how people live together and make sense of their world: their institutions, beliefs and everyday practices. The British tradition of social anthropology (A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, E.E. Evans-Pritchard) focused on social structure, while American cultural anthropology (Franz Boas, A.L. Kroeber) focused on culture, which E.B. Tylor (Primitive Culture, 1871) described as the complex whole that humans acquire as members of society. Today the two are treated as one field.

1. Scope

  • Social institutions: kinship, marriage, family, economy, polity, law and religion are studied as linked parts of one whole (holism); Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922) traced how the Kula exchange tied Trobriand trade, magic and politics together.
  • Culture and the individual: socialisation, personality and values, from Margaret Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) to present-day studies of emotion, gender and identity.
  • Change and continuity: diffusion, acculturation, modernisation and globalisation; M.N. Srinivas's Sanskritisation and S.C. Dube's Indian Village (1955) traced change in Indian rural life.
  • Distinct method: long fieldwork, participant observation, the genealogical method and cross-cultural comparison give an insider (emic) view along with the observer's (etic) view.
  • Widening field: medical, urban, legal, environmental, development, visual and digital anthropology now study cities, firms, hospitals and online communities, not only "simple" societies.

2. Relevance

  • Understanding diversity: cultural relativism counters ethnocentrism and racism, vital in a plural society; the Anthropological Survey of India's People of India project (led by K.S. Singh) documented 4,635 communities.
  • Tribal policy and development: Verrier Elwin's advice shaped Nehru's tribal Panchsheel; anthropologists contribute to social impact assessment, resettlement of displaced people and the working of the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Health: ethnography of burial customs helped contain the Ebola epidemic in West Africa (2014–16) and explains vaccine hesitancy; in India it guides maternal-health and sickle-cell programmes in tribal areas.
  • Governance and conflict: knowledge of ethnic identity, customary law and village institutions helps peace-building in the Northeast and the working of PESA, 1996.
  • Economy and technology: ethnographic methods are now used in market research, user-experience design and corporate studies.

Social-cultural anthropology has moved from describing "other" cultures to understanding all societies, including our own. Its holistic, people-centred lens makes it essential for inclusive development and culturally sensitive public policy.
free.upa-2023-an1-1b:
Iron AgePainted Grey WareMegalithic cultureSecond urbanisation

The Iron Age begins when smelted iron replaces bronze and stone as the main material for tools and weapons. Iron-working spread from Anatolia and the Near East (widely after about 1200 BCE) to Europe (Hallstatt and La Tène cultures) and Africa (Nok, Nigeria). In India iron appears in the Painted Grey Ware (PGW) culture of the Ganga–Yamuna doab and in the Megalithic burials of the Deccan and the south, with dates of about 1800–1000 BCE at sites such as Malhar (Uttar Pradesh) and Hallur (Karnataka).

1. Economic impact

  • Forest clearance and farming: iron axes, sickles and ploughshares opened the heavy, forested soils of the middle Ganga plain; D.D. Kosambi and later R.S. Sharma (Material Culture and Social Formations in Ancient India, 1983) linked this to wet-rice cultivation and a food surplus.
  • Craft specialisation: smiths became a distinct group; the craft survives among the Lohar and among the Agaria and Asur iron-smelting communities (Verrier Elwin, The Agaria, 1942).
  • Trade and money: surplus supported long-distance trade, punch-marked coins and the fine Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW, c. 700–200 BCE).

2. Social and political impact

  • Second urbanisation: towns such as Rajagriha, Kaushambi and Shravasti and the sixteen Mahajanapadas (6th century BCE) rose on this surplus, with taxation and standing armies; Magadha's rise has been linked to its access to iron ore.
  • Cheaper metal, wider use: V. Gordon Childe (What Happened in History, 1942) argued that cheap, abundant iron put tools and weapons in the hands of ordinary farmers and soldiers.
  • Stratification: control over land, cattle and metal deepened inequality between chiefs, warriors, peasants and artisans.

3. Ideological and cultural impact

  • Megalithic burials at Brahmagiri, Junapani and Adichanallur, with iron weapons, horse fittings and Black-and-Red Ware, suggest chiefdoms, ancestor cults and belief in an afterlife.
  • New religious ideas: Buddhism and Jainism, which rejected costly animal sacrifice, suited a peasant economy that needed its cattle (R.S. Sharma).
  • Living megalithic tradition: the Khasi, Jaintia, Naga and Munda still raise memorial stones, linking Iron Age burials to living tribal belief.

4. Debate

  • A. Ghosh and others argued that early iron was too scarce to clear forests and that fire did much of the work. Tamil Nadu's 2025 report dating iron at Sivagalai to about 3345 BCE, like the early Malhar dates, remains disputed.

The Iron Age was thus a technological and social turning point: it laid the material base for early states, cities and new faiths, working together with rice farming, trade and political ambition.
free.upa-2023-an1-1c:
RaceEthnicityClinesEthnic boundaries

Race was used in classical physical anthropology to divide humankind into groups by inherited physical traits such as skin colour, hair form and head shape, beginning with J.F. Blumenbach's five varieties (1795). Ethnicity refers to a group's shared cultural identity (language, religion, customs and a belief in common origin), which Fredrik Barth (Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, 1969) showed is maintained through social boundaries.

1. Race: from types to clines

  • Typological classifications: in India, H.H. Risley (The People of India, 1908) ranked groups by the nasal index, and B.S. Guha (Census of 1931) identified six racial elements; such schemes are now of historical interest only.
  • Scientific critique: human variation is continuous (clinal); Frank Livingstone (1962) wrote "there are no races, there are only clines", and R.C. Lewontin (1972) found that about 85% of human genetic variation lies within populations rather than between them.
  • Current position: the UNESCO statements (from 1950) and the American Association of Physical Anthropologists' statement on race and racism (2019) treat race as a social category rather than a natural biological unit. Genomics still finds population structure, such as the Ancestral North and South Indian components (David Reich and colleagues, 2009), but no sharp boundaries.

2. Ethnicity: a cultural and political identity

  • Primordial view: Clifford Geertz (1963) described ethnic loyalty as rooted in "primordial attachments" of blood, language, religion and custom.
  • Instrumental view: Abner Cohen (Custom and Politics in Urban Africa, 1969) showed Hausa traders in Ibadan using ethnic ties to control the cattle and kola trade; ethnicity is mobilised for resources and power.
  • Constructivist view: Barth showed that identities persist even when people and cultural traits cross the boundary; ethnicity is fluid and situational.
  • Indian examples: linguistic states, the Naga, Mizo and Bodo movements, and safeguards such as Articles 371A and 371G and the Sixth Schedule show ethnicity shaping federal politics.

3. Race, ethnicity and discrimination

  • Racism ranks people by supposed biology (apartheid, Nazi race laws), while ethnocentrism ranks them by culture. In India the Bezbaruah Committee (2014) recorded discrimination against people from the Northeast in large cities, and ethnic violence in Manipur since May 2023 shows how quickly boundaries can harden.

Race is best understood as a social construct with a troubled history, while ethnicity is a living cultural identity that can unite or divide. Anthropology studies both without hierarchy and helps counter discrimination built on either.
free.upa-2023-an1-1d:
Customary lawSacred grovesTraditional ecological knowledgeCommunity conservation

Customary law is the body of unwritten rules, handed down from ancestors and enforced by community institutions such as village councils, elders and clan heads. E. Adamson Hoebel (The Law of Primitive Man, 1954) showed that such rules are true law because they carry legitimate sanctions. Many of them govern the use of forests, water and wildlife and embody traditional ecological knowledge (Fikret Berkes, Sacred Ecology, 1999).

1. How customary law conserves nature

  • Sacred groves: forest patches dedicated to a deity where felling, hunting or grazing is forbidden, such as the law kyntang of the Khasi and Jaintia (Mawphlang, Meghalaya), the sarna of the Munda and Oraon, the devrai of Maharashtra and the kavu of Kerala; Madhav Gadgil and V.D. Vartak (1975) showed them to be refuges of biodiversity.
  • Totemic and seasonal taboos: clans do not kill or eat their totem, and closed seasons for hunting and fishing protect breeding stock.
  • Ritual regulation: Roy Rappaport (Pigs for the Ancestors, 1968) showed that the kaiko ritual cycle of the Tsembaga Maring of New Guinea kept pig herds within the carrying capacity of their land.
  • Religious ethic: the Bishnoi of Rajasthan follow Guru Jambheshwar's rules against cutting green trees; in 1730 Amrita Devi and 363 others gave their lives at Khejarli to save khejri trees.

2. Customary law in modern resource governance

  • Niyamgiri (Odisha): the Dongria Kondh revere the hill as the seat of Niyam Raja; after the Supreme Court's Orissa Mining Corporation judgment (2013), their gram sabhas rejected bauxite mining.
  • Community reserves: the Angami village of Khonoma (Nagaland) banned hunting in 1998 and set up a community sanctuary; Apatani clans of Ziro valley (Arunachal Pradesh) manage bamboo and pine groves alongside rice–fish farming.
  • Legal recognition: Article 13(3)(a) treats custom with the force of law as law; Article 371A protects Naga customary law and ownership of land and resources; PESA, 1996 and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (community forest resource rights and Section 5) empower gram sabhas to protect forests and biodiversity.

3. Limitations

  • Customary rules weaken under market pressure, migration, religious change and state control of forests, and some deny women land and council rights. Elinor Ostrom (Governing the Commons, 1990) showed that well-designed community rules can avoid the "tragedy of the commons" that Garrett Hardin (1968) predicted.

Customary law turns conservation into a moral duty rather than an external rule. Recognising it through FRA and PESA, while making it gender-just, is central to community-based conservation in India.
free.upa-2023-an1-1e:
Gene expressionCentral dogmaGene regulationEpigenetics

Gene expression is the process by which the information in a gene is used to make a functional product, a protein or a functional RNA, and so to produce a phenotype. It follows Francis Crick's central dogma (1958): DNA is transcribed into RNA, which is translated into protein. Every cell carries the same genome, but each expresses only a part of it at a given time; this selective gene regulation makes a liver cell different from a neuron.

1. Steps of gene expression

  • Transcription: RNA polymerase binds the promoter and copies the template strand of DNA into pre-mRNA in the nucleus.
  • RNA processing: a 5′ cap and a poly-A tail are added and introns are spliced out; alternative splicing lets one gene code for several proteins.
  • Translation: ribosomes read the mRNA codons while tRNAs bring the matching amino acids to build a polypeptide.
  • Post-translational modification: folding, cutting and chemical tagging make the protein functional.

2. Regulation of gene expression

  • Operon model: François Jacob and Jacques Monod (1961) showed with the lac operon of E. coli how a repressor switches genes on or off in response to the environment.
  • Transcription factors and enhancers: in humans, proteins binding to enhancers and silencers tune expression by tissue and stage of life; for example, haemoglobin switches from the foetal form (HbF) to the adult form (HbA) after birth.
  • Epigenetic control: DNA methylation and histone modification alter expression without changing the DNA sequence, as in X-chromosome inactivation (Mary Lyon, 1961; the Barr body) and genomic imprinting (Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes).

3. Anthropological significance

  • Penetrance and expressivity: the same genotype may not show, or may show to different degrees, because of modifier genes and environment (polydactyly is a classic example).
  • Human evolution: Mary-Claire King and Allan Wilson (1975) argued that humans and chimpanzees differ more in gene regulation than in protein sequence; lactase persistence in herding populations results from a regulatory variant near the LCT gene that keeps lactase switched on in adults.
  • Environment and health: people conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter (1944–45) showed altered methylation of the IGF2 gene six decades later. In India, hydroxyurea, which raises HbF expression, eases sickle cell disease, common in several tribal groups and targeted by the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023).

Gene expression links genotype to phenotype: when, where and how much a gene works depends on regulation and environment, so heredity is not destiny, a theme central to biocultural anthropology.
free.upa-2023-an1-2a:
AustralopithecinesTaung childRaymond Dart (1925)Gracile and robust forms

The australopithecines ("southern apes") were small-brained, bipedal hominins of Africa, living from about 4.2 to 2 million years ago (mya), while the robust forms (often placed in Paranthropus) survived to about 1 mya. The genus was named by Raymond Dart (1925) from the Taung child, the first australopithecine ever found.

1. Species from East Africa

  • Au. anamensis (4.2–3.8 mya): Kanapoi, Kenya (Meave Leakey and colleagues, 1995); a bipedal tibia, and a 3.8-million-year-old cranium (MRD) from Ethiopia reported in 2019.
  • Au. afarensis (3.9–2.9 mya): "Lucy" (Hadar, Ethiopia; Donald Johanson, 1974) and the Laetoli footprints (Tanzania, 3.66 mya; Mary Leakey) prove habitual bipedalism with a brain of about 400–500 cc.
  • Au. garhi (2.5 mya): Bouri, Ethiopia, near cut-marked bones, a possible ancestor of Homo; Au. deyiremeda (3.5–3.3 mya) shows that several species coexisted.
  • Robust forms: P. aethiopicus (the "Black Skull" of West Turkana) and P. boisei ("Zinjanthropus", Olduvai Gorge; Mary Leakey, 1959), the "Nutcracker Man" with huge molars.

2. Species from South Africa

  • Au. africanus (about 3–2 mya): Taung, Sterkfontein ("Mrs Ples", Robert Broom and John Robinson, 1947) and Makapansgat; gracile, with a rounded skull and small canines.
  • P. robustus (about 2–1 mya): Kromdraai (Broom, 1938) and Swartkrans; heavy jaws for tough plant food.
  • Au. sediba (about 1.98 mya): Malapa (named by Lee Berger, 2010); ape-like arms and feet with a human-like hand and pelvis.
  • "Little Foot" (StW 573): a nearly complete Sterkfontein skeleton dated to about 3.67 mya; its species is still debated.

3. Taung baby: discovery

  • In 1924 quarrying at the Buxton limeworks near Taung (South Africa) exposed a fossil-bearing block that reached Raymond Dart, anatomy professor at Witwatersrand University.
  • Dart described it in Nature (7 February 1925) as "Australopithecus africanus: The Man-Ape of South Africa". Its age is roughly 2.8–2.5 mya, though the dating is uncertain.

4. Physical features

  • A young child: milk teeth and just-erupting first permanent molars; dental growth (Bromage and Dean, 1985) suggests death at about three years.
  • Natural endocast: lime filled the braincase and preserved a brain cast of about 400 cc, ape-sized.
  • Human-like traits: a forward-placed foramen magnum implying upright posture, small canines, and a face less projecting than a young ape's, without heavy brow ridges.
  • Ape-like traits: small brain, projecting jaws and large molars.

5. Significance

  • Africa as the cradle: it supported Darwin's (1871) suggestion of African origins against the then-popular Asian theory.
  • Bipedalism before brain: it contradicted the "brain-first" view that the Piltdown forgery had encouraged.
  • Vindication: dismissed by Arthur Keith and others as a young ape, it was accepted after Broom's adult finds, Le Gros Clark's support (1947) and the exposure of Piltdown (1953).
  • Taphonomy: Lee Berger and Ron Clarke (1995) proposed that an eagle killed the child, supported by puncture marks in the eye sockets (Berger, 2006).

The australopithecines show mosaic evolution: bipedal bodies with ape-sized brains, in several coexisting lineages. The Taung child, once dismissed, made Africa the cradle of humankind.
free.upa-2023-an1-2b:
PleistoceneGlacial–interglacial cyclesPalaeoclimatic proxiesToba ash

The Palaeolithic largely coincides with the Pleistocene epoch (2.58 million to 11,700 years ago), a time of repeated glacial and interglacial cycles. In tropical regions such as India they appeared mainly as wetter (pluvial) and drier (interpluvial) phases driven by the monsoon. As there are no written records, the environment is reconstructed from geological, faunal, botanical and chemical evidence, read together with stone tools and dated deposits.

1. The global framework

  • Alpine model: Albrecht Penck and Eduard Brückner (1909) proposed four glaciations (Günz, Mindel, Riss and Würm), long used to date Palaeolithic cultures.
  • Marine isotope stages: oxygen-isotope records from deep-sea cores, pioneered by Cesare Emiliani (1955), show dozens of cycles; the Last Glacial Maximum (about 26–19 kya) was cold and dry in South Asia, with a weak monsoon.

2. Lines of evidence

  • Geological: river terraces, gravels and silts record changes in river flow; laterites, calcretes and wind-blown sands record humid and arid spells.
  • Faunal: hippopotamus, crocodile and turtles indicate perennial water, while horses, wild cattle and ostrich indicate open grassland.
  • Botanical: pollen and phytoliths in lake and river sediments show shifts between forest, grassland and desert scrub.
  • Chemical and dating methods: stable isotopes in soil carbonates, with luminescence, electron spin resonance and cosmogenic dating, fix these deposits in time.
  • Volcanic marker: ash from the Toba super-eruption in Sumatra (about 74 kya) forms a time-line across Indian river valleys.

3. Evidence from India

  • Kashmir and Potwar: the Yale–Cambridge expedition of Helmut de Terra and T.T. Paterson (1939) correlated Kashmir's glacial sequence with the Soan valley terraces, the first climatic framework for the Indian Palaeolithic.
  • Narmada valley: the Hathnora cranium (Arun Sonakia, 1982) came from gravels with fossil elephant (Palaeoloxodon), wild cattle (Bos namadicus) and hippopotamus, pointing to a large perennial river amid grassland and woodland.
  • Belan and Son valleys: G.R. Sharma's sequence of gravels with Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tools, separated by fine silts, shows alternating phases of flow; Toba ash lies within Son valley deposits.
  • Thar desert: at Didwana (Rajasthan; Singi Talav, V.N. Misra), Acheulian tools lie in old soils within dunes, showing that the desert was wetter and habitable during some phases.
  • South India: at Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu) Acheulian tools dated to about 1.5 mya (Shanti Pappu and colleagues, 2011) lie in clays of an old river; at Jwalapuram (Andhra Pradesh) Middle Palaeolithic tools occur below and above Toba ash (Michael Petraglia and colleagues, 2007).
  • Late Pleistocene aridity: ostrich eggshell at Patne (Maharashtra) and central Indian sites points to dry, open grassland near the last glacial maximum.

4. Human adaptation

  • Early humans favoured river banks, lake margins and rock shelters such as Bhimbetka; dry spells drew them to water, and blade and bone tools of the Upper Palaeolithic (Kurnool caves) reflect adjustment to the arid last glacial.

The Indian record shows that Palaeolithic people lived through shifting monsoons rather than ice sheets, and their tool traditions changed with these environmental fluctuations. Multi-proxy, well-dated research has replaced the old four-glacial scheme and the simple matching of glacials with pluvials.
free.upa-2023-an1-2c:
MalnutritionTriple burdenProtein-energy malnutritionKwashiorkor and marasmus

The World Health Organization defines malnutrition as deficiencies, excesses or imbalances in a person's intake of energy and nutrients. It covers both under- and over-nutrition, and India, like many developing countries, now faces a triple burden of undernutrition, micronutrient deficiency and rising obesity. Anthropologists treat it as a biocultural condition shaped by poverty, food beliefs, gender and disease.

1. Forms of malnutrition

  • Undernutrition: stunting (low height-for-age, a sign of chronic deprivation), wasting (low weight-for-height, acute) and underweight (low weight-for-age). NFHS-6 (2023–24) puts stunting among children under five at 29.3% (35.5% in NFHS-5) and underweight at 31.8% (32.1%); severe wasting fell from 7.7% to 5.2%, but overall wasting has barely changed.
  • Micronutrient deficiency ("hidden hunger"): iron (anaemia), iodine (goitre, cretinism), vitamin A (night blindness), vitamin D (rickets), zinc and folate.
  • Overnutrition: overweight, obesity and diet-related non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, rising with processed foods and sedentary work.
  • Secondary malnutrition: caused by illnesses such as diarrhoea, tuberculosis or worm infestation that reduce absorption or raise needs.

2. Protein-energy (protein-calorie) malnutrition

  • Meaning: PEM results from too little energy, protein or both, and mostly affects children under five. Gómez (1956) graded it by weight-for-age; the Wellcome classification (1970) combined weight-for-age with oedema; WHO now identifies severe acute malnutrition by weight-for-height below –3 SD, mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm, or oedema of both feet.
  • Kwashiorkor: described by Cicely Williams in the Gold Coast (Ghana) in the 1930s; the Ga word refers to the illness of a child displaced from the breast by a new baby. It typically appears at one to three years after abrupt weaning onto starchy food, with oedema, moon face, "flaky-paint" skin, thin pale hair, fatty liver and apathy. Its cause is now seen as more than protein lack, involving infection and gut microbes.
  • Marasmus: severe wasting from overall starvation, usually in the first year: "skin and bones", an old-man face, no oedema, and an alert, hungry child.
  • Marasmic kwashiorkor: wasting together with oedema.

3. Causes and Indian examples

  • Poverty and food insecurity, large families and short birth intervals.
  • Cultural practices: late start of breastfeeding, discarding of colostrum, food taboos in pregnancy and illness, and less food for girls.
  • Infection: repeated diarrhoea and worms cut appetite and absorption, while malnutrition weakens immunity.
  • Examples: child deaths from severe malnutrition have been repeatedly reported among the Korku of Melghat (Maharashtra) and the Sahariya of Sheopur (Madhya Pradesh), where seasonal migration, loss of forest foods and distant health services add to the problem.

4. Response

  • ICDS (1975), Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, PM POSHAN school meals, nutrition rehabilitation centres for severe cases, fortified foods and community-based management of acute malnutrition.

Malnutrition is not merely a shortage of food but a biocultural condition; reducing it needs diverse diets, maternal care, sanitation and culturally sensitive feeding advice, as the slow fall in underweight and wasting in NFHS-6 shows.
free.upa-2023-an1-3a:
HominizationBipedalismEncephalizationMosaic evolution

Hominization is the evolutionary process by which the human lineage acquired its distinctive anatomy, behaviour and culture after separating from the chimpanzee line about 7–6 million years ago (mya). The traits did not appear together but at different times (mosaic evolution): bipedalism came first, brain expansion much later, and language and symbolic culture last. Charles Darwin (The Descent of Man, 1871) first linked upright posture, free hands, tools and a larger brain in one feedback loop.

1. Bipedalism and upright posture

  • Skeletal changes: foramen magnum moved under the skull, S-shaped spine, short and broad bowl-shaped pelvis, thigh bones angled inward to the knee, arched foot and big toe in line with the others.
  • Evidence: Sahelanthropus (Chad, about 7 mya; debated), the Orrorin femur (Kenya, about 6 mya), Ardipithecus ramidus, "Ardi" (Ethiopia, 4.4 mya) and the Laetoli footprints (Tanzania, 3.66 mya).
  • Explanations: energy-efficient walking (Rodman and McHenry, 1980), keeping cool in open habitats (Wheeler, 1991), and carrying food to mates and young (Owen Lovejoy, 1981).

2. Hands, tools and diet

  • Precision grip: a long, opposable thumb allowed fine handling, as John Napier showed; the hand of Homo habilis from Olduvai (OH 7) suggested tool-making.
  • Tool traditions: Lomekwi (Kenya, about 3.3 mya), Oldowan (about 2.6 mya) and Acheulian handaxes (about 1.76 mya); in India, Acheulian tools at Attirampakkam are dated to about 1.5 mya.
  • Diet: meat, marrow and later cooked food supplied energy for a bigger brain while the gut became smaller, as argued in Leslie Aiello and Peter Wheeler's "expensive tissue" hypothesis (1995) and Richard Wrangham's cooking hypothesis.

3. Skull, face and teeth

  • Encephalization: cranial capacity rose from about 400–500 cc in Australopithecus to about 600–650 cc in H. habilis, 800–1,100 cc in H. erectus and about 1,350 cc in H. sapiens, with a rounded vault and high forehead.
  • Smaller face and teeth: canines shrank and the gap (diastema) closed, the dental arch became parabolic, the face flattened (orthognathism), brow ridges reduced and a chin appeared in H. sapiens.
