4. Life history and social life

  • Long childhood: slower growth and longer dependence on adults, which developed gradually within Homo, allowed more learning and cultural transmission.
  • Fire: controlled use at Wonderwerk Cave (South Africa, about 1 mya) and Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (Israel, about 780 kya) gave warmth, protection and cooked food.
  • Cooperation: food sharing, pair bonding and gendered sharing of work; the "Man the Hunter" model (Washburn and Lancaster, 1968) was balanced by Sally Slocum's "Woman the Gatherer" (1975).

5. Language and symbolic culture

  • Speech: a lowered larynx, a modern hyoid bone (Kebara Neanderthal) and the FOXP2 gene point to a capacity for speech.
  • Symbols: engraved ochre and shell beads at Blombos Cave (South Africa, about 100–75 kya), cave art and burials mark behavioural modernity; India's Bhimbetka rock shelters preserve a long record of rock art.

Hominization was biocultural: anatomy made culture possible, and culture (tools, fire, cooking, cooperation) in turn reshaped anatomy. This feedback continues today in gene–culture co-evolution such as adult lactose tolerance.
free.upa-2023-an1-3b:
Religion as a cultural systemClifford Geertz (1966)Symbols and meaningPsychological approach

Clifford Geertz (1926–2006), the leading figure of interpretive (symbolic) anthropology, set out his view in the essay "Religion as a Cultural System" (1966), reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures (1973). He shifted attention from the origins and social functions of religion to its meaning for believers, to be grasped through "thick description" of their symbols and practices.

1. Geertz's view of religion

  • Definition: religion is "a system of symbols which acts to establish powerful, pervasive, and long-lasting moods and motivations in men", by picturing a general order of existence and surrounding it with such an aura of factuality that these moods seem uniquely realistic.
  • "Model of" and "model for": sacred symbols both describe reality and shape conduct; they fuse a people's ethos (moral and aesthetic style) with its world view (picture of how things are).
  • Problem of meaning: religion helps people face what threatens order: bafflement (events beyond explanation), suffering (pain beyond endurance) and evil (injustice beyond moral sense).
  • Ritual: in ritual the world as lived and the world as imagined become one; in Bali, the dramatic combat of Rangda and Barong makes cosmic struggle real for performers and audience.
  • Ethnography: The Religion of Java (1960) described the abangan, santri and priyayi variants, and Islam Observed (1968) contrasted mystical Indonesian Islam with saint-centred Moroccan Islam.

2. Criticism

  • Talal Asad (Genealogies of Religion, 1993) argued that a universal definition reflects a modern, Protestant idea of religion as inner belief and ignores the power and discipline that produce religious dispositions.
  • Others found the approach hard to verify and inclined to read culture as a text, neglecting material and political conditions.

3. Anthropological and psychological approaches

  • Classic division: Evans-Pritchard (Theories of Primitive Religion, 1965) sorted earlier theories into psychological ones (intellectualist and emotionalist) and sociological ones.
  • Psychological approaches locate religion in the individual mind: E.B. Tylor's animism (Primitive Culture, 1871) saw it as early reasoning about dreams and death; R.R. Marett stressed awe and emotion; Sigmund Freud (Totem and Taboo, 1913; The Future of an Illusion, 1927) treated it as wish-fulfilment rooted in childhood and guilt; Carl Jung traced it to archetypes of the collective unconscious; and Malinowski (Magic, Science and Religion, 1925) saw ritual as relieving anxiety, as in Trobriand magic for risky open-sea fishing.
  • Anthropological (socio-cultural) approaches locate religion in group life and shared culture: Émile Durkheim (The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life, 1912) saw the sacred, through Australian Arunta totemism, as society worshipping itself; Radcliffe-Brown (The Andaman Islanders, 1922) stressed ritual's role in cohesion; Evans-Pritchard (Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande, 1937) showed witchcraft as a coherent logic of misfortune; Victor Turner and Geertz read ritual as symbol. In India, M.N. Srinivas's study of Coorg religion (1952) and L.P. Vidyarthi's "sacred complex" of Gaya (1961) follow this line.

The two approaches are complementary: Melford Spiro (1966) combined the psychological and social functions of religion. Geertz's lasting contribution was to make religion a matter of meaning, now extended by psychological anthropology and the cognitive science of religion.
free.upa-2023-an1-3c:
Mixed-longitudinal designOverlapping cohortsDistance and velocity curvesGrowth studies

Human growth can be studied by cross-sectional (different children of each age measured once), longitudinal (the same children measured repeatedly for years) and mixed-longitudinal designs. In the last, a sample is measured repeatedly while some children leave and others join; in its planned (linked or semi-longitudinal) form, several cohorts starting at different ages are followed for a few years so that their age ranges overlap.

1. The method

  • Design: for example, three cohorts aged 6, 9 and 12 years are measured every six months for four years; the study then spans ages 6 to 16 in four years instead of the ten that a pure longitudinal study would need.
  • Mixed samples: some children are measured on every occasion, others leave or join midway; data from both are pooled.
  • Analysis: distance curves (size at each age) use all measurements, while velocity curves (rate of growth) use successive measures on the same child; overlapping ages are linked to build continuous curves, today with multilevel (mixed-effects) models developed by Harvey Goldstein and others.
  • Indian example: Vaman Khadilkar and colleagues measured 2,949 schoolchildren aged 5–17 in Pune and Delhi every year from 2007 to 2013 to publish height-velocity percentiles (2019).
  • Choice of design: the design must suit the question. The WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study (1997–2003), which included South Delhi, combined a longitudinal follow-up from birth to 24 months with a cross-sectional survey of children aged 18–71 months to build the WHO Child Growth Standards (2006).

2. Merits

  • Saves time and money compared with a pure longitudinal study, so results reach health and nutrition policy sooner.
  • Gives both distance and velocity data, including the adolescent growth spurt for cohorts that pass through puberty during the study.
  • Copes with drop-outs: losses are partly made good by new entrants, keeping the sample at each age reasonably large.
  • Reveals secular trends: where cohorts overlap at the same age, differences between them show cohort effects such as earlier menarche or greater height in younger cohorts.
  • Less burden: fewer repeat visits reduce fatigue for subjects and staff and limit the "learning" effect of repeated testing.

3. Demerits

  • Complex analysis: unequal numbers of measurements per child make estimation of velocity and of peak height velocity difficult.
  • Joining errors: if cohorts differ in nutrition, socio-economic background or secular change, the joins between age segments are biased.
  • Incomplete individual curves: few children are followed through the whole of puberty, so individual tempo (early and late maturers) is poorly captured.
  • Sampling bias: selective drop-out, migration or new entrants from different backgrounds affect representativeness.
  • Logistics: standardising instruments and observers across cohorts and years needs careful planning and training.

The mixed-longitudinal design is a practical compromise between the speed of cross-sectional surveys and the depth of longitudinal studies. It suits countries such as India, where growth monitoring across diverse ethnic and nutritional settings is needed quickly but long follow-up is difficult.
free.upa-2023-an1-4a:
Marriage regulationsEndogamy and exogamyAlliance theorySocial solidarity

Marriage regulations are the rules that define whom a person may, must or must not marry. In traditional India they work through caste and tribal endogamy, clan and gotra exogamy, hypergamy and preferential unions. In the light of Émile Durkheim's idea of social solidarity and Claude Lévi-Strauss's alliance theory (The Elementary Structures of Kinship, 1949), these rules are not mere restrictions but devices that bind individuals, families and groups together.

1. Endogamy: solidarity within the group

  • Caste and tribal endogamy keeps marriage inside the group and preserves its identity, occupation, ritual status and property; G.S. Ghurye (Caste and Race in India, 1932) and B.R. Ambedkar (Castes in India, 1916) saw endogamy as the core of caste; it gives strong in-group cohesion, Durkheim's mechanical solidarity.
  • Tribal examples: the Santal, Gond and Bhil marry within the tribe, and among the Todas the Tartharol and Teivaliol sections are themselves endogamous (W.H.R. Rivers, The Todas, 1906).

2. Exogamy: solidarity between groups

  • Clan and gotra exogamy: members of one clan regard each other as kin and must marry outside it; the Munda and Oraon follow totemic clan exogamy, and the Santal have twelve exogamous clans.
  • Village and sapinda exogamy: Irawati Karve (Kinship Organisation in India, 1953) showed that North Indian Hindus avoid marriage within the village and among close kin, so each marriage links distant villages into a wide kin network.
  • Alliance: for Lévi-Strauss, the incest taboo and exogamy compel groups to exchange brides, turning potential rivals into in-laws who owe each other help.

3. Preferential and secondary marriages

  • Cross-cousin and uncle–niece marriage in South India (menarikam in Telugu areas) repeats alliances in each generation and keeps property within known families; Louis Dumont (1953) read Dravidian kin terms as a language of alliance. Among the Gond, cross-cousin marriage is called dudh lautawa, "returning the milk".
  • Levirate and sororate: the junior levirate of the Santal and the karewa of the Jats keep the widow and children within the husband's lineage, so the alliance survives a death.
  • Hypergamy (anuloma): among Rajputs, Kulin Brahmins of Bengal and in Nambudiri–Nayar sambandham unions in Kerala (Kathleen Gough), it linked ranked groups in a stable hierarchy.
  • Fraternal polyandry: among the Todas and the Khasa of Jaunsar-Bawar (D.N. Majumdar, Himalayan Polyandry, 1962) it kept land undivided and brothers united.
  • Marriage payments: bride price (gonong among the Ho) and marriage by service (lamsena among the Gond and Baiga) create lasting obligations between families.

4. Limits and change

  • The same rules sustain hierarchy and exclusion: caste endogamy reproduces inequality, and sanctions against inter-caste or same-gotra marriages have led to "honour" crimes, condemned by the Supreme Court in Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018).
  • Education, urbanisation, the Special Marriage Act, 1954 and the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 are loosening these rules.

Marriage regulations acted as the social glue of traditional India: endogamy secured unity within the group, while exogamy and preferential unions wove alliances outward. A constitutional society must keep their integrative value while protecting individual choice.
free.upa-2023-an1-4b:
Forensic anthropologyBiological profilePositive identificationOsteometry

Forensic anthropology applies physical anthropology to legal questions, above all the personal identification of skeletonised, burnt or badly decomposed remains. Identification moves from a general biological profile (sex, age, stature and ancestry) to individual features that allow a positive identification by comparison with records of a missing person. Wilton Krogman's The Human Skeleton in Forensic Medicine (1962) systematised these methods.

1. Preliminary questions

  • Bone or not, human or animal: gross shape, bone histology (osteon pattern) and, if needed, protein or DNA tests.
  • Number of individuals: duplicated elements, such as two right femurs, give the minimum number of individuals (MNI).
  • Time since death: soft tissue, odour, weathering, root marks and, for older bones, radiocarbon dating.

2. Biological profile

  • Sex: the pelvis is the best guide (wider subpubic angle and sciatic notch and a preauricular sulcus in females, and the ventral arc of the pubis described by T.W. Phenice, 1969), followed by the skull (larger mastoid, brow ridges, nuchal crest and square chin in males) and the size of long-bone heads; the pelvis alone gives about 95% accuracy. Children's skeletons cannot be reliably sexed without DNA.
  • Age: in children, tooth formation and eruption, the appearance of ossification centres and fusion of epiphyses; in adults, changes in the pubic symphysis (T.W. Todd, 1920; Suchey–Brooks method, 1990), the auricular surface of the ilium (Lovejoy and colleagues, 1985), sternal rib ends and closure of cranial sutures.
  • Stature: regression formulae from long bones, best from the femur and tibia (Karl Pearson, 1899; Mildred Trotter and Goldine Gleser, 1952); formulae must be population-specific, and Indian ones date back to Pan (1924).
  • Ancestry: skull and dental traits and measurements (for example with FORDISC software), used cautiously because human variation is continuous.

3. Individualising features

  • Dental evidence: fillings, crowns, missing teeth and dentures compared with dental records (forensic odontology).
  • Pathology and trauma: healed fractures, surgical plates and joint implants (often with serial numbers), arthritis and occupational markers.
  • Radiographic comparison: the unique outline of the frontal sinus and bone patterns matched with X-rays taken in life.
  • Superimposition and facial reconstruction: in the Buck Ruxton case (1935), John Glaister and James Brash superimposed a victim's skull on her photograph; Mikhail Gerasimov developed reconstruction of the face from the skull.

4. Molecular and chemical methods

  • DNA: extracted from teeth and dense bone such as the petrous part of the temporal bone, and compared with relatives (mitochondrial, Y-chromosome and autosomal markers); it was central to disaster victim identification after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
  • Stable isotopes in bone and teeth show diet and region of origin. At Roopkund lake (Uttarakhand), ancient DNA and isotope study (Éadaoin Harney and colleagues, 2019) showed that the skeletons came from distinct groups who died in separate events about a thousand years apart.

Personal identification combines osteology with odontology, radiology and DNA; no single method is decisive, so experts cross-check several. With frequent disasters and many unidentified bodies, India needs trained forensic anthropologists and population-specific standards.
free.upa-2023-an1-4c:
MesolithicMicrolithsComposite toolsEarly Holocene

The Mesolithic is the transitional stage between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic, broadly belonging to the warmer early Holocene. In India it begins around 10,000 BCE and in some regions lasted into the 2nd millennium BCE, alongside farming cultures. It is marked by hunting of smaller game, fishing and plant gathering, and above all by microliths, tiny stone tools hafted into composite tools. H.D. Sankalia, V.N. Misra, G.R. Sharma and others revealed hundreds of Indian sites.

1. Major Mesolithic sites of India

  • Rajasthan and Gujarat: Bagor on the Kothari river (V.N. Misra, from 1967), one of the largest Indian Mesolithic sites, with early evidence of domestic sheep and goat; Tilwara; and Langhnaj in north Gujarat (H.D. Sankalia), with human burials and bones of wild animals.
  • Central India: Adamgarh near Hoshangabad (R.V. Joshi), also with early domestic animals, and Bhimbetka (V.S. Wakankar, 1957; UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2003), whose painted shelters show hunting, dancing and honey collection.
  • Ganga plain (Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh): Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama, camps beside ox-bow lakes with hearths, hut floors and many burials, some of them double, with grave goods such as bone ornaments.
  • Vindhyas and Belan valley: Chopani Mando (G.R. Sharma), Lekhahia, Baghai Khor and Morhana Pahar; Chopani Mando shows a move towards settled life with huts, hand-made pottery and wild rice.
  • East and South: Birbhanpur in West Bengal (B.B. Lal), the Teri sites on red sand dunes of the Tamil Nadu coast, and Sanganakallu in Karnataka.

2. Typo-technological features

  • Raw material: fine-grained stones such as chert, chalcedony, agate, jasper and carnelian, and quartz in the south and east, where better stone was scarce.
  • Blade technology: small parallel-sided blades were detached from prepared, often fluted cores by pressure or indirect (punch) flaking, and then snapped into segments.
  • Retouch and microburin technique: one edge was blunted (backed) for hafting; notching and snapping (the microburin technique) produced geometric shapes.
  • Tool types: non-geometric forms (backed blades, points, scrapers, borers, burins) and geometric forms (lunates, triangles, trapezes); many sequences show non-geometric forms early and geometric forms and pottery later.
  • Composite tools: microliths were set in wooden or bone shafts with resin or gum to make arrows, harpoons, spears and sickles; the bow and arrow became a key weapon.
  • Other finds: ring stones, querns and grinders for seeds, bone tools and ornaments, hearths, post-holes and burials.

3. Significance

  • Microblade technology appears much earlier in India, about 45–35 thousand years ago at Mehtakheri (Madhya Pradesh) and Jwalapuram (Andhra Pradesh), so the Mesolithic is defined by its whole way of life, not by microliths alone.
  • Bagor and Adamgarh show the first steps towards herding, and Chopani Mando towards plant use and settled life, bridging hunting-gathering and farming; Bhimbetka art opens a window on ritual and social life.

The Indian Mesolithic shows adaptation to the Holocene through a light, versatile microlithic toolkit and a broad-based economy; with its burials, art and early herding it forms the bridge to food production.
free.upa-2023-an1-5a:
Polygenic inheritanceAdditive allelesContinuous variationMultifactorial traits

Polygenic inheritance is the inheritance of a trait governed by several genes (polygenes) at different loci, each contributing a small, additive effect. Such traits do not fall into Mendel's neat classes but show continuous variation. Herman Nilsson-Ehle (1909) demonstrated it with kernel colour in wheat, and R.A. Fisher (1918) showed that many Mendelian factors together produce the bell-shaped curves that Galton and the biometricians had measured.

1. Features

  • Many genes, small effects: every contributing allele adds a fixed increment to the phenotype; no single allele is fully dominant.
  • Graded classes: with n gene pairs a cross between two heterozygotes gives 2n + 1 phenotypic classes in binomial proportions (1:4:6:4:1 for two pairs, 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 for three), approaching a normal curve as genes increase.
  • Intermediate offspring: children of contrasting parents are usually intermediate, though some may fall outside the parental range (transgressive variation).
  • Environmental modification: nutrition, disease and climate act on the genetic base, so most such traits are multifactorial; their heritability is estimated from twin, adoption and family studies.

2. Human examples

  • Stature and body size: genome-wide studies have tied thousands of common variants to adult height, each with a tiny effect, while the secular rise in height shows the role of nutrition.
  • Skin colour: genes such as SLC24A5, SLC45A2, OCA2 and MC1R jointly shape pigmentation, giving continuous gradation within and between populations.
  • Dermatoglyphics: total finger ridge count is highly heritable and polygenic (Sarah Holt, The Genetics of Dermal Ridges, 1968).
  • Threshold traits: cleft lip and palate, neural tube defects and type 2 diabetes appear only when combined genetic and environmental liability crosses a threshold (D.S. Falconer's liability model, 1965).

3. Anthropological significance

  • Against racial typology: continuous, clinal variation in skin colour, stature or head form undermines fixed racial types such as H.H. Risley's ranking of Indian castes by nasal index.
  • Adaptation: skin pigmentation follows ultraviolet radiation (Jablonski and Chaplin, 2000), an example of selection acting on many genes at once.
  • Medicine: polygenic risk scores estimate susceptibility to heart disease or diabetes, but they work poorly in South Asian groups that are under-represented in reference data.

Polygenic inheritance links Mendelian genetics with the measurable, graded variation that physical anthropologists study, and reminds us that most human traits arise from the interplay of many genes and the environment, not from a single gene.
free.upa-2023-an1-5b:
RakhigarhiHarappan urbanismAncient DNABioarchaeology

Rakhigarhi (Hisar district, Haryana) lies in the Ghaggar basin and is among the largest Harappan settlements, a cluster of eleven mounds that Vasant Shinde's team estimated at about 550 ha, larger than Mohenjo-daro by that reckoning. First explored by Suraj Bhan in the 1960s, it was excavated by the ASI (Amarendra Nath, 1997–2000), Deccan College (Shinde, 2010s) and again by the ASI from 2021. Its cemetery made it a landmark for bioarchaeology.

1. A long cultural sequence

  • From village to city: Early Harappan (pre-urban) deposits lie beneath Mature Harappan levels, showing that urbanism grew locally in the Ghaggar plain and not only in the Indus heartland.
  • Urban traits: planned streets and lanes, mud- and burnt-brick houses, drains, fire altars, seals with Indus signs, and copper, gold and terracotta objects.
  • Craft specialisation: workshops for beads and ornaments of agate, carnelian and shell point to organised production and long-distance trade.

2. The cemetery and skeletal biology

  • Burial customs: extended burials at Mound 7, about 1 km west of the town, came with pots, shell bangles and beads as grave goods, suggesting belief in an afterlife and social differences.
  • Human biology: skeletons provide data on age, sex, stature, diet, disease and injury of a Bronze Age population. In June 2026, under an ASI–AnSI agreement, remains from eight burials found at Mound 7 in 2025–26 went to the Anthropological Survey of India, Kolkata, for ancient DNA, isotope and palaeopathology studies.

3. Ancient DNA and population history

  • First Harappan genome: Shinde, Narasimhan, Reich and colleagues (Cell, 2019) sequenced a woman from the cemetery. Her ancestry combined an Iranian-related strand that separated from Iranian plateau lineages more than 12,000 years ago with a strand related to South Asian hunter-gatherers (proxied by the Andamanese).
  • Implications: she had no steppe pastoralist or Anatolian farmer ancestry, suggesting that farming in South Asia was taken up largely by local foragers rather than brought by migrating Near Eastern farmers, and that steppe ancestry arrived later, around 2000–1500 BCE.
  • Caution: it is one genome without a direct radiocarbon date, so these conclusions remain tentative.

Rakhigarhi shifts the Harappan centre of gravity eastward into India and joins archaeology with osteology and genetics; its planned site museum can make it a living classroom on the origins of South Asians.
free.upa-2023-an1-5c:
GlottochronologyLexicostatisticsSwadesh listRetention rate

Glottochronology estimates how long ago two related languages separated from a common ancestor from the share of basic vocabulary they still have in common. It was developed by Morris Swadesh in the early 1950s and formalised by Robert Lees (1953), on the analogy of radiocarbon dating: core words were thought to be replaced at a steady rate, as carbon-14 decays at a known rate. It rests on lexicostatistics, the statistical comparison of vocabularies.

1. Assumptions and method

  • A culture-free core vocabulary: words for body parts, low numerals, pronouns, natural objects and simple actions exist in every language and are rarely borrowed. Swadesh drew up a 200-meaning list (1952), later reduced to 100 (1955).
  • Constant retention: about 81% of the 200-item list survives every thousand years (Lees), roughly 86% for the 100-item list, and the rate is assumed to be the same for all languages.
  • The formula: time depth t = log C ÷ (2 log r), where C is the proportion of shared cognates and r the retention rate; the factor 2 reflects independent loss in both daughter languages.
  • Worked example: two languages sharing 66% cognates on the 200-item list would have separated about 1,000 years ago (log 0.66 ÷ 2 log 0.81 ≈ 0.99 millennium).

2. Uses

  • Prehistory of non-literate peoples: it offered dates for splits in language families of the Americas, Africa and the Pacific, which could be matched with archaeological cultures and migrations.
  • Indian studies: lexicostatistics has been applied to Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman and Dravidian speech forms; a Bayesian phylogenetic study of twenty Dravidian languages (Kolipakam and colleagues, 2018) placed the family's origin about 4,500 years ago.

3. Criticism

  • Rates are not constant: Bergsland and Vogt (1962) showed that Icelandic kept far more basic words than Norwegian over the same centuries, so dates can be badly wrong.
  • Borrowing and taboo: contact with prestige languages (Sanskrit, Persian, English) and replacement of tabooed words distort counts.
  • Subjectivity: deciding what is a true cognate, and whether the list is really culture-free, depends on the analyst.
  • Successors: computational methods (Gray and Atkinson, 2003, on Indo-European) allow rates to vary and give date ranges rather than single figures.

Glottochronology is today valued more as a relative measure of closeness than as a clock, but its idea lives on in phylogenetic linguistics, which, together with archaeology and genetics, reconstructs the human past.
free.upa-2023-an1-5d:
MenopauseOestrogen declineVasomotor symptomsLocal biologies

Menopause is the permanent end of menstruation caused by the exhaustion of ovarian follicles, confirmed after twelve months without a period. The transition years (perimenopause or climacteric) bring symptoms because the ovaries secrete less oestrogen and progesterone while FSH rises. Indian women usually reach menopause in their mid-to-late forties, a few years earlier than Western women, so symptoms affect a large share of adult life.

1. Somatic symptoms

  • Vasomotor: hot flushes and night sweats are the hallmark symptoms; falling oestrogen narrows the heat-regulating zone of the hypothalamus, so small temperature changes trigger flushing. They may last several years.
  • Sleep and fatigue: insomnia, palpitations, headache and tiredness are common.
  • Bones and joints: joint and muscle aches; faster bone loss raises the risk of osteoporosis and fractures of the spine, hip and wrist.
  • Heart and metabolism: weight gain around the waist and adverse changes in blood lipids raise the risk of heart disease after menopause.

2. Urogenital symptoms

  • Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: vaginal dryness, painful intercourse, urinary urgency and repeated urinary infections follow thinning of oestrogen-dependent tissues.
  • End of fertility: cycles become irregular in perimenopause before they stop.

3. Psychological symptoms

  • Mood and cognition: irritability, anxiety, low mood, poor concentration and forgetfulness.
  • Life events: these often coincide with children leaving home, widowhood or caring for elders, so social stress and hormonal change act together.

4. Biocultural variation

  • Culture shapes the experience: Marcha Flint (1975) found that Rajput women in India reported few complaints apart from menstrual changes, since menopause freed them from purdah and raised their standing.
  • Local biologies: Margaret Lock (Encounters with Aging, 1993) found Japanese women reporting hot flushes far less often than North American women, and Yewoubdar Beyene (1989) found that Maya women of Yucatán did not report them at all; diet, reproductive history and meaning all matter.
  • Indian context: symptoms are often under-reported and seldom treated, as reproductive health services focus on younger women.

Menopausal symptoms are thus biocultural: a universal hormonal change felt through diet, status and belief. Lifestyle care, calcium and vitamin D, counselling and, where suitable, hormone therapy can make this phase a healthy one, which matters as women's life expectancy rises.
free.upa-2023-an1-5e:
Cultural lagMaterial cultureAdaptive cultureSocial change

William Fielding Ogburn (1886–1959), an American sociologist, introduced the idea of cultural lag in Social Change with Respect to Culture and Original Nature (1922). He held that material culture (tools, machines, technology) changes faster than non-material culture, and that the delay before customs, laws and values adjust to it produces strain and social problems.

1. Ogburn's theory of social change

  • Four processes: invention, accumulation (the cultural base grows as inventions pile up), diffusion and adjustment explain why change speeds up over time.
  • Adaptive culture: the part of non-material culture that must adjust to material conditions, such as family, law, government and education. The lag is the interval between a material change and this adjustment.
  • His illustrations: machines caused many industrial accidents in the United States long before employers' liability and workmen's compensation laws were passed; forests were cut far faster than conservation policy developed.

2. Uses of the concept

  • Explaining social problems: dowry inflation alongside modern consumer goods, or road deaths as vehicles outpace traffic discipline, can be read as lags.
  • Tribal and rural change: rapid entry of money, markets and new technology often outruns customary institutions, leading to land alienation, debt and generational conflict.
  • Policy foresight: it encourages anticipating the social effects of new technology, as in present debates on artificial intelligence and gene editing.

3. Criticism

  • Technological determinism: it assumes that material culture always leads. Max Weber (The Protestant Ethic, 1905) showed that ideas can drive economic change, and movements such as Gandhian satyagraha show non-material innovation leading.
  • Artificial dichotomy: tools embody knowledge and values, so material and non-material culture cannot be neatly separated.
  • Subjective and hard to measure: deciding which element lags, and from what standard, is a value judgement; some delay is useful as a period of testing.
  • Uneven change: in plural societies different groups adjust at different speeds, so there is no single lag.

Despite these limits, cultural lag remains a handy lens for technological change, from AI to climate policy, and reminds planners that new tools need matching institutional adjustment.
free.upa-2023-an1-6a:
Participant observationMalinowski's DiaryMead–Freeman controversyReflexivity

Bronislaw Malinowski (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922) and Margaret Mead (Coming of Age in Samoa, 1928) made long, first-hand fieldwork the hallmark of anthropology. Both later faced controversies over the objectivity, ethics and authority of the ethnographer, which helped give rise to reflexive anthropology.

1. Controversies around Malinowski

  • The Diary (1967): his private field diaries of 1914–18, published posthumously as A Diary in the Strict Sense of the Term, revealed loneliness, irritation, sexual fantasies and contemptuous, even racist, words about the islanders. This clashed with his image as the empathetic participant observer; Clifford Geertz replied that understanding the native's point of view comes from interpreting symbols, not from fellow-feeling.
  • Colonial setting: an Austrian subject caught in Australia by the First World War, he worked with the consent of the colonial administration. His functionalism painted a timeless Trobriand society that ignored colonial rule, missions and traders; Talal Asad's Anthropology and the Colonial Encounter (1973) linked such silences to colonial power.
  • Male bias: Annette Weiner's restudy (Women of Value, Men of Renown, 1976) showed that women's banana-leaf bundles and skirts, exchanged at mortuary rites, were major wealth that Malinowski had largely missed.
  • Textual authority: James Clifford (1983) and Geertz (Works and Lives, 1988) showed how Argonauts builds authority through vivid scenes of "being there".

2. Controversies around Mead

  • Short, interview-based fieldwork: aged 23, Mead spent about nine months in American Samoa (1925–26), mostly on Ta'ū, lodged with an American naval family and relied on interviews with adolescent girls.
  • Freeman's attack: Derek Freeman (Margaret Mead and Samoa: The Making and Unmaking of an Anthropological Myth, 1983), published after her death, argued that Samoans prized virginity (the taupou system) and knew much rivalry, punishment and violence. He claimed her stress-free adolescence served Boas's cultural determinism.
  • The "hoaxing" claim: in The Fateful Hoaxing of Margaret Mead (1999) he relied on a 1987 interview in which Fa'apua'a Fa'amū said she and a friend had jokingly fed Mead tall tales about night-time affairs.
  • Defence of Mead: Lowell Holmes, who restudied Ta'ū in 1954 (Quest for the Real Samoa, 1987), judged her broadly right though she overstated sexual freedom. Paul Shankman (The Trashing of Margaret Mead, 2009) showed that her conclusions rested on far more than that joke, while Freeman drew on Western Samoa decades later.

3. Critical assessment

  • Restudies differ: as with Robert Redfield (1930) and Oscar Lewis (1951) on Tepoztlán, different periods and informants yield different pictures, which Karl Heider (1988) called the "Rashomon effect".
  • Theory and ideology: Freeman claimed to defend falsifiable, biologically informed science; critics saw a nature–nurture crusade. Both cases show ethnography to be positioned, partial knowledge.
  • Indian parallel: M.N. Srinivas wrote The Remembered Village (1976) from memory after his Rampura field notes burned at Stanford in 1970, showing that ethnography rests on memory and selection.

The controversies did not discredit participant observation; they matured it through reflexivity, restudies and ethics codes. Fieldwork is now seen as a dialogue shaped by power, gender and the observer's self, whose authority rests on transparency and ethical responsibility.
free.upa-2023-an1-6b:
GlobalisationDisembeddingAccumulation by dispossessionIndigenous livelihoods

Globalisation is the growing flow of capital, goods, technology, people and ideas across borders; in India it gathered pace after the economic reforms of 1991. It draws indigenous economies, built on subsistence, reciprocity, redistribution and common property, into the market. Karl Polanyi (The Great Transformation, 1944) described this as the economy being disembedded from kinship, religion and community.

1. Change in the principles of exchange

  • From gift to price: barter, reciprocity and feast-based redistribution give way to money, wages and profit, and prestige items become commodities.
  • Classic cases: Lauriston Sharp's "Steel Axes for Stone-Age Australians" (1952) showed how steel axes handed out by missionaries to the Yir Yoront upset the authority of elders, gender relations and trade partnerships. Richard Salisbury (From Stone to Steel, 1962) found that steel tools freed Siane men's time for politics and ceremonial exchange.

2. Adverse impacts

  • Land and resource alienation: mines, dams, plantations and industrial corridors take tribal land, a process David Harvey (2003) calls accumulation by dispossession. The Dongria Kondh of Niyamgiri, Odisha, resisted bauxite mining; after the Supreme Court (2013) left the decision to gram sabhas, all twelve chosen villages rejected it.
  • Unequal markets: forest produce such as tendu leaves, mahua and sal seed reaches distant buyers through middlemen, leaving gatherers with low prices, debt and over-harvesting.
  • Distress migration: loss of land and forests sends young people to brick kilns, construction sites and plantations, weakening the household as a unit of production.
  • Biopiracy and commodified culture: traditional knowledge and designs are copied or patented, and tourism can turn rituals into spectacles, as in the "human safaris" to Jarawa areas of the Andamans exposed in 2012.
  • Diet and health: cash crops and packaged food replace varied forest and millet diets.

3. Opportunities and indigenous responses

  • New markets: Geographical Indication tags and branding help, as with Araku Valley Arabica coffee grown by tribal farmers in Andhra Pradesh (GI, 2019); TRIFED's Tribes India outlets and e-commerce sell crafts.
  • Benefit sharing: the Kani of Kerala received a share of licence fees for the herbal drug Jeevani, developed from their knowledge of the plant arogyapacha.
  • Collective rights: under the Forest Rights Act, Mendha-Lekha in Gadchiroli won community forest rights (2009) and, after receiving a bamboo transit pass in 2011, began selling its own bamboo, bargaining with the market on its own terms.
  • Global solidarity: the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) and transnational networks amplify local struggles.

The impact of globalisation is therefore uneven: it destroys where communities lose control of land and knowledge, and empowers where they negotiate from secure rights. Laws such as PESA and FRA, fair prices and cooperatives make self-determined development, in the spirit of Nehru's tribal Panchsheel, possible.
free.upa-2023-an1-6c:
DNA technologyDNA profilingGenome editingAncient DNA

DNA technology covers the tools to isolate, copy, cut, join, read and edit genetic material: recombinant DNA (1970s), the polymerase chain reaction (PCR, Kary Mullis, 1983), high-throughput sequencing and CRISPR–Cas9 editing (Nobel Prize to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna, 2020). Cheaper sequencing has carried these tools from the laboratory into medicine, law, agriculture and anthropology.

1. Medicine and public health

  • Screening and diagnosis: carrier, prenatal and newborn testing for thalassaemia, sickle-cell disease and other disorders. India's National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (launched July 2023, aiming at elimination by 2047) screens people in 278 districts of 17 high-focus states, mainly in tribal areas, and gives genetic status cards with counselling.
  • Gene therapy and editing: Casgevy, the first CRISPR-based therapy to be approved anywhere, was cleared in the UK in November 2023 for sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassaemia (and soon after in the USA), disorders common in many Indian tribal and caste groups.
  • Recombinant products and vaccines: human insulin, hepatitis B vaccine and nucleic-acid vaccines; India's ZyCoV-D (2021) was the first DNA vaccine authorised for human use against COVID-19.
  • Genomic surveillance and pharmacogenomics: the INSACOG network tracked SARS-CoV-2 variants, and variants in drug-metabolising genes guide the choice and dose of medicines.

2. Forensic and legal uses

  • DNA profiling: pioneered by Alec Jeffreys (1984) and in India by Lalji Singh, it now identifies offenders, settles paternity and identifies disaster victims; victims of the Air India crash at Ahmedabad (June 2025) were identified by matching with relatives' DNA.
  • Genetic genealogy and wildlife forensics: the US "Golden State Killer" was traced in 2018 through relatives in a public genealogy database, and DNA tests trace poached tiger parts and ivory.
  • Regulation: the DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill, 2019, which proposed national DNA data banks, was withdrawn from the Lok Sabha in July 2023; the government said the Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 already covered most of it, while critics had raised privacy concerns.

3. Anthropology and human evolution

  • Ancient DNA: Svante Pääbo's Neanderthal genome and the discovery of the Denisovans (Nobel Prize, 2022) showed interbreeding with early modern humans; the Rakhigarhi genome (2019) shed light on Harappan ancestry.
  • Peopling of India: mitochondrial, Y-chromosome and genome-wide data reveal Ancestral North and South Indian components (Reich and colleagues, 2009), the deep roots of the Andamanese and strong founder effects created by endogamy. The GenomeIndia project (launched 2020) released whole-genome data of about 10,000 Indians in January 2025.
  • Historical puzzles: DNA from the Roopkund lake skeletons (2019) showed distinct groups who died centuries apart.

4. Agriculture and environment

  • Crops: Bt cotton (2002) and India's first genome-edited rice varieties, DRR Dhan 100 (Kamala) and Pusa DST Rice 1, released by ICAR in May 2025.
  • Environmental DNA and barcoding: monitoring biodiversity and checking adulteration of food and herbal drugs.

DNA technology is now part of everyday public life, but the Havasupai blood-sample case in the USA and the illegal gene-edited babies in China (2018) show that consent, privacy and equity must keep pace. Anthropologists help make genomics ethically and culturally sensitive.
free.upa-2023-an1-7a:
CodingGrounded theoryThick descriptionCAQDAS

Qualitative data in anthropology are words and images rather than numbers: field notes, interview transcripts, life histories, genealogies, myths, songs, photographs and recordings. Qualitative data analysis turns them into patterns and explanations through repeated coding, comparison and interpretation, aiming at the insider's (emic) view and what Clifford Geertz (1973) called thick description. Analysis begins in the field and continues through writing.

1. Methods of qualitative data analysis

  • Thematic analysis: finding recurring patterns of meaning across interviews or texts; Braun and Clarke (2006) set out six phases, from familiarisation to writing up.
  • Grounded theory: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss (The Discovery of Grounded Theory, 1967) build theory from the data through constant comparison until no new categories appear (theoretical saturation); Strauss and Corbin later named open, axial and selective coding.
  • Content analysis: systematic categorising, and often counting, of words, themes or images in documents, media and folklore.
  • Narrative and life-history analysis: how people order experience in stories, as in Oscar Lewis's The Children of Sánchez (1961).
  • Discourse and conversation analysis: how talk builds identity, authority and social order.
  • Cognitive and domain analysis: James Spradley's domain, taxonomic and componential analysis (The Ethnographic Interview, 1979), with free lists and pile sorts, uncovers folk classifications such as Harold Conklin's work on Hanunóo colour terms.
  • Structural, symbolic and situational analysis: Lévi-Strauss's binary oppositions in myth, Victor Turner's reading of Ndembu ritual symbols, and Max Gluckman's analysis of a bridge-opening ceremony in Zululand (1940) as a "social situation".

2. Ensuring rigour

  • Triangulation: cross-checking across data sources, methods, investigators and theories (Norman Denzin, The Research Act, 1970).
  • Member checking and audit trail: returning interpretations to participants, and keeping memos that show how codes and conclusions were reached.
  • Reflexivity: recording how the researcher's caste, gender, language and status shape what is seen and heard.

3. Computer software for qualitative analysis

Computer-assisted qualitative data analysis software (CAQDAS) stores, codes, retrieves and links data but does not think for the researcher.

  • Recent trends: cloud collaboration, automatic transcription, and AI-assisted suggestions of codes and summaries in ATLAS.ti, NVivo and MAXQDA.
  • Advantages: speed with large data sets, transparent audit trails, easy retrieval and teamwork.
  • Limits: coding can cut quotations from their context and encourage mechanical counting; licences are costly; and sensitive field data on cloud servers raise confidentiality issues. Indigenous groups increasingly assert control over data about them (the CARE principles, 2019).

Qualitative analysis remains an act of interpretation: software organises meaning, but the anthropologist's long immersion, reflexivity and theoretical imagination turn coded fragments into ethnographic understanding.
free.upa-2023-an1-7b:
Hardy–Weinberg principleGene poolRandom matingForces of evolution

The Hardy–Weinberg principle, stated independently by the mathematician G.H. Hardy and the physician Wilhelm Weinberg in 1908, holds that in an ideal population allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. For two alleles with frequencies p and q (p + q = 1), genotypes settle at p² + 2pq + q² = 1 after a single generation of random mating. Such a population is in genetic equilibrium: it is not evolving.

1. Assumptions for genetic equilibrium

  • Very large population: chance changes in allele frequency (genetic drift) must be negligible.
  • Random mating (panmixia): each individual is equally likely to mate with any other, irrespective of genotype, with no inbreeding, endogamy or assortative mating.
  • No mutation: no new alleles appear and none change into another.
  • No migration: no gene flow into or out of the population.
  • No natural selection: all genotypes survive and reproduce equally well.
  • Other conditions: sexual reproduction in diploids, normal Mendelian segregation, equal allele frequencies in both sexes and non-overlapping generations.

2. Importance of genetic equilibrium

  • Null model of evolution: since evolution is a change in allele frequencies, a significant departure from equilibrium shows that some force (drift, selection, migration, mutation or non-random mating) is acting. This makes the principle the starting point of population genetics.
  • Estimating carriers: from the frequency of a recessive disorder (q²) one can work out the share of healthy carriers (2pq), the basis of screening and genetic counselling.
  • Detecting inbreeding and structure: an excess of homozygotes reveals consanguinity or a population divided into isolates. Nakatsuka and colleagues (2017) found strong founder events in many endogamous Indian groups, raising the risk of recessive disease.
  • Quality checks and forensics: genome-wide studies discard markers that depart sharply from equilibrium in controls as likely genotyping errors, and forensic match probabilities assume equilibrium in a reference population.
  • Anthropological comparison: frequencies of ABO, Rh and haemoglobin variants across tribes and castes are judged against equilibrium; high sickle-cell frequencies in central Indian tribal belts fit the malaria hypothesis of J.B.S. Haldane (1949), which A.C. Allison (1954) confirmed for the sickle-cell trait.

3. Limits

  • An ideal, not a reality: no human population fully meets the assumptions, and equilibrium at one locus says nothing about others.
  • Neutral, not self-correcting: a disturbed population settles at a new equilibrium rather than returning to the old one.

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is valuable precisely because it is rarely met: as a yardstick, it lets anthropologists measure and explain how evolutionary forces shape human gene pools.
free.upa-2023-an1-7c:
National characterCulture at a distanceModal personalityAnthropology and the state

National character studies extended the culture-and-personality approach from small communities to modern nations, asking which personality traits are typical of, say, Japanese or Russians, and how child-rearing and institutions produce them. They flourished during and after World War II, when Ruth Benedict, Margaret Mead, Geoffrey Gorer and Gregory Bateson studied enemy and allied peoples "at a distance" for the American and British governments.

1. Political aspects

  • Born of war needs: Benedict's work at the Office of War Information led to The Chrysanthemum and the Sword (1946) on Japan, used in planning the occupation; Mead's And Keep Your Powder Dry (1942) addressed American morale.
  • Cold War continuation: Columbia University's Research in Contemporary Cultures (1947–52), funded by the Office of Naval Research, studied Russia, China, France and other cultures; Gorer and Rickman (The People of Great Russia, 1949) linked tight swaddling to adult attitudes to authority.
  • Scholarship serving power: critics saw anthropology turned into intelligence work, recalling Boas's 1919 protest against anthropologists acting as spies; Project Camelot (1965) and the US Army's Human Terrain System (2007–14), which the American Anthropological Association opposed, revived the concern.
  • Stereotypes as policy: fixed national images can feed propaganda and justify domination (Edward Said, Orientalism, 1978). In India, colonial ethnography gave groups fixed "characters", such as "martial races" and the communities notified under the Criminal Tribes Act, 1871, whose stigma still burdens denotified tribes.

2. Methodological aspects

  • Culture at a distance: without fieldwork, scholars used immigrants, prisoners of war, novels, films, propaganda and newspapers (Mead and Métraux, The Study of Culture at a Distance, 1953).
  • Neo-Freudian assumptions: adult character was traced to toilet training, swaddling or weaning; critics mocked this as "diaperology".
  • Sampling and homogeneity: a few informants stood for millions, ignoring class, region, religion, gender and history; Benedict's Japan reflected samurai-class ethics.
  • Circular and untestable: traits were inferred from culture and then used to explain it, and projective tests such as the Rorschach were culture-bound.
  • Refinements: Cora Du Bois's modal personality (The People of Alor, 1944) and Alex Inkeles and Daniel Levinson (1954) treated character as a statistical spread of traits, not a single type.

3. Contemporary relevance

  • Business and diplomacy: Hofstede's dimensions and the World Values Survey guide cross-cultural management, negotiation and the training of diplomats and multinational teams, a quantified heir to national character.
  • Security and soft power: "cultural intelligence" for conflict zones and public diplomacy revive both the method and its ethical dilemmas.
  • Testing stereotypes: Terracciano and colleagues (Science, 2005) found that perceived national character in 49 cultures did not match measured average personality, showing stereotypes to be social constructions.
  • Identity politics: national stereotypes shape debates on migration, populism and profiling; anthropology now stresses diversity within nations and person-centred ethnography, as in Sudhir Kakar's study of Indian childhood (The Inner World, 1978).

National character studies are discredited in their wartime form, yet their questions survive: how culture shapes persons, and whom such knowledge serves. Empirical rigour and professional ethics must accompany any revival.
free.upa-2023-an1-8a:
Global cultural economyFive scapesDisjunctureImagination as social practice

In his essay "Disjuncture and Difference in the Global Cultural Economy" (1990), expanded in Modernity at Large: Cultural Dimensions of Globalization (1996), Arjun Appadurai argued that the global cultural economy cannot be grasped through centre–periphery models. It is a complex, overlapping and disjunctive order of flows, which he mapped as five "scapes", in which imagination itself has become a social practice.

1. The conceptual framework

  • Beyond homogenisation: global forms do not simply Americanise the world; they are indigenised. His essay on Indian cricket shows an English game made Indian through vernacular commentary, media and national passion.
  • Five scapes: ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes and ideoscapes. The suffix "-scape" marks fluid, irregular landscapes that look different from each standpoint: a nation-state, a diaspora, a firm or a village.
  • Disjuncture: the scapes move at different speeds and in different directions; money moves in seconds, people face visas, images travel instantly. The gaps between them breed new cultural forms and new conflicts.
  • Imagined worlds and deterritorialisation: extending Benedict Anderson's "imagined communities" (1983), he showed how media and migration let people imagine lives elsewhere; diasporas sustain long-distance nationalism and loosen the bond of culture to territory.

2. Strengths

  • Decentring globalisation: it replaces one-way models with multiple centres; India itself exports films, yoga and software services.
  • Agency: local people appropriate and rework global forms instead of passively receiving them.
  • New methods: it encouraged multi-sited ethnography (George Marcus, 1995) and studies of diaspora, media and transnational lives.

3. Critical examination

  • Flows without structure: Josiah Heyman and Howard Campbell (2009) argued that the "flows" metaphor hides the capitalism, states and borders that channel movement; political economists such as David Harvey see globalisation as driven by capital accumulation, not free-floating culture.
  • Unequal access: Zygmunt Bauman's contrast of mobile "tourists" and immobile "vagabonds" (1998) shows that mobility and imagination are shaped by class, gender and race; tribal and rural Indians enter the scapes on very unequal terms.
  • Nation-state not withering: visa regimes, citizenship laws, data localisation and resurgent nationalism, such as Brexit (2016), show the state's continuing grip.
  • Vague metaphors: the scapes overlap and are hard to measure or test. Anna Tsing ("The Global Situation", 2000; Friction, 2005) urged ethnographies of concrete encounters rather than celebration of flows.
  • Consumption over production: labour, environment and material inequality get less attention than media and imagination.
  • His own later view: in Fear of Small Numbers (2006) Appadurai himself showed how global uncertainty breeds majoritarian violence against minorities.

Appadurai's model remains a landmark for thinking about cultural globalisation without assuming sameness. Combined with political economy and grounded fieldwork, it explains both creative glocalisation and the new inequalities of the global age.
free.upa-2023-an1-8b:
Structural aberrationsChromosome breakageUnequal crossing overClastogens

Structural abnormalities are changes in the arrangement of chromosome material: deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations, ring chromosomes and isochromosomes. Unlike numerical changes (aneuploidy), they almost always begin with a double-strand break in DNA that is wrongly repaired, or with mispairing between similar DNA sequences. They may be balanced or unbalanced, inherited or new (de novo), and present in all cells or only in a tumour.

1. Mechanisms that produce them

  • Break and wrong rejoining: when two breaks occur, repair by end-joining may join the wrong ends. A lost segment gives a deletion; a segment turned round gives an inversion; an exchange between two chromosomes gives a reciprocal translocation; breaks at both ends of one chromosome that fuse give a ring.
  • Non-allelic homologous recombination: blocks of repeated DNA (low-copy repeats) on either side of a region misalign at meiosis, and unequal crossing over produces a deletion on one chromatid and a duplication on the other. This explains recurrent syndromes such as 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge), Williams (7q11.23) and Smith–Magenis (17p11.2).
  • Centric fusion: two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22) join near their centromeres and lose their tiny short arms, forming a Robertsonian translocation.
  • Faulty splitting of the centromere: a transverse rather than lengthwise split forms an isochromosome with two identical arms, as i(Xq) in some cases of Turner syndrome.
  • Chromothripsis: a chromosome shatters and is stitched back at random in a single event, described in cancers by Stephens and colleagues (2011).

2. Agents and risk factors

  • Ionising radiation: X-rays and gamma rays break chromosomes; survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and radiation workers show more aberrations, and dicentric counts in blood cells are used to estimate radiation dose.
  • Chemical clastogens: benzene, alkylating anticancer drugs, some pesticides and tobacco smoke.
  • Defective DNA repair: inherited chromosome-instability syndromes such as Bloom syndrome, Fanconi anaemia and ataxia-telangiectasia show spontaneous breakage and a high cancer risk.
  • Somatic events in cancer: the Philadelphia chromosome, a translocation t(9;22) first seen by Nowell and Hungerford (1960) and explained by Janet Rowley (1973), creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene of chronic myeloid leukaemia.

3. Inheritance from carrier parents

  • Balanced translocation carriers: healthy themselves, they form unbalanced gametes at meiosis, causing repeated miscarriage or affected children; a small share of Down syndrome results from a Robertsonian translocation such as t(14;21), which can be inherited from a balanced carrier parent and then tends to recur in the family.
  • Inversion carriers: crossing over inside the inversion loop yields recombinant chromosomes with duplications and deficiencies (pericentric) or dicentric and acentric fragments (paracentric).

Karyotyping, FISH and chromosomal microarrays detect these changes. Their study supports genetic counselling, especially in consanguineous communities, and protection from mutagens at work and in the environment.
free.upa-2023-an1-8c:
Kinship terminologyClassificatory systemsEight principlesPsychology versus sociology

A.L. Kroeber (1876–1960), Franz Boas's first doctoral student at Columbia, reshaped the study of kinship terms with his paper "Classificatory Systems of Relationship" (1909). Rejecting the sorting of kinship systems into "classificatory" and "descriptive" in Systems of Consanguinity and Affinity of the Human Family (Lewis Henry Morgan, 1871), he analysed kin terms through a small set of universal principles (categories) found in all languages.

1. Critique of Morgan

  • No system is purely descriptive: the English word "uncle" covers father's brother, mother's brother and the husbands of both aunts, and "cousin" merges many relatives, so English also classifies; it simply uses fewer distinctions than many Native American systems.
  • Against evolutionary guesswork: Morgan read terms as survivals of earlier forms such as group marriage; Kroeber held that they are poor evidence of past social stages.

2. The eight principles

Kroeber showed that every terminology selects some of eight distinctions and ignores others, so systems can be compared by the principles they use.

3. The psychology versus sociology debate

  • Kroeber's thesis: kin terms are primarily linguistic and reflect ways of thinking; he concluded that "terms of relationship reflect psychology, not sociology", so they can support inferences about social life only with great caution.
  • Rivers's reply: W.H.R. Rivers (Kinship and Social Organisation, 1914) argued that terms are shaped by social institutions; where cross-cousin marriage is practised, the mother's brother and the father-in-law share one term.
  • Later support for Rivers: A.R. Radcliffe-Brown (1941) treated terminology as part of the social structure defining rights and duties, and Louis Dumont (1953) showed that Dravidian terminology expresses marriage alliance; in Tamil and Telugu, mama denotes both mother's brother and father-in-law.

4. Evaluation

  • Lasting tools: G.P. Murdock (Social Structure, 1949) used Kroeber's criteria, adding polarity to make nine, for his cross-cultural typology; Ward Goodenough and Floyd Lounsbury (1956) turned them into componential analysis of kin terms as bundles of semantic features.
  • Neutral comparison: freed from evolutionary ranking, the principles suit Boasian historical particularism and Kroeber's own studies of Californian and Zuni kinship (1917).
  • Criticism: the approach is formal and static, deals with words rather than behaviour, underrates marriage rules and descent groups, and assumes a universal genealogical grid that David Schneider (A Critique of the Study of Kinship, 1984) later questioned.

Kroeber turned kinship terminology into a field of systematic, comparative analysis. The debate he opened with Rivers still frames how anthropologists relate language to social structure.
free.upa-2023-an2-1a:
Material cultureArchaeological recordFormation processesEthnoarchaeology

Material culture is the physical world that people make, use and throw away: tools, pots, houses, ornaments, graves and altered landscapes. Archaeology studies past societies almost entirely through such remains, so the two are inseparable. Because objects do not speak, archaeologists turn to ethnoarchaeology, the study of material culture among living communities, to read behaviour from things.

1. Material culture as archaeological evidence

  • Artefacts, ecofacts and features: portable objects (handaxes, microliths, beads), organic remains (seeds, animal bones) and fixed traces (hearths, post-holes, burials) together make up the archaeological record.
  • Cultures as assemblages: V. Gordon Childe (The Danube in Prehistory, 1929) treated an archaeological culture as a recurring set of pottery, tools, house forms and burial rites; Indian sequences such as Ochre Coloured Pottery followed by Painted Grey Ware are built in this way.
  • Objects carry meaning: Ian Hodder (Symbols in Action, 1982), working in Kenya's Baringo district, showed that people use dress, ornaments and pottery to mark group identity, so material culture is active, not a passive mirror.

2. From objects to behaviour

  • Formation processes: Michael Schiffer (Behavioral Archeology, 1976) separated the living "systemic context" from the "archaeological context"; discard, reuse, decay and later disturbance decide what survives.
  • Middle-range theory: Lewis Binford (Nunamiut Ethnoarchaeology, 1978) recorded how Nunamiut caribou hunters of Alaska butchered, stored and discarded bones, giving rules for reading ancient bone scatters.
  • Analogy: direct historical analogy where living people descend from the excavated ones, and general comparative analogy between societies in similar environments.

3. Indian applications

  • Megalithic survivals: Khasi memorial stones (upright "male" and flat "female" slabs), Munda burial slabs (sasandiri) and Maria Gond memorial pillars help interpret the Iron Age megaliths of the peninsula.
  • Crafts: Carol Kramer's Pottery in Rajasthan (1997) studied potters in two cities, showing how caste, workshops and markets shape the making and spread of pots, a guide for reading ancient pottery.
  • Harappan analogies: from John Marshall onward, excavators read terracotta bullock carts, ploughs and bangles through their present-day village equivalents.
  • Prehistoric landscapes: K. Paddayya used present-day seasonal patterns of water, plants and game in the Hunsgi–Baichbal valleys (Karnataka) to model Acheulian settlement.

4. Limits

  • Living people are not fossils: steel and plastic vessels, markets and migration have transformed crafts, so analogies need caution, and fieldwork needs informed consent.

Material culture is the bridge between present and past; joined with ethnoarchaeology and scientific dating, it lets archaeology move from describing objects to explaining human behaviour.
free.upa-2023-an2-1b:
PurusharthaAshramaDharmaMoksha

In the classical Hindu scheme, Purushartha names the four legitimate aims of life (dharma, artha, kama and moksha), while Ashrama divides the ideal life of a twice-born man into four stages. P.H. Prabhu (Hindu Social Organization, 1954) showed that the two were designed together: the stages are the social settings in which the aims are pursued in turn, always under the guidance of dharma.

1. Each stage emphasises different aims

  • Brahmacharya (student): begins with upanayana; celibacy, study and obedience to the guru teach dharma and prepare the youth for later duties.
  • Grihastha (householder): begins with marriage (vivaha); artha (wealth) and kama (desire and family life) are pursued within dharma, the debts (rinas) to gods, sages and ancestors are repaid, and the Dharmashastras praise this stage as the support of all the others.
  • Vanaprastha (forest dweller): when grandchildren arrive, worldly pursuits are reduced and dharma is turned towards preparing for liberation.
  • Sannyasa (renouncer): all ties are given up in search of moksha, release from the cycle of birth and rebirth.

2. Principles that join the two

  • Dharma as regulator: artha and kama are valid only when bounded by dharma; Kautilya's Arthashastra and Vatsyayana's Kamasutra treat these aims as sciences, yet within a moral order.
  • Pravritti and nivritti: the first two stages engage with the world and the last two withdraw from it, balancing material and spiritual life across a lifetime.
  • Links with samskara and karma: life-cycle rites mark entry into each stage, and right action in each stage shapes the next birth.

3. Anthropological appraisal

  • An ideal, not a universal practice: the Dharmashastras addressed the scheme to twice-born men; women and Shudras were largely outside upanayana, and Manu treats marriage as a woman's equivalent of initiation.
  • Historical change: Patrick Olivelle (The Asrama System, 1993) shows that the ashramas were first alternative lifelong paths and only later became a fixed sequence.
  • Householder and renouncer: Louis Dumont (1960) contrasted the man-in-the-world with the renouncer as an individual outside society, while T.N. Madan (Non-renunciation, 1987) found Kashmiri Pandits valuing detachment within household life.

Few follow the stages literally today, yet the ideal survives in retirement, pilgrimage and service to family, and its lesson, a balance of material and spiritual aims, remains relevant.
free.upa-2023-an2-1c:
Jajmani systemJajman–kaminReciprocityMonetisation

The jajmani system is the hereditary exchange of services and goods between landowning patron families (jajman) and service and artisan castes (kamin or praja), paid mainly in kind: a fixed share of grain at harvest plus gifts at festivals and life-cycle rites. William Wiser (The Hindu Jajmani System, 1936) described it from Karimpur village in Uttar Pradesh; the baluta system of Maharashtra is a regional variant.

1. Traditional features

  • Hereditary and many-stranded: ties linked particular families over generations, covering economic, ritual and social duties, and were enforced by caste panchayats and village opinion.
  • Ritual core: the priest, barber and washerman were needed for purity at birth, marriage and death; Louis Dumont (Homo Hierarchicus, 1966) read the system as an expression of the pure–impure hierarchy rather than as mere economics.
  • Rival readings: Wiser stressed reciprocity, with every caste serving others and being served in turn, master and servant by turns; T.O. Beidelman (1959) called it feudal and exploitative, and Oscar Lewis and Victor Barnouw (1956) showed landowning Jats dominating the service castes of Rampur near Delhi.

2. Change

  • Money and markets: mill cloth, aluminium and plastic vessels and tractors displaced weavers, potters and carpenters, and cash wages replaced harvest shares.
  • Agrarian transformation: the Green Revolution, land reforms and smaller holdings led patrons to hire labour by the day or season instead of keeping clients.
  • Assertion and law: schooling, migration and Dalit movements led many castes to refuse caste-marked tasks such as removing carcasses; bonded labour was abolished by law in 1976.
  • Karimpur revisited: Susan Wadley (Struggling with Destiny in Karimpur, 1925–1984, 1994) found most of Wiser's ties replaced by cash relations.

3. Continuity

  • Ritual services persist: priests still call their clients "jajman", and barbers and washermen serve at weddings and funerals, now for cash and customary gifts.
  • Patronage in new forms: Jan Breman (Patronage and Exploitation, 1974) traced the hali bond of South Gujarat turning into casual wage labour, while credit, labour contracting and vote banks recreate dependence.
  • Caste-linked work: sanitation and leather work remain concentrated among Dalits.

Jajmani has largely dissolved as an economic system but survives as a ritual and patronage idiom, showing how caste adapts to markets rather than simply disappearing.
free.upa-2023-an2-1d:
Rock artLakhudiyarKumaon HimalayaMesolithic affinity

Rock art covers paintings (pictographs) and engravings or cup-marks (petroglyphs) on rock shelters and boulders. In Uttarakhand it is concentrated in the Kumaon hills of Almora district, with smaller sites in Garhwal; the best-known site is Lakhudiyar on the Suyal river near Barechhina. Yashodhar Mathpal's Rock Art in Kumaon Himalaya (1995) remains the main survey.

1. Main sites

  • Lakhudiyar (Lakhu Udyar), Almora: painted overhangs beside the Almora–Barechhina road, first reported by M.P. Joshi in the 1960s; the name is usually explained as "a lakh caves".
  • Phalsima–Dalband cluster, Almora: about a dozen painted rocks close together, also reported by Joshi.
  • Garhwal: Gwarkha Udiyar (Chamoli), high above the Alaknanda, with red figures of hunters, deer and goats; Kimni (Chamoli); and Hudoli near Purola (Uttarkashi), with greyish bird and creeper-like motifs.
  • Engravings: cup-marks and carved hollows at Devidhura (Champawat), described as early as 1856, and at Deoli (Almora).

2. Themes, colours and technique

  • Human figures: stick-like people, often in long rows dancing hand in hand, with drummers and hunters; Mathpal regarded the dance scenes as the most striking.
  • Animals and signs: animals with long snouts, a fox-like creature, wavy lines, clusters of dots and rectangles filled with patterns.
  • Pigments: black (charcoal), red ochre (haematite) and white, applied mostly with fingers; overlapping layers suggest that black is the oldest and white the latest.

3. Dating and significance

  • Uncertain age: no absolute dates exist; some scholars link the paintings to the Mesolithic on grounds of style, while Mathpal related them to the megalith-building communities of Kumaon in the first millennium BCE.
  • A cultural window: they record hunting, herding and collective ritual in the central Himalaya, and the chain dances invite comparison with Kumaoni group dances such as the jhora.
  • Threats: weathering, soot, graffiti and careless tourism; many Gwarkha figures have reportedly been defaced.

Uttarakhand's rock art extends India's prehistoric art map from the Vindhyas to the Himalaya; scientific dating, digital recording and community-led protection are urgently needed.
free.upa-2023-an2-1e:
Religious pluralismSocial solidarityShared sacred spacesConstitutional secularism

Religious pluralism is more than many faiths side by side: it is coexistence with mutual recognition and exchange. Social solidarity is the bond that holds a society together; Émile Durkheim (The Elementary Forms of Religious Life, 1912) saw religion as its main source. India (Hindus 79.8%, Muslims 14.2%, Christians 2.3%, Sikhs 1.7%, Buddhists 0.7%, Jains 0.4%; Census 2011) tests whether many faiths can sustain one society.

1. How pluralism builds solidarity

  • Shared sacred spaces: Hindus and Muslims visit the dargah of Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and the Nagore dargah; Sabarimala pilgrims stop at the Vavar mosque at Erumeli; the Velankanni church draws people of all faiths.
  • Syncretic traditions: Bhakti and Sufi saints such as Kabir and Guru Nanak, and cults such as Satya Pir in Bengal, blend idioms; the Meos of Mewat long combined Hindu and Muslim customs (Shail Mayaram, Resisting Regimes, 1997).
  • Economic interdependence: in Varanasi's silk industry Muslim weavers and Hindu traders depend on each other, a case of Durkheim's organic solidarity based on interdependence.
  • Civic networks: Ashutosh Varshney (Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life, 2002) showed that associations of traders, unions and parties cutting across communities kept Calicut peaceful, while Aligarh, lacking them, was riot-prone.

2. Beyond Durkheim

  • Civic glue: where no single religion unites all, shared constitutional values act as a "civil religion" (Robert Bellah, 1967); Articles 25–28 guarantee religious freedom, Article 51A(e) asks citizens to promote harmony, and S.R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.
  • Indian secularism means equal respect for all faiths and principled distance from each, not mere separation of religion and state.

3. Strains

  • Communal violence and polarisation: Paul Brass (2003) described an "institutionalized riot system" that local leaders activate for political gain.
  • Segregation: residential ghettoisation and online hate reduce everyday contact.
  • Conversion and identity debates turn religion into a political boundary.

Pluralism yields solidarity only when everyday interaction, civic association and equal citizenship are nurtured; India's composite culture shows that it is possible, but it must be renewed in each generation.
free.upa-2023-an2-2a:
G.S. GhuryeBackward HindusAssimilationTribe–caste continuum

G.S. Ghurye (1893–1983), who headed the Department of Sociology at Bombay University and founded the Indian Sociological Society (1951), approached tribes through Indology, census data and history. In The Aborigines "So-called" and Their Future (1943; retitled The Scheduled Tribes in later editions) he argued that most tribes were "backward Hindus", imperfectly integrated sections of Hindu society, and pleaded for assimilation against Verrier Elwin's protective approach.

1. Ghurye's argument

  • No separate "aboriginal" category: he criticised British censuses for listing "animism" or "tribal religion" apart from Hinduism, a line drawn by administrators rather than by social reality.
  • A difference of degree: tribes worshipped Hindu deities, kept Hindu festivals, used Hinduised priests and borrowed caste norms, as census and gazetteer evidence showed.
  • Historical absorption: over centuries some tribal chiefs became Rajputs while many groups entered caste society, so tribes belonged to one civilisation.
  • Policy: he opposed the Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas of the Government of India Act, 1935 and Elwin's "national park" proposal, and sought education, economic uplift and protection from moneylenders and landlords.

2. His contributions

  • Documentation: he assembled census, gazetteer and ethnographic evidence of tribal–Hindu interaction, an early systematic treatment of the question.
  • Exploitation highlighted: he linked tribal distress to land alienation and debt, problems later commissions confirmed.
  • Wider legacy: Caste and Race in India (1932) and students such as M.N. Srinivas, Irawati Karve and A.R. Desai shaped Indian sociology and anthropology.

3. Critical assessment

  • Elwin's opposing view: in The Loss of Nerve (1941) Elwin argued that Hinduisation brought caste disabilities and the loss of dormitories, dances and women's freedom.
  • Absorption as subordination: N.K. Bose (Hindu Method of Tribal Absorption, 1941) showed groups such as the Juang entering Hindu society mainly at its lower rungs.
  • Continuum, not identity: F.G. Bailey (Tribe, Caste and Nation, 1960) and Surajit Sinha ("Tribe-caste and tribe-peasant continua in Central India", 1965) placed tribe and caste at two ends of a continuum; some groups moved towards caste, others did not.
  • Regional exceptions: most tribes of the North-East, such as the Nagas, Mizos and Khasis, are Christian or follow indigenous faiths (Donyi-Polo, Seng Khasi).
  • Self-identity and law: the Jharkhand Assembly's 2020 resolution for a Sarna religion code, and the Hindu Marriage Act (1955) and Hindu Succession Act (1956), which apply to STs only if the Centre notifies, recognise distinct custom; Virginius Xaxa (1999) argued that tribes should be defined by their own societies, not by distance from caste Hindus.
  • Overlooked institutions: clan land, bride price and women's relatively higher status do not fit a "backward caste" model.

4. Relevance today

  • The middle path won: the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Article 46, PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) protect distinct ways of life while integrating tribes.
  • A valid insight: Ghurye rightly saw long interaction with Hindu society, as Sanskritisation and the tribe–caste continuum confirm.

Ghurye's thesis was historically informed but assimilationist; anthropology today accepts interaction while respecting tribal self-identification, as the Constitution's integration approach intends.
free.upa-2023-an2-2b:
Harappan civilisationUrban revolutionEarly HarappanMehrgarh

The Harappan or Indus civilisation, whose mature urban phase lasted c. 2600–1900 BCE, was identified at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921) and Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji, 1922). It marks South Asia's first urban revolution, V. Gordon Childe's term (Man Makes Himself, 1936; ten criteria listed in 1950) for the rise of cities, writing and specialised crafts. The claim fits its scale and urbanism, not the idea of a first settlement or of the world's first civilisation.

1. Why it was a "big civilisation"

  • Extent: over a thousand mature-phase sites, from Sutkagen-dor on the Makran coast to Alamgirpur in western Uttar Pradesh and from Manda (Jammu) to Daimabad (Maharashtra), with an outpost at Shortugai in Afghanistan; no Bronze Age civilisation covered more ground.
  • Cities: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira had planned streets, citadels, covered drains, standard bricks (1:2:4) and binary-decimal weights.
  • Childe's urban traits: script and seals, full-time crafts (beads, shell, metal), storehouses and long-distance trade with Mesopotamia, whose texts call the region Meluhha.

2. Not the first settlement: a long local build-up

  • Neolithic roots: at Mehrgarh (Balochistan), excavated by J.-F. Jarrige from 1974, people grew barley and wheat and herded cattle, sheep and goats in mud-brick villages from about 7000 BCE.
  • Early Harappan phase (c. 3300–2600 BCE): Kot Diji, Amri, Rehman Dheri, Kalibangan I and the Ravi phase at Harappa already show walled settlements, planned layouts and early signs; M. Rafique Mughal's concept of the "Early Harappan" established this continuity.
  • Endogenous origin: this refutes Mortimer Wheeler's view that the idea of city life came from Mesopotamia; the Rakhigarhi genome (Shinde et al., Cell, 2019) shows ancestry from South Asian hunter-gatherers and ancient Iranian-related groups, with no steppe ancestry.

3. Not the world's first civilisation

  • Earlier centres: Sumerian cities such as Uruk, with writing by about 3200 BCE, and a unified Egyptian state (c. 3100 BCE) predate mature Harappa, which was contemporary with Akkad and Old Kingdom Egypt.
  • A different model: no palaces, royal tombs or monumental temples have been identified, and the script is undeciphered, so its political organisation is still debated.
