  • Name and geography: many sites lie on the Ghaggar-Hakra and in Gujarat, so "Harappan" is preferred to "Indus Valley".

The Harappan civilisation was thus South Asia's first urban civilisation and the most extensive of its age, but it grew out of millennia of local village farming and was preceded elsewhere by Mesopotamia and Egypt.
free.upa-2023-an2-2c:
AhimsaAnekantavadaTriratnaShramana tradition

Jainism is a shramana (ascetic) tradition that rejects a creator god and Vedic sacrifice. It traces its teaching through 24 tirthankaras ("ford-makers"), from Rishabhanatha to Parshvanatha (23rd) and Vardhamana Mahavira (24th, 6th–5th century BCE), who attained kevala jnana after twelve years of austerity and nirvana at Pavapuri. Its core values are ahimsa and anekantavada.

1. Basic tenets

  • Jiva and ajiva: the universe is eternal and uncreated, made of countless souls (jiva) and non-living matter (ajiva); every living being, down to plants and minute organisms, has a soul.
  • Karma as matter: passions attract fine karmic particles that bind the soul; liberation comes by stopping their inflow and shedding them through austerity.
  • Triratna: right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together lead to moksha.
  • Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya (non-stealing), aparigraha (non-possession) and brahmacharya, which Mahavira added to Parshvanatha's four; monks keep them fully (mahavratas), lay people partially (anuvratas).
  • Anekantavada and syadvada: reality has many aspects, so every statement holds only "in some respect" (syat); this sevenfold logic encourages tolerance of other views.
  • Two sects: Digambara monks renounce clothing and hold that women must be reborn as men to be liberated; Svetambaras wear white and accept women's liberation; the Svetambara canon was written down at Valabhi (5th century CE).

2. Impact on Indian society

  • Ethics and diet: strict non-violence spread vegetarianism, especially in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Karnataka, and inspired pinjrapoles (animal shelters); Gandhi's ahimsa and fasting owed much to his Jain mentor Shrimad Rajchandra.
  • Economy: since farming harms life, lay Jains turned to trade and banking; James Laidlaw (Riches and Renunciation, 1995) shows Jaipur's Jain merchants combining wealth with ascetic ideals, echoing Max Weber's The Religion of India.
  • Language and literature: the canon is in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit; Jain poets enriched Kannada (Pampa, Ponna, Ranna) and Tamil (Jivaka Chintamani); Prakrit was declared a classical language in 2024.
  • Art and architecture: Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves (Odisha), the Jain caves of Ellora, the Gommateshwara monolith at Shravanabelagola (c. 983 CE), Dilwara (Mount Abu), Ranakpur and the temple hill of Palitana; illustrated Kalpasutra manuscripts.
  • Social structure: Jainism rejected ritual hierarchy and admitted women as nuns in large numbers, yet its laity is organised in endogamous jatis such as the Oswals and Porwals.
  • Today: Jains (about 45 lakh, Census 2011) were notified as a national minority in 2014; in 2015 the Supreme Court stayed a Rajasthan High Court ruling that had treated sallekhana (ritual fasting unto death) as an offence.

Jainism's non-violence, pluralist logic and ethic of restraint left a lasting mark on India's diet, trade, art and politics, and speak directly to sustainable living today.
free.upa-2023-an2-3a:
SanskritisationM.N. SrinivasPositional changeReference group

Sanskritisation was introduced by M.N. Srinivas in his 1952 study Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India; he preferred it to the narrower "Brahminisation". In Social Change in Modern India (1966) he defined it: "Sanskritization is the process by which a 'low' Hindu caste, or tribal or other group, changes its customs, ritual, ideology, and way of life in the direction of a high, and frequently, 'twice-born' caste." Rooted in the caste order, it is called culture-bound.

1. The concept

  • Process: a group that has gained wealth or power adopts vegetarianism, teetotalism, the sacred thread, Sanskritic deities and restrictions on widows, then claims a higher varna; acceptance may take a generation or two.
  • Several models: besides the Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and local dominant castes serve as models; Surajit Sinha (1962) described the "Rajputisation" of the Bhumij.
  • Cases: the Nadars of Tamil Nadu (Robert Hardgrave, 1969), the Jatavs of Agra (Owen Lynch, 1969) and the Tana Bhagats among the Oraons.

2. Why it is culture-bound

  • Hindu referent: the model is the Sanskritic great tradition, so the concept presumes caste, purity and pollution and a Brahmanical scale of values.
  • Orthogenetic change: Yogendra Singh (Modernization of Indian Tradition, 1973) classed it as change from within tradition, unlike Westernisation, which comes from outside.
  • Ambiguous term: J.F. Staal (1963) noted that "Sanskritic" mixes language, text and practice, and much that groups adopted was not Sanskritic at all.

3. Strengths as a framework

  • Dynamic view of caste: it replaced the book-view of a frozen hierarchy with field evidence of mobility.
  • Links culture with power: Srinivas noted that economic or political gain usually comes first; F.G. Bailey's Boad Distillers of Bisipara (1957) grew rich from liquor, bought land and then sought ritual rank.
  • Generalisable core: read as status emulation or reference-group behaviour (Merton), it travels; "Ashrafisation" among Indian Muslims, as when Julaha weavers took the name Ansari, and N.K. Bose's Hindu absorption of tribes are parallels.
  • Bridges levels: with McKim Marriott's Kishan Garhi study (1955), it links village little traditions with the great tradition.

4. Limitations

  • Positional, not structural: Srinivas himself admitted that castes change places while the hierarchy remains.
  • Upward, Brahmanical bias: it misses de-Sanskritisation, as in the Self-Respect Movement (1925), Dalit conversion to Buddhism (1956) and the Sarna revival among tribes.
  • Culture over class: Harold Gould (1961) saw its driving force less in imitation than in lower castes' challenge to their deprivation; the concept underplays land, labour and the state.
  • Weak prediction: it cannot say which groups will Sanskritise, and Marriott found Sanskritic rites added beside local ones, not replacing them.
  • Gender cost: dowry, seclusion and bans on widow remarriage tightened control over women.
  • Waning relevance: mobility now runs through education, reservations and votes (Rajni Kothari, Caste in Indian Politics, 1970), and dominant castes even seek backward status.

Sanskritisation is culture-bound in content but general in logic; combined with Westernisation, dominant caste and modernisation, it remains a useful though partial framework for social change in India.
free.upa-2023-an2-3b:
MesolithicSedentismBroad-spectrum economyMicroliths

The Mesolithic, the Middle Stone Age marked by microliths (tiny blades hafted into composite tools), flourished in India in the early Holocene, after about 10,000 years ago. Sedentism means living at one place for most or all of the year. A warmer, wetter climate encouraged a broad-spectrum economy (Kent Flannery, 1969) of hunting, fishing and plant collecting, which allowed longer stays and, in some regions, the first settled camps.

1. Evidence that the Mesolithic took the first step

  • Lake-side camps of the Ganga plain: at Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama (Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh), excavated by Allahabad University, oxbow lakes gave fish, turtles and game for much of the year; hut floors, post-holes, hearths, grinding stones and dozens of burials, some double, inside the camps show attachment to place.
  • Belan valley: at Chopani Mando (Prayagraj), excavated by G.R. Sharma, the late phase has clusters of round huts, handmade pottery and wild rice, leading on to the Neolithic villages of Koldihwa and Mahagara.
  • Rajasthan and central India: Bagor (Bhilwara), excavated by V.N. Misra, has stone-paved floors and bones of domestic sheep and goat in its first phase; Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh), excavated by R.V. Joshi, yielded bones claimed as domestic.
  • Rock shelters and burials: repeated occupation at Bhimbetka, with paintings of family and group life, and burials at Lekhahia (Mirzapur) and Langhnaj (Gujarat, H.D. Sankalia) show return to familiar places.

2. Parallels elsewhere

  • Natufian of the Levant (c. 12,500–9,500 BCE): round stone-based houses at Ain Mallaha, sickles, mortars and storage long before farming.
  • Jomon of Japan: foragers who made pottery and lived in long-lasting villages.
  • The lesson: sedentism can precede agriculture, as Lewis Binford's "post-Pleistocene adaptations" (1968) argued.

3. Why it was only a first step

  • Partial, seasonal settlement: most sites were seasonal or semi-permanent camps, and mobility remained central for most groups.
  • Contested claims: the domestic status of the Adamgarh and Bagor animals and some very early Ganga-plain dates are debated.
  • Uneven change: hunter-gatherers persisted in the forests beside farmers for millennia, trading with them.
  • Full sedentism came with farming: Mehrgarh (c. 7000 BCE) and later Neolithic villages had permanent houses, granaries and domesticated crops.

The Mesolithic was a threshold rather than a revolution: by reducing mobility, burying the dead at camps and experimenting with plants and animals, it prepared the ground for the Neolithic village.
free.upa-2023-an2-3c:
Customary self-governancePESA 1996Gram sabhaElite capture

Tribal societies have long governed themselves through customary institutions: Santhal manjhi–pargana councils, the manki–munda system of the Mundas and Hos, the Oraon parha, the Khasi dorbar shnong and Naga village councils. Since 1950 these have been overlaid by modern democratic institutions: adult franchise, reserved seats (Articles 330 and 332), Panchayati Raj, the PESA Act (1996), Sixth Schedule councils and Forest Rights Act (2006) gram sabhas.

1. Positive impacts

  • Voice and representation: reserved seats have produced tribal legislators, ministers and Chief Ministers, and in 2022 Droupadi Murmu, a Santhal, became India's first tribal President; elections have also raised a young, educated leadership aware of constitutional rights.
  • Gram sabha as self-rule: Mendha-Lekha, a Gond village in Gadchiroli (Maharashtra), decides by consensus in its gram sabha and was among the first to win community forest rights (2009) and the right to sell its bamboo (2011).
  • Consent over resources: in 2013, after a Supreme Court order, twelve Dongria Kondh gram sabhas in Niyamgiri (Odisha) rejected bauxite mining.
  • Women in office: reservation in panchayats has brought tribal women into public roles.

2. Negative and contradictory impacts

  • Dual authority: where statutory panchayats ignore customary bodies, the pahan and parha of the Oraons lose authority and are confined to marriage and family disputes.
  • Elite capture: educated, better-off families corner reserved posts and benefits, and party politics splits clans; F.G. Bailey (Politics and Social Change: Orissa in 1959, 1963) showed villagers, including those of the Kond hills, reaching the state through brokers who gained at others' expense.
  • Gender within custom: Khasi dorbars traditionally excluded women despite matriliny, and Naga bodies opposed 33% reservation for women in urban local bodies, leading to violence in 2017; the elections were finally held with the quota in 2024.
  • Law versus practice: several States delayed or diluted PESA rules; in the Pathalgadi movement (Khunti, Jharkhand, 2017–18), Munda villages carved PESA provisions on stone slabs and faced sedition cases, later withdrawn.

3. Way forward

  • Harmonise, not replace: as the Bhuria Committee (1995) and B.D. Sharma, a former Commissioner for SCs and STs, urged, customary councils should work through the gram sabha with clear roles.
  • Real devolution: funds, functions and staff for gram sabhas, and accountable, gender-inclusive district councils.

Democracy has given tribes voice, rights and new leaders, but also stratification and friction with custom; it succeeds where elected bodies are rooted in tribal traditions of collective decision-making.
free.upa-2023-an2-4a:
PVTGsDhebar CommissionPM-JANMANHabitat rights

Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs) are the most disadvantaged among the Scheduled Tribes. The Dhebar Commission (1960–61) first noted deep inequality among tribes; 52 such groups were identified in 1975 and 23 more in 1993, making 75 PVTGs in 18 States and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Called "Primitive Tribal Groups" until 2006, they are identified by pre-agricultural technology, very low literacy, economic backwardness and a stagnant or declining population.

1. Problems faced by PVTGs

  • Fragile demography and health: the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa, Sentinelese and Shompen number from a few dozen to a few hundred; contact has brought epidemics such as measles among the Jarawa, and malnutrition and tuberculosis affect the Saharia of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
  • Insecure livelihoods: foraging and shifting cultivation (Birhor, Chenchu, Juang, Bondo) clash with forest and wildlife laws; Baiga families in Kanha and Chenchus in the Nagarjunasagar–Srisailam tiger reserve face pressure to relocate.
  • Displacement and land loss: mining (Dongria Kondh of Niyamgiri) and strategic projects such as the Great Nicobar plan (Shompen) threaten habitats; Katkari families of Maharashtra migrate to brick kilns and fall into debt bondage.
  • Exclusion from services: scattered, roadless hamlets lack schools, health centres and documents such as Aadhaar, ration cards and caste certificates; teaching is rarely in their languages.
  • Cultural vulnerability: "human safaris" along the Andaman Trunk Road, forced sedentarisation and stigma erode identity and dignity.

2. Policy so far

  • Earlier measures: micro-projects from the Fifth Plan, a Central Sector scheme (from 1998–99) funding States' Conservation-cum-Development plans, and habitat rights under Section 3(1)(e) of the Forest Rights Act, first granted to the Baiga of Madhya Pradesh (2015) and since to a few others, such as the Bharia, Kamar and eight Odisha PVTGs.
  • PM-JANMAN: launched on 15 November 2023 with ₹24,104 crore, it brings 11 interventions of nine ministries (housing, roads, piped water, mobile medical units, hostels, anganwadis, Van Dhan centres) to PVTG habitations.

3. Challenges in designing special programmes

  • Heterogeneity: the 75 groups range from isolated foragers (Sentinelese) to pastoralists (Toda) and settled cultivators; a uniform package of pucca houses and roads does not suit mobile groups such as the Birhor.
  • Weak data: many PVTGs are sections of larger tribes (Dongria Kondh, Hill Kharia), so Census tables do not show them separately; the list has stayed at 75 since 1993, names overlap (Birhor and Mankidia in Odisha), and identification varies between neighbouring States.
  • Isolation versus integration: the Andaman administration's Jarawa (2004) and Shompen (2015) policies show the difficulty of protecting autonomy while providing health care.
  • Top-down delivery: time-bound targets and many ministries hamper convergence, and PVTGs rarely shape plans, though PESA and FRA require gram sabha consent.
  • Competing priorities: conservation, mining and strategic projects often override PVTG needs.

4. Way forward

  • Group-specific plans made with community consent and anthropological input, mother-tongue schooling, full habitat rights, targeted health care (nutrition, sickle-cell disease) and periodic review of the list.

PVTG policy must follow Nehru's Tribal Panchsheel, development "along the lines of their own genius", with consent and dignity rather than uniform schemes.
free.upa-2023-an2-4b:
Racial classificationAnthropometryNasal and cephalic indexAustraloid substratum

Early physical anthropology tried to sort India's people into racial types. H.H. Risley, Census Commissioner for 1901, did so through anthropometry in The People of India (1908), tying race to caste. The physical anthropologist S.S. Sarkar proposed a different scheme in The Aboriginal Races of India (1954), giving the Australoid tribes the place of India's oldest population.

1. Risley's approach

  • Data and method: measurements of head, nose and stature collected from the late 1880s, chiefly the nasal index and cephalic index, read against caste and region.
  • Seven types: Turko-Iranian, Indo-Aryan, Scytho-Dravidian, Aryo-Dravidian, Mongolo-Dravidian, Mongoloid and Dravidian; he treated the Dravidian, Indo-Aryan and Mongoloid as primary stocks and most others as crosses.
  • Race explains caste: he held that a caste's rank fell as its nasal index rose, and traced caste to Aryan conquerors' contact with darker natives; his 1901 Census ranking of castes set off petitions for higher status.

2. Sarkar's approach

  • Method: the 1954 scheme rests mainly on the cephalic index; his team's later work added ABO blood groups and dermatoglyphics.
  • Six elements: Australoid, Indo-Aryan, Irano-Scythian, Mundari-speaking, Far Eastern and Mongolian.
  • Key claims: Australoids (many tribes of central and southern India) form the earliest substratum; the Mundari-speakers of Chota Nagpur are a distinct group with eastern links; and his team's study of the Kadar (1959) found no Negrito element, unlike B.S. Guha's scheme (1935).

3. Critical comparison

  • Common ground: both were typological, treated averages as fixed types and mixed racial with linguistic labels.
  • Risley's weaknesses: uneven samples, a racial theory of caste and a colonial purpose; Franz Boas (1912) showed that head form changes within a generation in a new environment, undermining the cephalic index, and Nicholas Dirks (Castes of Mind, 2001) showed how such census work hardened caste.
  • Sarkar's advance: his team later added blood-group and dermatoglyphic evidence, and he recognised the tribal substratum and the separate identity of Munda-speakers, a point echoed by later genetic work linking the paternal lineages of Austroasiatic speakers to Southeast Asia.
  • Sarkar's limits: cephalic index stayed central, the "Far Eastern" element was vague, and race remained the unit of analysis.

4. Present position

  • Clines, not races: Richard Lewontin (1972) found that most human genetic variation lies within populations, and Reich and colleagues (Nature, 2009) described Indian groups as mixtures of Ancestral North Indian and Ancestral South Indian components, kept distinct by long endogamy rather than by race.

Risley's scheme is now of historical interest, while Sarkar's recognition of the tribal substratum and later use of blood groups pointed towards population genetics; both remind us that classifying people must never imply a racial hierarchy.
free.upa-2023-an2-4c:
Caste mobilityIndological viewEmpirical viewPositional change

Caste mobility is the movement of a caste or sub-caste, usually as a group, up or down the local hierarchy. The Indological view, drawn from texts (Dumont, Prabhu), tended to see caste as a fixed order; the empirical view, drawn from fieldwork and census data (Srinivas, Bailey, Béteille), found movement everywhere. Srinivas held that mobility was always possible, especially in the middle ranks.

1. Indological and historical evidence: mobility is ancient

  • Fluid varna in early texts: in the Chandogya Upanishad, Satyakama Jabala, whose father was unknown, was accepted as a student for his truthfulness; Vishvamitra rose from Kshatriya to Brahmarshi.
  • Categories of change: the Dharmashastras discuss mixed castes (anuloma and pratiloma), vratyas and occupations allowed in distress (apaddharma), all implying shifts in rank.
  • Power made Kshatriyas: many ruling houses were of non-Kshatriya origin, from the Nandas to early medieval Rajput clans, whose fire-pit (agnikula) myth absorbed new groups; K.M. Panikkar and Surajit Sinha (1962) saw Kshatriya status as open to those who held power.
  • Sects and devotion: Basava's Virashaiva movement (12th century) and saints such as Kabir and Ravidas created identities that bypassed Brahmanical rank.

2. Empirical evidence: colonial and modern

  • Census as arena: Risley's 1901 ranking spurred caste associations to petition for Kshatriya or Vaishya status, as the Kayasthas and Kurmis did.
  • Sanskritisation: the Coorgs (Srinivas, 1952), the Bhumij (Sinha), the Nadars (Mahajana Sangam, 1910) and the Ezhavas (SNDP Yogam, 1903) rose through reform and emulation.
  • Economic routes: F.G. Bailey (Caste and the Economic Frontier, 1957) showed Bisipara's distillers buying land and seeking rank; railways, mills and the army opened new jobs.
  • After 1947: reservations, land reform and electoral politics lifted backward castes, as in the Yadav movement studied by M.S.A. Rao, and created a Dalit middle class; Mahars turned to Buddhism (1956), and powerful castes such as Jats, Marathas and Patidars now seek backward status.

3. What is recent

  • New channels: secular routes (education, jobs, votes) have overtaken ritual ones, and mobility is increasingly individual and class-based.
  • Limits remain: endogamy, honour-related violence and attacks on assertive Dalits show that mobility is often positional rather than structural.

Caste mobility is not a recent phenomenon; it is as old as caste itself, but democracy and the market have changed its speed, scale and means.
free.upa-2023-an2-5a:
Fifth ScheduleArticle 244(1)Tribes Advisory CouncilPESA 1996

Scheduled Areas are tribal tracts declared by the President under the Fifth Schedule, read with Article 244(1), so that the Scheduled Tribes living there enjoy special protection of their land, customs and self-rule. They cover parts of ten States: the two Telugu States, Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh. Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram come under the Sixth Schedule instead.

1. How an area is declared

  • Presidential order (Para 6): the President declares, alters or rescinds a Scheduled Area after consulting the Governor; such orders have been issued since 1950.
  • Working criteria: the Constitution sets no test, but in practice the area should have a tribal majority, be compact and of reasonable size, form a viable unit (district, block or taluk) and be markedly more backward than its neighbours.

2. A special regime of governance

  • Governor's power (Para 5): the Governor may bar or modify the application of any Act to the area and make regulations to restrict transfer of tribal land and control money-lending. The Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation, 1959 (tightened in 1970) protects Agency tracts such as Bhadrachalam and Paderu.
  • Tribes Advisory Council (Para 4): up to 20 members, about three-fourths of them ST legislators, advise on tribal welfare; Tamil Nadu and West Bengal have TACs on Presidential direction though they have no Scheduled Areas.
  • Union oversight (Para 3): the Governor reports annually to the President, and the Union may issue directions.

3. Extensions, judgments and concerns

  • PESA 1996: on the Bhuria Committee's advice, panchayats were extended to these areas, with gram sabhas empowered to protect customs, community resources and minor forest produce and to be consulted on land acquisition.
  • Courts: Samatha (1997) voided leases of tribal land to private mining firms, and in the Niyamgiri case (2013) Dongria Kondh gram sabhas were allowed to decide on bauxite mining, which they rejected; but Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020) struck down 100% ST reservation of teacher posts in these areas.
  • Gaps: TACs meet irregularly, Governors' reports are routine, PESA rules came late in several States, and many tribal-majority villages lie outside any Scheduled Area.

Scheduled Areas give territorial form to protective discrimination. Their promise of self-rule will be met only when Governors use Para 5 actively, TACs work in earnest and gram sabhas gain real control over land and resources.
free.upa-2023-an2-5b:
RamapithecusSivapithecusOrangutan lineageMolecular clock

Miocene ape jaws from the Siwalik Hills once seemed to place the beginnings of the human line in South Asia. Sivapithecus was named by Guy Pilgrim (1910) and Ramapithecus brevirostris by G. Edward Lewis (1934), both from Siwalik fossils. The debate was whether Ramapithecus was the earliest hominid or merely an ape; today it is treated as part of Sivapithecus, an ape close to the orangutan lineage.

1. The hominid claim (1960s–1970s)

  • Simons and Pilbeam: Elwyn Simons (from 1961) and David Pilbeam argued that Ramapithecus, about 14–12 million years old, was the first member of the human line: it had small canines, thick molar enamel, a short face and, as reconstructed, a curved, human-like tooth row.
  • African parallel: Louis Leakey's Kenyapithecus from Fort Ternan, Kenya (about 14 mya), was seen as a similar form, implying an early and widespread hominid stage.
  • Ecological reading: heavy jaws and thick enamel suggested hard foods in open woodland, a step towards a ground-living hominid.

2. Why the claim collapsed

  • Molecular clock: Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson (1967) used protein differences to date the split of humans from African apes to about 5 mya, far too late for a 12-million-year-old hominid.
  • Fuller jaws: complete mandibles found in the mid-1970s, especially on the Potwar Plateau of Pakistan, showed an ape-like tooth row, not the curved arcade of the old reconstruction.
  • The GSP 15000 face: Pilbeam (1982) described a Sivapithecus face with orangutan features, such as a narrow space between the eyes, tall orbits and a concave profile.
  • Sexual dimorphism: the small "Ramapithecus" specimens fitted the females of a strongly dimorphic ape. Peter Andrews and John Cronin (1982) placed the whole group near the orangutan, and Ramapithecus was absorbed into Sivapithecus.

3. Present position

  • Species and dates: Sivapithecus indicus (about 12.5–10.5 mya), S. parvada (about 10 mya) and S. sivalensis (about 9.5–8.5 mya) are generally recognised.
  • The "Sivapithecus dilemma": arm bones described by Pilbeam and colleagues (1990) suit a generalised tree-climbing ape rather than an orangutan-like suspensory climber, so face and limbs send conflicting signals.
  • Meaning for India: no hominin is known from the Neogene Siwaliks; their value lies in recording ape evolution in Asia.

The debate is a classic lesson in palaeoanthropological method: a partial jaw, a hopeful reconstruction and an attractive theory gave way before fuller fossils and molecular data. Ramapithecus now stands as an ape, not a human ancestor.
free.upa-2023-an2-5c:
Little republicsCharles Metcalfe (1830)Myth of self-sufficiencyVillage studies

The description of Indian villages as "little republics" comes from colonial administrators, above all Charles Metcalfe, whose minute of 1830 called them "little republics, having nearly everything they can want within themselves". The image was developed by Henry Maine and Karl Marx and idealised by Gandhi, but village studies by anthropologists since the 1950s have shown it to be only a partial truth.

1. The idea and its sources

  • Metcalfe (1830): villages were self-governing, almost independent of outside relations and outlived the fall of dynasties: "They seem to last where nothing else lasts."
  • Henry Maine, Village-Communities in the East and West (1871): treated the Indian village as a survival of an ancient form of joint landholding, comparable to early European communities.
  • Karl Marx (1853): saw the self-sufficient village, uniting farming and handicraft, as the unchanging base of "Oriental despotism".
  • Gandhi: made the village the unit of gram swaraj, echoed in Article 40.

2. The anthropological critique

  • Not self-sufficient: M.N. Srinivas and A.M. Shah (1960) called self-sufficiency a myth, since villages depended on weekly markets, specialist castes living elsewhere, towns, pilgrim centres and the revenue demands of the state.
  • Not isolated: marriage ties, caste councils spanning many villages and religious networks linked each village to its region. McKim Marriott's study of Kishan Garhi (1955) showed constant exchange between little and great traditions, and S.C. Dube's Indian Village (1955) traced Shamirpet's ties with nearby Hyderabad.
  • Not a republic of equals: power lay with a landowning dominant caste, as in Srinivas's Rampura, and the jajmani system bound service castes to patrons (W.H. Wiser, 1936). B.R. Ambedkar asked in the Constituent Assembly (1948), "What is the village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism?"
  • A colonial construction: Louis Dumont (1966) traced how the "village community" idea passed from Munro to Maine, serving administrative needs more than describing reality.

3. What remains valid

  • Vertical unity: Srinivas noted that villagers of all castes shared a sense of belonging to their village, with common deities, festivals and boundaries; headmen, caste panchayats and common lands gave real, if unequal, self-management.
  • Democratic revival: the 73rd Amendment (1992) and PESA (1996) seek to rebuild the village as a self-governing unit, now on the basis of equal citizenship.

The village was neither a little republic nor a mere fragment of the State, but a relatively integrated yet open unit of a wider civilisation; decentralisation must build on its solidarity while dismantling its hierarchy.
free.upa-2023-an2-5d:
Dravidian familyRobert Caldwell (1856)Four subgroupsTribal Dravidian languages

Dravidian is India's second-largest language family. Census 2011 grouped 17 Dravidian languages (each with 10,000 or more speakers) spoken by about 23.8 crore people, or 19.64% of the population. F.W. Ellis showed in 1816 that Tamil, Telugu and Kannada were related, and Robert Caldwell's Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages (1856) established the name. Bhadriraju Krishnamurti's The Dravidian Languages (2003) gives the standard subgrouping.

1. Subgroups

  • Basis: languages are grouped by sound changes and grammatical forms they share after splitting from Proto-Dravidian, not by geography.
  • Four branches: South (South Dravidian I), South-Central (South Dravidian II), Central and North; the first two are often treated as one southern branch.
  • Literary and tribal languages: the four literary languages are in the Eighth Schedule and have classical status (Tamil 2004, Telugu and Kannada 2008, Malayalam 2013); Telugu, with about 8.1 crore speakers in 2011, is the largest. Most of the remaining languages are spoken by tribal communities.

2. Common features

  • Agglutinative structure: words are built by adding suffixes one after another, the verb comes at the end (subject–object–verb) and postpositions replace prepositions.
  • Retroflex sounds: consonants such as ṭ, ḍ and ṇ, which also spread into Indo-Aryan languages through long contact.
  • Gender and person: nouns are classed as rational (human) or non-rational, and many languages separate an inclusive "we" (with the listener) from an exclusive "we", as in Tamil nām and nāṅkaḷ.

3. Anthropological significance

  • Not only southern: Dravidian is the speech of large tribal peoples of central and eastern India. Gondi had about 30 lakh speakers in Census 2011 but is outside the Eighth Schedule, and Kurukh ties the Oraons to this family though their neighbours speak Munda languages.
  • The Brahui puzzle: Brahui, spoken in Pakistan's Balochistan far from the Dravidian core, keeps alive the hypothesis that Dravidian was once spoken further north-west, perhaps in the Harappan region; this remains unproven.
  • Language is not race: the colonial use of "Dravidian" as a racial type (H.H. Risley's The People of India, 1908) has been abandoned; genetic studies show that Indian groups mix ancestral northern and southern strands in different proportions.
  • Endangerment: small languages such as Toda, Kota and Kolami are shifting towards dominant regional languages.

The Dravidian family reveals the linguistic depth of Indian civilisation and links the literate south with the tribal centre. Mother-tongue education in Gondi, Kui and Kurukh would help these languages survive.
free.upa-2023-an2-5e:
KarmaSamsaraTheodicyMoksha

In Hindu thought karma is the moral law by which every deliberate act yields consequences, and samsara (the cycle of rebirth) is the process by which the self carries these consequences into new lives until it attains moksha. First stated clearly in the early Upanishads (Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya), the doctrine became, with dharma and varnashrama, a pillar of the traditional Indian social system.

1. The doctrine

  • Kinds of karma: Vedanta distinguishes accumulated karma (sanchita), the portion working itself out in this life (prarabdha) and the karma now being made (kriyamana or agami).
  • Birth as reward or penalty: the Chandogya Upanishad says that those of good conduct are born from a Brahmin, Kshatriya or Vaishya womb and those of foul conduct as a dog, a pig or a Chandala, tying caste rank to past deeds.
  • Duty without attachment: the Bhagavad Gita teaches nishkama karma, action without craving its fruits, as a path to release.
  • Other traditions: Buddhism explains rebirth without a permanent soul, and Jainism treats karma as subtle matter clinging to the soul.

2. Sociological significance

  • A theodicy: Max Weber (The Religion of India, 1916–17) called the union of karma and caste "the most consistent theodicy ever produced by history": it explains unequal fortune and promises a better birth to those who keep their caste duty, discouraging revolt.
  • Support for varnashrama: svadharma, the purusharthas and the three debts (rinas) turn karma into rules for each stage of life, and fear of a lower birth reinforces caste duty.

3. Anthropological evidence and critique

  • Everyday belief: studies in Charles Keyes and E. Valentine Daniel's Karma: An Anthropological Inquiry (1983), and Ursula Sharma's work in a Himachal Pradesh village (1973), show that people invoke karma as one explanation of misfortune among several, alongside deities, spirits, sorcery and planets.
  • Comparison: Gananath Obeyesekere's Imagining Karma (2002) shows that rebirth beliefs exist in many small-scale societies, such as the Trobriand belief, recorded by Malinowski, that spirits of the dead return as babies; Indic religions made rebirth depend on ethical conduct.
  • Challenge and reinterpretation: Phule and Ambedkar rejected karma as a justification for untouchability, while Milton Singer (When a Great Tradition Modernizes, 1972) found Madras industrialists reinterpreting karma and the Gita to support enterprise, questioning Weber's view that the doctrine blocks change.

Karma and rebirth gave Indian society a moral explanation of inequality and a path to liberation. Their stress on individual responsibility endures, but their use to justify birth-based hierarchy has been rejected by the Constitution.
free.upa-2023-an2-6a:
Annihilation of Caste (1936)Protective discriminationEndogamyCaste as identity

In Annihilation of Caste (1936), his undelivered address for the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal of Lahore, B.R. Ambedkar argued that caste rested on religious sanction and endogamy and could be destroyed only by inter-caste marriage and by rejecting the authority of the shastras. Independent India chose protective discrimination and anti-discrimination law as its main tools. Caste has since weakened as a ritual hierarchy but endures as kinship and political identity.

1. Ambedkar's case for annihilation

  • Division of labourers: caste is "not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers", graded one above another and fixed by birth.
  • A state of mind: because "Caste is a notion, it is a state of the mind", laws alone cannot end it; belief in the sanctity of the shastras must go.
  • Remedy: inter-dining was too weak a step: "The real remedy for breaking Caste is inter-marriage." Gandhi's reply in Harijan (1936) defended varna as a division of duties without high and low, which Ambedkar rejected.

2. Proactive measures of the State

  • Reservation: quotas in jobs, education and legislatures have built a Dalit, Adivasi and OBC middle class and leadership, loosening the tie between caste and occupation.
  • Data: the decision of April 2025 to enumerate all castes in Census 2027, the first full count since 1931, aims at better targeting, not abolition.

3. Evidence that caste is weakening

  • Ritual decline: rules of purity and pollution in eating, dress and public places have weakened with cities, factories and travel; M.N. Srinivas noted that caste lost ritual force even as it gained political strength.
  • Caste–class disjunction: André Béteille's Caste, Class and Power (1965), on Sripuram village in Tanjore, showed land, education and power no longer matching caste rank.
  • Dalit assertion: Dalit parties, writers and entrepreneurs (the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, 2005) challenge the old order.

4. Why annihilation remains distant

  • Endogamy holds: the India Human Development Survey (2011–12) found only about 5% of marriages to be inter-caste and 27% of households admitting some practice of untouchability; "honour" killings punish those who cross the line.
  • From hierarchy to identity: Louis Dumont called this the "substantialisation" of caste; Rajni Kothari's Caste in Indian Politics (1970) and Dipankar Gupta's Interrogating Caste (2000) show castes acting as competing interest groups.
  • The policy paradox: reservation and enumeration need caste categories, so groups mobilise to gain them, as in the quota agitations of Jats, Patidars and Marathas.

5. Future of caste

  • Likely path: caste will weaken further as ritual rank and hereditary occupation but survive in marriage, networks and politics.
  • What could change it: inter-caste marriage, mixed urban neighbourhoods, secular education and the constitutional morality Ambedkar urged, carried by society and not by the State alone.

Annihilation in Ambedkar's sense has not happened; caste is changing form rather than disappearing. State measures have removed its legal sanction and much of its cruelty, but the final step must come from social reform.
free.upa-2023-an2-6b:
EthnicityEthnic identityBoundary maintenanceTribal ethnic conflict

Ethnicity is the social organisation of cultural difference: the way groups that claim common descent, history and culture draw boundaries and relate to others. Fredrik Barth (Ethnic Groups and Boundaries, 1969) argued that it is the boundary, not the cultural content within it, that keeps a group distinct. In India's tribal regions, especially the North-East and Jharkhand, ethnicity has become the main idiom of political mobilisation and, at times, of conflict.

1. Ethnic identity and ethnicity distinguished

  • Ethnic identity is the sense of belonging: a person's or group's self-ascription to a people, carried by name, language, dress, origin myths and attachment to a territory. It can remain private or latent.
  • Ethnicity is the wider process by which such identities are activated and organised in relations with others, often in competition for land, power or recognition. Identity is the raw material; ethnicity is its social and political expression.
  • Theories: Clifford Geertz (1963) stressed "primordial" ties of blood, language and custom; Abner Cohen (1969) and Paul Brass (1991) showed how elites mobilise ethnicity for political ends.

2. Factors responsible for ethnic conflict in tribal areas

  • Land and in-migration: in Tripura, migration from East Bengal reduced the tribal share of the population to 31.8% (Census 2011), feeding insurgency and the riots of 1980; in western Assam, Bodo groups clashed with Bengali-speaking Muslims (2012) and with Adivasi tea-garden communities (1996, 2014).
  • Contested ST status: a Manipur High Court direction (March 2023) on the Meitei demand for ST status triggered violence between Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities from May 2023; in Kandhamal (2008), a dispute over ST status between Kandhas and Pana Christians sharpened communal violence.
  • Overlapping homelands: rival territorial claims caused Naga–Kuki clashes in the 1990s, Karbi–Dimasa violence in 2005 and the flight of Bru (Reang) people from Mizoram to Tripura in 1997.
  • Colonial legacies: the Inner Line (1873), "excluded areas" and missionary schooling created sharp identities and boundaries that cut across peoples.
  • Resources and development: mines, dams and forest laws set Adivasis against "diku" outsiders, a theme of the Jharkhand movement.
  • Recognition and elites: demands for a Sarna religion code, scripts and languages (Santali and Bodo entered the Eighth Schedule in 2003), and leaders and armed groups who gain from polarisation.

3. Anthropological reading

  • Changing movements: K.S. Singh (Tribal Movements in India, 1982–83) traced a shift from agrarian and forest struggles to ethno-political demands for autonomy and statehood.
  • Not primordial: conflicts flare when identity meets scarcity and political opportunity, which is why autonomy arrangements (the Bodoland Territorial Region under the 2020 accord), the Bru resettlement agreement of 2020 and land protection have eased some of them.

Ethnic identity is a source of dignity; it turns into conflict when competition and insecurity politicise it. Secure land rights, fair recognition and shared development are the surest ways to keep plural identities peaceful.
free.upa-2023-an2-6c:
Siwalik GroupNeogene primatesSivapithecusFragmentary record

The Siwalik Group is a thick series of river-laid sediments in the Himalayan foothills, stretching from Jammu and Himachal Pradesh through Pakistan's Potwar Plateau to Nepal. Ranging from the Miocene into the Pleistocene, it holds one of Asia's richest records of Neogene (23–2.6 mya) mammals, including several kinds of primates. The statement is valid, but the primate record is fragmentary and has often been over-read.

1. The Siwalik sequence

  • Divisions: Guy Pilgrim's classic scheme divides the Siwaliks into Lower (Kamlial, Chinji), Middle (Nagri, Dhok Pathan) and Upper (Tatrot, Pinjor) levels; most fossil apes come from the Chinji and Nagri levels of the Middle and Late Miocene.
  • Key localities: Haritalyangar (Himachal Pradesh), Ramnagar (Jammu and Kashmir) and the Pinjor beds near Chandigarh in India, and the Potwar Plateau in Pakistan, where palaeomagnetic dating gives a finely dated sequence.

2. A variety of Neogene primates

  • Breadth: the fauna spans strepsirrhines (adapiforms and lorises) and catarrhines (apes and monkeys) within one long sequence.
  • Dispersal from Africa: Kapi and early Sivapithecus appear at roughly the same time, suggesting that ancestors of lesser and great apes reached Asia along similar routes.
  • Turnover: apes are common in the Middle and Late Miocene, while monkeys dominate the later deposits.

3. Strengths of the evidence

  • Long dated record: few regions let primate change be tied to so continuous and well-dated a sequence.
  • Environmental link: carbon-isotope studies of ancient soils and teeth show forests giving way to C4 grasslands in the late Miocene; most Siwalik apes, Sivapithecus included, disappear by about 8 mya, linking their extinction to climate change.
  • Phylogenetic insight: the GSP 15000 face (Pilbeam, 1982) ties Sivapithecus to the orangutan line, and Kapi pushes the gibbon record back by several million years.

4. Limitations: a critical view

  • Fragmentary fossils: most specimens are isolated teeth and jaws; skulls and limb bones are rare, and the face (1982) and arm bones (1990) of Sivapithecus give conflicting signals about the orangutan link.
  • Taxonomic confusion: Pilgrim, Lewis and others named many genera, such as Bramapithecus, Sugrivapithecus and Ramapithecus, from scraps; Simons and Pilbeam (1965) merged them, and Ramapithecus' standing as a hominid was later rejected.
  • Uneven work: Indian sections are less precisely dated and less systematically collected than the Potwar sequence, and primates are rare beside other mammals.
  • No Neogene hominin: claims of very early human activity, such as cut-marked bones at Masol near Chandigarh (about 2.6 mya, reported in 2016) and stone tools at Riwat in Pakistan (about 2 mya, reported in 1988), lie at or after the Neogene–Pleistocene boundary and remain debated.

The Siwaliks do preserve a remarkable variety of Neogene primates and are central to the story of Asian apes. But the variety is known largely from fragments, and finds such as Kapi show that systematic fieldwork in Indian sections can still change the picture.
free.upa-2023-an2-7a:
IsolationAssimilationIntegration (Panchsheel)Rights-based approach

India's tribal policy has crossed several terrains: colonial control and exclusion, a late-colonial debate between isolation and assimilation, Nehru's integration through the Panchsheel, a rights-based turn from the 1990s and, lately, mission-mode schemes to saturate basic services. Each shift reflected a changing view of tribal people: subjects, wards, citizens and right-holders.

1. Colonial period: revenue, forests and exclusion

  • Opening the tracts: the Permanent Settlement (1793) and new courts brought landlords, moneylenders and traders ("diku") into tribal lands; the Forest Acts of 1865, 1878 and 1927 made forests state property.
  • Revolt and concession: the Kol rising (1831–32) led to the South-West Frontier Agency (1833), the Santhal Hul (1855) to a separate Santhal Parganas district, and Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899–1900) to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908).
  • Exclusion: the Inner Line (1873), the Scheduled Districts Act (1874), "backward tracts" (1919) and "excluded" and "partially excluded areas" (1935) kept tribal regions outside normal administration.

2. The late-colonial debate

  • Verrier Elwin (The Loss of Nerve, 1941) urged protection from exploitation and hasty change; his early proposal of a protected "national park" for groups such as the Baiga was attacked as isolationist.
  • G.S. Ghurye (The Aborigines—"So-called"—and Their Future, 1943) saw tribes as "backward Hindus" who should be assimilated.

3. Integration after Independence (1950–1990)

  • Constitutional frame: Article 46, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, grants under Article 275(1), reserved seats and ST lists under Article 342.
  • Panchsheel (1959): in his foreword to Elwin's A Philosophy for NEFA, Nehru asked for development along the people's own genius, respect for land and forest rights, training of tribal teams, no over-administration, and judging results by human character rather than money spent.
  • Programmes: Multipurpose Tribal Blocks (1954), Tribal Development Blocks after the Elwin (1959) and Dhebar (1960–61) reviews, the Tribal Sub-Plan with Integrated Tribal Development Projects from the Fifth Plan (1974–75), and special help for primitive tribal groups from 1975 (now 75 PVTGs).
  • Contradiction: dams, mines and forest policy displaced lakhs of tribal people, making development a source of alienation.

4. Rights-based turn (1990s–2010s)

  • Self-rule and rights: PESA (1996), on the Bhuria Committee's advice, empowered gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas; the Forest Rights Act (2006) recognised individual and community forest rights and acknowledged a "historical injustice".
  • Institutions and courts: a Ministry of Tribal Affairs (1999), a separate National Commission for STs (Article 338A, 2003), and judgments such as Samatha (1997) and Niyamgiri (2013); the Xaxa Committee (2014) found land loss and weak implementation persisting.

5. Recent phase

  • Saturation schemes: PM-JANMAN (2023, about ₹24,000 crore for PVTG habitations) and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024, ₹79,156 crore for over 63,000 tribal villages); Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November) since 2021.
  • Tension: critics see a return to top-down delivery and a dilution of forest safeguards through the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023.

The terrain has shifted from control to rights, but the tension between national development and tribal autonomy persists. Policy will succeed when gram sabhas, not distant offices, decide how development reaches tribal homelands.
free.upa-2023-an2-7b:
Development-induced displacementGendered impoverishmentCernea's IRR modelSardar Sarovar

Large dams are among the biggest causes of development-induced displacement in India, and Walter Fernandes estimates that tribal people make up about two-fifths of all those displaced since Independence. For tribal women the loss is double: they lose the river, forest and commons on which their work and status rested, while compensation is built around a male "head of household". Michael Cernea's Impoverishment Risks and Reconstruction model (1997) shows how each risk weighs more heavily on women.

1. Loss of the economic base

  • Commons: tribal women gather fuel, fodder, fish, minor forest produce and medicinal plants; submergence and distant resettlement colonies cut them off from these sources of food and cash.
  • Titles in men's names: land and cash compensation go to recorded owners, usually men, so women's customary use rights vanish; Bina Agarwal (A Field of One's Own, 1994) showed how such privatisation erodes women's claims to land.
  • From producer to wage worker: many women become casual labourers or migrants, while cash in men's hands is often lost to debt or drink.

2. Social and cultural effects

  • Broken networks: scattering of villages and clans weakens the kin support on which women rely in childbirth, illness and widowhood.
  • Violence and insecurity: alcohol abuse, domestic violence, harassment near construction camps and trafficking increase in uprooted settings.
  • Sacred loss: submergence of shrines, groves and burial grounds weakens rituals in which women have roles, and women are seldom consulted on rehabilitation.

3. Ethnographic illustrations

  • Sardar Sarovar (Narmada): Amita Baviskar's In the Belly of the River (1995) on the Bhilala of Alirajpur shows how a forest and river economy was destroyed; the Narmada tribunal treated adult sons, but not adult daughters, as separate families for land, a gap criticised by feminist scholars.
  • Kariba Dam (Zambia): Elizabeth Colson's study of the resettled Gwembe Tonga (1971) found relocation straining family and kin ties, and her later work urged a gendered view of the uprooted; Scudder and Colson's four-stage model (1982) shows stress peaking during transition.
  • Koel-Karo (Jharkhand): Munda villagers, women among them, resisted this project for decades; after police firing at Tapkara (2001) killed eight protesters, it was shelved in 2003.
  • Polavaram (Godavari): Koya and Konda Reddi villages of the Godavari Agency tracts face submergence, raising the same concerns about women's access to podu fields and forest produce.

4. Critical assessment and safeguards

  • Not one-sided: some women gain roads, schools and health centres, and women have shown agency in movements such as the Narmada Bachao Andolan; Lyla Mehta and Bina Srinivasan, in a gender review for the World Commission on Dams (report 2000), argued that dam planning overlooks gendered costs.
  • Law: the RFCTLARR Act, 2013 counts widows, divorcees and deserted women as separate families, treats every adult as a separate family, and needs gram sabha consent in Scheduled Areas; the Forest Rights Act, 2006 bars relocation before rights are settled.

Dams turn tribal women from producers into dependants unless resettlement is gender-just. Joint land titles, land-for-land, women's voice in gram sabhas and gender-disaggregated social impact assessment are the minimum safeguards.
free.upa-2023-an2-7c:
Nation buildingApplied anthropologyUnity in diversityPeople of India

Nation building means forging a shared political community out of many peoples while ensuring justice and development for all. Anthropology contributes through its holistic, fieldwork-based knowledge of diversity: it documents India's peoples, advises tribal and social policy, and supports unity in diversity. The Anthropological Survey of India (1945) and applied anthropology after Independence gave this role an institutional base.

1. Understanding diversity and unity

  • People of India project: launched by the Anthropological Survey of India under K.S. Singh in 1985, it profiled 4,635 communities and found extensive sharing of traits across religion, region and language, supporting the idea of a composite culture.
  • Civilisational studies: concepts such as Sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas), little and great traditions (McKim Marriott, 1955) and the sacred complex of Gaya (L.P. Vidyarthi, 1961) showed how local communities are linked to a pan-Indian civilisation.
  • Population genetics: studies such as Reich and colleagues (2009) showed that most Indian groups mix ancestral northern and southern strands, and the GenomeIndia project (2025) released data on about 10,000 genomes for health research.

2. Policy, governance and justice

  • Identification: anthropological criteria guided the Lokur Committee (1965) in defining Scheduled Tribes, and ethnographic study still informs claims for inclusion.
  • Development and impact: S.C. Dube's India's Changing Villages (1958) evaluated the Community Development Programme; social impact assessment under the RFCTLARR Act, 2013 and the work of Tribal Research Institutes rest on anthropological methods.
  • Health: surveys of sickle-cell disease and nutrition among tribes underpin the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023); anthropometry guides child-growth monitoring.
  • Peace and autonomy: knowledge of clans, village councils and customary law in the North-East informs Sixth Schedule arrangements and accords.
  • Forensic and ergonomic uses: physical anthropologists help identify disaster victims and skeletal remains, and body measurements guide the design of uniforms, equipment and work spaces.

3. Limits and critique

  • Colonial baggage: H.H. Risley's caste rankings in the 1901 Census and the "criminal tribes" label show how anthropology could also divide and stigmatise.
  • Advice ignored: displacement by dams and mines continued despite anthropologists' warnings, and policy has swung between isolation and assimilation.
  • Need for reflexivity: participatory and action anthropology, with tribal scholars and communities as partners, makes the discipline more democratic.

Anthropology helps the nation see itself plural yet connected. By turning local knowledge into inclusive policy, it supports a nation built on integration without assimilation.
free.upa-2023-an2-8a:
Tribal regionsL.P. VidyarthiCensus 2011Institutional features

India's Scheduled Tribes numbered 10.43 crore (8.6% of the population) in Census 2011, spread over 705 notified communities and about 90% rural. Only Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry have no notified STs. L.P. Vidyarthi and B.K. Rai (The Tribal Culture of India, 1977) grouped them into five regions — Himalayan, Middle Indian, Western, Southern and Island — each with distinct institutional features shaped by ecology, history and contact.

1. Pattern of distribution

  • Central belt: seven States, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, hold about two-thirds of India's STs; Madhya Pradesh has the largest number.
  • High proportion, small numbers: in Lakshadweep and Mizoram tribal people form about 95% and 94% of the population, and in Nagaland and Meghalaya about 86%, though their absolute numbers are small.

2. Himalayan and North-Eastern region

  • Clan and village polity: Naga villages are governed by councils and once trained youth in the morung (dormitory); the Adi kebang and the Apatani village councils, the latter studied by Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf, settle disputes and manage land.
  • Matriliny: the Khasi pass property to the youngest daughter (khadduh) and the Garo to a chosen heiress (nokna), with men holding political office.
  • Western and central Himalaya: fraternal polyandry among the Jaunsari (D.N. Majumdar, Himalayan Polyandry, 1962) and Kinnaura, transhumant herding among the Gaddi, and trans-Himalayan trade among the Bhotia.

3. Middle India

  • Traditional polities: the Santhal manjhi–pargana system, the Munda manki–munda system and the Oraon parha federation of villages; Munda khuntkatti land belongs to the founding lineage.
  • Youth dormitories: the Oraon dhumkuria (described by S.C. Roy) and the Muria ghotul (Verrier Elwin, 1947) train the young in work, song and social rules.
  • Economy and belief: mostly settled plough farming, with shifting cultivation among the Baiga (bewar) and Kondh (podu); totemic patrilineal clans and Sarna worship at sacred groves.

4. Western and Southern India

  • Western India: the Bhil, Mina, Garasia, Warli and Dubla are patrilineal, strongly influenced by neighbouring Hindu castes, with village panchayats; reform movements such as Govind Guru's Bhagat movement grew among the Bhils.
  • Nilgiri complex: Toda buffalo herders (W.H.R. Rivers, 1906), with sacred dairies and fraternal polyandry, exchanged goods and services with Kota artisans, Badaga farmers and Kurumba forest dwellers.
  • Forest communities: the Chenchu (Haimendorf, 1943) and Kadar live by gathering, the Koya and Konda Reddi practise podu cultivation in the Godavari valley, and the Kurichiya of Wayanad keep large matrilineal joint households; cross-cousin marriage is common.

5. Island region

  • Andaman Islands: the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese live in small, egalitarian hunting–gathering bands (A.R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders, 1922).
  • Nicobar and Lakshadweep: Nicobarese land and coconut groves are held by the tuhet (joint family group), the Shompen are forest foragers, and Lakshadweep islanders are Muslim with matrilineal inheritance.

Tribal India is diverse, not uniform: ecology and contact have produced distinct kinship, polity and economy in each region. Policy must respect this diversity, which is why the Fifth and Sixth Schedules offer different models of self-rule.
free.upa-2023-an2-8b:
Sarat Chandra RoyFather of Indian ethnographyMan in India (1921)Chotanagpur tribes

Sarat Chandra Roy (1871–1942), a lawyer at Ranchi with degrees in English and law, turned his concern for the tribal litigants he met in court into a lifetime of fieldwork. His monographs on the tribes of Chotanagpur and the journal Man in India (1921) laid the foundations of anthropology in India, earning him the title "father of Indian ethnography".

1. Ethnographic monographs

  • The Mundas and Their Country (1912): the first full-length monograph on an Indian tribe by an Indian, tracing Munda history, the khuntkatti land system and the Birsa movement.
  • The Oraons of Chota Nagpur (1915) and Oraon Religion and Customs (1928): described the parha federation of villages and the dhumkuria youth dormitory in detail.
  • Later works: The Birhors (1925) on a small hunting and rope-making community, The Hill Bhuiyas of Orissa (1935) and The Kharias (1937, with his son R.C. Roy).

2. Method and institution building

  • Holistic fieldwork: he combined history, customary law, economy, religion and physical measurements, used tribal languages and the people's own accounts, and gave space to how communities saw themselves.
  • Man in India: the first anthropological journal of India, it gave Indian scholars a forum alongside foreign ones and still continues.
  • Prehistory: he located Asur sites in the Ranchi plateau and linked local legends of the Asura to an earlier metal-working people.

3. Applied anthropology and advocacy

  • Law and land: as a pleader he used ethnographic knowledge to explain tribal tenures, such as khuntkatti and bhuinhari, to colonial courts, supporting the protective spirit of the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908).
  • Voice for tribes: he wrote against exploitation by landlords and moneylenders and argued that administrators must understand tribal custom before changing it.

4. Critical evaluation

  • Strengths: he was a pioneer who made Indian tribes known to world anthropology; A.C. Haddon wrote the introduction to The Oraons.
  • Weaknesses: his reconstructions of origins and migrations are speculative, his studies predate functional analysis of how institutions work together, and his terms ("primitive", racial types) reflect the evolutionist and colonial thinking of the period.
  • Legacy: L.P. Vidyarthi's history of Indian anthropology treats him as the leading Indian figure of its early phases, and Vidyarthi's own Chotanagpur research built on his work.

S.C. Roy gave Indian anthropology its empirical base, its first journal and a tradition of anthropology in the service of tribal people. His limitations were those of his age; his commitment to tribal rights remains a model.

Other Backward Classes (OBCs) are the "socially and educationally backward classes" of Articles 15(4) and 16(4) other than SCs and STs. Their identification rests mainly on caste as a unit, judged by social, educational and economic indicators, as laid down by the Mandal Commission (1980) and upheld in Indra Sawhney (1992). Mandal estimated them at 52% of the population; Bihar's caste survey (2023) put backward and extremely backward classes together at about 63%.

1. How OBCs are identified

  • Commissions under Article 340: the Kalelkar Commission (report 1955) listed 2,399 castes but the Union rejected it; the B.P. Mandal Commission (appointed 1979, reported 1980) identified 3,743 castes and recommended 27% reservation, implemented in 1990.
  • Indicators: Mandal used eleven indicators (social, educational, economic) with weighted scores; a caste scoring at least half the total was treated as backward.
  • Judicial tests: Indra Sawhney accepted caste as a class, required exclusion of the "creamy layer" (₹8 lakh a year, unrevised since 2017), fixed a 50% ceiling and asked for a permanent commission; in Rohith Nathan (2026) the Supreme Court held that parental salary alone cannot fix creamy-layer status.
  • Present procedure: the National Commission for Backward Classes became constitutional under Article 338B (102nd Amendment, 2018); the President notifies the Central List (Article 342A), and the 105th Amendment (2021) restored the States' power to keep their own lists. Many States sub-divide OBCs, as in the BC-A to BC-E groups of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.

2. Important features

  • Heterogeneity: landowning peasant castes (Yadav, Kurmi, Koeri), artisans (Kumhar, Lohar), service castes (Nai, Dhobi), herders (Kuruba, Gadaria), fishers (Mallah, Besta) and Muslim OBCs (Ansari, Qureshi).
  • Middle position: most belong to the broad Shudra category, above Dalits and below the twice-born, and many sought upward mobility through Sanskritisation (M.N. Srinivas).
  • Local dominance: several are dominant castes in Srinivas's sense, combining numbers and land, while artisan and service groups remain poor.

3. Recent social changes

  • Political rise: Christophe Jaffrelot's India's Silent Revolution (2003) traced OBC leadership in north Indian politics after Mandal; Bharat Ratna to Karpoori Thakur (2024) reflects this mobilisation.
  • Assertion over imitation: pride in OBC heroes and "Bahujan" identity, and the Pasmanda movement among backward Muslims, replace Sanskritisation.
  • Education: OBC quotas in central institutions (2006) and the medical All-India Quota (2021) widened access.
  • Inner inequality: the Rohini Commission (report 2023) was set up because a few castes took most benefits; States such as Bihar separate extremely backward classes.

4. Recent economic changes

  • From land to diversification: Green Revolution gains made many OBC farmers "bullock capitalists" (Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, In Pursuit of Lakshmi, 1987); later generations moved into business, transport and services.
  • Agrarian distress: shrinking holdings fuel quota demands from landed castes such as Jats, Patidars and Marathas.
  • Artisans under pressure: factory goods erode craft incomes; PM Vishwakarma (2023) offers credit and training for 18 traditional trades.

OBC identification is moving from colonial caste lists towards data and sub-categorisation, and the caste count in Census 2027 will test it. Their story shows mobility for some and stagnation for many.
